text: Example 16.16.2 (Pointwise variation depends on the representative) . 78C1D3DF08E9 The function $u=\chi _{\mathbb Q\cap (0,1)}$ is zero almost everywhere, belongs to $BV(0,1)$ and has distributional variation zero. As a specified pointwise function it has infinite classical variation. Its canonical right-continuous BV representative is identically zero. Proof Countability makes the rationals Lebesgue null, so all distributional pairings agree with those of zero. To obtain arbitrarily large pointwise variation, choose an arbitrarily long increasing sequence alternating between rational and irrational points, possible by density of both sets. Every successive function increment has absolute value one. The regulated representative theorem applies to the almost-everywhere class and gives the zero representative; it does not assign finite classical variation to every null modification of that class. $\square$

title: Example 16.16.3 (A boundary layer can retain a trace while disappearing in the interior)
search_title: A boundary layer can retain a trace while disappearing in the interior
section: 16.16 Jumps, representatives, and boundary traces
text: Example 16.16.3 (A boundary layer can retain a trace while disappearing in the interior) . 3A54E25A86CC Let $u_ j=\chi _{(0,1/j)}$ on $I=(0,1)$, $j\geq 2$. Then $u_ j\to 0$ in $L^1(I)$, $|Du_ j|(I)=1$, and $Du_ j\rightharpoonup 0$ against compactly supported continuous tests in $I$. Yet $u_ j(0+)=1$ for every $j$. The zero extensions to $\mathbb R$ have derivative $\delta _0-\delta _{1/j}$ and total variation two. Proof The $L^1$ norm is $1/j$. Within the open interval there is only the right endpoint, so $Du_ j=-\delta _{1/j}$ by Theorem 4.7.4 . Every compact support stays away from zero and eventually misses that atom. The interior right trace at zero is one. Proposition 4.7.5 adds the missing boundary atom $\delta _0$, whose support is distinct from $1/j$. The example shows that an $L^1$ limit with uniformly bounded variation does not alone preserve boundary traces. $\square$

title: Example 16.16.4 (Three derivative types in one BV function)
search_title: Three derivative types in one BV function
section: 16.16 Jumps, representatives, and boundary traces
text: Example 16.16.4 (Three derivative types in one BV function) . 49385BB539FF Let $C$ be the Cantor distribution function on $[0,1]$, and let $0<c<1$. The function $u(x)=x+C(x)+\chi _{[c,1)}(x)$ on $(0,1)$ is in $BV(0,1)$ and \[  Du=\mathcal L^1\lfloor (0,1)+\mu _ C\lfloor (0,1)+\delta _ c, \qquad |Du|((0,1))=3.  \] Its absolutely continuous, singular-continuous and atomic summands are mutually singular, even when $c$ belongs to the Cantor set. Proof Differentiate each summand in distributions, using Example 16.1.11 and the interval endpoint formula. The Cantor measure is singular to Lebesgue measure and has no atoms, including at the endpoints and at $c$. All three measures are positive of mass one, so their sum has total variation three. Nonatomicity lets one remove $c$ from a full-measure support of the Cantor part to obtain disjoint carriers for the three types. This also shows why absence of jumps does not by itself imply absolute continuity. $\square$

title: 16.17 A radial obstacle problem and its contact transition
search_title: A radial obstacle problem and its contact transition
section: 16.17 A radial obstacle problem and its contact transition
text: We solve the normalized obstacle problem in a ball, with obstacle zero and constant boundary height. The normalization is [ Fig18 ] , equation (5.2), p. 9, and Definition 13.3.4 ; the explicit radial computations below illustrate that equation and the regular and singular models of Sections 7.1–7.2 of the source. Proposition 16.17.1 (A radial profile with a prescribed contact ball) . 3A54999BC942 Let $n\geq 2$ and $a>0$. Put $U_ a(r)=0$ for $0\leq r\leq a$ and, for $r>a$, set \[  U_ a(r)=\int _ a^ r\frac{s^ n-a^ n}{ns^{n-1}}\, ds.  \] Then $u_ a(x)=U_ a(|x|)$ is a globally $C^{1,1}$ normalized obstacle solution on $\mathbb R^ n$, with contact set $\overline B_ a$ and positivity outside that ball. Explicitly, \[  U_ a(r)=\begin{cases}  \dfrac {r^2-a^2}{4}-\dfrac {a^2}{2}\log (r/a),& n=2,\\[4pt] \dfrac {r^2-a^2}{2n}+\dfrac {a^ n}{n(n-2)}(r^{2-n}-a^{2-n}),& n>2 \end{cases}\qquad (r>a).  \] Proof The radial equation is $(r^{n-1}U')'=r^{n-1}$. Integrating with $U'(a)=0$ gives $U'(r)=(r^ n-a^ n)/(nr^{n-1})$, and a second integration with $U(a)=0$ gives the stated formulas. For $r>a$ the derivative is positive, so the contact set is exactly the closed ball. The tangential and radial eigenvalues of its Hessian there are \[  \frac{U_ a'}r=\frac1n\left(1-(a/r)^ n\right),\qquad U_ a''=\frac1n+\frac{n-1}{n}(a/r)^ n.  \] They lie in $[0,1]$ and have sum, with tangential multiplicity $n-1$, equal to one. On the contact ball the gradient and Hessian vanish. Since $U_ a(a)=U_ a'(a)=0$, the gradient is continuous across the sphere and no surface measure appears in its distributional derivative. Its bounded weak Hessian makes the gradient globally Lipschitz, with bound one. The function is therefore $C^{1,1}$ and has Laplacian equal to one outside contact and zero inside, as required. It is not $C^2$ across the sphere: the radial second derivative jumps from zero to one. $\square$ Theorem 16.17.2 (All constant-height Dirichlet cases in a ball) . C9817DF3B271 Fix $n\geq 2$, $R>0$ and $h\geq 0$. The unique minimizer of \[  J(v)=\int _{B_ R}\left(\tfrac 12|Dv|^2+v\right),\qquad v\geq 0,\quad v-h\in H^1_0(B_ R),  \] is as follows, with $h_*=R^2/(2n)$: \[  u_ h(x)=\begin{cases}  0,& h=0,\\  U_ a(|x|),\quad U_ a(R)=h,\  0<a<R,& 0<h<h_*,\\  |x|^2/(2n),& h=h_*,\\  h-h_*+|x|^2/(2n),& h>h_*. \end{cases}  \] In the middle range the contact radius $a$ is uniquely determined and decreases strictly as $h$ increases. These explicit solutions illustrate the normalized obstacle equation in [ Fig18 ] ; the proof below verifies minimality against all admissible competitors. Proof Existence and uniqueness follow from Theorem 13.2.1 with forcing $f=-1$. For $0<a<R$ set $g(a)=U_ a(R)$. Differentiating its integral expression, whose integrand vanishes at the moving lower endpoint, gives \[  g'(a)=-a^{n-1}\int _ a^ R s^{1-n}\, ds<0.  \] The explicit formulas show $g(a)\to h_*$ as $a\downarrow 0$ and $g(a)\to 0$ as $a\uparrow R$. Continuity and strict monotonicity supply exactly one radius for each intermediate $h$. Every displayed function is nonnegative, has boundary value $h$, and is $C^{1,1}$ with $\Delta u_ h=\chi _{\{ u_ h>0\} }$ almost everywhere. For a competitor $v$, integration by parts yields \[  \int _{B_ R}Du_ h\cdot D(v-u_ h)+\int _{B_ R}(v-u_ h) =\int _{\{ u_ h=0\} \cap B_ R}v\geq 0.  \] Thus each candidate satisfies the variational inequality and is the unique minimizer. This verifies the global boundary-value problem directly; rotational symmetry alone is not used to assume away possible nonradial competitors. $\square$ Proposition 16.17.3 (Contact is not the same as positive reaction mass) . 20576B580998 For $0<h<h_*$ the reaction measure of $u_ h$ is $\lambda _ h=\chi _{B_ a}\mathcal L^ n$ and its mass is $\omega _ n a^ n$. At $h=h_*$ the contact set is the singleton $\{ 0\} $ but the reaction is zero. At $h>h_*$ contact is empty and the reaction remains zero; at $h=0$ the whole ball is in contact and $\lambda _0=\mathcal L^ n\lfloor B_ R$. Proof With forcing $f=-1$, Proposition 13.2.5 gives $\lambda _ h=1-\Delta u_ h$. Substitute the Laplacians computed in Theorem 16.17.2 . The sphere $\partial B_ a$ has zero Lebesgue measure and carries no singular reaction, since the gradient is continuous across it. At the threshold the Laplacian of $|x|^2/(2n)$ is one even at zero, while its value vanishes there. Thus a nonempty contact set need not carry nonzero reaction measure. $\square$ Proposition 16.17.4 (The regular sphere and the singular point have different blow-ups) . DE855AC5E65E For $0<h<h_*$ and $p=ae\in \partial B_ a$, $|e|=1$, the full family of quadratic rescalings satisfies \[  \frac{u_ h(p+ry)}{r^2}\longrightarrow \frac12((y\cdot e)^+)^2 \quad \text{in }C^1_{\mathrm{loc}}(\mathbb R^ n)\quad (r\downarrow 0).  \] At $h=h_*$ the blow-up at the sole contact point is exactly $|y|^2/(2n)$ at every scale. Hence the contact sphere consists of regular points, whereas the threshold point is singular with a positive-definite blow-up matrix. Proof Near $a$, Taylor's theorem on the exterior side gives $U_ a(a+t)=\frac12(t^+)^2+O(|t|^3)$ and $U_ a'(a+t)=t^++O(t^2)$, with zero values for $t\leq 0$. On bounded $y$ sets, \[  |p+ry|-a=r(y\cdot e)+O(r^2),\qquad \frac{p+ry}{|p+ry|}=e+O(r).  \] Substitution into the function and radial gradient formulas gives uniform convergence of both the rescaled function and gradient. The estimates remain valid across the changing positivity interface because $t\mapsto t^+$ is Lipschitz. At the threshold, exact quadratic homogeneity gives the second assertion. Apply Definitions 13.3.12 and 13.3.13 ; the singular matrix is $I/n$ and has zero-dimensional kernel. $\square$ Proposition 16.17.5 (How the contact radius approaches its endpoints) . EED8D8469AD3 As $h\downarrow 0$, the contact radius satisfies $R-a\sim \sqrt{2h}$. As $h\uparrow h_*$, it tends to zero. In dimension two the exact deficit is \[  h_*-h=\frac{a^2}{2}\log (R/a)+\frac{a^2}{4}.  \] In dimensions $n>2$ it is \[  h_*-h=\frac{a^2}{2(n-2)}-\frac{a^ nR^{2-n}}{n(n-2)}, \qquad a\sim \sqrt{2(n-2)(h_*-h)}.  \] Here $f\sim g$ means $f/g\to 1$ in the indicated limit. Proof Subtract the explicit value $U_ a(R)$ from $h_*$ to obtain the deficit identities. For $n>2$ the second term is lower order than $a^2$ as $a\downarrow 0$, giving the stated asymptotic. In dimension two the logarithm grows without bound and cannot be dropped. At the other endpoint, differentiate the formula for $g'(a)$ in Theorem 16.17.2 ; it gives $g(R)=g'(R)=0$ and $g''(R)=1$ by continuous extension from the left. Taylor's theorem yields $h=g(a)=(R-a)^2/2+o((R-a)^2)$, proving the first assertion. These calculations exhibit a change in contact geometry even though the minimizer remains controlled in $C^{1,1}$. $\square$ Proposition 16.17.6 (The derivative of the minimized energy) . AEA8FAF2A27B Let $E(h)=J(u_ h)$ for $h\geq 0$. It is continuously differentiable from the right at zero and differentiable elsewhere, with \[  E'(h)=\begin{cases}  \omega _ n(R^ n-a(h)^ n),& 0<h<h_*,\\  \omega _ nR^ n,& h\geq h_*, \end{cases} \qquad E'(0+)=0.  \] It is strictly convex on $(0,h_*)$ and affine on $[h_*,\infty )$. Proof In the intermediate range, $g'(a)<0$ makes $a(h)$ smooth. Differentiate the energy as a radial integral over $a<|x|<R$. There is no moving-interface contribution because both $U_ a$ and its gradient vanish at $r=a$. Integration by parts in the resulting first variation leaves only the outer boundary term: the interior term has coefficient $1-\Delta u_ h=0$ on positivity, and the parameter derivative is zero in contact. The boundary derivative with respect to $h$ is one. Consequently \[  E'(h)=\mathcal H^{n-1}(\partial B_ R)U_ a'(R) =n\omega _ nR^{n-1}\frac{R^ n-a^ n}{nR^{n-1}} =\omega _ n(R^ n-a^ n).  \] This derivative is strictly increasing because $a'(h)<0$. Above threshold the solution is the threshold solution plus the constant $h-h_*$, so its gradient energy is unchanged and its linear energy increases by $(h-h_*)|B_ R|$. The explicit profiles and their gradients converge uniformly on the closed ball at both limiting heights, so $E$ is continuous there. The interior derivative has limits zero at $h=0$ and $\omega _ nR^ n$ at $h=h_*$. The mean value theorem, applied on one-sided intervals and then taking their endpoints to the threshold, gives the claimed matching derivatives. This proves the endpoint assertions without differentiating an undefined inverse radius at zero. $\square$

text:
This section expands Definition 10.1.1 . All integrals are over the parameter surface with its induced metric, retaining immersion multiplicity. We use the trace mean curvature vector $\vec H=\Delta F$ in Euclidean space. For a two-sided hypersurface, $A=D
u $, $H=\operatorname {tr}A$ and $\vec H=-H
u $. The conformal mechanism is described in [ LY82 ] , Proposition 1, p. 279, and the spherical formulation in [ MNWill ] , pp. 684–685. The formulas below are derived explicitly. Definition 10.3.1 (Vector normalization and the trace-free second fundamental form) . 6C2509083AF7 For a smooth immersion $F:M^2	o \mathcal N^ d$ into a space of constant sectional curvature $\kappa $, let $B$ be its normal-vector-valued second fundamental form, $\vec H=\operatorname {tr}_ gB$, and \[  B^0=B-	frac 12g\otimes \vec H, \qquad \mathcal W_\kappa (F)=\int _ M\left(\kappa +	frac 14|\vec H|^2ight)d\mu .  \] For a closed Euclidean surface write $\mathcal W=\mathcal W_0$. In a two-sided three-dimensional ambient space, $B=-A
u $, so $|\vec H|^2=H^2$. Li–Yau use averaged mean curvature in [ LY82 ] ; Simon uses the trace vector and the factor $1/4$ in [ SimW93 ] , p. 281. Lemma 10.3.2 (Conformal changes of the normal geometry) . 147F594395A4 Let $\widetilde{ ar g}=e^{2\phi } ar g$ be a smooth conformal change of ambient metric near an immersed surface, and set $\varphi =\phi \circ F$. Tangent and normal spaces as vector subspaces are unchanged. Regarding normal-valued tensors as vectors in the same ambient tangent bundle, \[  \widetilde g=e^{2\varphi }g,\qquad \widetilde B(U,V)=B(U,V)-g(U,V)( ar
abla \phi )^\perp ,  \] \[  \widetilde{\vec H}=e^{-2\varphi }(\vec H-2( ar
abla \phi )^\perp ), \qquad \widetilde B^0=B^0, \qquad |\widetilde B^0|_{\widetilde g,\widetilde{ ar g}}^2\, d\widetilde\mu =|B^0|_{g, ar g}^2\, d\mu .  \] For a hypersurface with $\widetilde
u =e^{-\phi }
u $, the shape operators instead satisfy $\widetilde A=e^{-\phi }(A+
u (\phi )I)$. Proof The ambient connection changes by \[  \widetilde{ ar
abla }_ UV= ar
abla _ UV+U(\phi )V+V(\phi )U- ar g(U,V) ar
abla \phi .  \] To check this identity, the right-hand connection is torsion free, and substituting it into the derivative of $e^{2\phi } ar g(V,W)$ gives metric compatibility. Uniqueness of the Levi-Civita connection proves the formula. The two middle terms are tangent when $U,V$ are tangent to the surface. Taking the normal part gives the formula for $\widetilde B$. Tracing uses $\widetilde g^{-1}=e^{-2\varphi }g^{-1}$, which gives the stated vector mean curvature. Subtracting $\widetilde g\otimes \widetilde{\vec H}/2$ cancels the added pure-trace normal term. For the norm of a normal-valued bilinear form, two inverse induced metrics contribute $e^{-4\varphi }$ and the ambient vector norm contributes $e^{2\varphi }$. Hence the squared norm of $B^0$ changes by $e^{-2\varphi }$; the area element changes by $e^{2\varphi }$. Finally differentiate $e^{-\phi }
u $ using the connection formula and take its tangential part. The terms involving $U(\phi )
u $ cancel, leaving $e^{-\phi }(AU+
u (\phi )U)$, as claimed. This last scalar formula uses the convention $A=D
u $. $\square$ Lemma 10.3.3 (The intrinsic curvature density under a conformal change) . 6DBF2123A3DF For a smooth surface metric $\widetilde g=e^{2\varphi }g$, \[  \widetilde K=e^{-2\varphi }(K-\Delta _ g\varphi ),\qquad \widetilde K\, d\widetilde\mu =(K-\Delta _ g\varphi )\, d\mu .  \] Consequently the integrals of Gauss curvature agree on a closed surface. Proof The difference of induced connections is $C_{ij}^{k}=\varphi _ i\delta _ j^ k+\varphi _ j\delta _ i^ k-g_{ij}\varphi ^ k$. At a point choose $g$-geodesic coordinates with orthonormal coordinate vectors. The three relevant coefficient vectors are \[  (C_{11}^1,C_{11}^2)=(\varphi _1,-\varphi _2),\quad (C_{12}^1,C_{12}^2)=(\varphi _2,\varphi _1),\quad (C_{22}^1,C_{22}^2)=(-\varphi _1,\varphi _2).  \] In the component of $\widetilde R(e_1,e_2)e_2$ along $e_1$, the derivative terms contribute $-\varphi _{11}-\varphi _{22}$. The products of the displayed $C$ coefficients cancel. The remaining curvature term is $K$. Pairing in $\widetilde g$ contributes $e^{2\varphi }$ and dividing by the squared area of the coordinate parallelogram contributes $e^{-4\varphi }$. This gives the first identity and then the density identity. On a closed surface the integral of $\Delta _ g\varphi $ vanishes by the divergence theorem, including on a nonorientable surface using its Riemannian measure or orientation double cover. $\square$ Proposition 10.3.4 (The conformally invariant energy density modulo curvature) . BACD0400946D For a surface in a space of constant sectional curvature $\kappa $, \[  \kappa +	frac 14|\vec H|^2=K+	frac 12|B^0|^2.  \] If an ambient conformal diffeomorphism maps a neighborhood of a closed immersed surface in one space form into another, its Willmore energy with the corresponding ambient curvature term is unchanged. Proof In an orthonormal tangent frame the Gauss equation reads \[  K=\kappa +\langle B_{11},B_{22}angle -|B_{12}|^2 =\kappa +	frac 12(|\vec H|^2-|B|^2).  \] The orthogonal trace decomposition gives $|B|^2=|B^0|^2+|\vec H|^2/2$, proving the first assertion. Pull back the target ambient metric by the conformal map. Lemma 10.3.2 preserves the trace-free norm density, and Lemma 10.3.3 preserves the integral of Gauss curvature. Integrate the displayed identity on each side. The ambient map must be smooth on a neighborhood of the entire image; a pole lying on the surface is excluded here and is treated separately below. This proof does not require the Gauss–Bonnet theorem. $\square$ Proposition 10.3.5 (Stereographic projection preserves the normalized energy) . 72FC663C3366 Let $F:M^2	o S^ N\setminus \{ p\} $ be a smooth closed immersion in the unit sphere, and let $\pi _ p$ be stereographic projection. Then \[  \mathcal W_0(\pi _ p\circ F)=\mathcal W_1(F) =\int _ M\left(1+	frac 14|\vec H_{S^ N}|^2ight)d\mu .  \] In particular, the Euclidean energy of the projection of a closed minimal surface in the sphere equals its spherical area. The identity is equation (1) of [ MNWill ] , p. 684, in trace-vector notation. Proof Take $p=(0,\ldots ,0,1)$. The inverse projection is \[  Y(x)=\left( rac{2x}{1+|x|^2}, rac{|x|^2-1}{1+|x|^2}ight).  \] A direct derivative gives, for every $v$, \[  |dY_ x(v)|^2= rac{4}{(1+|x|^2)^2}|v|^2.  \] For example, the first component has derivative $2v/(1+r^2)-4x(x\cdot v)/(1+r^2)^2$ and the last has derivative $4(x\cdot v)/(1+r^2)^2$; their squared cross terms cancel. Thus projection is conformal. Compactness and avoidance of $p$ ensure a smooth conformal factor near the entire surface, so Proposition 10.3.4 applies with ambient curvatures one and zero. Minimality removes the mean-curvature term in the spherical integral. $\square$ Theorem 10.3.6 (First variation of Willmore energy in a three-dimensional space form) . 439BE1C2C30D Let $F:M^2	o N^3_\kappa $ be a smooth closed two-sided immersion and let its normal variation have initial velocity $f
u $. With $H=\operatorname {tr}A$ and $A^0=A-HI/2$, \[  \left. rac{d}{dt}ight|_{0}\mathcal W_\kappa (F_ t) =- rac12\int _ M igl (\Delta H+H|A^0|^2 igr )f\, d\mu .  \] Thus critical points satisfy $\Delta H+H|A^0|^2=0$. In averaged notation $h=H/2$, this is \[  \Delta h+2h(h^2+\kappa -K)=0.  \] This is the Willmore variational problem discussed in [ MNWill ] , p. 685; the displayed formula retains the ambient curvature term explicitly. Proof The area variation is $\dot{d\mu }=Hf\, d\mu $. The mean-curvature linearization is $\dot H=-\Delta f-(|A|^2+2\kappa )f$, since the ambient Ricci curvature in the normal direction is $2\kappa $. Differentiate the energy to obtain \[  \dot{\mathcal W}_\kappa =\int \left[-	frac 12H\Delta f-	frac 12H(|A|^2+2\kappa )f +(\kappa +H^2/4)Hfight]d\mu .  \] The two explicit $\kappa Hf$ terms cancel. Self-adjointness of the Laplacian on a closed surface moves $\Delta $ from $f$ to $H$. Since $|A|^2-H^2/2=|A^0|^2$, this is the asserted formula. The Gauss equation $K=\kappa +\det A$ gives $|A^0|^2=2(h^2+\kappa -K)$, proving the averaged expression. Arbitrary smooth normal speeds imply the Euler–Lagrange equation. Tangential velocities only reparametrize the immersion and do not change the energy. $\square$ Corollary 10.3.7 (Minimal spherical surfaces give Euclidean Willmore surfaces) . 9A078B2B51E7 A closed two-sided minimal surface in a three-dimensional space form is a Willmore critical point. A stereographic projection of a closed minimal surface of $S^3$ avoiding the pole is a Euclidean Willmore critical point. Its energy equals the original area. Proof The equation of Theorem 10.3.6 vanishes when $H=0$. For the second assertion, every sufficiently small smooth variation of the projected compact surface pulls back to a spherical variation avoiding the pole. Proposition 10.3.5 identifies their energies for all small parameters. Differentiating therefore transfers stationarity. If the spherical immersion is one-sided, apply the preceding first-variation formula on its normal orientation double cover: the lifted energy and its first derivative are twice those downstairs, so stationarity descends. The energy value follows from the same identity. This only proves criticality, not minimizing or stability among all variations. $\square$

text: Lemma 10.3.3 (The intrinsic curvature density under a conformal change) . 6DBF2123A3DF For a smooth surface metric $\widetilde g=e^{2\varphi }g$, \[  \widetilde K=e^{-2\varphi }(K-\Delta _ g\varphi ),\qquad \widetilde K\, d\widetilde\mu =(K-\Delta _ g\varphi )\, d\mu .  \] Consequently the integrals of Gauss curvature agree on a closed surface. Proof The difference of induced connections is $C_{ij}^{k}=\varphi _ i\delta _ j^ k+\varphi _ j\delta _ i^ k-g_{ij}\varphi ^ k$. At a point choose $g$-geodesic coordinates with orthonormal coordinate vectors. The three relevant coefficient vectors are \[  (C_{11}^1,C_{11}^2)=(\varphi _1,-\varphi _2),\quad (C_{12}^1,C_{12}^2)=(\varphi _2,\varphi _1),\quad (C_{22}^1,C_{22}^2)=(-\varphi _1,\varphi _2).  \] In the component of $\widetilde R(e_1,e_2)e_2$ along $e_1$, the derivative terms contribute $-\varphi _{11}-\varphi _{22}$. The products of the displayed $C$ coefficients cancel. The remaining curvature term is $K$. Pairing in $\widetilde g$ contributes $e^{2\varphi }$ and dividing by the squared area of the coordinate parallelogram contributes $e^{-4\varphi }$. This gives the first identity and then the density identity. On a closed surface the integral of $\Delta _ g\varphi $ vanishes by the divergence theorem, including on a nonorientable surface using its Riemannian measure or orientation double cover. $\square$

title: 10.4 Willmore energy, multiplicity and inversion
search_title: Willmore energy, multiplicity and inversion
section: 10.4 Willmore energy, multiplicity and inversion
text:
The multiplicity inequality is due to Li–Yau [ LY82 ] , Theorem 6, p. 286. We give a direct smooth proof through the radial identity underlying Simon's equations (1.2') and (1.5) in [ SimW93 ] , p. 285. The scope is smooth compact immersions; this section does not assert a corresponding theorem for arbitrary weak surfaces or branched maps. Write $\vec H=\Delta F$ and $\mathcal W(F)= rac14\int |\vec H|^2d\mu $. Lemma 10.4.1 (The differential and curvature of an inversion) . 86AC490C5917 Let $F:M^2	o \mathbb R^ N\setminus \{ y\} $ be a smooth immersion. Write $X=F-y$, $r=|X|$, and let $R_ X=I-2r^{-2}X\otimes X$ be reflection across the hyperplane orthogonal to $X$; the notation $X^\perp $ below denotes projection onto the surface normal space. The inversion $I_ y(z)=(z-y)/|z-y|^2$ satisfies \[  dI_ y=r^{-2}R_ X,\quad d\widetilde\mu =r^{-4}d\mu ,\quad \widetilde{\vec H}=r^2R_ X\left(\vec H+4 rac{X^\perp }{r^2}ight).  \] Consequently on every measurable parameter set, \[   rac14\int |\widetilde{\vec H}|^2d\widetilde\mu =4\int \left| rac{\vec H}{4}+ rac{X^\perp }{r^2}ight|^2d\mu ,  \] with equality also when the integrals are infinite. Proof Differentiate $X/r^2$ to obtain the differential. The map $R_ X$ is orthogonal, so lengths scale by $r^{-2}$ and surface area by $r^{-4}$. Pullback of the Euclidean ambient metric is $r^{-4}$ times that metric, a conformal change with $\phi =-2\log r$. Lemma 10.3.2 gives the mean curvature in that pullback metric as $r^4(\vec H+4X^\perp /r^2)$. The inversion is an isometry from the pullback metric to the target metric; pushing forward by $dI_ y$ proves the formula. Squaring, multiplying by the transformed area element and retaining the factor $1/4$ proves the integral identity. $\square$ Lemma 10.4.2 (The puncture flux at a smooth immersed sheet) . 3C733C121AC2 Let $F:M^2	o \mathbb R^ N$ be a smooth compact immersion, possibly with smooth boundary, and let $y
otin F(\partial M)$. Its preimage is a finite set of interior points, of cardinality $m$. For small $\varepsilon >0$, remove from each such sheet the region $|F-y|<\varepsilon $. Along the resulting inner boundary, the outward conormal $\eta _\varepsilon $ of the remaining surface satisfies \[  \int _{	ext{inner boundary}} rac{X^ T}{r^2}\cdot \eta _\varepsilon \, ds\longrightarrow -2\pi m.  \] Near each puncture, $X^\perp =O(r^2)$; hence $X^\perp /r^2$ is bounded and locally square integrable. Proof An immersion is an embedding on a neighborhood of each parameter point. The preimage of $y$ is closed in the compact domain and each of its points is isolated. An infinite preimage would have an accumulation point contradicting local injectivity, so it is finite. Compactness excludes any further image points near $y$ outside the chosen sheet neighborhoods. Translate $y$ to zero and write a sheet as a graph $F(z)=(z,u(z))$ over its tangent plane, with $u(0)=0$, $Du(0)=0$, $u(z)=O(|z|^2)$ and $Du(z)=O(|z|)$. Its radial function is $r=|z|(1+O(|z|^2))$, and its gradient has $|
abla _ Mr|=1+O(r^2)$. The small radial level is a smooth perturbation of a circle, with length $2\pi \varepsilon +O(\varepsilon ^3)$. The graph expansion also gives $|X^\perp |=O(r^2)$, since the leading linear vector lies in the tangent plane and the tangent plane changes by $O(r)$. At the inner level, $\eta _\varepsilon =-
abla _ Mr/|
abla _ Mr|$ and $X^ T=r
abla _ Mr$. Thus the integrand is $-|
abla _ Mr|/\varepsilon $, and its integral is $-2\pi +O(\varepsilon ^2)$ for each sheet. Sum over the finite preimage. If $m=0$, a small ball misses the image and there is no puncture flux. $\square$ Theorem 10.4.3 (A square identity for a compact immersed surface) . A6413522A6DE Let $F:M^2	o \mathbb R^ N$ be a smooth compact immersion with smooth boundary allowed. For $y
otin F(\partial M)$ let $m=\# F^{-1}(y)$, and let $\eta $ be the outward unit conormal on the original boundary. Then \[  \pi m+\int _{M\setminus F^{-1}(y)} \left| rac{\vec H}{4}+ rac{(F-y)^\perp }{|F-y|^2}ight|^2d\mu = rac{\mathcal W(F)}4+  rac12\int _{\partial M} rac{(F-y)\cdot \eta }{|F-y|^2}\, ds.  \] The boundary integral is zero for a closed surface. All integrals retain parameter multiplicity. This is the smooth immersed form of the identity used in [ SimW93 ] , equation (1.5). Proof On the punctured surface, set $V=X/r^2$. Ambient tangential divergence gives \[  \operatorname {div}_ M V= rac2{r^2}-2 rac{|X^ T|^2}{r^4} =2 rac{|X^\perp |^2}{r^4}.  \] The intrinsic divergence of $V^ T$ is $\operatorname {div}_ MV+\vec H\cdot V$. To see the sign, for an orthonormal tangent frame, differentiating $\langle V^\perp ,e_ iangle =0$ gives $\operatorname {div}_ MV^\perp =-\vec H\cdot V$. Therefore \[  \operatorname {div}_ M(V^ T) =2\left| rac{\vec H}{4}+ rac{X^\perp }{r^2}ight|^2- rac18|\vec H|^2.  \] Integrate over the surface with the small sheet disks removed. The original boundary contributes the displayed flux, and Lemma 10.4.2 gives the limiting inner flux $-2\pi m$. The same lemma and smoothness of $\vec H$ give integrability of both terms near each puncture. Letting the radii tend to zero and rearranging proves the identity. Smoothness of the image as a set at a multiple point is not required: each parameter sheet has its own puncture. $\square$ Theorem 10.4.4 (The Li–Yau multiplicity bound for smooth immersions) . 572AC3C13DF8 For a smooth closed immersion $F:M^2	o \mathbb R^ N$ and any $y\in \mathbb R^ N$, \[  \mathcal W(F)\geq 4\pi \, \# F^{-1}(y).  \] In particular $\mathcal W(F)\geq 4\pi $ for every nonempty domain, and $\mathcal W(F)<8\pi $ implies that $F$ is an embedding. The multiplicity inequality is [ LY82 ] , Theorem 6, p. 286. Proof Drop the nonnegative square integral in Theorem 10.4.3 . If the domain is nonempty, choose a point of its image to obtain the first universal lower bound. If the energy is less than $8\pi $, no two distinct parameter points can have the same image, so $F$ is injective. A continuous injective map from a compact space to a Hausdorff space is a homeomorphism onto its image. Together with the immersion hypothesis and its local smooth charts, this makes $F$ a smooth embedding. The energy threshold is strict; equality at $8\pi $ does not yield injectivity by this argument. $\square$ Proposition 10.4.5 (The energy lost at an inversion pole) . 447BFBA2C2DD Under the closed-surface hypotheses above, inversion at $y$ gives an immersion of $M\setminus F^{-1}(y)$ with finite Willmore energy and \[  \mathcal W(I_ y\circ F)=\mathcal W(F)-4\pi m, \qquad m=\# F^{-1}(y).  \] Thus energy is unchanged if the pole misses the image; if it lies on $m$ smooth sheets, inversion subtracts $4\pi $ per sheet. In the equality case $\mathcal W(F)=4\pi m$, the punctured inverted immersion is minimal. Proof Lemma 10.4.1 identifies the inverted energy with four times the square integral in Theorem 10.4.3 . With no boundary that integral is $\mathcal W(F)/4-\pi m$, proving the formula and finiteness. If it vanishes, the transformed mean curvature has zero squared integral. It is smooth on the punctured domain and must vanish everywhere there. No assertion about a smooth compactification at infinity or a classification of that minimal surface is needed. $\square$ Theorem 10.4.6 (Equality in the universal Willmore bound) . 19BB9C12AF07 Let $M$ be connected, closed and nonempty, and $F:M^2	o \mathbb R^ N$ a smooth immersion. Then $\mathcal W(F)=4\pi $ if and only if $F$ is a parametrization without multiplicity of a round two-sphere in an affine three-plane. This is the round-sphere equality case discussed in [ SimW93 ] , pp. 281–282; a direct proof follows. Proof Suppose the energy is $4\pi $. Theorem 10.4.4 makes $F$ an embedding. For every $q\in M$, choose the pole $y=F(q)$ in Theorem 10.4.3 . Its square integral is zero, so for every $x
e q$, \[   rac{\vec H(x)}4+ rac{(F(x)-F(q))^{\perp _ x}}{|F(x)-F(q)|^2}=0.  \] Fix $x$ and a unit tangent vector $v$. Along a geodesic $q(t)$ with $q(0)=x$, $q'(0)=v$, the immersion expansion is $F(q(t))=F(x)+t\, dF_ x(v)+	frac 12t^2B_ x(v,v)+o(t^2)$. Taking the limit in the preceding identity gives $B_ x(v,v)=\vec H(x)/2$. Polarization yields $B=	frac 12g\otimes \vec H$ at every point. Codazzi now implies that $\vec H$ is parallel in the normal bundle. Indeed, in orthonormal tangent directions $e_1,e_2$ the equation $(
abla ^\perp _{e_1}B)(e_2,e_2)=(
abla ^\perp _{e_2}B)(e_1,e_2)$ gives $
abla ^\perp _{e_1}\vec H=0$, and interchanging the two directions gives the other derivative. Therefore $|\vec H|=c$ is constant. It cannot be zero: if $\vec H=\Delta F=0$ on a closed connected surface, integration of $F^\alpha \Delta F^\alpha $ makes all coordinate functions constant, contradicting immersion. Differentiating $\langle \vec H,dF(V)angle =0$ gives $\langle D_ U\vec H,dF(V)angle =-\langle \vec H,B(U,V)angle =-(c^2/2)g(U,V)$. Since the normal derivative vanishes, $D_ U\vec H=-(c^2/2)dF(U)$. It follows that $F+2\vec H/c^2=C$ is constant and $|F-C|=2/c$. The three-dimensional subspace spanned by $F-C$ and the tangent plane is fixed along every curve: derivatives of $F-C$ are tangent, and derivatives of tangent fields have normal part $B$, which is parallel to $F-C$. Parallel transport of a frame for this subspace therefore keeps it in one fixed ambient three-plane. The image lies in the round two-sphere of radius $2/c$ in that plane. Its tangent spaces agree with those of the sphere, so it is open there by the inverse function theorem, and compactness makes it closed. Connectedness of the sphere gives the full image, with no multiplicity since $F$ is injective. Conversely a round sphere of radius $R$ has $|\vec H|=2/R$ and area $4\pi R^2$, so its energy is $4\pi $. $\square$ Corollary 10.4.7 (Multiplicity bounds in the unit sphere) . E284F9A1175C For a smooth closed immersion $F:M^2	o S^ N$, $N\geq 3$, and a point $y\in S^ N$ with $m$ preimages, \[  \mathcal W_1(F)\geq 4\pi m.  \] In particular a closed minimal spherical immersion with area below $8\pi $ is embedded. This is the consequence stated in [ LY82 ] , Corollary 10, p. 286. Proof A compact smooth two-dimensional immersed image has zero $N$-dimensional volume for $N>2$, by covering it with finitely many smooth Lipschitz charts and the dimension estimate for Lipschitz images. Choose a pole outside the image. Stereographic projection preserves multiplicities, and Proposition 10.3.5 preserves the normalized energy. Apply Theorem 10.4.4 . In the minimal case the energy is area, and the same injectivity argument gives embeddedness. $\square$ Example 10.4.8 (The boundary flux of a flat disk) . 4CF7F912975D For the radius-$R$ disk in a two-plane, with pole at its center, the Willmore energy and the square term in Theorem 10.4.3 both vanish, but the boundary flux is $2\pi $. Thus the identity reads $\pi =	frac 12(2\pi )$; the closed-surface lower bound cannot be applied to a disk. Proof The plane has $\vec H=0$ and $X^\perp =0$. At the boundary $\eta =X/R$, so $X\cdot \eta /r^2=1/R$. The boundary length is $2\pi R$, giving the stated flux. There is exactly one preimage of the pole. This verifies the sign and factor in the boundary identity independently of a curved example. $\square$ Corollary 10.4.9 (From the embedded theorem to all orientable positive-genus immersions) . 9065CAA9C92F Let $F:M^2	o \mathbb R^3$ be a smooth closed connected immersion of an orientable surface of genus at least one. Then $\mathcal W(F)\geq 2\pi ^2$. Equality requires embeddedness and, after inverse stereographic projection, a conformal image of the Clifford torus. The same statement holds for immersions in $S^3$ with energy $\mathcal W_1$. This deduction uses the external Marques–Neves theorem 10.1.2 , as explained in [ MNWill ] , p. 685. Proof If an immersion is not injective, Theorem 10.4.4 , or Corollary 10.4.7 in the sphere, gives energy at least $8\pi >2\pi ^2$. Otherwise compactness makes it an embedding. A Euclidean embedding becomes a spherical embedding by inverse stereographic projection, with the same energy by Proposition 10.3.5 . Apply Theorem 10.1.2 and its equality classification. Conversely the Clifford torus and its conformal images have that energy by the explicit calculation and conformal invariance. The deep embedded theorem is an input to this argument, not proved by the multiplicity bound. $\square$

title: Lemma 10.4.1 (The differential and curvature of an inversion)
search_title: The differential and curvature of an inversion
section: 10.4 Willmore energy, multiplicity and inversion
text: Lemma 10.4.1 (The differential and curvature of an inversion) . 86AC490C5917 Let $F:M^2\to \mathbb R^ N\setminus \{ y\} $ be a smooth immersion. Write $X=F-y$, $r=|X|$, and let $R_ X=I-2r^{-2}X\otimes X$ be reflection across the hyperplane orthogonal to $X$; the notation $X^\perp $ below denotes projection onto the surface normal space. The inversion $I_ y(z)=(z-y)/|z-y|^2$ satisfies \[  dI_ y=r^{-2}R_ X,\quad d\widetilde\mu =r^{-4}d\mu ,\quad \widetilde{\vec H}=r^2R_ X\left(\vec H+4\frac{X^\perp }{r^2}\right).  \] Consequently on every measurable parameter set, \[  \frac14\int |\widetilde{\vec H}|^2d\widetilde\mu =4\int \left|\frac{\vec H}{4}+\frac{X^\perp }{r^2}\right|^2d\mu ,  \] with equality also when the integrals are infinite. Proof Differentiate $X/r^2$ to obtain the differential. The map $R_ X$ is orthogonal, so lengths scale by $r^{-2}$ and surface area by $r^{-4}$. Pullback of the Euclidean ambient metric is $r^{-4}$ times that metric, a conformal change with $\phi =-2\log r$. Lemma 10.3.2 gives the mean curvature in that pullback metric as $r^4(\vec H+4X^\perp /r^2)$. The inversion is an isometry from the pullback metric to the target metric; pushing forward by $dI_ y$ proves the formula. Squaring, multiplying by the transformed area element and retaining the factor $1/4$ proves the integral identity. $\square$

title: Lemma 10.4.2 (The puncture flux at a smooth immersed sheet)
search_title: The puncture flux at a smooth immersed sheet
section: 10.4 Willmore energy, multiplicity and inversion
text:
Lemma 10.4.2 (The puncture flux at a smooth immersed sheet) . 3C733C121AC2 Let $F:M^2	o \mathbb R^ N$ be a smooth compact immersion, possibly with smooth boundary, and let $y
otin F(\partial M)$. Its preimage is a finite set of interior points, of cardinality $m$. For small $\varepsilon >0$, remove from each such sheet the region $|F-y|<\varepsilon $. Along the resulting inner boundary, the outward conormal $\eta _\varepsilon $ of the remaining surface satisfies \[  \int _{	ext{inner boundary}} rac{X^ T}{r^2}\cdot \eta _\varepsilon \, ds\longrightarrow -2\pi m.  \] Near each puncture, $X^\perp =O(r^2)$; hence $X^\perp /r^2$ is bounded and locally square integrable. Proof An immersion is an embedding on a neighborhood of each parameter point. The preimage of $y$ is closed in the compact domain and each of its points is isolated. An infinite preimage would have an accumulation point contradicting local injectivity, so it is finite. Compactness excludes any further image points near $y$ outside the chosen sheet neighborhoods. Translate $y$ to zero and write a sheet as a graph $F(z)=(z,u(z))$ over its tangent plane, with $u(0)=0$, $Du(0)=0$, $u(z)=O(|z|^2)$ and $Du(z)=O(|z|)$. Its radial function is $r=|z|(1+O(|z|^2))$, and its gradient has $|
abla _ Mr|=1+O(r^2)$. The small radial level is a smooth perturbation of a circle, with length $2\pi \varepsilon +O(\varepsilon ^3)$. The graph expansion also gives $|X^\perp |=O(r^2)$, since the leading linear vector lies in the tangent plane and the tangent plane changes by $O(r)$. At the inner level, $\eta _\varepsilon =-
abla _ Mr/|
abla _ Mr|$ and $X^ T=r
abla _ Mr$. Thus the integrand is $-|
abla _ Mr|/\varepsilon $, and its integral is $-2\pi +O(\varepsilon ^2)$ for each sheet. Sum over the finite preimage. If $m=0$, a small ball misses the image and there is no puncture flux. $\square$

title: Theorem 10.4.3 (A square identity for a compact immersed surface)
search_title: A square identity for a compact immersed surface
section: 10.4 Willmore energy, multiplicity and inversion
text: Theorem 10.4.3 (A square identity for a compact immersed surface) . A6413522A6DE Let $F:M^2\to \mathbb R^ N$ be a smooth compact immersion with smooth boundary allowed. For $y\notin F(\partial M)$ let $m=\# F^{-1}(y)$, and let $\eta $ be the outward unit conormal on the original boundary. Then \[  \pi m+\int _{M\setminus F^{-1}(y)} \left|\frac{\vec H}{4}+\frac{(F-y)^\perp }{|F-y|^2}\right|^2d\mu =\frac{\mathcal W(F)}4+ \frac12\int _{\partial M}\frac{(F-y)\cdot \eta }{|F-y|^2}\, ds.  \] The boundary integral is zero for a closed surface. All integrals retain parameter multiplicity. This is the smooth immersed form of the identity used in [ SimW93 ] , equation (1.5). Proof On the punctured surface, set $V=X/r^2$. Ambient tangential divergence gives \[  \operatorname {div}_ M V=\frac2{r^2}-2\frac{|X^ T|^2}{r^4} =2\frac{|X^\perp |^2}{r^4}.  \] The intrinsic divergence of $V^ T$ is $\operatorname {div}_ MV+\vec H\cdot V$. To see the sign, for an orthonormal tangent frame, differentiating $\langle V^\perp ,e_ i\rangle =0$ gives $\operatorname {div}_ MV^\perp =-\vec H\cdot V$. Therefore \[  \operatorname {div}_ M(V^ T) =2\left|\frac{\vec H}{4}+\frac{X^\perp }{r^2}\right|^2-\frac18|\vec H|^2.  \] Integrate over the surface with the small sheet disks removed. The original boundary contributes the displayed flux, and Lemma 10.4.2 gives the limiting inner flux $-2\pi m$. The same lemma and smoothness of $\vec H$ give integrability of both terms near each puncture. Letting the radii tend to zero and rearranging proves the identity. Smoothness of the image as a set at a multiple point is not required: each parameter sheet has its own puncture. $\square$

title: Theorem 10.4.4 (The Li–Yau multiplicity bound for smooth immersions)
search_title: The Li–Yau multiplicity bound for smooth immersions
section: 10.4 Willmore energy, multiplicity and inversion
text: Theorem 10.4.4 (The Li–Yau multiplicity bound for smooth immersions) . 572AC3C13DF8 For a smooth closed immersion $F:M^2\to \mathbb R^ N$ and any $y\in \mathbb R^ N$, \[  \mathcal W(F)\geq 4\pi \, \# F^{-1}(y).  \] In particular $\mathcal W(F)\geq 4\pi $ for every nonempty domain, and $\mathcal W(F)<8\pi $ implies that $F$ is an embedding. The multiplicity inequality is [ LY82 ] , Theorem 6, p. 286. Proof Drop the nonnegative square integral in Theorem 10.4.3 . If the domain is nonempty, choose a point of its image to obtain the first universal lower bound. If the energy is less than $8\pi $, no two distinct parameter points can have the same image, so $F$ is injective. A continuous injective map from a compact space to a Hausdorff space is a homeomorphism onto its image. Together with the immersion hypothesis and its local smooth charts, this makes $F$ a smooth embedding. The energy threshold is strict; equality at $8\pi $ does not yield injectivity by this argument. $\square$

title: Proposition 10.4.5 (The energy lost at an inversion pole)
search_title: The energy lost at an inversion pole
section: 10.4 Willmore energy, multiplicity and inversion
text: Proposition 10.4.5 (The energy lost at an inversion pole) . 447BFBA2C2DD Under the closed-surface hypotheses above, inversion at $y$ gives an immersion of $M\setminus F^{-1}(y)$ with finite Willmore energy and \[  \mathcal W(I_ y\circ F)=\mathcal W(F)-4\pi m, \qquad m=\# F^{-1}(y).  \] Thus energy is unchanged if the pole misses the image; if it lies on $m$ smooth sheets, inversion subtracts $4\pi $ per sheet. In the equality case $\mathcal W(F)=4\pi m$, the punctured inverted immersion is minimal. Proof Lemma 10.4.1 identifies the inverted energy with four times the square integral in Theorem 10.4.3 . With no boundary that integral is $\mathcal W(F)/4-\pi m$, proving the formula and finiteness. If it vanishes, the transformed mean curvature has zero squared integral. It is smooth on the punctured domain and must vanish everywhere there. No assertion about a smooth compactification at infinity or a classification of that minimal surface is needed. $\square$

title: Theorem 10.4.6 (Equality in the universal Willmore bound)
search_title: Equality in the universal Willmore bound
section: 10.4 Willmore energy, multiplicity and inversion
text:
Theorem 10.4.6 (Equality in the universal Willmore bound) . 19BB9C12AF07 Let $M$ be connected, closed and nonempty, and $F:M^2	o \mathbb R^ N$ a smooth immersion. Then $\mathcal W(F)=4\pi $ if and only if $F$ is a parametrization without multiplicity of a round two-sphere in an affine three-plane. This is the round-sphere equality case discussed in [ SimW93 ] , pp. 281–282; a direct proof follows. Proof Suppose the energy is $4\pi $. Theorem 10.4.4 makes $F$ an embedding. For every $q\in M$, choose the pole $y=F(q)$ in Theorem 10.4.3 . Its square integral is zero, so for every $x
e q$, \[   rac{\vec H(x)}4+ rac{(F(x)-F(q))^{\perp _ x}}{|F(x)-F(q)|^2}=0.  \] Fix $x$ and a unit tangent vector $v$. Along a geodesic $q(t)$ with $q(0)=x$, $q'(0)=v$, the immersion expansion is $F(q(t))=F(x)+t\, dF_ x(v)+	frac 12t^2B_ x(v,v)+o(t^2)$. Taking the limit in the preceding identity gives $B_ x(v,v)=\vec H(x)/2$. Polarization yields $B=	frac 12g\otimes \vec H$ at every point. Codazzi now implies that $\vec H$ is parallel in the normal bundle. Indeed, in orthonormal tangent directions $e_1,e_2$ the equation $(
abla ^\perp _{e_1}B)(e_2,e_2)=(
abla ^\perp _{e_2}B)(e_1,e_2)$ gives $
abla ^\perp _{e_1}\vec H=0$, and interchanging the two directions gives the other derivative. Therefore $|\vec H|=c$ is constant. It cannot be zero: if $\vec H=\Delta F=0$ on a closed connected surface, integration of $F^\alpha \Delta F^\alpha $ makes all coordinate functions constant, contradicting immersion. Differentiating $\langle \vec H,dF(V)angle =0$ gives $\langle D_ U\vec H,dF(V)angle =-\langle \vec H,B(U,V)angle =-(c^2/2)g(U,V)$. Since the normal derivative vanishes, $D_ U\vec H=-(c^2/2)dF(U)$. It follows that $F+2\vec H/c^2=C$ is constant and $|F-C|=2/c$. The three-dimensional subspace spanned by $F-C$ and the tangent plane is fixed along every curve: derivatives of $F-C$ are tangent, and derivatives of tangent fields have normal part $B$, which is parallel to $F-C$. Parallel transport of a frame for this subspace therefore keeps it in one fixed ambient three-plane. The image lies in the round two-sphere of radius $2/c$ in that plane. Its tangent spaces agree with those of the sphere, so it is open there by the inverse function theorem, and compactness makes it closed. Connectedness of the sphere gives the full image, with no multiplicity since $F$ is injective. Conversely a round sphere of radius $R$ has $|\vec H|=2/R$ and area $4\pi R^2$, so its energy is $4\pi $. $\square$

title: Corollary 10.4.7 (Multiplicity bounds in the unit sphere)
search_title: Multiplicity bounds in the unit sphere
section: 10.4 Willmore energy, multiplicity and inversion
text: Corollary 10.4.7 (Multiplicity bounds in the unit sphere) . E284F9A1175C For a smooth closed immersion $F:M^2\to S^ N$, $N\geq 3$, and a point $y\in S^ N$ with $m$ preimages, \[  \mathcal W_1(F)\geq 4\pi m.  \] In particular a closed minimal spherical immersion with area below $8\pi $ is embedded. This is the consequence stated in [ LY82 ] , Corollary 10, p. 286. Proof A compact smooth two-dimensional immersed image has zero $N$-dimensional volume for $N>2$, by covering it with finitely many smooth Lipschitz charts and the dimension estimate for Lipschitz images. Choose a pole outside the image. Stereographic projection preserves multiplicities, and Proposition 10.3.5 preserves the normalized energy. Apply Theorem 10.4.4 . In the minimal case the energy is area, and the same injectivity argument gives embeddedness. $\square$

title: Example 10.4.8 (The boundary flux of a flat disk)
search_title: The boundary flux of a flat disk
section: 10.4 Willmore energy, multiplicity and inversion
text: Example 10.4.8 (The boundary flux of a flat disk) . 4CF7F912975D For the radius-$R$ disk in a two-plane, with pole at its center, the Willmore energy and the square term in Theorem 10.4.3 both vanish, but the boundary flux is $2\pi $. Thus the identity reads $\pi =\tfrac 12(2\pi )$; the closed-surface lower bound cannot be applied to a disk. Proof The plane has $\vec H=0$ and $X^\perp =0$. At the boundary $\eta =X/R$, so $X\cdot \eta /r^2=1/R$. The boundary length is $2\pi R$, giving the stated flux. There is exactly one preimage of the pole. This verifies the sign and factor in the boundary identity independently of a curved example. $\square$

title: Corollary 10.4.9 (From the embedded theorem to all orientable positive-genus immersions)
search_title: From the embedded theorem to all orientable positive-genus immersions
section: 10.4 Willmore energy, multiplicity and inversion
text: Corollary 10.4.9 (From the embedded theorem to all orientable positive-genus immersions) . 9065CAA9C92F Let $F:M^2\to \mathbb R^3$ be a smooth closed connected immersion of an orientable surface of genus at least one. Then $\mathcal W(F)\geq 2\pi ^2$. Equality requires embeddedness and, after inverse stereographic projection, a conformal image of the Clifford torus. The same statement holds for immersions in $S^3$ with energy $\mathcal W_1$. This deduction uses the external Marques–Neves theorem 10.1.2 , as explained in [ MNWill ] , p. 685. Proof If an immersion is not injective, Theorem 10.4.4 , or Corollary 10.4.7 in the sphere, gives energy at least $8\pi >2\pi ^2$. Otherwise compactness makes it an embedding. A Euclidean embedding becomes a spherical embedding by inverse stereographic projection, with the same energy by Proposition 10.3.5 . Apply Theorem 10.1.2 and its equality classification. Conversely the Clifford torus and its conformal images have that energy by the explicit calculation and conformal invariance. The deep embedded theorem is an input to this argument, not proved by the multiplicity bound. $\square$

title: 10.5 Local area and diameter estimates from Willmore energy
search_title: Local area and diameter estimates from Willmore energy
section: 10.5 Local area and diameter estimates from Willmore energy
text: Throughout this section $F:M^2\to \mathbb R^ N$ is a smooth compact immersion of a nonempty surface without boundary. Set $X=F-y$, $r=|X|$, $M_ s=\{ r<s\} $, $A(s)=\mu (M_ s)$ and $\mathcal W(E)=\frac14\int _ E|\vec H|^2d\mu $. The cutoff calculation follows [ SimW93 ] , pp. 284–286. We keep the annular energy and the two boundary-radius terms explicit before deriving inequalities. Proposition 10.5.1 (The two-radius square identity) . 1EB2A47C45B3 For positive regular values $0<\sigma <\rho $ of $r$, let $M_{\sigma ,\rho }=\{ \sigma <r<\rho \} $. Then \[  \frac{A(\sigma )}{\sigma ^2} +\int _{M_{\sigma ,\rho }}\left|\frac{\vec H}4+\frac{X^\perp }{r^2}\right|^2d\mu =\frac{A(\rho )}{\rho ^2}+\frac14\mathcal W(M_{\sigma ,\rho }) +\frac1{2\rho ^2}\int _{M_\rho }X\cdot \vec H\, d\mu -\frac1{2\sigma ^2}\int _{M_\sigma }X\cdot \vec H\, d\mu .  \] There is no contribution from the intrinsic boundary of $M$, since it is empty. Proof Use the compactly supported Lipschitz ambient vector field \[  V(X)=\bigl (\max (r,\sigma )^{-2}-\rho ^{-2}\bigr )_+X  \] in the first variation identity $\int \operatorname {div}_ MV=-\int \vec H\cdot V$. Its nonsmooth radii can be approximated by smooth radial cutoffs; the coefficients and tangential derivatives are uniformly bounded for fixed $\sigma >0$, and the two regular level sets have zero surface measure. Dominated convergence therefore justifies the Lipschitz test. On $M_\sigma $ its tangential divergence is $2(\sigma ^{-2}-\rho ^{-2})$. On the annulus it is $2|X^\perp |^2/r^4-2\rho ^{-2}$, and outside $M_\rho $ it is zero. Substitution and division by two give \[  \frac{A(\sigma )}{\sigma ^2}+\int _{M_{\sigma ,\rho }} \left(\frac{|X^\perp |^2}{r^4}+\frac{X\cdot \vec H}{2r^2}\right)d\mu =\frac{A(\rho )}{\rho ^2}+\frac1{2\rho ^2}\int _{M_\rho }X\cdot \vec H -\frac1{2\sigma ^2}\int _{M_\sigma }X\cdot \vec H.  \] Completing the square inside the annulus adds $|\vec H|^2/16$ on that annulus, exactly $\mathcal W(M_{\sigma ,\rho })/4$ on the right. This explains why the energy in the exact two-radius formula is annular, before any enlargement used in an estimate. $\square$ Proposition 10.5.2 (A corrected area ratio is monotone) . 06FDAA574FA5 For $s>0$ define \[  \Phi _ y(s)=\frac{A(s)}{s^2}+\frac1{2s^2}\int _{M_ s}X\cdot \vec H\, d\mu +\frac14\mathcal W(M_ s).  \] Then $\Phi _ y$ is nondecreasing and \[  \Phi _ y(s)=\pi m+\int _{M_ s\setminus F^{-1}(y)} \left|\frac{\vec H}4+\frac{X^\perp }{r^2}\right|^2d\mu , \qquad m=\# F^{-1}(y).  \] In particular $\Phi _ y(0+)=\pi m$ and $\Phi _ y(+\infty )=\mathcal W(F)/4$. The uncorrected area ratio need not be monotone for a nonminimal surface. Proof Move the inner curvature-radius term in Proposition 10.5.1 to the left and add $\mathcal W(M_\sigma )/4$ to both sides. The result is $\Phi _ y(\rho )-\Phi _ y(\sigma )$ equal to the nonnegative square integral over the annulus. The graph calculation of Lemma 10.4.2 gives $A(\sigma )/\sigma ^2\to \pi m$. It also gives $X^\perp =O(r^2)$ near each preimage, whence $\sigma ^{-2}\int _{M_\sigma }X\cdot \vec H=O(\sigma ^2)$; the inner energy tends to zero. If the pole misses the image, all three terms vanish for small $\sigma $. Letting $\sigma \downarrow 0$ proves the formula for regular $s$. For any other $s>0$, choose regular values increasing to $s$. The corresponding open sublevel sets increase to $M_ s$. Monotone convergence for the nonnegative terms, and dominated convergence for the bounded signed curvature term, yield the same formula. It makes monotonicity immediate at every radius. Finally compactness of $M$ makes both radius-denominator terms tend to zero at infinity, while the energy tends to its full value. The correction terms involving mean curvature are essential in this computation. $\square$ Proposition 10.5.3 (A local comparison with an explicit constant) . 2124DA17B73F For $0<\sigma <\rho $, \[  \frac{A(\sigma )}{\sigma ^2}\leq 3\frac{A(\rho )}{\rho ^2}+\frac52\mathcal W(M_\rho ).  \] If $y$ has $m$ preimages, then \[  \pi m\leq 3\frac{A(\rho )}{\rho ^2}+\frac52\mathcal W(M_\rho ).  \] These estimates do not assume embeddedness or a pointwise bound on mean curvature. Proof First use regular radii in Proposition 10.5.1 and discard its square term. Put $a_ s=A(s)/s^2$ and $E=\int _{M_\rho }|\vec H|^2$. The two radius terms are bounded in absolute value by $\tfrac 12\sqrt{a_\rho E}$ and $\tfrac 12\sqrt{a_\sigma E}$, using $r\leq s$ on $M_ s$ and Cauchy–Schwarz. The annular energy term is at most $E/16$. Since \[  \tfrac 12\sqrt{aE}\leq \tfrac 12a+\tfrac 18E,  \] we obtain $a_\sigma \leq a_\rho +E/16+(a_\rho +a_\sigma )/2+E/4$. Rearrangement gives $a_\sigma \leq 3a_\rho +5E/8$, which is the claim. Approximation from below by regular radii gives the formula at arbitrary radii; open sublevel sets and their integrals converge from below. Letting $\sigma \downarrow 0$ gives the multiplicity consequence by the local sheet area expansion. $\square$ Theorem 10.5.4 (Global energy controls every local area ratio) . 6850DAD0C60F For every $y\in \mathbb R^ N$ and $s>0$, \[  \mu \bigl (F^{-1}(B_ s(y))\bigr )\leq \mathcal W(F)s^2.  \] The constant is independent of the total area, diameter and number of components. This is a consequence of the radial first-variation mechanism of [ SimW93 ] , pp. 284–285; the following proof retains separate inside and outside energies. Proof Fix a regular value $s$ and let $\rho \to \infty $ in Proposition 10.5.1 . Compactness eliminates the outer radius terms. Let $a=A(s)/s^2$, $w=\mathcal W(M_ s)$ and $W=\mathcal W(F)$. Dropping the exterior square term gives \[  a\leq \frac{W-w}{4}-\frac1{2s^2}\int _{M_ s}X\cdot \vec H \leq \frac{W-w}{4}+\sqrt{aw}.  \] The last estimate again uses $r\leq s$ and Cauchy–Schwarz. Consequently \[  \left(\sqrt a-\frac{\sqrt w}{2}\right)^2\leq \frac W4, \qquad \sqrt a\leq \frac{\sqrt w+\sqrt W}{2}\leq \sqrt W.  \] This proves $a\leq W$. For arbitrary $s$, take regular values increasing to $s$ and use convergence of the open-ball area. No limit surface or weak mean-curvature theory enters the argument. $\square$ Corollary 10.5.5 (Willmore energy gives a Gaussian-area bound) . 779189C9B6ED Every smooth closed immersed surface in Euclidean space satisfies, for all centers $y$ and scales $t>0$, \[  F_{y,t}(M)=\frac1{4\pi t}\int _ Me^{-|F-y|^2/(4t)}d\mu \leq \frac{\mathcal W(F)}\pi .  \] Thus the supremum over centers and scales obeys the same bound. This estimate is not asserted to be sharp. Proof For $r\geq 0$, write $e^{-r^2/(4t)}=\int _ r^\infty \frac{s}{2t}e^{-s^2/(4t)}ds$. Tonelli's theorem gives \[  F_{y,t}=\frac1{8\pi t^2}\int _0^\infty s\, e^{-s^2/(4t)}A(s)\, ds.  \] The choice of open or closed sublevel sets does not affect this integral in $s$. Apply Theorem 10.5.4 and substitute $u=s^2/(4t)$. Since $\int _0^\infty s^3e^{-s^2/(4t)}ds=8t^2$, the result follows. Taking the supremum preserves the inequality. This connects an extrinsic bending-energy bound to the Gaussian functional used in mean curvature flow without claiming that Willmore energy is itself monotone along that flow. $\square$ Proposition 10.5.6 (A containing ball bounds area by energy) . D11A3941C16D If $R>0$ and the image lies in $\overline B_ R(y)$, then $\mu (M)\leq R^2\mathcal W(F)$. Equality holds exactly when the immersion lies in $\partial B_ R(y)$ and is minimal as a surface of that sphere. Proof Use the vector field $F-y$ in the closed-surface first variation. Its tangential divergence is two, so \[  2\mu (M)=-\int _ M(F-y)\cdot \vec H \leq R\sqrt{\mu (M)}\left(\int _ M|\vec H|^2\right)^{1/2}.  \] This gives the inequality. Equality in the two estimates requires $|F-y|=R$ almost everywhere, hence everywhere, and $\vec H$ to be a fixed negative scalar multiple of $F-y$. The first-variation integral identifies that scalar as $2/R^2$. For a surface in a radius-$R$ sphere, the Euclidean and spherical mean curvature vectors satisfy $\vec H_{\mathbb R^ N}=\vec H_{S^{N-1}(R)}-2(F-y)/R^2$. Therefore equality is equivalent to spherical minimality. Conversely that identity and $|F-y|=R$ give $\mathcal W=\mu (M)/R^2$ directly. $\square$ Theorem 10.5.7 (Area-energy bounds for extrinsic diameter) . 2289A5287A63 If $M$ is connected and nonempty, its extrinsic diameter $D=\operatorname {diam}F(M)$ satisfies \[  \sqrt{\frac{\mu (M)}{\mathcal W(F)}}\leq D \leq \frac{29}{2\pi }\sqrt{\mu (M)\mathcal W(F)}.  \] The upper constant is merely an explicit choice. The qualitative estimate is Lemma 1.1 of [ SimW93 ] , p. 283; the proof below also works with immersion multiplicity. Proof Fix a point of the image. The entire image lies in its closed radius-$D$ ball, so Proposition 10.5.6 gives the lower estimate. Write $A=\mu (M)$, $W=\mathcal W(F)>0$ and $\ell =\sqrt{A/W}$. Choose image points whose distance is $D$ and use one as center $y_0$. Connectedness makes the continuous distance function on the image attain every value in $[0,D]$. Hence for $j=0,\ldots ,\lfloor D/\ell \rfloor $ choose image points $y_ j$ with $|y_ j-y_0|=j\ell $. Distinct points have pairwise distance at least $\ell $, so their open radius-$\ell /2$ balls are disjoint. Each $y_ j$ has at least one preimage. Apply Proposition 10.5.3 with outer radius $\ell /2$ at that center and sum. Disjointness of the preimages of these balls gives \[  \pi \bigl (1+\lfloor D/\ell \rfloor \bigr ) \leq \frac{12A}{\ell ^2}+\frac52W=\frac{29}{2}W.  \] Since $D/\ell <1+\lfloor D/\ell \rfloor $, the upper bound follows, with a non-strict inequality as stated. This is an extrinsic diameter bound; it does not control intrinsic distances along a surface with long narrow geometry. $\square$

text: Proposition 10.5.2 (A corrected area ratio is monotone) . 06FDAA574FA5 For $s>0$ define \[  \Phi _ y(s)=\frac{A(s)}{s^2}+\frac1{2s^2}\int _{M_ s}X\cdot \vec H\, d\mu +\frac14\mathcal W(M_ s).  \] Then $\Phi _ y$ is nondecreasing and \[  \Phi _ y(s)=\pi m+\int _{M_ s\setminus F^{-1}(y)} \left|\frac{\vec H}4+\frac{X^\perp }{r^2}\right|^2d\mu , \qquad m=\# F^{-1}(y).  \] In particular $\Phi _ y(0+)=\pi m$ and $\Phi _ y(+\infty )=\mathcal W(F)/4$. The uncorrected area ratio need not be monotone for a nonminimal surface. Proof Move the inner curvature-radius term in Proposition 10.5.1 to the left and add $\mathcal W(M_\sigma )/4$ to both sides. The result is $\Phi _ y(\rho )-\Phi _ y(\sigma )$ equal to the nonnegative square integral over the annulus. The graph calculation of Lemma 10.4.2 gives $A(\sigma )/\sigma ^2\to \pi m$. It also gives $X^\perp =O(r^2)$ near each preimage, whence $\sigma ^{-2}\int _{M_\sigma }X\cdot \vec H=O(\sigma ^2)$; the inner energy tends to zero. If the pole misses the image, all three terms vanish for small $\sigma $. Letting $\sigma \downarrow 0$ proves the formula for regular $s$. For any other $s>0$, choose regular values increasing to $s$. The corresponding open sublevel sets increase to $M_ s$. Monotone convergence for the nonnegative terms, and dominated convergence for the bounded signed curvature term, yield the same formula. It makes monotonicity immediate at every radius. Finally compactness of $M$ makes both radius-denominator terms tend to zero at infinity, while the energy tends to its full value. The correction terms involving mean curvature are essential in this computation. $\square$

title: Proposition 10.5.3 (A local comparison with an explicit constant)
search_title: A local comparison with an explicit constant
section: 10.5 Local area and diameter estimates from Willmore energy
text: Proposition 10.5.3 (A local comparison with an explicit constant) . 2124DA17B73F For $0<\sigma <\rho $, \[  \frac{A(\sigma )}{\sigma ^2}\leq 3\frac{A(\rho )}{\rho ^2}+\frac52\mathcal W(M_\rho ).  \] If $y$ has $m$ preimages, then \[  \pi m\leq 3\frac{A(\rho )}{\rho ^2}+\frac52\mathcal W(M_\rho ).  \] These estimates do not assume embeddedness or a pointwise bound on mean curvature. Proof First use regular radii in Proposition 10.5.1 and discard its square term. Put $a_ s=A(s)/s^2$ and $E=\int _{M_\rho }|\vec H|^2$. The two radius terms are bounded in absolute value by $\tfrac 12\sqrt{a_\rho E}$ and $\tfrac 12\sqrt{a_\sigma E}$, using $r\leq s$ on $M_ s$ and Cauchy–Schwarz. The annular energy term is at most $E/16$. Since \[  \tfrac 12\sqrt{aE}\leq \tfrac 12a+\tfrac 18E,  \] we obtain $a_\sigma \leq a_\rho +E/16+(a_\rho +a_\sigma )/2+E/4$. Rearrangement gives $a_\sigma \leq 3a_\rho +5E/8$, which is the claim. Approximation from below by regular radii gives the formula at arbitrary radii; open sublevel sets and their integrals converge from below. Letting $\sigma \downarrow 0$ gives the multiplicity consequence by the local sheet area expansion. $\square$

title: Theorem 10.5.4 (Global energy controls every local area ratio)
search_title: Global energy controls every local area ratio
section: 10.5 Local area and diameter estimates from Willmore energy
text: Theorem 10.5.4 (Global energy controls every local area ratio) . 6850DAD0C60F For every $y\in \mathbb R^ N$ and $s>0$, \[  \mu \bigl (F^{-1}(B_ s(y))\bigr )\leq \mathcal W(F)s^2.  \] The constant is independent of the total area, diameter and number of components. This is a consequence of the radial first-variation mechanism of [ SimW93 ] , pp. 284–285; the following proof retains separate inside and outside energies. Proof Fix a regular value $s$ and let $\rho \to \infty $ in Proposition 10.5.1 . Compactness eliminates the outer radius terms. Let $a=A(s)/s^2$, $w=\mathcal W(M_ s)$ and $W=\mathcal W(F)$. Dropping the exterior square term gives \[  a\leq \frac{W-w}{4}-\frac1{2s^2}\int _{M_ s}X\cdot \vec H \leq \frac{W-w}{4}+\sqrt{aw}.  \] The last estimate again uses $r\leq s$ and Cauchy–Schwarz. Consequently \[  \left(\sqrt a-\frac{\sqrt w}{2}\right)^2\leq \frac W4, \qquad \sqrt a\leq \frac{\sqrt w+\sqrt W}{2}\leq \sqrt W.  \] This proves $a\leq W$. For arbitrary $s$, take regular values increasing to $s$ and use convergence of the open-ball area. No limit surface or weak mean-curvature theory enters the argument. $\square$

title: Corollary 10.5.5 (Willmore energy gives a Gaussian-area bound)
search_title: Willmore energy gives a Gaussian-area bound
section: 10.5 Local area and diameter estimates from Willmore energy
text: Corollary 10.5.5 (Willmore energy gives a Gaussian-area bound) . 779189C9B6ED Every smooth closed immersed surface in Euclidean space satisfies, for all centers $y$ and scales $t>0$, \[  F_{y,t}(M)=\frac1{4\pi t}\int _ Me^{-|F-y|^2/(4t)}d\mu \leq \frac{\mathcal W(F)}\pi .  \] Thus the supremum over centers and scales obeys the same bound. This estimate is not asserted to be sharp. Proof For $r\geq 0$, write $e^{-r^2/(4t)}=\int _ r^\infty \frac{s}{2t}e^{-s^2/(4t)}ds$. Tonelli's theorem gives \[  F_{y,t}=\frac1{8\pi t^2}\int _0^\infty s\, e^{-s^2/(4t)}A(s)\, ds.  \] The choice of open or closed sublevel sets does not affect this integral in $s$. Apply Theorem 10.5.4 and substitute $u=s^2/(4t)$. Since $\int _0^\infty s^3e^{-s^2/(4t)}ds=8t^2$, the result follows. Taking the supremum preserves the inequality. This connects an extrinsic bending-energy bound to the Gaussian functional used in mean curvature flow without claiming that Willmore energy is itself monotone along that flow. $\square$

title: Proposition 10.5.6 (A containing ball bounds area by energy)
search_title: A containing ball bounds area by energy
section: 10.5 Local area and diameter estimates from Willmore energy
text: Proposition 10.5.6 (A containing ball bounds area by energy) . D11A3941C16D If $R>0$ and the image lies in $\overline B_ R(y)$, then $\mu (M)\leq R^2\mathcal W(F)$. Equality holds exactly when the immersion lies in $\partial B_ R(y)$ and is minimal as a surface of that sphere. Proof Use the vector field $F-y$ in the closed-surface first variation. Its tangential divergence is two, so \[  2\mu (M)=-\int _ M(F-y)\cdot \vec H \leq R\sqrt{\mu (M)}\left(\int _ M|\vec H|^2\right)^{1/2}.  \] This gives the inequality. Equality in the two estimates requires $|F-y|=R$ almost everywhere, hence everywhere, and $\vec H$ to be a fixed negative scalar multiple of $F-y$. The first-variation integral identifies that scalar as $2/R^2$. For a surface in a radius-$R$ sphere, the Euclidean and spherical mean curvature vectors satisfy $\vec H_{\mathbb R^ N}=\vec H_{S^{N-1}(R)}-2(F-y)/R^2$. Therefore equality is equivalent to spherical minimality. Conversely that identity and $|F-y|=R$ give $\mathcal W=\mu (M)/R^2$ directly. $\square$

title: Theorem 10.5.7 (Area-energy bounds for extrinsic diameter)
search_title: Area-energy bounds for extrinsic diameter
section: 10.5 Local area and diameter estimates from Willmore energy
text: Theorem 10.5.7 (Area-energy bounds for extrinsic diameter) . 2289A5287A63 If $M$ is connected and nonempty, its extrinsic diameter $D=\operatorname {diam}F(M)$ satisfies \[  \sqrt{\frac{\mu (M)}{\mathcal W(F)}}\leq D \leq \frac{29}{2\pi }\sqrt{\mu (M)\mathcal W(F)}.  \] The upper constant is merely an explicit choice. The qualitative estimate is Lemma 1.1 of [ SimW93 ] , p. 283; the proof below also works with immersion multiplicity. Proof Fix a point of the image. The entire image lies in its closed radius-$D$ ball, so Proposition 10.5.6 gives the lower estimate. Write $A=\mu (M)$, $W=\mathcal W(F)>0$ and $\ell =\sqrt{A/W}$. Choose image points whose distance is $D$ and use one as center $y_0$. Connectedness makes the continuous distance function on the image attain every value in $[0,D]$. Hence for $j=0,\ldots ,\lfloor D/\ell \rfloor $ choose image points $y_ j$ with $|y_ j-y_0|=j\ell $. Distinct points have pairwise distance at least $\ell $, so their open radius-$\ell /2$ balls are disjoint. Each $y_ j$ has at least one preimage. Apply Proposition 10.5.3 with outer radius $\ell /2$ at that center and sum. Disjointness of the preimages of these balls gives \[  \pi \bigl (1+\lfloor D/\ell \rfloor \bigr ) \leq \frac{12A}{\ell ^2}+\frac52W=\frac{29}{2}W.  \] Since $D/\ell <1+\lfloor D/\ell \rfloor $, the upper bound follows, with a non-strict inequality as stated. This is an extrinsic diameter bound; it does not control intrinsic distances along a surface with long narrow geometry. $\square$

title: 6.12 Quadratic curvature energy under varifold convergence
search_title: Quadratic curvature energy under varifold convergence
section: 6.12 Quadratic curvature energy under varifold convergence
text: The first-variation convention is Definition 6.1.3 , based on [ Sim18 ] , Chapter 8, equations (2.3)–(2.10), pp. 239–240. A singular boundary part must not be discarded when discussing continuity of curvature energy. We formulate an extended energy through smooth ambient tests and prove its lower semicontinuity using the representation results already established in the measure chapter. Definition 6.12.1 (An extended quadratic first-variation energy) . A25C61F4660D For an $m$-varifold $V$ in an open set $U\subset \mathbb R^ N$, with weight $\mu =\| V\| $, define \[  \mathcal E_ U(V)=\sup _{X\in C_ c^1(U;\mathbb R^ N)} \left\{ \delta V(X)-\int _ U|X|^2d\mu \right\} \in [0,+\infty ].  \] The zero test makes the supremum nonnegative. This definition uses the entire first variation. In dimension two it agrees with one quarter of the squared generalized mean curvature when that curvature represents the first variation without a singular part and is globally square integrable, as proved next. Theorem 6.12.2 (Finite quadratic energy is equivalent to square-integrable mean curvature) . 03E7797CCA57 The quantity $\mathcal E_ U(V)$ is finite if and only if there is $H\in L^2(\mu ;\mathbb R^ N)$ such that \[  \delta V(X)=-\int _ UH\cdot X\, d\mu \quad \text{for every }X\in C_ c^1(U;\mathbb R^ N).  \] In that case $H$ is unique up to $\mu $-null sets and \[  \mathcal E_ U(V)=\frac14\int _ U|H|^2d\mu .  \] The first variation therefore has no singular boundary part in $U$. This is a dual formulation of the mean-curvature representation in [ Sim18 ] , pp. 239–240; the $L^2$ equivalence is proved here. Proof Suppose $E=\mathcal E_ U(V)<\infty $. For a fixed test $X$, applying the definition to $tX$ for every real $t$ gives \[  t\delta V(X)-t^2\| X\| _{L^2(\mu )}^2\leq E.  \] If $\| X\| _2=0$, this forces $\delta V(X)=0$. Otherwise optimize the quadratic polynomial in $t$ to obtain $|\delta V(X)|\leq 2\sqrt E\| X\| _2$. Thus the first variation is well defined and bounded on the $L^2$ equivalence classes of smooth compactly supported fields. These fields are dense in $L^2(\mu ;\mathbb R^ N)$. Indeed Theorem 2.3.8 approximates each component by a continuous compactly supported function. Extending such a function by zero and mollifying gives uniform smooth approximation with support in a fixed compact neighborhood inside $U$; local finiteness of $\mu $ converts uniform convergence to $L^2$ convergence. The bounded functional extends to the Hilbert space. Lemma 5.7.1 gives a unique vector field $-H$ representing it, with $\| H\| _2\leq 2\sqrt E$. Conversely, if such $H$ exists, completion of the square gives \[  \delta V(X)-\int |X|^2d\mu =\frac14\int |H|^2d\mu -\int |X+H/2|^2d\mu .  \] The right side is bounded above by the claimed energy. Smooth compactly supported approximations to $-H/2$ in $L^2$ make the last term tend to zero, proving equality. The same density proves uniqueness. The representing vector measure $-H\mu $ is locally finite by Cauchy–Schwarz and local finiteness of $\mu $, and is absolutely continuous with respect to $\mu $, so there is no additional singular first-variation measure. $\square$ Theorem 6.12.3 (Lower semicontinuity of quadratic varifold energy) . 365150F73639 If $V_ j\rightharpoonup V$ as varifolds in $U$, then \[  \mathcal E_ U(V)\leq \liminf _{j\to \infty }\mathcal E_ U(V_ j).  \] In particular, if the liminf is finite, the limit has a generalized mean curvature in $L^2(\| V\| )$ representing its entire first variation, with the corresponding squared-norm bound. This argument uses the first-variation formula of [ Sim18 ] , equation (2.3), and does not assume integrality. Proof For a fixed $X\in C_ c^1(U;\mathbb R^ N)$, both $(x,S)\mapsto \operatorname {div}_ SX(x)$ and $(x,S)\mapsto |X(x)|^2$ are continuous with compact support on the Grassmann bundle. Thus \[  \delta V_ j(X)-\int |X|^2d\| V_ j\|  \longrightarrow \delta V(X)-\int |X|^2d\| V\| .  \] Each term before the limit is bounded above by $\mathcal E_ U(V_ j)$. For every fixed test the limiting expression is therefore at most the liminf of the energies. Taking the supremum over tests proves the inequality, including an infinite liminf. If it is finite, apply Theorem 6.12.2 to identify the limit curvature and its norm. The proof does not interchange a supremum with a limit as an equality. $\square$ Proposition 6.12.4 (Comparison with the energy of a smooth immersion) . DF57C01B9F0F Let $F:M^2\to \mathbb R^ N$ be a smooth closed immersion, and let $V_ F$ be its induced varifold with parameter multiplicity. Then \[  \mathcal E_{\mathbb R^ N}(V_ F)\leq \mathcal W(F).  \] For an embedding there is equality. For every compact set $K\subset U$ and any varifold of finite quadratic energy, \[  \| \delta V\| (K)\leq 2\sqrt{\mathcal E_ U(V)}\sqrt{\| V\| (K)}.  \] Proof The smooth first variation gives $\delta V_ F(X)=-\int _ M\vec H_ F\cdot X(F)d\mu _ M$, and the weight identity gives $\int |X|^2d\| V_ F\| =\int _ M|X(F)|^2d\mu _ M$. Completing the square on the parameter surface bounds their difference by $\frac14\int _ M|\vec H_ F|^2$. Take the supremum. For an embedding, the geometric mean curvature defines a vector field on the image representing the entire first variation, so Theorem 6.12.2 gives equality. The weaker assertion for an arbitrary immersion suffices here and avoids requiring a separate identification of curvatures on coincident sheets. For the last estimate, finite energy represents the first variation by $-H\| V\| $. Its total variation on $K$ is $\int _ K|H|d\| V\| $. Cauchy–Schwarz bounds this by $\sqrt{\| V\| (K)}\| H\| _{L^2(U)}$, and the norm identity gives the claimed constant. The same argument applies to relatively compact Borel sets. $\square$ Corollary 6.12.5 (An integral compactness consequence, with its external input) . 71DC1770F6D7 Let $V_ j$ be integral two-varifolds in $U$ with locally uniformly bounded weights and $\sup _ j\mathcal E_ U(V_ j)<\infty $. Then a subsequence converges to an integral two-varifold $V$, and $\mathcal E_ U(V)\leq \liminf _ j\mathcal E_ U(V_ j)$ after taking a subsequence attaining the energy liminf. The integrality conclusion uses the externally proved Allard compactness theorem 6.2.1 ; it is not a consequence of the Hilbert-space duality alone. Proof First pass to a subsequence whose energies tend to the liminf. Proposition 6.12.4 bounds the total variation of $\delta V_ j$ uniformly on each relatively compact set from the assumed weight and energy bounds. Apply Theorem 6.2.1 , whose hypotheses are now verified, to obtain an integral varifold subsequential limit. Theorem 6.12.3 supplies the energy inequality. This proves the deduction conditional on the explicitly named external compactness theorem; it does not replace its geometric proof. $\square$ Corollary 6.12.6 (A bounded-energy sequence of closed surfaces has local compactness) . 12AB1072F745 Let $F_ j:M_ j^2\to \mathbb R^ N$ be smooth closed embedded surfaces with $\mathcal W(F_ j)\leq \Lambda $. Their induced varifolds have a subsequence converging locally to an integral two-varifold $V$ with $\mathcal E_{\mathbb R^ N}(V)\leq \Lambda $. Its weight satisfies \[  \| V\| (B_ r(y))\leq \Lambda r^2  \] for every ball, and has no atoms. The limit is allowed to be zero. Integrality again uses Theorem 6.2.1 externally. Proof Theorem 10.5.4 gives uniform mass bounds on every ball and hence on every compact set. Proposition 6.12.4 identifies the energy of each embedding with its classical Willmore energy. Corollary 6.12.5 gives the claimed limit and energy bound. Weak varifold convergence implies weak convergence of the weights, since the Grassmannian is compact. The open-set lower semicontinuity of Radon measures then yields $\| V\| (B_ r(y))\leq \liminf _ j\| V_ j\| (B_ r(y))\leq \Lambda r^2$. Let $r\downarrow 0$ to get $\| V\| (\{ y\} )=0$. No fixed area lower bound, tightness at infinity or nonvanishing limit was assumed. $\square$

text:
These calculations use the averaged energy $\mathcal W= rac14\int H^2$ in Euclidean space and $\mathcal W_1=\int (1+H^2/4)$ in the unit three-sphere, where $H$ is the trace. The circular torus and its relation to the Clifford torus appear in [ MNWill ] , p. 684; the calculations here supply their metrics, curvature and exact energies. The global positive-genus theorem remains the separate Theorem 10.1.2 . Proposition 16.18.1 (Geometry of a circular ring torus) . 737F11A69F2E For $R>r>0$, the map \[  T(	heta ,\varphi )= igl ((R+r\cos 	heta )\cos \varphi , (R+r\cos 	heta )\sin \varphi ,r\sin 	heta  igr ), \qquad (	heta ,\varphi )\in (\mathbb R/2\pi \mathbb Z)^2,  \] is an embedded torus with metric $r^2d	heta ^2+(R+r\cos 	heta )^2d\varphi ^2$ and area $4\pi ^2Rr$. With the outward normal $
u =(\cos 	heta \cos \varphi ,\cos 	heta \sin \varphi ,\sin 	heta )$, its principal curvatures are $1/r$ and $\cos 	heta /(R+r\cos 	heta )$. Proof Differentiate the parametrization. The two coordinate derivatives are orthogonal and have respective lengths $r$ and $R+r\cos 	heta >0$, so it is an immersion with the stated metric. The positive distance to the rotation axis determines $\varphi $, while that distance minus $R$ together with height determines $(r\cos 	heta ,r\sin 	heta )$ and hence $	heta $. This proves injectivity and thus embeddedness by compactness. The area density is $r(R+r\cos 	heta )$, whose double integral is $4\pi ^2Rr$. Differentiating the stated normal gives $
u _	heta =T_	heta /r$ and $
u _\varphi =\cos 	heta \, T_\varphi /(R+r\cos 	heta )$, proving the principal curvatures with $A=D
u $. $\square$ Theorem 16.18.2 (The energy minimum within the circular ring family) . Its energy tends to infinity as $R/r\downarrow 1$ or $R/r	o \infty $. text: The catenoid of Example 16.2.2 and the inversion identity of Section 10.4 give an explicit warning about compactification. The calculations use the first-variation boundary flux in [ SimW93 ] , equation (1.5), but do not assert a removable-singularity theorem. Proposition 16.19.1 (The inverted catenoid has energy eight pi) . A26F36C721D5 For $a>0$, let \[  C_ a(\theta ,v)=(a\cosh v\cos \theta ,a\cosh v\sin \theta ,av), \qquad \theta \in \mathbb R/2\pi \mathbb Z,\  v\in \mathbb R.  \] It avoids zero, and $I_0\circ C_ a$ is a smooth embedded noncompact surface of finite Willmore energy $8\pi $. For its portion with $|v|<T$, $T>0$, the energy is \[  8\pi \frac{\cosh T\sinh T+T}{\cosh ^2T+T^2}.  \] Both ends converge to the origin in the target. Proof The original catenoid is embedded and minimal, and $|C_ a|^2=a^2(\cosh ^2v+v^2)\geq a^2$, so inversion is a diffeomorphism on its image. Lemma 10.4.1 expresses the inverted energy on $|v|<T$ as $4\int |C_ a^\perp |^2/|C_ a|^4$. Apply Theorem 10.4.3 to the compact truncated catenoid with pole zero. It has no pole preimages and zero original mean curvature, so this energy is twice its boundary flux. At $v=T$, the outward conormal is $C_{a,v}/(a\cosh T)$ and the boundary arclength is $a\cosh T\, d\theta $. Therefore that circle contributes \[  \int _0^{2\pi }\frac{C_ a\cdot C_{a,v}}{|C_ a|^2}d\theta =2\pi \frac{\cosh T\sinh T+T}{\cosh ^2T+T^2}.  \] The lower boundary gives the same value, because both $v$ and the outward derivative reverse sign. D49D00FDACD8 Each end of the inverted catenoid can be filled at zero as a rotational graph that is continuously differentiable with horizontal tangent plane, but it has no $C^2$ graph extension there.
