title: 16.20 Curvature concentration and boundary energy
search_title: Curvature concentration and boundary energy
section: 16.20 Curvature concentration and boundary energy
text: These examples test the hypotheses in Section 6.12 . They distinguish the area measure, the squared-curvature measure and the singular part of first variation. The weak framework is that of [ Sim18 ] , Chapter 8, Section 2. Example 16.20.1 (A collapsing sphere loses mass and concentrates curvature energy) . BA6CFF390155 Let $S_ j=\partial B_{r_ j}(0)\subset \mathbb R^3$ with $r_ j\downarrow 0$ and multiplicity one. Then $V_{S_ j}\rightharpoonup 0$ as varifolds and $\mathcal W(S_ j)=4\pi $, but their curvature-energy measures satisfy \[  \frac14|\vec H_ j|^2\mathcal H^2\llcorner S_ j\rightharpoonup 4\pi \delta _0.  \] Thus the weak limit's zero curvature energy does not account for all the energy in the approximating sequence. Proof The sphere has area $4\pi r_ j^2$ and $|\vec H_ j|=2/r_ j$. Its varifold mass therefore tends to zero, bounding every compactly supported test integral by its supremum times that mass. The energy is $4\pi $. For a continuous compactly supported scalar test $\phi $, changing variables $x=r_ j\omega $ gives \[  \frac14\int _{S_ j}\phi (x)|\vec H_ j|^2d\mu _ j =\int _{S^2}\phi (r_ j\omega )d\mu _{S^2}\longrightarrow 4\pi \phi (0).  \] Uniform continuity or dominated convergence proves the limit. The zero varifold has zero first variation and zero extended energy. This is strict lower semicontinuity and concentration, not an equality of limit energies. $\square$ Example 16.20.2 (Energy can escape to infinity) . 01D295A558FF The unit spheres centered at $je_1$ converge locally as varifolds to zero while each has area and Willmore energy $4\pi $. Their curvature-energy measures converge vaguely to zero, rather than to a nonzero point mass. Proof Every fixed compact subset of Euclidean space misses those spheres for all sufficiently large $j$. Hence every compactly supported varifold or scalar measure test is eventually zero. Translation does not change either area or mean curvature, giving the constant totals. The loss occurs at infinity and shows why local convergence alone cannot preserve global mass or energy. $\square$ Example 16.20.3 (A disk has zero classical bending energy but infinite full first-variation energy) . 1A05A5759283 Let $V$ be the multiplicity-one varifold of a closed planar disk $D_ R\subset \mathbb R^3$, considered in all of $\mathbb R^3$. Its smooth interior mean curvature is zero, but $\mathcal E_{\mathbb R^3}(V)=+\infty $. The singular boundary first variation is essential. Proof The divergence theorem gives $\delta V(X)=\int _{\partial D_ R}X\cdot \eta \, ds$. Choose smooth compactly supported ambient fields $X_\varepsilon $ that equal the outward radial unit vector on the boundary circle and are supported, on the disk, in an annulus of width at most $\varepsilon $, with uniformly bounded magnitude. Such fields come from smooth radial cutoffs near $r=R$ and a cutoff in the normal coordinate. Then \[  \delta V(X_\varepsilon )=2\pi R,\qquad b_\varepsilon =\int |X_\varepsilon |^2d\| V\| =O(\varepsilon ).  \] The energy definition tested with $tX_\varepsilon $ gives a supremum over $t$ equal to $(2\pi R)^2/(4b_\varepsilon )$, which tends to infinity. If instead one works in an ambient open set not meeting the boundary circle, its first variation is zero there. The ambient domain is therefore part of the assertion. $\square$ Example 16.20.4 (Real multiplicity scales the energy) . 7B753EE4AB09 For the round sphere varifold $V=q|S_ R^2|$ with a constant real multiplicity $q>0$, \[  \mathcal E_{\mathbb R^3}(V)=4\pi q.  \] If $0<q<1$, this is below the smooth closed-surface bound $4\pi $. For every noninteger $q$ the varifold is rectifiable but not integral, and cannot come from a closed immersion counted with ordinary parameter multiplicity. For positive integer $q$ it is integral. Proof Multiplying both first variation and weight by $q$ does not change the representing geometric mean curvature. Its norm is $2/R$ and its weighted area is $4\pi qR^2$. Theorem 6.12.2 therefore gives $4\pi q$. Its density is the real number $q$, so it is nonintegral for $q\notin \mathbb N$. The case $0<q<1$ demonstrates why no unqualified extension of Theorem 10.4.4 to all nonzero varifolds is being asserted. $\square$

title: 15.3 From a circular torus to a min-max theorem
search_title: From a circular torus to a min-max theorem
section: 15.3 From a circular torus to a min-max theorem
text: The sources here are the authors' papers: [ LY82 ] , the opening pages of [ SimW93 ] , and the introduction of [ MNWill ] . The entries distinguish the historical questions of identifying a candidate, proving existence of an optimizer, and determining the sharp value. They do not replace the mathematical statements and proof dependencies linked below. Remark 15.3.1 (A family calculation suggested a global conjecture) . E15742E4F29E Marques–Neves date Willmore's torus conjecture to 1965 in [ MNWill ] , Section 1.1, p. 684. The circular torus with ratio $R/r=\sqrt2$ attains energy $2\pi ^2$, but a calculation over circular tori leaves all other immersions untreated. The same candidate is a stereographic image of the Clifford torus in $S^3$. Theorems 16.18.2 and 10.3.6 , and Example 16.18.5 , explain why this candidate is natural without assuming the eventual global theorem. Remark 15.3.2 (Conformal area separated the multiple-point obstruction) . 07DE29ED0FC2 In their 1982 paper [ LY82 ] , Li–Yau introduced conformal volume and proved a multiplicity bound for the bending energy of an immersed surface; see the introduction and Theorem 6, p. 286. A double point forces energy at least $8\pi $, already above the conjectured torus minimum $2\pi ^2$. Thus the unresolved low-energy problem concerned embeddings. Theorem 10.4.4 gives a direct radial proof of that obstruction, while Corollary 10.4.9 shows precisely how it combines with the later embedded theorem. The two numerical thresholds serve different purposes. Remark 15.3.3 (Existence and the exact minimum were separate achievements) . F2980A8D4351 Simon's 1993 paper [ SimW93 ] , pp. 281–283, established a smooth embedded torus minimizing Willmore energy among embedded tori in each Euclidean ambient dimension at least three. This supplied an optimizer without identifying its sharp energy in three-space. The 2014 paper of Marques–Neves [ MNWill ] , Theorem A, p. 685, determined the positive-genus bound in $S^3$ and its equality case through min-max theory. Their Corollary D, p. 687, realizes the Clifford torus through a five-parameter min-max family. The local square identities developed here illuminate Simon's estimates; neither his full existence proof nor the five-parameter min-max proof has been replaced by those local calculations.

section: 10.6 The logarithmic cost of a Euclidean catenoidal neck
text:
This section develops the explicit Euclidean calculation in [ KMN ] , Section 2.1, Proposition 2.1 and Remark 2.2, pp. 4–6 of the supplied manuscript. It explains the scale in Remark 10.1.3 . It does not construct the manifold sweepout of that paper's Theorem 2.4, and it makes no conclusion about multiplicity in an unspecified min-max class. Proposition 10.6.1 (Two rotational catenoids with the same circular boundary) . 81AF723B08AA Fix $R>0$ and $h>0$. A rotational catenoid of waist radius $a>0$, centered at height zero, meets the planes $z=\pm h$ in circles of radius $R$ exactly when \[  R=a\cosh (h/a).  \] There is a unique $t_*>0$ satisfying $t_*	anh t_*=1$. Set $q_*=t_*/\cosh t_*$. If $0<h/R<q_*$, there are exactly two such waist radii. At equality there is exactly one, and above it there is none. The smaller waist corresponds to the larger solution $t=h/a>t_*$. The same threshold parameter occurs in the free-boundary catenoid of Example 16.7.5 ; the present assertion counts rotational solutions for prescribed boundary circles. Proof The catenoid parametrization in Example 16.2.2 has radius $a\cosh v$ at height $av$, giving the equation. On putting $t=h/a$, it becomes $h/R=t/\cosh t$. The derivative of the right side is $(1-t	anh t)/\cosh t$. The function $t	anh t$ is strictly increasing from zero to infinity, since its derivative is $	anh t+t/\cosh ^2t>0$. Thus the ratio increases strictly to a unique maximum and then decreases strictly to zero; its limit at zero is also zero. The number of roots follows by the intermediate value theorem and strict monotonicity. Since $a=h/t$, the larger root has the smaller waist. This argument counts rotational solutions and does not assert uniqueness among all surfaces spanning the two circles, or prove their stability indices. $\square$ Proposition 10.6.2 (Exact excess over two disks) . 6672A8E926D4 For a truncated catenoid with waist $a$ and parameter range $|v|\leq T$, put $h=aT$ and $R=a\cosh T$. Its area $A$ and excess over the two radius-$R$ disks are \[  A=2\pi a^2(T+\sinh T\cosh T),\qquad A-2\pi R^2=2\pi a^2\left(T- rac12- rac12e^{-2T}ight).  \] In particular the excess is positive for all sufficiently large $T$, although its ratio to $h^2$ tends to zero as $T	o \infty $. Proof The induced metric is $a^2\cosh ^2v(dv^2+d	heta ^2)$. Integrating the area density over a full angular period and $[-T,T]$ gives the first formula. For the second, subtract $2\pi a^2\cosh ^2T$ and use \[  \sinh T\cosh T-\cosh ^2T=-\cosh T e^{-T} =- rac12(1+e^{-2T}).  \] Finally divide the excess by $h^2=a^2T^2$. The resulting expression is $2\pi (T-1/2-e^{-2T}/2)/T^2$, positive eventually and tending to zero. No limiting interchange with an area-minimizing problem is involved. $\square$ Theorem 10.6.3 (The sharp leading logarithmic neck cost) . AB484D5A03C6 Fix $R>0$ and let $h\downarrow 0$. Choose the smaller waist solution $a(h)$ of Proposition 10.6.1 . If $L=\log (R/h)$ and $T=h/a(h)$, then \[   rac{T}{L}\longrightarrow 1,\qquad T=L+\log L+\log 2+o(1),\qquad  rac{ igl (A(h)-2\pi R^2 igr )L}{h^2}\longrightarrow 2\pi .  \] Consequently, for every $\varepsilon >0$ and all sufficiently small $h>0$, \[  A(h)\leq 2\pi R^2+ rac{2\pi (1+\varepsilon )h^2}{\log (R/h)}.  \] This is the dimensionless version of the leading estimate in [ KMN ] , Proposition 2.1 and Remark 2.2; it concerns the explicit rotational neck. Proof The larger root $T$ tends to infinity: on the strictly decreasing branch of $t/\cosh t$, its value $h/R$ tends to zero, and no bounded sequence on that branch can have this limit. The boundary equation yields \[  L=\log \cosh T-\log T =T-\log 2+\log (1+e^{-2T})-\log T.  \] Divide by $T$ to obtain $L/T	o 1$. Rearrangement and $\log T-\log L	o 0$ then give the second expansion. By Proposition 10.6.2 , \[   rac{(A-2\pi R^2)L}{h^2} =2\pi  rac{L}{T}\left(1- rac{1+e^{-2T}}{2T}ight)\longrightarrow 2\pi .  \] The asserted bound is the definition of this limit, with $L>0$ once $h<R$. The logarithm uses a ratio of lengths, so it is invariant under a common change of length units. $\square$ Example 10.6.4 (A cylindrical connector has a larger leading cost) . 2AE5C3C55721 For $0<h<R$, remove a disk of radius $ho \in [0,R]$ from each of the planar radius-$R$ disks at heights $\pm h$, and join the inner boundary circles by a cylinder of radius $ho $. The resulting piecewise smooth comparison set has area \[  2\pi R^2+4\pi hho -2\pi ho ^2.  \] The maximum along this explicit radius family is $2\pi R^2+2\pi h^2$, attained at $ho =h$. For fixed $R$ and $h\downarrow 0$, this excess is larger by an asymptotic factor $\log (R/h)$ than the thin catenoid's excess. Proof The two annuli contribute $2\pi (R^2-ho ^2)$ and the cylinder, of height $2h$, contributes $4\pi hho $. The excess is $2\pi h^2-2\pi (ho -h)^2$, which has the stated maximum because $h$ lies in the allowed interval. The ratio assertion follows from Theorem 10.6.3 . At the joins this comparison set has corners; the displayed calculation alone neither supplies a smooth sweepout with controlled smoothing errors nor identifies a variational width. Those additional requirements belong to the deformation theorem, not this elementary area comparison. $\square$ Proposition 10.6.5 (The exact planar annulus capacity) . C9FC5ED9776D Let $0<a<R$ and $\mathcal A=\{ x\in \mathbb R^2:a<|x|<R\} $. Among smooth functions on the closed annulus with boundary values zero on the inner circle and one on the outer circle, the unique minimizer of $\int _{\mathcal A}|
abla u|^2$ is \[  u_0(x)= rac{\log (|x|/a)}{\log (R/a)},\qquad \int _{\mathcal A}|
abla u_0|^2= rac{2\pi }{\log (R/a)}.  \] For every such function $u$, the exact excess identity is \[  \int _{\mathcal A}|
abla u|^2 = rac{2\pi }{\log (R/a)}+\int _{\mathcal A}|
abla (u-u_0)|^2.  \] Proof The radial Laplacian of $\log |x|$ is zero away from zero, so $u_0$ is harmonic. Its radial derivative is $1/(|x|\log (R/a))$; polar integration gives the stated energy. Write $u=u_0+v$, where $v$ vanishes on both boundary circles. Integration by parts gives $\int 
abla u_0\cdot 
abla v=0$. Expanding the square gives the identity. Equality forces $
abla v=0$, and the boundary value then forces $v=0$. This is an exact minimization on a fixed planar annulus. Lemma 7.11.2 already uses the logarithmic profile to remove punctures; the present identity specifies the optimal constant and its equality case. $\square$ Proposition 10.6.6 (Quadratic sheet gain dominates a logarithmic error) . 4A98911260BF Let $\Sigma $ be a smooth closed embedded two-sided minimal surface in a smooth three-manifold, with chosen unit normal $
u $. Suppose $\phi >0$ is smooth and its area second variation satisfies $Q(\phi ,\phi )=-q<0$. For small $t$, set \[  \Sigma _ t=\{ \exp _ p(t\phi (p)
u (p)):p\in \Sigma \} .  \] Then \[  |\Sigma _ t|+|\Sigma _{-t}|=2|\Sigma |-qt^2+O(t^4).  \] If a collection of comparison surfaces $S_{t,s}$ additionally satisfies, uniformly in its parameter $s$, \[  |S_{t,s}|\leq |\Sigma _ t|+|\Sigma _{-t}| + rac{Ct^2}{\log (1/|t|)}  \] for some fixed $C$ and all sufficiently small $0<|t|<1$, then every surface in that collection has area at most $2|\Sigma |-(q/2)t^2$ once $t$ is small enough. The existence, topology and continuity of such a collection are additional hypotheses here, not conclusions of this estimate. Proof For small $t$, the normal exponential map is a tubular coordinate map on the compact embedded surface. The positivity of $\phi $ makes the two graphs disjoint when $t
e 0$. Their area function $A(t)$ is smooth, with $A'(0)=0$ by minimality and $A''(0)=-q$ by Theorem 7.1.3 . Taylor expansion through the cubic term gives $A(t)+A(-t)=2A(0)-qt^2+O(t^4)$, because the odd terms cancel. Choose $t$ small enough that the absolute remainder is at most $(q/4)t^2$ and $C/\log (1/|t|)\leq q/4$. Substituting into the assumed uniform comparison gives the result. This algebra explains the competition described in [ KMN ] , p. 2; proving a uniformly controlled manifold deformation requires the separate geometric construction of its Section 2.2. $\square$

text: Proposition 10.6.1 (Two rotational catenoids with the same circular boundary) . 81AF723B08AA Fix $R>0$ and $h>0$. A rotational catenoid of waist radius $a>0$, centered at height zero, meets the planes $z=\pm h$ in circles of radius $R$ exactly when \[  R=a\cosh (h/a).  \] There is a unique $t_*>0$ satisfying $t_*\tanh t_*=1$. Set $q_*=t_*/\cosh t_*$. If $0<h/R<q_*$, there are exactly two such waist radii. At equality there is exactly one, and above it there is none. The smaller waist corresponds to the larger solution $t=h/a>t_*$. The same threshold parameter occurs in the free-boundary catenoid of Example 16.7.5 ; the present assertion counts rotational solutions for prescribed boundary circles. Proof The catenoid parametrization in Example 16.2.2 has radius $a\cosh v$ at height $av$, giving the equation. On putting $t=h/a$, it becomes $h/R=t/\cosh t$. The derivative of the right side is $(1-t\tanh t)/\cosh t$. The function $t\tanh t$ is strictly increasing from zero to infinity, since its derivative is $\tanh t+t/\cosh ^2t>0$. Thus the ratio increases strictly to a unique maximum and then decreases strictly to zero; its limit at zero is also zero. The number of roots follows by the intermediate value theorem and strict monotonicity. Since $a=h/t$, the larger root has the smaller waist. This argument counts rotational solutions and does not assert uniqueness among all surfaces spanning the two circles, or prove their stability indices. $\square$

title: Proposition 10.6.2 (Exact excess over two disks)
search_title: Exact excess over two disks
section: 10.6 The logarithmic cost of a Euclidean catenoidal neck
text: Proposition 10.6.2 (Exact excess over two disks) . 6672A8E926D4 For a truncated catenoid with waist $a$ and parameter range $|v|\leq T$, put $h=aT$ and $R=a\cosh T$. Its area $A$ and excess over the two radius-$R$ disks are \[  A=2\pi a^2(T+\sinh T\cosh T),\qquad A-2\pi R^2=2\pi a^2\left(T-\frac12-\frac12e^{-2T}\right).  \] In particular the excess is positive for all sufficiently large $T$, although its ratio to $h^2$ tends to zero as $T\to \infty $. Proof The induced metric is $a^2\cosh ^2v(dv^2+d\theta ^2)$. Integrating the area density over a full angular period and $[-T,T]$ gives the first formula. For the second, subtract $2\pi a^2\cosh ^2T$ and use \[  \sinh T\cosh T-\cosh ^2T=-\cosh T e^{-T} =-\frac12(1+e^{-2T}).  \] Finally divide the excess by $h^2=a^2T^2$. The resulting expression is $2\pi (T-1/2-e^{-2T}/2)/T^2$, positive eventually and tending to zero. No limiting interchange with an area-minimizing problem is involved. $\square$

title: Theorem 10.6.3 (The sharp leading logarithmic neck cost)
search_title: The sharp leading logarithmic neck cost
section: 10.6 The logarithmic cost of a Euclidean catenoidal neck
text: Theorem 10.6.3 (The sharp leading logarithmic neck cost) . AB484D5A03C6 Fix $R>0$ and let $h\downarrow 0$. Choose the smaller waist solution $a(h)$ of Proposition 10.6.1 . If $L=\log (R/h)$ and $T=h/a(h)$, then \[  \frac{T}{L}\longrightarrow 1,\qquad T=L+\log L+\log 2+o(1),\qquad \frac{\bigl (A(h)-2\pi R^2\bigr )L}{h^2}\longrightarrow 2\pi .  \] Consequently, for every $\varepsilon >0$ and all sufficiently small $h>0$, \[  A(h)\leq 2\pi R^2+\frac{2\pi (1+\varepsilon )h^2}{\log (R/h)}.  \] This is the dimensionless version of the leading estimate in [ KMN ] , Proposition 2.1 and Remark 2.2; it concerns the explicit rotational neck. Proof The larger root $T$ tends to infinity: on the strictly decreasing branch of $t/\cosh t$, its value $h/R$ tends to zero, and no bounded sequence on that branch can have this limit. The boundary equation yields \[  L=\log \cosh T-\log T =T-\log 2+\log (1+e^{-2T})-\log T.  \] Divide by $T$ to obtain $L/T\to 1$. Rearrangement and $\log T-\log L\to 0$ then give the second expansion. By Proposition 10.6.2 , \[  \frac{(A-2\pi R^2)L}{h^2} =2\pi \frac{L}{T}\left(1-\frac{1+e^{-2T}}{2T}\right)\longrightarrow 2\pi .  \] The asserted bound is the definition of this limit, with $L>0$ once $h<R$. The logarithm uses a ratio of lengths, so it is invariant under a common change of length units. $\square$

title: Example 10.6.4 (A cylindrical connector has a larger leading cost)
search_title: A cylindrical connector has a larger leading cost
section: 10.6 The logarithmic cost of a Euclidean catenoidal neck
text: Example 10.6.4 (A cylindrical connector has a larger leading cost) . 2AE5C3C55721 For $0<h<R$, remove a disk of radius $\rho \in [0,R]$ from each of the planar radius-$R$ disks at heights $\pm h$, and join the inner boundary circles by a cylinder of radius $\rho $. The resulting piecewise smooth comparison set has area \[  2\pi R^2+4\pi h\rho -2\pi \rho ^2.  \] The maximum along this explicit radius family is $2\pi R^2+2\pi h^2$, attained at $\rho =h$. For fixed $R$ and $h\downarrow 0$, this excess is larger by an asymptotic factor $\log (R/h)$ than the thin catenoid's excess. Proof The two annuli contribute $2\pi (R^2-\rho ^2)$ and the cylinder, of height $2h$, contributes $4\pi h\rho $. The excess is $2\pi h^2-2\pi (\rho -h)^2$, which has the stated maximum because $h$ lies in the allowed interval. The ratio assertion follows from Theorem 10.6.3 . At the joins this comparison set has corners; the displayed calculation alone neither supplies a smooth sweepout with controlled smoothing errors nor identifies a variational width. Those additional requirements belong to the deformation theorem, not this elementary area comparison. $\square$

Proposition 10.6.5 (The exact planar annulus capacity) . C9FC5ED9776D Let $0<a<R$ and $\mathcal A=\{ x\in \mathbb R^2:a<|x|<R\} $. Among smooth functions on the closed annulus with boundary values zero on the inner circle and one on the outer circle, the unique minimizer of $\int _{\mathcal A}|
abla u|^2$ is \[  u_0(x)= rac{\log (|x|/a)}{\log (R/a)},\qquad \int _{\mathcal A}|
abla u_0|^2= rac{2\pi }{\log (R/a)}.  \] For every such function $u$, the exact excess identity is \[  \int _{\mathcal A}|
abla u|^2 = rac{2\pi }{\log (R/a)}+\int _{\mathcal A}|
abla (u-u_0)|^2.  \] Proof The radial Laplacian of $\log |x|$ is zero away from zero, so $u_0$ is harmonic. Its radial derivative is $1/(|x|\log (R/a))$; polar integration gives the stated energy. Write $u=u_0+v$, where $v$ vanishes on both boundary circles. Integration by parts gives $\int 
abla u_0\cdot 
abla v=0$. Expanding the square gives the identity. Equality forces $
abla v=0$, and the boundary value then forces $v=0$. This is an exact minimization on a fixed planar annulus. Lemma 7.11.2 already uses the logarithmic profile to remove punctures; the present identity specifies the optimal constant and its equality case. $\square$

text:
Proposition 10.6.6 (Quadratic sheet gain dominates a logarithmic error) . 4A98911260BF Let $\Sigma $ be a smooth closed embedded two-sided minimal surface in a smooth three-manifold, with chosen unit normal $
u $. Suppose $\phi >0$ is smooth and its area second variation satisfies $Q(\phi ,\phi )=-q<0$. For small $t$, set \[  \Sigma _ t=\{ \exp _ p(t\phi (p)
u (p)):p\in \Sigma \} .  \] Then \[  |\Sigma _ t|+|\Sigma _{-t}|=2|\Sigma |-qt^2+O(t^4).  \] If a collection of comparison surfaces $S_{t,s}$ additionally satisfies, uniformly in its parameter $s$, \[  |S_{t,s}|\leq |\Sigma _ t|+|\Sigma _{-t}| + rac{Ct^2}{\log (1/|t|)}  \] for some fixed $C$ and all sufficiently small $0<|t|<1$, then every surface in that collection has area at most $2|\Sigma |-(q/2)t^2$ once $t$ is small enough. The existence, topology and continuity of such a collection are additional hypotheses here, not conclusions of this estimate. Proof For small $t$, the normal exponential map is a tubular coordinate map on the compact embedded surface. The positivity of $\phi $ makes the two graphs disjoint when $t
e 0$. Their area function $A(t)$ is smooth, with $A'(0)=0$ by minimality and $A''(0)=-q$ by Theorem 7.1.3 . Taylor expansion through the cubic term gives $A(t)+A(-t)=2A(0)-qt^2+O(t^4)$, because the odd terms cancel. Choose $t$ small enough that the absolute remainder is at most $(q/4)t^2$ and $C/\log (1/|t|)\leq q/4$. Substituting into the assumed uniform comparison gives the result. This algebra explains the competition described in [ KMN ] , p. 2; proving a uniformly controlled manifold deformation requires the separate geometric construction of its Section 2.2. $\square$

section: 12.8 The linearized operator of a single transition
text: We use $q(t)=\tanh (t/\sqrt2)$, $\psi =q'>0$, $V(t)=W''(q(t))=2-3\operatorname {sech}^2(t/\sqrt2)$ and \[  \mathscr L=-\frac{d^2}{dt^2}+V(t),\qquad Q(f)=\int _{\mathbb R}(|f'|^2+Vf^2),\qquad \| \psi \| _2^2=c_ W=\frac{2\sqrt2}{3}.  \] The positive-gap and kernel questions are posed in [ ChAC ] , Appendix B, Problem 2, pp. 28–29. We compute the sharp constant for this particular quartic potential. The ground-state identity of Proposition 12.6.2 is already available; the new point is coercivity after removing translation. Lemma 12.8.1 (Two first-order factorizations) . AFBF4999E313 Set \[  \mathcal A=\frac d{dt}+\sqrt2\tanh (t/\sqrt2),\qquad \mathcal B=\frac d{dt}+\frac1{\sqrt2}\tanh (t/\sqrt2).  \] Their formal $L^2$ adjoints reverse the derivative sign, and on smooth functions \[  \mathscr L=\mathcal A^*\mathcal A,\qquad \mathcal A\mathcal A^*=\mathcal B^*\mathcal B+\frac32, \qquad \mathcal B\mathcal B^*=-\frac{d^2}{dt^2}+\frac12.  \] For $f\in H^1(\mathbb R)$, $Q(f)=\| \mathcal A f\| _2^2$. Its zero space is exactly $\operatorname {span}\{ \psi \} $. Proof For $D=d/dt$ and a real function $b$, $(D+b)^*(D+b)=-D^2+b^2-b'$ and $(D+b)(D+b)^*=-D^2+b^2+b'$. Insert $b=\sqrt2\tanh (t/\sqrt2)$ and then $b=\tanh (t/\sqrt2)/\sqrt2$, using $\tanh ^2+\operatorname {sech}^2=1$. Integration by parts proves the quadratic identity for compactly supported smooth functions. Boundedness of the coefficients and density extend it to $H^1$. Since $\psi '/\psi =-\sqrt2\tanh (t/\sqrt2)$, $\mathcal A\psi =0$. If $Q(f)=0$, the weak first-order equation gives $(f/\psi )'=0$ on every bounded interval, where $\psi $ is smooth and bounded away from zero. The constants agree on overlaps, so $f=c\psi $ globally. Conversely these functions lie in $H^1$ and have zero quadratic form. $\square$ Proposition 12.8.2 (The bounded kernel on the line) . CF5564CA311E Every bounded $C^2$ solution of $\mathscr Lf=0$ on $\mathbb R$ is a constant multiple of $\psi $. More generally, all solutions have the form \[  f(t)=\psi (t)\left(c_1+c_2\int _0^ t\psi (s)^{-2}ds\right).  \] The second independent solution grows exponentially as $t\to +\infty $ and is unbounded. Proof Write $f=\psi v$ and use $\mathscr L\psi =0$. The equation becomes $(\psi ^2v')'=0$, yielding the formula. Since $\psi (t)=2\sqrt2 e^{-\sqrt2t}(1+o(1))$ as $t\to +\infty $, its second solution is asymptotic to a nonzero constant times $e^{\sqrt2t}$. A bounded solution therefore has $c_2=0$. Conversely $\psi $ is bounded. This proves the one-dimensional assertion in [ ChAC ] , Problem 2(b), without assuming that a bounded solution is square integrable in advance. $\square$ Lemma 12.8.3 (An adjoint primitive for compact orthogonal data) . DF91D11FE50F If $f\in C_ c^\infty (\mathbb R)$ satisfies $\int f\psi =0$, then \[  g(t)=-\frac1{\psi (t)}\int _{-\infty }^ t f(s)\psi (s)ds  \] is smooth and compactly supported, $\mathcal A^*g=f$, and \[  Q(f)-\frac32\| f\| _2^2 =\| \mathcal B^*\mathcal B g\| _2^2+\frac32\| \mathcal B g\| _2^2.  \] Moreover $\| g\| _2^2\leq (2/3)\| f\| _2^2$. Proof The integral vanishes to the left of the support, and orthogonality makes it vanish to the right as well. Differentiate $\psi g$ to obtain $\mathcal A^*g=f$. Put $T=\mathcal A\mathcal A^*=\mathcal B^*\mathcal B+3/2$. Then $Q(f)=\| Tg\| _2^2$ and $\| f\| _2^2=\langle Tg,g\rangle $. Expand $T$ in these two expressions and integrate by parts; subtracting $3\langle Tg,g\rangle /2$ gives exactly the asserted sum. The lower bound $\langle Tg,g\rangle \geq (3/2)\| g\| _2^2$ gives the final estimate. All integrations here have compact support, so no endpoint behavior is assumed. $\square$ Theorem 12.8.4 (The exact gap away from translation) . 864856B2C443 If $f\in H^1(\mathbb R)$ and $\int f\psi =0$, then \[  Q(f)\geq \frac32\| f\| _2^2.  \] Equality holds precisely for multiples of $\zeta (t)=\operatorname {sech}(t/\sqrt2)\tanh (t/\sqrt2)$. Thus $3/2$ is the optimal gap. For arbitrary $f\in H^1$, \[  Q(f)\geq \frac32\left(\| f\| _2^2- \frac{|\int f\psi |^2}{c_ W}\right).  \] The existence of a positive gap is the assertion in [ ChAC ] , Problem 2(c); the factorization determines its exact value here. Proof First apply Lemma 12.8.3 to compact orthogonal tests. For an arbitrary orthogonal $f$, approximate in $H^1$ by compact smooth functions and subtract a coefficient tending to zero times a fixed compact smooth function having nonzero pairing with $\psi $. This produces orthogonal $f_ j\to f$ in $H^1$, proving the inequality by continuity. Let $g_ j$ be their adjoint primitives. Applied to differences, the last estimate of the lemma makes $g_ j$ Cauchy in $L^2$. Since $g_ j'=\sqrt2\tanh (t/\sqrt2)g_ j-f_ j$, the derivatives are also Cauchy in $L^2$. Thus $g_ j\to g$ in $H^1$ and $\mathcal A^*g=f$. If equality holds for $f$, the sum identity implies $\mathcal B g_ j\to 0$ in $L^2$, hence $\mathcal B g=0$. Solving this first-order equation gives $g=c\chi $, where $\chi =\operatorname {sech}(t/\sqrt2)$. Direct differentiation gives $\mathcal A^*\chi =(3/\sqrt2)\zeta $, so equality forces the stated form. Conversely $\mathcal B\chi =0$ and the factorization give $\mathscr L\zeta =(3/2)\zeta $. This function is in $H^1$ and is orthogonal to the even function $\psi $, so it realizes equality. For general $f$, subtract its $L^2$ projection onto $\psi $. The quadratic form is unchanged because $\mathcal A\psi =0$, while the squared norm loses exactly the displayed projection term. This proves the last formula. $\square$ Proposition 12.8.5 (All square-integrable eigenfunctions of the normal operator) . 0D25EFCEBA69 If a nonzero real $f\in H^2(\mathbb R)$ satisfies $\mathscr Lf=\lambda f$, then either $\lambda =0$ and $f$ is a multiple of $\psi $, or $\lambda =3/2$ and $f$ is a multiple of $\zeta $. This classifies square-integrable eigenfunctions; it is not a statement about the full continuous spectrum. Proof The quadratic identity gives $\lambda \geq 0$. At zero the kernel was identified in Lemma 12.8.1 . Suppose $\lambda >0$ and set $g=\mathcal A f$. It is nonzero, and intertwining yields $(\mathcal A\mathcal A^*)g=\lambda g$. Set $h=\mathcal B g$. The second factorization gives \[  -h''+2h=\lambda h.  \] These operations are justified in $L^2$: the eigen-equation and bounded derivatives of $V$ imply successively that all derivatives of $f$ lie in $L^2$, starting from $f\in H^2$ and differentiating $f''=(V-\lambda )f$. No nonzero solution of the displayed constant-coefficient equation belongs to $L^2(\mathbb R)$. For $\lambda <2$ its solutions are linear combinations of opposite exponentials, for $\lambda =2$ affine functions, and for $\lambda >2$ sines and cosines. Each nonzero combination fails square integrability at one or both ends. Hence $h=0$, so $g=c\chi $ and the nonzero equation for $g$ forces $\lambda =3/2$. Finally $\lambda f=\mathcal A^*g$ gives the stated eigenfunction. The converse eigen-equations have already been checked. $\square$ Theorem 12.8.6 (A normal inverse after fixing translation) . 3BF96C4734D7 For every $F\in L^2(\mathbb R)$ with $\int F\psi =0$, there is a unique $u\in H^2(\mathbb R)$ satisfying \[  \mathscr Lu=F,\qquad \int u\psi =0.  \] With $\| u\| _{H^2}^2=\| u\| _2^2+\| u'\| _2^2+\| u''\| _2^2$, one has \[  \| u\| _2\leq \frac23\| F\| _2,\qquad \| u\| _{H^2}\leq \sqrt7\| F\| _2.  \] Orthogonality of $F$ is necessary for any $H^2$ solution. This supplies an elementary normal-direction solvability statement for the linearized problem discussed in [ ChAC ] , Problems 2 and 3; it is not a uniform inverse on a curved or noncompact interface. Proof On the closed subspace $\mathcal H=\{ u\in H^1:\int u\psi =0\} $, the gap and $V\geq -1$ give \[  \| u\| _2^2\leq \frac23Q(u),\qquad \| u'\| _2^2\leq Q(u)+\| u\| _2^2\leq \frac53Q(u).  \] Thus $Q$ is an inner product with norm equivalent to the complete $H^1$ norm on this subspace. Hilbert representation, Lemma 5.7.1 , applied to $v\mapsto \int Fv$, gives a unique $u\in \mathcal H$ with $Q(u,v)=\int Fv$ for every $v\in \mathcal H$. Both sides vanish on $\psi $, so decomposing a general $H^1$ test into its orthogonal part and its multiple of $\psi $ proves the equation weakly against all tests. Since $u''=Vu-F\in L^2$, $u\in H^2$. Testing with $u$ gives $Q(u)\leq \| F\| _2\| u\| _2$ and hence the first estimate. It also gives $Q(u)\leq (2/3)\| F\| _2^2$, so $\| u'\| _2^2\leq (10/9)\| F\| _2^2$. Since $|V|\leq 2$, $\| u''\| _2\leq 2\| u\| _2+\| F\| _2\leq (7/3)\| F\| _2$. Adding the three squared estimates gives the constant seven. Uniqueness follows from the gap. Finally any $H^2$ solution paired with $\psi $ has $\int F\psi =Q(u,\psi )=0$, proving necessity. $\square$ Corollary 12.8.7 (The gap at a physical interface scale) . FCE16961822E For $\varepsilon >0$, if $f\in H^1(\mathbb R)$ and $\int f(t)\psi (t/\varepsilon )dt=0$, then \[  \int \left(\varepsilon |f'|^2+\varepsilon ^{-1}V(t/\varepsilon )f^2\right)dt \geq \frac3{2\varepsilon }\int f^2dt.  \] The operator $-\varepsilon ^2d^2/dt^2+V(t/\varepsilon )$ instead has gap $3/2$, while $-d^2/dt^2+\varepsilon ^{-2}V(t/\varepsilon )$ has gap $3/(2\varepsilon ^2)$. These are different normalizations of the same one-dimensional estimate. Proof Use $s=t/\varepsilon $ and apply Theorem 12.8.4 to $f(\varepsilon s)$. The energy on the left becomes its unscaled quadratic form, while its squared norm is $\varepsilon ^{-1}\int f^2$. Multiplying the resulting inequality by $\varepsilon $ or by $\varepsilon ^{-1}$ gives the other two normalizations. Equality is attained by the correspondingly rescaled function $\zeta $, so the constants remain sharp. $\square$

text: Theorem 12.8.6 (A normal inverse after fixing translation) . 3BF96C4734D7 For every $F\in L^2(\mathbb R)$ with $\int F\psi =0$, there is a unique $u\in H^2(\mathbb R)$ satisfying \[  \mathscr Lu=F,\qquad \int u\psi =0.  \] With $\| u\| _{H^2}^2=\| u\| _2^2+\| u'\| _2^2+\| u''\| _2^2$, one has \[  \| u\| _2\leq \frac23\| F\| _2,\qquad \| u\| _{H^2}\leq \sqrt7\| F\| _2.  \] Orthogonality of $F$ is necessary for any $H^2$ solution. This supplies an elementary normal-direction solvability statement for the linearized problem discussed in [ ChAC ] , Problems 2 and 3; it is not a uniform inverse on a curved or noncompact interface. Proof On the closed subspace $\mathcal H=\{ u\in H^1:\int u\psi =0\} $, the gap and $V\geq -1$ give \[  \| u\| _2^2\leq \frac23Q(u),\qquad \| u'\| _2^2\leq Q(u)+\| u\| _2^2\leq \frac53Q(u).  \] Thus $Q$ is an inner product with norm equivalent to the complete $H^1$ norm on this subspace. Hilbert representation, Lemma 5.7.1 , applied to $v\mapsto \int Fv$, gives a unique $u\in \mathcal H$ with $Q(u,v)=\int Fv$ for every $v\in \mathcal H$. Both sides vanish on $\psi $, so decomposing a general $H^1$ test into its orthogonal part and its multiple of $\psi $ proves the equation weakly against all tests. Since $u''=Vu-F\in L^2$, $u\in H^2$. Testing with $u$ gives $Q(u)\leq \| F\| _2\| u\| _2$ and hence the first estimate. It also gives $Q(u)\leq (2/3)\| F\| _2^2$, so $\| u'\| _2^2\leq (10/9)\| F\| _2^2$. Since $|V|\leq 2$, $\| u''\| _2\leq 2\| u\| _2+\| F\| _2\leq (7/3)\| F\| _2$. Adding the three squared estimates gives the constant seven. Uniqueness follows from the gap. Finally any $H^2$ solution paired with $\psi $ has $\int F\psi =Q(u,\psi )=0$, proving necessity. $\square$

text: Corollary 12.8.7 (The gap at a physical interface scale) . FCE16961822E For $\varepsilon >0$, if $f\in H^1(\mathbb R)$ and $\int f(t)\psi (t/\varepsilon )dt=0$, then \[  \int \left(\varepsilon |f'|^2+\varepsilon ^{-1}V(t/\varepsilon )f^2\right)dt \geq \frac3{2\varepsilon }\int f^2dt.  \] The operator $-\varepsilon ^2d^2/dt^2+V(t/\varepsilon )$ instead has gap $3/2$, while $-d^2/dt^2+\varepsilon ^{-2}V(t/\varepsilon )$ has gap $3/(2\varepsilon ^2)$. These are different normalizations of the same one-dimensional estimate. Proof Use $s=t/\varepsilon $ and apply Theorem 12.8.4 to $f(\varepsilon s)$. The energy on the left becomes its unscaled quadratic form, while its squared norm is $\varepsilon ^{-1}\int f^2$. Multiplying the resulting inequality by $\varepsilon $ or by $\varepsilon ^{-1}$ gives the other two normalizations. Equality is attained by the correspondingly rescaled function $\zeta $, so the constants remain sharp. $\square$

text: Write $x=(y,t)\in \mathbb R^ d\times \mathbb R$, $d\geq 1$, and retain $\psi =q'$, $V=W''(q)$ from Section 12.8 . We develop the bounded-kernel argument of [ ChAC ] , Appendix B, Problem 2(d)–(g), pp. 28–29. Interior elliptic derivative estimates are explicitly retained as an analytic input in the decay step. Lemma 12.9.1 (A bounded positive subsolution cannot persist on all of Euclidean space) . 0A781005EAC2 If $G\in C^2(\mathbb R^ d)$ is bounded above and $\Delta G\geq cG$ for a constant $c>0$, then $G\leq 0$ everywhere. In particular a nonnegative bounded such function is zero. Proof If $G(y_0)>0$, choose $\eta >0$ with $2d\eta <cG(y_0)$. The function $G(y)-\eta |y-y_0|^2$ tends to minus infinity at infinity and attains its maximum at some $y_\eta $. At that point $G(y_\eta )\geq G(y_0)$ and $\Delta G(y_\eta )\leq 2d\eta $. These inequalities contradict $\Delta G\geq cG$. This proof uses only a penalized maximum on the full Euclidean domain; the conclusion need not hold on a bounded domain with positive boundary data. $\square$ Lemma 12.9.2 (Uniform decay in the normal direction) . 53B06602A64D Let $w\in C^2(\mathbb R^{d+1})\cap L^\infty $ solve \[  \Delta _ yw+w_{tt}-V(t)w=0.  \] For every $0<\sigma <\sqrt2$ there is $C_\sigma $ such that \[  |w(y,t)|+|Dw(y,t)|+|D^2w(y,t)| \leq C_\sigma e^{-\sigma |t|}  \] for every $(y,t)$. The constants are uniform in the tangential variable $y$. Proof Choose $0<\delta <1$ and then $\Lambda $ so large that $V(t)>\max \{ \sigma ^2,2\delta ^2\} $ for $|t|\geq \Lambda $. On the upper half-space $t\geq \Lambda $, put \[  B_\eta (y,t)=e^{\sigma (\Lambda -t)}+ \eta \cosh (\delta t)\sum _{i=1}^ d\cosh (\delta y_ i),\qquad \eta >0.  \] The operator $P=\Delta _ y+\partial _ t^2-V(t)$ is strictly negative on each positive summand. In particular the product summands have Laplacian $2\delta ^2$ times themselves; the coefficient is not multiplied by the number of tangential dimensions. The barrier is at least one on $t=\Lambda $ and tends to infinity along every sequence escaping to infinity in the half-space. Let $M=\| w\| _\infty $. If $M=0$ there is nothing to prove. Each of $\pm w-MB_\eta $ is nonpositive on the finite boundary, negative outside a sufficiently large compact set, and has $P(\pm w-MB_\eta )>0$. A positive interior maximum would have $P(\pm w-MB_\eta )<0$ because $V>0$, a contradiction. Therefore $|w|\leq MB_\eta $. Send $\eta \downarrow 0$ at a fixed point to obtain $|w(y,t)|\leq Me^{\sigma (\Lambda -t)}$. The lower half-space is identical, and the remaining strip is handled by increasing the constant. The coefficient $V$ and all its derivatives are uniformly bounded. Interior elliptic estimates on unit balls, followed by bootstrapping, bound first and second derivatives by a constant times the supremum of $|w|$ on a slightly larger ball. These estimates are the external local elliptic input used here. The proved exponential bound on that larger ball differs by at most a fixed factor, so it gives the displayed derivative bounds uniformly in $y$. This justifies the decay step requested in [ ChAC ] , Problem 2(e). $\square$ Proposition 12.9.3 (The translation coefficient is constant) . 8FC283F8B3D2 For a bounded solution as in Lemma 12.9.2 , define \[  a(y)=\frac1{c_ W}\int _{\mathbb R}w(y,t)\psi (t)dt.  \] Then $a$ is bounded and harmonic on $\mathbb R^ d$, and hence constant. The remainder $v=w-a\psi $ solves the same linearized equation and satisfies $\int v(y,t)\psi (t)dt=0$ for every $y$. Proof The decay estimates and the exponential decay of $\psi $ justify two tangential derivatives under the integral and integrations by parts in $t$, with vanishing endpoint terms. Thus \[  c_ W\Delta _ y a=\int (Vw-w_{tt})\psi =\int w(V\psi -\psi '')=0.  \] Boundedness follows either from the decay or directly from bounded $w$ and integrable $\psi $. To recall the needed Liouville argument, the mean-value formula for a bounded harmonic function and differentiation of the moving ball give $|D a(y)|\leq C_ d\| a\| _\infty /R$ for every $R>0$. This can also be seen by writing the derivative of its ball average as a boundary integral. Let $R\to \infty $ to conclude $Da=0$. Subtracting the constant multiple of the kernel function gives both remaining assertions. The projection is defined before any conclusion about the entire kernel; no separation-of-variables assumption is used. $\square$ Theorem 12.9.4 (Bounded solutions of the flat linearized equation) . 4372C7E46BA5 Every bounded $C^2$ solution of \[  \Delta w-W''(q(x_{d+1}))w=0 \quad \text{on }\mathbb R^{d+1}  \] is $w(y,t)=a\psi (t)$ for one constant $a$. Together with Proposition 12.8.2 , this holds in every ambient dimension at least one. This is the kernel assertion in [ ChAC ] , Appendix B, Problem 2, with its normal decay and orthogonality steps made explicit. Proof Take the orthogonal remainder $v$ from Proposition 12.9.3 and define $G(y)=\int _{\mathbb R}v(y,t)^2dt$. It is nonnegative, bounded and twice continuously differentiable by Lemma 12.9.2 . Differentiation, the equation and integration by parts give the exact identity \[  \Delta _ yG=2\int |D_ yv|^2dt+ 2\int \bigl (|v_ t|^2+V(t)v^2\bigr )dt.  \] Each normal slice lies in $H^1$ and is orthogonal to $\psi $. Theorem 12.8.4 therefore implies \[  \Delta _ yG\geq 2\int |D_ yv|^2dt+3G\geq 3G.  \] Lemma 12.9.1 forces $G=0$. Continuity then gives $v=0$, proving the claim. The displayed gradient term is tangential; the inequality is derived from the exact slice energy rather than by discarding the potentially negative normal potential. $\square$ Proposition 12.9.5 (Splitting the full quadratic form into translation and normal parts) . 4A01EE1BF148 For $f\in H^1(\mathbb R^ d\times \mathbb R)$ set \[  a(y)=c_ W^{-1}\int f(y,t)\psi (t)dt,\qquad v(y,t)=f(y,t)-a(y)\psi (t).  \] Then $a\in H^1(\mathbb R^ d)$, $v\in H^1$, and \[  \int \bigl (|Df|^2+Vf^2\bigr ) =c_ W\int |D_ ya|^2+ \int _{\mathbb R^ d}\left(\int _{\mathbb R}|D_ yv|^2dt+Q(v(y,\cdot ))\right)dy.  \] In particular the rightmost term is at least $\int |D_ yv|^2+(3/2)\int v^2$. Proof Cauchy–Schwarz in the normal variable bounds $a$ and each weak tangential derivative in $L^2$. Since $\psi ,\psi '\in L^2$, the product $a\psi $ lies in $H^1$, hence so does $v$. The normal pairing with $\psi $ is zero, including after a tangential weak derivative. Therefore tangential cross terms vanish on integrating in $t$. The normal cross term is $Q(\psi ,v)=0$ by the factorization, and $Q(\psi )=0$. Expanding the quadratic form proves the identity, first for smooth approximations and then by $H^1$ continuity. Apply the sharp normal gap on almost every slice and integrate by Fubini to obtain the estimate. $\square$ Example 12.9.6 (A normal gap does not give a full-space spectral gap) . 09EF9F42AC39 For $d\geq 1$, the full quadratic form of Proposition 12.9.5 is strictly positive on every nonzero $H^1(\mathbb R^{d+1})$ function, but its Rayleigh infimum is zero. Consequently it has no nonzero $H^1$ null vector despite the bounded translation solution $\psi (t)$. Proof If the form is zero, the splitting forces $v=0$ and $D_ ya=0$. A constant in $L^2(\mathbb R^ d)$ is zero, proving strict positivity. For a nonzero $\eta \in C_ c^\infty (\mathbb R^ d)$, take $f_ R(y,t)=\eta (y/R)\psi (t)$. Its Rayleigh quotient is \[  R^{-2}\frac{\int |D\eta |^2}{\int \eta ^2}\longrightarrow 0.  \] These are $H^1$ functions; cutting off the exponentially decaying normal factor approximates them by compactly supported tests with the same limiting quotients. The bounded function $\psi (t)$ is not in $L^2(\mathbb R^{d+1})$ because the tangential factor has infinite volume. This separates bounded-kernel rigidity, normal coercivity and a positive spectral gap on the whole space. $\square$

text:
We follow the local calculations of [ ChAC ] , Appendix B, Problem 3, pp. 29–31, with explicit signs, boundedness conditions and error norms. Let $\Sigma ^2\subset \mathbb R^3$ be a smooth two-sided embedded surface, $
u $ a chosen unit normal, and $A=D
u $. Work on a relatively compact coordinate patch $K$ inside a larger patch $U$ on which \[  F(y,z)=y+z
u (y),\qquad |z|<ho ,  \] is an injective tubular parametrization, with $I+zA$ uniformly positive definite on a neighborhood of $K	imes [-ho ,ho ]$. All estimates below are uniform on this fixed tube over $K$, with constants depending on its geometry and the stated smooth functions. We write $H=\operatorname {tr}A$, $K_\Sigma =\det A$, and retain the quartic potential, profile $q$, and $\psi =q'$ from Section 12.8 . No closed nonflat minimal surface in Euclidean space is assumed. Lemma 12.10.1 (The exact metric, Jacobian and parallel curvature) . 5C6FEA2AE720 In these coordinates the Euclidean metric, volume density relative to $d\mu _\Sigma \, dz$, and parallel shape operator are \[  g_{\mathbb R^3}=dz^2+g_ z,\qquad g_ z(v,w)=g((I+zA)v,(I+zA)w),\qquad D(y,z)=\det (I+zA)=1+Hz+K_\Sigma z^2,  \] \[  A_ z=A(I+zA)^{-1},\qquad H_ z=\partial _ z\log D=\sum _{i=1}^2 rac{\kappa _ i}{1+z\kappa _ i}, \qquad \partial _ zH_ z=-|A_ z|^2.  \] Here $\kappa _1,\kappa _2$ are the principal curvatures at $y$, and $A_ z$ is identified through the parallel tangent planes. Proof Differentiate $F$ tangentially to get $dF(v)=(I+zA)v$, while $\partial _ zF=
u $ is orthogonal to every tangential derivative and has length one. This proves the metric formula. Diagonalizing $A$ gives the positive volume ratio $(1+z\kappa _1)(1+z\kappa _2)$ and its stated polynomial. The normal of each parallel surface is still $
u (y)$, so differentiation along its tangent vector $(I+zA)v$ gives $Av$. Thus its shape operator is $A(I+zA)^{-1}$. Taking its trace and differentiating each eigenvalue proves both remaining formulas. Positivity and injectivity of the chosen tube are used to avoid a focal point or a self-intersection, not inferred merely from the formulas. $\square$ Proposition 12.10.2 (The Laplacian and the special cancellation for minimal surfaces) . 022784D6AABA For every smooth function $f$ in the tube, \[  \Delta f=f_{zz}+H_ zf_ z+\Delta _{g_ z}f.  \] If $\Sigma $ is minimal and $a(y)=|A(y)|^2$, then \[  D=1- rac{a z^2}{2},\qquad H_ z=- rac{az}{1-az^2/2}=-az+O(z^3).  \] For a smooth function $h(y)$ independent of $z$, $\Delta _{g_ z}h=\Delta _\Sigma h+O(|z|)$ uniformly on the fixed patch, with the last constant controlled by its first two derivatives and the local geometry. Proof In block diagonal coordinates the divergence formula for the Laplacian separates into $D^{-1}\partial _ z(Df_ z)$ and the tangential Laplace–Beltrami operator. Lemma 12.10.1 gives the coefficient of $f_ z$. For a minimal surface the principal curvatures are $\kappa ,-\kappa $, hence $a=2\kappa ^2$ and $D=1-az^2/2$. Differentiating its logarithm gives the exact rational expression. Its difference from $-az$ is $-a^2z^3/[2(1-az^2/2)]$, uniformly of order $z^3$ on the chosen tube. Finally the coefficients of $\Delta _{g_ z}$ and their first tangential derivatives vary smoothly with $z$. Subtract their values at zero in the coordinate formula; every difference is bounded by $C|z|$. This gives the last estimate without asserting an equality between the metrics at nonzero $z$. $\square$ Proposition 12.10.3 (When the distance profile is an exact solution) . 8A22C57A90B9 Put $u_\varepsilon (F(y,z))=q(z/\varepsilon )$ and $R_\varepsilon =\varepsilon ^2\Delta u_\varepsilon -W'(u_\varepsilon )$. Then $R_\varepsilon =\varepsilon H_ z\psi (z/\varepsilon )$, which is uniformly $O(\varepsilon )$, and is uniformly $O(\varepsilon ^2)$ when $\Sigma $ is minimal. If this profile is an exact solution throughout a tube for even one $\varepsilon >0$, then $A=0$ on its base; every connected base patch is contained in a plane. If $H(y_0)
e 0$, the general $O(\varepsilon )$ estimate is sharp at $(y_0,0)$. Proof The equation $q''=W'(q)$ cancels the normal second derivative, leaving precisely the residual already identified in Proposition 12.4.4 . The boundedness of $H_ z$ gives the general estimate. In the minimal case $|H_ z|\leq C|z|$, and $|t|\psi (t)$ is bounded, giving $C\varepsilon ^2$. If the residual vanishes identically, positivity of $\psi $ forces $H_ z=0$ for every $z$ in the tube. Differentiate at zero using Lemma 12.10.1 : $0=-|A|^2$. The normal is therefore constant on each connected patch, and $y\cdot 
u $ is constant along it, proving planarity. Finally $R_\varepsilon (y_0,0)=\varepsilon H(y_0)\psi (0)$ proves sharpness when the mean curvature does not vanish. $\square$ Lemma 12.10.4 (The bounded odd normal corrector) . C4389C0124F3 There is exactly one bounded solution $j$ of \[  j''-Vj=t\psi ,\qquad j(0)=0.  \] It is odd, belongs to $H^2(\mathbb R)$, and is given by \[  j(t)=\psi (t)\int _0^ t\psi (s)^{-2} \left(\int _{-\infty }^ s	au \psi (	au )^2\, d	au ight)ds.  \] It is negative for $t>0$, orthogonal to $\psi $, and satisfies $|j|+|j'|+|j''|\leq C(1+t^2)e^{-\sqrt2|t|}$. Proof The total integral of $	au \psi (	au )^2$ is zero by oddness. Its primitive $I(s)$ from minus infinity is even and strictly negative at every finite $s$: for $s\leq 0$ this is immediate, and for $s>0$ use $I(s)=-\int _ s^\infty 	au \psi (	au )^2d	au $. Thus $\psi ^{-2}I$ is even and negative, proving the claimed parity and sign of the formula. Writing $j=\psi v$ gives \[  (\psi ^2v')'=t\psi ^2,\qquad j''-Vj=\psi v''+2\psi 'v'=t\psi ,  \] so the formula solves the correct equation with the prescribed value at zero. For $s\geq 0$, the exponential bounds on $\psi $ give $|I(s)|\leq C(1+s)e^{-2\sqrt2s}$ and $\psi (s)^{-2}|I(s)|\leq C(1+s)$. Therefore $|v(t)|\leq C(1+t^2)$ and $|v'(t)|\leq C(1+|t|)$; parity handles the other end. These bounds give the estimates for $j$ and $j'$, and the differential equation gives the bound for $j''$. They imply $j\in H^2$ and justify its orthogonality to the even function $\psi $. The difference of two bounded solutions is a multiple of $\psi $ by Proposition 12.8.2 ; its zero value at the origin forces that multiple to vanish. Both boundedness and the value at zero are needed for this uniqueness statement. The linear coefficient is $V=W''(q)$, as dictated by linearization of $W'$. $\square$ Proposition 12.10.5 (A fourth-order residual for the unshifted corrected layer) . text: Lemma 12.10.1 (The exact metric, Jacobian and parallel curvature) . 5C6FEA2AE720 In these coordinates the Euclidean metric, volume density relative to $d\mu _\Sigma \, dz$, and parallel shape operator are \[  g_{\mathbb R^3}=dz^2+g_ z,\qquad g_ z(v,w)=g((I+zA)v,(I+zA)w),\qquad D(y,z)=\det (I+zA)=1+Hz+K_\Sigma z^2,  \] \[  A_ z=A(I+zA)^{-1},\qquad H_ z=\partial _ z\log D=\sum _{i=1}^2\frac{\kappa _ i}{1+z\kappa _ i}, \qquad \partial _ zH_ z=-|A_ z|^2.  \] Here $\kappa _1,\kappa _2$ are the principal curvatures at $y$, and $A_ z$ is identified through the parallel tangent planes. Proof Differentiate $F$ tangentially to get $dF(v)=(I+zA)v$, while $\partial _ zF=\nu $ is orthogonal to every tangential derivative and has length one. This proves the metric formula. The normal of each parallel surface is still $\nu (y)$, so differentiation along its tangent vector $(I+zA)v$ gives $Av$. Thus its shape operator is $A(I+zA)^{-1}$. text: Proposition 12.10.2 (The Laplacian and the special cancellation for minimal surfaces) . 022784D6AABA For every smooth function $f$ in the tube, \[  \Delta f=f_{zz}+H_ zf_ z+\Delta _{g_ z}f.  \] If $\Sigma $ is minimal and $a(y)=|A(y)|^2$, then \[  D=1-\frac{a z^2}{2},\qquad H_ z=-\frac{az}{1-az^2/2}=-az+O(z^3).  \] For a smooth function $h(y)$ independent of $z$, $\Delta _{g_ z}h=\Delta _\Sigma h+O(|z|)$ uniformly on the fixed patch, with the last constant controlled by its first two derivatives and the local geometry. Proof In block diagonal coordinates the divergence formula for the Laplacian separates into $D^{-1}\partial _ z(Df_ z)$ and the tangential Laplace–Beltrami operator. Lemma 12.10.1 gives the coefficient of $f_ z$. For a minimal surface the principal curvatures are $\kappa ,-\kappa $, hence $a=2\kappa ^2$ and $D=1-az^2/2$. Differentiating its logarithm gives the exact rational expression. Its difference from $-az$ is $-a^2z^3/[2(1-az^2/2)]$, uniformly of order $z^3$ on the chosen tube. Subtract their values at zero in the coordinate formula; every difference is bounded by $C|z|$. This gives the last estimate without asserting an equality between the metrics at nonzero $z$. $\square$

C4389C0124F3 There is exactly one bounded solution $j$ of \[  j''-Vj=t\psi ,\qquad j(0)=0.  \] It is odd, belongs to $H^2(\mathbb R)$, and is given by \[  j(t)=\psi (t)\int _0^ t\psi (s)^{-2} \left(\int _{-\infty }^ s\tau \psi (\tau )^2\, d\tau \right)ds.  \] It is negative for $t>0$, orthogonal to $\psi $, and satisfies $|j|+|j'|+|j''|\leq C(1+t^2)e^{-\sqrt2|t|}$. Proof The total integral of $\tau \psi (\tau )^2$ is zero by oddness. Its primitive $I(s)$ from minus infinity is even and strictly negative at every finite $s$: for $s\leq 0$ this is immediate, and for $s>0$ use $I(s)=-\int _ s^\infty \tau \psi (\tau )^2d\tau $. Thus $\psi ^{-2}I$ is even and negative, proving the claimed parity and sign of the formula. Writing $j=\psi v$ gives \[  (\psi ^2v')'=t\psi ^2,\qquad j''-Vj=\psi v''+2\psi 'v'=t\psi ,  \] so the formula solves the correct equation with the prescribed value at zero. For $s\geq 0$, the exponential bounds on $\psi $ give $|I(s)|\leq C(1+s)e^{-2\sqrt2s}$ and $\psi (s)^{-2}|I(s)|\leq C(1+s)$. Therefore $|v(t)|\leq C(1+t^2)$ and $|v'(t)|\leq C(1+|t|)$; parity handles the other end. These bounds give the estimates for $j$ and $j'$, and the differential equation gives the bound for $j''$. They imply $j\in H^2$ and justify its orthogonality to the even function $\psi $. The difference of two bounded solutions is a multiple of $\psi $ by Proposition 12.8.2 ; its zero value at the origin forces that multiple to vanish. Both boundedness and the value at zero are needed for this uniqueness statement. The linear coefficient is $V=W''(q)$, as dictated by linearization of $W'$. $\square$

Here $(M^ n,g)$ is a smooth nonempty closed Riemannian manifold, $n\geq 1$, and $\varepsilon >0$ is fixed. We develop the compactness calculation suggested in [ ChAC ] , Exercise 4.4, p. 14. The residual retains the correct $\varepsilon ^2$ factor. The needed Sobolev compactness is proved in Section 7.18 ; elliptic regularity remains an analytic input identified in the proofs. The resulting compactness statement alone is not a mountain-pass existence theorem. Proposition 12.11.1 (An energy identity for every closed critical point) . 1605E7AF7DC3 A smooth solution of $\varepsilon ^2\Delta _ g u=u^3-u$ satisfies \[  \varepsilon ^2\int _ M|
abla u|^2=\int _ M(u^2-u^4),\qquad E_\varepsilon (u;M)= rac{\operatorname {Vol}(M)-\int _ Mu^4}{4\varepsilon }.  \] In particular $0\leq E_\varepsilon (u;M)\leq \operatorname {Vol}(M)/(4\varepsilon )$ and $\int _ M|
abla u|^2\leq \operatorname {Vol}(M)/(4\varepsilon ^2)$. Equality in the energy upper bound occurs precisely for $u=0$. Proof Multiply the equation by $u$ and integrate by parts on the closed manifold. This gives the first identity. Substitute its gradient term into $E_\varepsilon =\varepsilon \int |
abla u|^2/2+(4\varepsilon )^{-1}\int (1-2u^2+u^4)$; the $u^2$ terms cancel and give the second. Nonnegativity follows from the original energy definition. Proposition 12.2.3 gives $|u|\leq 1$, and $u^2-u^4\leq 1/4$, proving the gradient bound. The energy upper bound follows from $u^4\geq 0$, and equality forces $u=0$ by continuity. The identities concern critical points, not arbitrary functions with the same pointwise bound. $\square$ Theorem 12.11.2 (Strong compactness for a bounded residual sequence) . A1F06EA746A2 Let $u_ j\in H^1(M)$ satisfy $|u_ j|\leq 1$ almost everywhere and $E_\varepsilon (u_ j;M)\leq C$. Suppose that \[  r_ j=-\varepsilon ^2\Delta _ g u_ j+W'(u_ j)\longrightarrow 0 \quad 	ext{in }H^{-1}(M),  \] where $H^{-1}$ is the dual of $H^1(M)$ with its full norm. Then a subsequence converges strongly in $H^1$ and in every finite $L^ p$ to a smooth critical point $u$, with $|u|\leq 1$ and $E_\varepsilon (u_ j;M)	o E_\varepsilon (u;M)$. This develops the bounded-range compactness mechanism in [ ChAC ] , Exercise 4.4, with the residual normalized to the displayed $\varepsilon $-equation. For this same residual, convergence in $L^2$ implies the $H^{-1}$ convergence assumed here. Proof The pointwise bound controls the $L^2$ norms, and the energy controls the gradients because $\varepsilon $ is fixed. Weak $H^1$ compactness and Theorem 7.18.2 supply a subsequence with $u_ jightharpoonup u$ in $H^1$ and $u_ j	o u$ strongly in $L^2$ and almost everywhere. The limit lies in $[-1,1]$. Since $W'$ is Lipschitz on this interval, $W'(u_ j)	o W'(u)$ in $L^2$. Passing to the equation against smooth tests shows that $u$ is a weak solution, and density gives the equation against every $H^1$ test. Subtract the limit equation and test with $u_ j-u$: \[  \varepsilon ^2\int |
abla (u_ j-u)|^2 =\langle r_ j,u_ j-uangle -\int (W'(u_ j)-W'(u))(u_ j-u).  \] The dual pairing tends to zero because the tests stay bounded in $H^1$, and the second term tends to zero by strong $L^2$ convergence. Thus convergence is strong in $H^1$. Boundedness by one upgrades it to every finite $L^ p$: for $p\geq 2$ use $|u_ j-u|^ p\leq 2^{p-2}|u_ j-u|^2$, and for smaller $p$ use finite volume. The potential $W$ is Lipschitz on $[-1,1]$, so its integrals converge; strong gradient convergence then gives energy convergence. Finally a bounded weak solution of this smooth semilinear equation is smooth by interior elliptic $W^{2,p}$ estimates followed by Sobolev embedding and bootstrapping in finitely many coordinate charts. These elliptic regularity inputs are external here. There is no restriction $n\leq 4$: the assumed uniform range bound supplies the integrability of the nonlinearity even when $H^1$ alone would not embed into $L^4$. $\square$ Corollary 12.11.3 (The entire critical set is compact for fixed epsilon) . AC5DCB969E47 For a fixed $\varepsilon >0$ and fixed smooth closed $(M,g)$, every sequence of smooth Allen–Cahn critical points has a subsequence converging in $C^ k(M)$ for every finite $k$ to a smooth critical point. The constants in these compactness estimates may depend on $\varepsilon $. Proof The maximum bound and Proposition 12.11.1 supply all assumptions of Theorem 12.11.2 , with residual zero. For the stronger convergence, the equation has uniformly bounded right-hand side after division by the fixed $\varepsilon ^2$. Global estimates obtained from the finitely many local elliptic charts give uniform $W^{2,p}$ bounds for every finite $p$. Choose $p>n$ to control $C^{1,\alpha }$, and bootstrap the smooth polynomial nonlinearity to uniform bounds of all derivative orders. These are the same external elliptic estimates used in the theorem. Arzela–Ascoli and a diagonal subsequence give every $C^ k$ convergence. The limit equation follows either from this convergence or from the preceding weak argument. These estimates do not assert compactness as $\varepsilon \downarrow 0$. $\square$ Proposition 12.11.4 (Index cannot increase in a bounded-range strong limit) . 30298CFE6EFF Fix $\varepsilon >0$. If $|u_ j|,|u|\leq 1$ almost everywhere and $u_ j	o u$ in $L^2(M)$, define the index of each quadratic form \[  Q_{\varepsilon ,u}(\phi )=\int _ M  igl (\varepsilon |
abla \phi |^2+\varepsilon ^{-1}(3u^2-1)\phi ^2 igr )  \] as the supremum of dimensions of negative definite subspaces of smooth tests. Then $\operatorname {index}(Q_{\varepsilon ,u}) \leq \liminf _ j\operatorname {index}(Q_{\varepsilon ,u_ j})$. In particular a fixed upper bound for the indices of the critical points passes to the limit in Theorem 12.11.2 . Proof Take any finite-dimensional negative subspace for the limit form and a smooth basis $\phi _1,\ldots ,\phi _ m$. Since $|u_ j^2-u^2|\leq 2|u_ j-u|$, the potential terms in every matrix entry $Q_{\varepsilon ,u_ j}(\phi _ r,\phi _ s)$ converge to those of the limit form by $L^2$ convergence and boundedness of the fixed tests. The negative definite limit matrix is bounded above by $-\delta $ times the Euclidean norm squared on its coefficient vectors for some $\delta >0$, using compactness of the unit sphere in $\mathbb R^ m$. Entrywise convergence preserves negative definiteness for all large $j$. Therefore the approximating indices are eventually at least $m$. Taking all possible finite $m$ proves the claim, including the case of an infinite limit index. No convergence of eigenfunction bases is assumed. $\square$ Proposition 12.11.5 (A sharp necessary parameter range for nonconstant solutions) . 8EFAD482DAF6 Assume $M$ is connected, and let \[  \lambda _1=\inf _{\substack {v\in H^1(M),\  \int _ Mv=0\ v
e 0}}  rac{\int _ M|
abla v|^2}{\int _ Mv^2}>0.  \] If $\varepsilon ^2\lambda _1\geq 1$, every smooth Allen–Cahn critical point is a constant in $\{ -1,0,1\} $. On a circle this threshold is sharp, as the periodic examples exist for every $\varepsilon ^2\lambda _1<1$. Proof Corollary 7.18.3 gives positivity of $\lambda _1$ and the Poincare inequality. Let $ ar u$ be the average of a critical point and set $v=u- ar u$. Testing its equation with $v$ gives \[  \varepsilon ^2\int |
abla u|^2-\int v^2 +\int (u^3- ar u^3)(u- ar u)=0.  \] The first two terms together are nonnegative by $\varepsilon ^2\lambda _1\geq 1$ and Poincare. The final integrand is nonnegative because the cubic is strictly increasing, and vanishes only when $u= ar u$. It follows that $u$ is constant, including in the equality case of the threshold. The equation then forces one of the three stated values. On the circle of length $\ell $, $\lambda _1=(2\pi /\ell )^2$, from the Fourier modes. Example 16.21.6 supplies a one-oscillation solution exactly for $\varepsilon <\ell /(2\pi )$, proving sharpness on this model. No sufficiency claim for a general manifold is made. $\square$

Suppose that \[  r_ j=-\varepsilon ^2\Delta _ g u_ j+W'(u_ j)\longrightarrow 0 \quad \text{in }H^{-1}(M),  \] where $H^{-1}$ is the dual of $H^1(M)$ with its full norm. This develops the bounded-range compactness mechanism in [ ChAC ] , Exercise 4.4, with the residual normalized to the displayed $\varepsilon $-equation. For this same residual, convergence in $L^2$ implies the $H^{-1}$ convergence assumed here. Proof The pointwise bound controls the $L^2$ norms, and the energy controls the gradients because $\varepsilon $ is fixed. Weak $H^1$ compactness and Theorem 7.18.2 supply a subsequence with $u_ j\rightharpoonup u$ in $H^1$ and $u_ j\to u$ strongly in $L^2$ and almost everywhere. The limit lies in $[-1,1]$. Since $W'$ is Lipschitz on this interval, $W'(u_ j)\to W'(u)$ in $L^2$. Passing to the equation against smooth tests shows that $u$ is a weak solution, and density gives the equation against every $H^1$ test. Subtract the limit equation and test with $u_ j-u$: \[  \varepsilon ^2\int |\nabla (u_ j-u)|^2 =\langle r_ j,u_ j-u\rangle -\int (W'(u_ j)-W'(u))(u_ j-u).  \] The dual pairing tends to zero because the tests stay bounded in $H^1$, and the second term tends to zero by strong $L^2$ convergence. Thus convergence is strong in $H^1$. Boundedness by one upgrades it to every finite $L^ p$: for $p\geq 2$ use $|u_ j-u|^ p\leq 2^{p-2}|u_ j-u|^2$, and for smaller $p$ use finite volume. The potential $W$ is Lipschitz on $[-1,1]$, so its integrals converge; strong gradient convergence then gives energy convergence. Finally a bounded weak solution of this smooth semilinear equation is smooth by interior elliptic $W^{2,p}$ estimates followed by Sobolev embedding and bootstrapping in finitely many coordinate charts. These elliptic regularity inputs are external here. There is no restriction $n\leq 4$: the assumed uniform range bound supplies the integrability of the nonlinearity even when $H^1$ alone would not embed into $L^4$. $\square$

AC5DCB969E47 For a fixed $\varepsilon >0$ and fixed smooth closed $(M,g)$, every sequence of smooth Allen–Cahn critical points has a subsequence converging in $C^ k(M)$ for every finite $k$ to a smooth critical point. The constants in these compactness estimates may depend on $\varepsilon $. Proof The maximum bound and Proposition 12.11.1 supply all assumptions of Theorem 12.11.2 , with residual zero. For the stronger convergence, the equation has uniformly bounded right-hand side after division by the fixed $\varepsilon ^2$. text: Proposition 12.11.4 (Index cannot increase in a bounded-range strong limit) . 30298CFE6EFF Fix $\varepsilon >0$. If $|u_ j|,|u|\leq 1$ almost everywhere and $u_ j\to u$ in $L^2(M)$, define the index of each quadratic form \[  Q_{\varepsilon ,u}(\phi )=\int _ M \bigl (\varepsilon |\nabla \phi |^2+\varepsilon ^{-1}(3u^2-1)\phi ^2\bigr )  \] as the supremum of dimensions of negative definite subspaces of smooth tests. Then $\operatorname {index}(Q_{\varepsilon ,u}) \leq \liminf _ j\operatorname {index}(Q_{\varepsilon ,u_ j})$. In particular a fixed upper bound for the indices of the critical points passes to the limit in Theorem 12.11.2 . Proof Take any finite-dimensional negative subspace for the limit form and a smooth basis $\phi _1,\ldots ,\phi _ m$. Since $|u_ j^2-u^2|\leq 2|u_ j-u|$, the potential terms in every matrix entry $Q_{\varepsilon ,u_ j}(\phi _ r,\phi _ s)$ converge to those of the limit form by $L^2$ convergence and boundedness of the fixed tests. The negative definite limit matrix is bounded above by $-\delta $ times the Euclidean norm squared on its coefficient vectors for some $\delta >0$, using compactness of the unit sphere in $\mathbb R^ m$. Entrywise convergence preserves negative definiteness for all large $j$. Therefore the approximating indices are eventually at least $m$. Taking all possible finite $m$ proves the claim, including the case of an infinite limit index. No convergence of eigenfunction bases is assumed. $\square$

Proposition 12.11.5 (A sharp necessary parameter range for nonconstant solutions) . 8EFAD482DAF6 Assume $M$ is connected, and let \[  \lambda _1=\inf _{\substack {v\in H^1(M),\  \int _ Mv=0\ v
e 0}}  rac{\int _ M|
abla v|^2}{\int _ Mv^2}>0.  \] If $\varepsilon ^2\lambda _1\geq 1$, every smooth Allen–Cahn critical point is a constant in $\{ -1,0,1\} $. On a circle this threshold is sharp, as the periodic examples exist for every $\varepsilon ^2\lambda _1<1$. Proof Corollary 7.18.3 gives positivity of $\lambda _1$ and the Poincare inequality. Let $ ar u$ be the average of a critical point and set $v=u- ar u$. Testing its equation with $v$ gives \[  \varepsilon ^2\int |
abla u|^2-\int v^2 +\int (u^3- ar u^3)(u- ar u)=0.  \] The first two terms together are nonnegative by $\varepsilon ^2\lambda _1\geq 1$ and Poincare. The final integrand is nonnegative because the cubic is strictly increasing, and vanishes only when $u= ar u$. It follows that $u$ is constant, including in the equality case of the threshold. The equation then forces one of the three stated values. On the circle of length $\ell $, $\lambda _1=(2\pi /\ell )^2$, from the Fourier modes. Example 16.21.6 supplies a one-oscillation solution exactly for $\varepsilon <\ell /(2\pi )$, proving sharpness on this model. No sufficiency claim for a general manifold is made. $\square$

title: 16.21 Periodic phases and the long-period transition limit

section: 16.21 Periodic phases and the long-period transition limit
text: The Hamiltonian in Lemma 12.2.5 describes many solutions outside the finite-energy class. We develop the infinite-energy examples suggested in [ ChAC ] , Section 2.2 and Exercise 2.2, and unpack the periodic orbit appearing in Lemma 12.6.9 . Throughout this section $\varepsilon =1$ unless explicitly rescaled. Proposition 16.21.1 (Every bounded entire profile stays between the wells) . 828FD329FEDF If $f\in C^2(\mathbb R)$ is bounded and solves $f''=f^3-f$, then $|f|\leq 1$. If it takes the value $+1$ or $-1$, it is that constant. For its Hamiltonian $C=(f')^2/2-W(f)$ one has $-1/4\leq C\leq 0$. Proof Suppose $f(t_0)=b>1$. Reverse time if necessary so that $f'(t_0)\geq 0$. As long as $f\geq b$, its second derivative is at least $b^3-b>0$. Integration shows that it remains above $b$ with increasing derivative for every later time, contradicting boundedness. Apply the same argument to $-f$ to exclude values below $-1$. At a well, a nonzero derivative would cross outside the allowed range; with zero derivative, ODE uniqueness gives the constant solution. Since $W(f)\leq 1/4$, the Hamiltonian is at least $-1/4$. If it were positive, the identity $(f')^2=2(W(f)+C)\geq 2C$ would make $f'$ nonvanishing with constant sign and magnitude bounded below on the line. That again contradicts boundedness. This proves both endpoints of the permitted range without assuming that a global maximum is attained. $\square$ Theorem 16.21.2 (Classification of bounded entire profiles) . C7DBCCB764C2 Every bounded entire solution is a constant in $\{ -1,0,1\} $, a translated and possibly reversed heteroclinic, or a periodic profile with amplitude $a\in (0,1)$ oscillating between $-a$ and $a$. For each amplitude there is, up to translation and reversal, exactly one such periodic solution. It satisfies \[  (f')^2=\frac12(a^2-f^2)(2-a^2-f^2),\qquad C=-W(a).  \] The periodic profiles and the zero constant have infinite total energy on the line. This extends the finite-energy classification of Theorem 12.2.6 , rather than identifying these distinct classes, and supplies the bounded infinite-energy examples asked for in [ ChAC ] , Exercise 2.2. Proof Proposition 16.21.1 treats the wells. At $C=0$, separation on $(-1,1)$ gives precisely the heteroclinics already classified. At $C=-1/4$, the identity forces $f'=0$ and $W(f)=1/4$, so $f=0$. For $-1/4<C<0$, there is a unique $a\in (0,1)$ with $W(a)=-C$, since $W$ is strictly decreasing on $(0,1)$. Factoring $2(W(f)-W(a))$ gives the displayed expression. On the permitted range $(-1,1)$ this is nonnegative exactly when $|f|\leq a$. The separated time integral from $-a$ to $a$ is finite: both endpoint zeros are simple. Starting at $(f,f')=(0,\sqrt{2(W(0)-W(a))})$, the solution reaches $a$, turns because $f''=a^3-a<0$, reaches $-a$ and turns again. Reflection at the extrema and ODE uniqueness produce a smooth periodic solution. The conserved orbit contains every possible nonconstant datum at this energy, proving uniqueness up to its phase and reversal. Its energy over a period is positive, so summing disjoint periods gives infinite total energy. The constant zero has the positive constant energy density $1/4$. $\square$ Proposition 16.21.3 (The fundamental period is strictly increasing) . BF7D7DE9DC38 For amplitude $a\in (0,1)$ the least period is \[  T(a)=4\sqrt2\int _0^{\pi /2} \frac{d\theta }{\sqrt{\, 2-a^2(1+\sin ^2\theta )\, }}.  \] It is smooth and strictly increasing, with $\lim _{a\downarrow 0}T(a)=2\pi $ and $\lim _{a\uparrow 1}T(a)=+\infty $. For $a\geq 1/2$ it satisfies $T(a)\leq C(1+|\log (1-a^2)|)$. Proof One quarter-period is the time from $0$ to $a$. In its separated integral substitute $f=a\sin \theta $; the factor $a\cos \theta $ cancels and yields the formula. This orbit is strictly monotone between successive extrema, so the resulting full return is the least period. On any compact amplitude subinterval the denominator stays positive. Differentiating under the integral gives \[  T'(a)=4\sqrt2\, a\int _0^{\pi /2} \frac{1+\sin ^2\theta }{[2-a^2(1+\sin ^2\theta )]^{3/2}}\, d\theta >0.  \] Dominated convergence at zero gives $2\pi $. At one, the integrand increases to $1/\cos \theta $, whose integral diverges, proving the other limit by monotone convergence. Write the squared denominator as $2(1-a^2)+a^2\cos ^2\theta $. For $a\geq 1/2$ and $r=\pi /2-\theta $, use $\cos \theta =\sin r\geq 2r/\pi $. The integral is bounded by a constant times $\int _0^{\pi /2}((1-a^2)+r^2)^{-1/2}dr$. Its elementary antiderivative gives the logarithmic upper bound. $\square$ Example 16.21.4 (Small oscillations and a single long-period layer) . 257BC8D7226F Normalize the increasing zero of the periodic profile by $f_ a(0)=0$ and $f_ a'(0)>0$. Then \[  a^{-1}f_ a(t)\longrightarrow \sin t\quad (a\downarrow 0),\qquad f_ a(t)\longrightarrow q(t)\quad (a\uparrow 1)  \] in $C^\infty $ on every compact interval. Each long-period solution contains both an increasing and a decreasing transition; the second moves outside every fixed interval under this normalization. Proof The initial derivative is $f_ a'(0)=a\sqrt{1-a^2/2}$. Thus $v_ a=f_ a/a$ solves $v_ a''=a^2v_ a^3-v_ a$ with $v_ a(0)=0$ and $v_ a'(0)=\sqrt{1-a^2/2}$. Since $|v_ a|\leq 1$, the integral form of this ODE and Gronwall's inequality give convergence with first derivatives to the solution of $v''=-v$, $v(0)=0$, $v'(0)=1$. The equation and successive differentiations give every higher derivative. This limit is $\sin t$. At the other endpoint the initial data converge to $(0,1/\sqrt2)$ for the unchanged equation $f''=f^3-f$. The same continuous-dependence argument, using $|f_ a|\leq 1$, yields the heteroclinic $q$ on compact intervals. Its decreasing zero occurs at $T(a)/2$, which diverges by Proposition 16.21.3 . This explains why local convergence to one layer is compatible with a second transition in every full period. $\square$ Proposition 16.21.5 (Energy of one periodic cell) . 29FB8961950E Let $\mathcal E(a)=\int _0^{T(a)}((f_ a')^2/2+W(f_ a))dt$. Then \[  \mathcal E(a)=4\int _0^ a\sqrt{2(W(s)-W(a))}\, ds+W(a)T(a), \qquad \mathcal E'(a)=W(a)T'(a)>0.  \] Its endpoint limits are $\pi /2$ at $a=0$ and $2c_ W$ at $a=1$. Proof The Hamiltonian says that the energy density is $(f_ a')^2+W(a)$. Substitution of the profile value on each quarter-period therefore gives the first formula. Write the first term as $J(a)$. The integrand vanishes at its upper endpoint, and its parameter derivative has only an integrable inverse-square-root singularity there. Differentiation, justified either by the substitution $s=a\sin \theta $ or by truncation followed by that bound, yields \[  J'(a)=-4W'(a)\int _0^ a\frac{ds}{\sqrt{2(W(s)-W(a))}} =-W'(a)T(a).  \] The derivative of $J+WT$ is consequently $WT'$, proving strict increase. At zero $J\to 0$, $W(a)\to 1/4$, and $T\to 2\pi $. At one the integrand of $J$, extended by zero from $[0,a]$ to $[0,1]$, is bounded by $\sqrt{2W(s)}$ and converges to it. Hence $J\to 4\int _0^1\sqrt{2W}=2c_ W$. Finally $W(a)=(1-a^2)^2/4$ times the logarithmic period bound tends to zero. This proves the second limit without confusing a full period with one transition. $\square$ Example 16.21.6 (All nonconstant phases on a circle) . 9C4D3AAD2ECB On a circle of length $\ell $, the equation $\varepsilon ^2u''=u^3-u$ has a nonconstant solution with exactly $m$ full oscillations precisely when \[  m\in \mathbb N,\qquad 2\pi m\varepsilon <\ell .  \] Its amplitude is the unique $a\in (0,1)$ solving $T(a)=\ell /(m\varepsilon )$, and it is unique up to translation and reversal. At equality no nonconstant solution of that oscillation number exists. Proof Lift a solution periodically to the line and rescale its independent variable by $\varepsilon $. The bounded classification excludes heteroclinics and leaves exactly the periodic profiles. Their least period in the physical coordinate is $\varepsilon T(a)$, so fitting $m$ complete periods is equivalent to the displayed equation. Proposition 16.21.3 maps $(0,1)$ strictly increasingly onto $(2\pi ,\infty )$, proving existence and uniqueness exactly under the strict inequality. At the endpoint the amplitude would be zero, giving the constant zero rather than a new periodic profile. $\square$ Example 16.21.7 (An explicit negative eigenfunction in every periodic cell) . 6F88FAC155AE For a periodic profile of amplitude $a$, set \[  d_ a=\sqrt{1+3(1-a^2)^2},\qquad b_ a=\frac{2+d_ a}{3},\qquad v_ a(t)=b_ a-f_ a(t)^2.  \] Then $v_ a>0$ is periodic and \[  \left(-\frac{d^2}{dt^2}+3f_ a^2-1\right)v_ a =\lambda _ a v_ a,\qquad \lambda _ a=1-d_ a<0.  \] On a circle comprising one or any integer number of periods, $\lambda _ a$ is the least Rayleigh quotient, attained only by multiples of $v_ a$. Moreover $\lambda _ a=-\tfrac 32(1-a^2)^2+O((1-a^2)^4)$ as $a\uparrow 1$. Proof Put $B=a^2(2-a^2)$. The Hamiltonian gives $(f_ a')^2=f_ a^4/2-f_ a^2+B/2$, whence $(f_ a^2)''=3f_ a^4-4f_ a^2+B$. Consequently, for a constant $b$, \[  \left(-D^2+3f_ a^2-1\right)(f_ a^2-b) =(3-3b)f_ a^2+b-B.  \] It is an eigenfunction with eigenvalue $3-3b$ precisely when $3b^2-4b+B=0$. The larger root is $b_ a$, giving $\lambda _ a=1-d_ a$. Since $a<1$, $d_ a>1$ and $b_ a>1>a^2$, so $v_ a$ is strictly positive. For any periodic $H^1$ test $\phi $, expansion and integration by parts around the circle give \[  Q_ f(\phi )-\lambda _ a\int \phi ^2 =\int v_ a^2\left|(\phi /v_ a)'\right|^2.  \] There is no endpoint term because the functions and coefficients are periodic. This proves the least-quotient assertion and its equality characterization without a spectral completeness theorem. Taylor expansion of $\sqrt{1+3(1-a^2)^2}$ gives the final estimate. The negative direction becomes small in a long cell, but it remains negative at every finite amplitude. $\square$ Proposition 16.21.8 (Periodic profiles have infinite index on the line) . 49D79826FC5E Every nonconstant periodic entire profile has infinite Morse index for compactly supported variations. Its extension $u(y,t)=f_ a(t)$ to every $\mathbb R^{d+1}$, $d\geq 1$, also has infinite index. Here infinite index means that the quadratic form is negative definite on compactly supported test subspaces of arbitrarily large finite dimension. Proof Example 16.21.7 supplies a positive bounded periodic eigenfunction $v_ a$ with negative eigenvalue $\lambda _ a$. For a nonzero compact smooth cutoff $\chi $, the same integration by parts on the line gives \[  Q_ f(v_ a\chi (t/R)) =\lambda _ a\int v_ a^2\chi (t/R)^2+ R^{-2}\int v_ a^2\chi '(t/R)^2<0  \] for large $R$: the first term is bounded above by a negative constant times $R$, while the second is $O(R^{-1})$. Thus there is a compactly supported smooth negative test $\phi $. This also gives a concrete alternative to the endpoint-pairing proof of instability in Lemma 12.6.9 . Translate $\phi $ by sufficiently separated integer multiples of $T(a)$. The potential is periodic, each form value is the same negative number, and disjoint supports eliminate all cross terms. Their span has negative definite form, with arbitrarily large dimension. In higher dimension test with $\phi (t)\eta (y/R)$ for a fixed nonzero compact smooth $\eta $. Dividing by $\int \eta (y/R)^2$ leaves $Q_ f(\phi )+R^{-2}C_\eta \int \phi ^2$, which is negative for large $R$. Separate copies by integer periods in $t$ to obtain the same arbitrarily large negative subspaces. This strengthens the instability conclusion without needing a full Floquet-spectrum calculation. $\square$

Proposition 16.21.3 maps $(0,1)$ strictly increasingly onto $(2\pi ,\infty )$, proving existence and uniqueness exactly under the strict inequality. At the endpoint the amplitude would be zero, giving the constant zero rather than a new periodic profile. $\square$
