text: Example 16.21.7 (An explicit negative eigenfunction in every periodic cell) . 6F88FAC155AE For a periodic profile of amplitude $a$, set \[  d_ a=\sqrt{1+3(1-a^2)^2},\qquad b_ a=\frac{2+d_ a}{3},\qquad v_ a(t)=b_ a-f_ a(t)^2.  \] Then $v_ a>0$ is periodic and \[  \left(-\frac{d^2}{dt^2}+3f_ a^2-1\right)v_ a =\lambda _ a v_ a,\qquad \lambda _ a=1-d_ a<0.  \] On a circle comprising one or any integer number of periods, $\lambda _ a$ is the least Rayleigh quotient, attained only by multiples of $v_ a$. Moreover $\lambda _ a=-\tfrac 32(1-a^2)^2+O((1-a^2)^4)$ as $a\uparrow 1$. Proof Put $B=a^2(2-a^2)$. The Hamiltonian gives $(f_ a')^2=f_ a^4/2-f_ a^2+B/2$, whence $(f_ a^2)''=3f_ a^4-4f_ a^2+B$. Consequently, for a constant $b$, \[  \left(-D^2+3f_ a^2-1\right)(f_ a^2-b) =(3-3b)f_ a^2+b-B.  \] It is an eigenfunction with eigenvalue $3-3b$ precisely when $3b^2-4b+B=0$. The larger root is $b_ a$, giving $\lambda _ a=1-d_ a$. Since $a<1$, $d_ a>1$ and $b_ a>1>a^2$, so $v_ a$ is strictly positive. For any periodic $H^1$ test $\phi $, expansion and integration by parts around the circle give \[  Q_ f(\phi )-\lambda _ a\int \phi ^2 =\int v_ a^2\left|(\phi /v_ a)'\right|^2.  \] There is no endpoint term because the functions and coefficients are periodic. This proves the least-quotient assertion and its equality characterization without a spectral completeness theorem. Taylor expansion of $\sqrt{1+3(1-a^2)^2}$ gives the final estimate. The negative direction becomes small in a long cell, but it remains negative at every finite amplitude. $\square$

title: Proposition 16.21.8 (Periodic profiles have infinite index on the line)
search_title: Periodic profiles have infinite index on the line
section: 16.21 Periodic phases and the long-period transition limit
text: Proposition 16.21.8 (Periodic profiles have infinite index on the line) . 49D79826FC5E Every nonconstant periodic entire profile has infinite Morse index for compactly supported variations. Its extension $u(y,t)=f_ a(t)$ to every $\mathbb R^{d+1}$, $d\geq 1$, also has infinite index. Here infinite index means that the quadratic form is negative definite on compactly supported test subspaces of arbitrarily large finite dimension. Proof Example 16.21.7 supplies a positive bounded periodic eigenfunction $v_ a$ with negative eigenvalue $\lambda _ a$. For a nonzero compact smooth cutoff $\chi $, the same integration by parts on the line gives \[  Q_ f(v_ a\chi (t/R)) =\lambda _ a\int v_ a^2\chi (t/R)^2+ R^{-2}\int v_ a^2\chi '(t/R)^2<0  \] for large $R$: the first term is bounded above by a negative constant times $R$, while the second is $O(R^{-1})$. Thus there is a compactly supported smooth negative test $\phi $. This also gives a concrete alternative to the endpoint-pairing proof of instability in Lemma 12.6.9 . Translate $\phi $ by sufficiently separated integer multiples of $T(a)$. The potential is periodic, each form value is the same negative number, and disjoint supports eliminate all cross terms. Their span has negative definite form, with arbitrarily large dimension. In higher dimension test with $\phi (t)\eta (y/R)$ for a fixed nonzero compact smooth $\eta $. Dividing by $\int \eta (y/R)^2$ leaves $Q_ f(\phi )+R^{-2}C_\eta \int \phi ^2$, which is negative for large $R$. Separate copies by integer periods in $t$ to obtain the same arbitrarily large negative subspaces. This strengthens the instability conclusion without needing a full Floquet-spectrum calculation. $\square$

title: 16.22 Exact phase-layer energies and geometric limits
search_title: Exact phase-layer energies and geometric limits
section: 16.22 Exact phase-layer energies and geometric limits
text: These examples refine the smooth-interface recovery calculation from [ ChAC ] , Section 3.1, and the periodic ODE examples from Section 16.21 . They distinguish a particular competitor's energy from the existence or minimality of a critical point. The potential, $q$, $\psi $ and $c_ W$ retain their normalization from Definition 12.1.1 . Example 16.22.1 (Vertical graph layers retain an area excess) . CB8ACA2FE3D2 Let $\Omega \subset \mathbb R^ d$ be bounded and open, and $h\in C^2(\Omega )\cap W^{1,\infty }(\Omega )$. On $\Omega \times \mathbb R$ put $u_\varepsilon (y,z)=q((z-h(y))/\varepsilon )$. On this unbounded cylinder, energy and discrepancy mean the integrals of the local densities; the function is locally Sobolev but need not be globally in $L^2$. Then, for every $\varepsilon >0$, \[  E_\varepsilon (u_\varepsilon ;\Omega \times \mathbb R) =c_ W\int _\Omega \left(1+\frac{|Dh|^2}{2}\right)dy, \qquad \xi _\varepsilon ^{u_\varepsilon }(\Omega \times \mathbb R) =\frac{c_ W}{2}\int _\Omega |Dh|^2dy.  \] The excess over $c_ W$ times the graph area is exactly \[  \frac{c_ W}{2}\int _\Omega \left(\sqrt{1+|Dh|^2}-1\right)^2dy.  \] In particular this unnormalized vertical profile is generally not a recovery sequence for the graph perimeter. Proof Write $t=(z-h(y))/\varepsilon $. Then $|Du_\varepsilon |^2=\varepsilon ^{-2}\psi (t)^2(1+|Dh|^2)$ and $W(q(t))=\psi (t)^2/2$. The energy density is therefore $\varepsilon ^{-1}\psi (t)^2(1+|Dh|^2/2)$ and the discrepancy density is $\varepsilon ^{-1}\psi (t)^2|Dh|^2/2$. Integrate in $z$, using $dz=\varepsilon \, dt$ and $\int \psi ^2=c_ W$, to obtain both identities. The graph area is $\int _\Omega \sqrt{1+|Dh|^2}$ by the area formula. The elementary identity $1+s/2-\sqrt{1+s}=(\sqrt{1+s}-1)^2/2$ proves the excess formula. It vanishes precisely when $Dh=0$ almost everywhere; the error does not disappear merely by taking a thinner transition layer. $\square$ Example 16.22.2 (The residual detects the same normalization error) . F91CC32ACDDD For the preceding layer, \[  \varepsilon ^2\Delta u_\varepsilon -W'(u_\varepsilon ) =q''(t)|Dh|^2-\varepsilon \psi (t)\Delta h.  \] If this is identically zero for all $(y,z)$, then $Dh=0$, so $h$ is constant on every connected component. When $h(y)=b\cdot y+c$, the correctly normalized tilted-plane solution is instead \[  \widetilde u_\varepsilon (y,z) =q\left(\frac{z-b\cdot y-c}{\varepsilon \sqrt{1+|b|^2}}\right).  \] Its energy per base area is $c_ W\sqrt{1+|b|^2}$ and its discrepancy vanishes. Proof Twice differentiating the composition gives $\varepsilon ^2\Delta u=q''(t)(1+|Dh|^2)-\varepsilon \psi (t)\Delta h$. Subtract $W'(q)=q''$ to obtain the residual. Divide by $\psi >0$ at a fixed $y$: the factor $q''(t)/\psi (t)=-\sqrt2\tanh (t/\sqrt2)$ varies with $z$, whereas $Dh$ and $\Delta h$ do not. The identity for all $z$ forces $|Dh|^2=0$. For an affine graph the normalized argument is signed Euclidean distance divided by $\varepsilon $, so the planar-interface calculation of Proposition 12.4.1 applies. Direct integration in $z$ gives the stated energy factor $\sqrt{1+|b|^2}$. The unit norm of the distance gradient gives equipartition pointwise. $\square$ Proposition 16.22.3 (The second-order energy of a distance layer in three-space) . DEB92BC85E40 Let $\Sigma \subset \mathbb R^3$ be a smooth compact embedded two-sided surface without boundary, and choose an injective symmetric tube $F(y,z)=y+z\nu (y)$, $|z|<\rho $, as in Lemma 12.10.1 . For $u_\varepsilon (F(y,z))=q(z/\varepsilon )$ define \[  m_2=\int _{\mathbb R}t^2\psi (t)^2dt\in (0,\infty ).  \] The energy on this tube satisfies \[  E_\varepsilon (u_\varepsilon ;\operatorname {Tube}_\rho (\Sigma )) =c_ W\operatorname {Area}(\Sigma ) +\varepsilon ^2m_2\int _\Sigma K_\Sigma \, d\mu +O(e^{-2\sqrt2\rho /\varepsilon }).  \] There is no linear term in $\varepsilon $. Proof The normal coordinate has unit gradient. Hence the energy density times the volume ratio is $\varepsilon ^{-1}\psi (z/\varepsilon )^2(1+Hz+K_\Sigma z^2)$. Change variables $z=\varepsilon t$. On the symmetric interval the term $t\psi (t)^2$ is odd, so its integral is exactly zero. The remaining terms give the exact finite-interval formula \[  \operatorname {Area}(\Sigma )\int _{-\rho /\varepsilon }^{\rho /\varepsilon }\psi ^2dt +\varepsilon ^2\left(\int _\Sigma K_\Sigma \, d\mu \right) \int _{-\rho /\varepsilon }^{\rho /\varepsilon }t^2\psi ^2dt.  \] The exponential decay $\psi ^2\leq Ce^{-2\sqrt2|t|}$ makes $m_2$ positive and finite. The omitted zeroth moment is $O(e^{-2\sqrt2\rho /\varepsilon })$. The second-moment tail, multiplied by $\varepsilon ^2$, is bounded by $C(\rho ^2+\varepsilon \rho +\varepsilon ^2)e^{-2\sqrt2\rho /\varepsilon }$ and has the same stated order for fixed $\rho $. This proves the formula. It is an expansion for the specified layer on the tube; extending the function to an ambient domain requires a separate tail estimate such as the one in Theorem 12.4.3 . $\square$ Example 16.22.4 (Spherical and toroidal corrections) . C3A0BCB3BC29 For a round sphere of radius $R$, the second-order term in Proposition 16.22.3 is $4\pi m_2\varepsilon ^2$, independent of $R$. For every circular ring torus it is zero. This correction is governed by total Gauss curvature, whereas the Willmore energy of the same ring tori is positive and varies with the radius ratio. Proof On the sphere, $K_\Sigma =R^{-2}$ and its area is $4\pi R^2$, so $\int K_\Sigma =4\pi $. For a ring torus the already computed identity in Example 16.18.3 gives $\int K_\Sigma =0$. Insert these values in the tube formula. The ring-torus energy in Theorem 16.18.2 is $\pi ^2R^2/(r\sqrt{R^2-r^2})$. Thus no identification of the tube correction with the Willmore energy is justified by this example; the two curvature integrals are different. $\square$ Example 16.22.5 (An exact periodic solution converges to two interfaces) . E2F3056BDF26 Fix a circle of length $\ell $. For $0<\varepsilon <\ell /(2\pi )$ choose $a_\varepsilon $ by $T(a_\varepsilon )=\ell /\varepsilon $ and set $u_\varepsilon (x)=f_{a_\varepsilon }(x/\varepsilon )$, normalized by the increasing zero at $x=0$. These are exact critical points, and \[  u_\varepsilon \longrightarrow \begin{cases}  +1,& 0<x<\ell /2,\\  -1,& \ell /2<x<\ell \end{cases} \quad \text{in every finite }L^ p(S^1_\ell ).  \] Their energy measures converge weakly to $c_ W(\delta _0+\delta _{\ell /2})$, and their total energy tends to $2c_ W$. Proof The period equation implies $a_\varepsilon \to 1$. For any fixed $b\in (0,1)$, the time for $f_ a$ to rise from zero to $b$ converges, as $a\to 1$, to $\int _0^ b(2W(s))^{-1/2}ds<\infty $. On the positive half-period the profile stays above $b$ except within this uniformly bounded time of either zero, by reflection about its maximum. Multiplication by $\varepsilon $ shows that $u_\varepsilon \to 1$ uniformly on compact subintervals of $(0,\ell /2)$. The symmetry $f_ a(t+T(a)/2)=-f_ a(t)$ handles the negative half. Boundedness by one then gives every finite $L^ p$ convergence. Change variables $x=\varepsilon t$ in the energy: the total is exactly $\mathcal E(a_\varepsilon )\to 2c_ W$ by Proposition 16.21.5 . Around either zero, for every fixed $L$ the rescaled profiles converge smoothly to a heteroclinic on $[-L,L]$. Their energy on the physical interval of radius $\varepsilon L$ therefore tends to $\int _{-L}^ L\psi ^2$. Sending $L\to \infty $ shows that every fixed neighborhood of either zero carries limiting energy at least $c_ W$. Since the total limit is exactly their sum, energy outside any disjoint pair of such neighborhoods tends to zero. For a continuous test function, replace it on each small neighborhood by its value at the center and use uniform continuity. The resulting error tends to zero as the neighborhoods shrink, proving the stated weak convergence. This limit has two perimeter points of multiplicity one, even though each approximating critical point is unstable. $\square$

section: 7.18 Sobolev compactness on closed manifolds
text:
The mollification argument used for BV compactness in Theorem 4.2.7 also gives the $L^2$ compactness needed for fixed-parameter elliptic problems. The translation-and-smoothing method parallels [ Sim18 ] , Chapter 2, Theorem 2.6; the phase-field application is the compactness step in [ ChAC ] , Exercise 4.4. We give the $H^1$ version explicitly. Lemma 7.18.1 (The quadratic translation estimate) . 14BA3E3305C8 For $f\in H^1(\mathbb R^ n)$ and $h\in \mathbb R^ n$, \[  \| f(\, \cdot +h)-f\| _{L^2}\leq |h|\, \| Df\| _{L^2}.  \] If $ho _\delta $ is a nonnegative smooth mollifier of integral one supported in $B_\delta $, then $\| ho _\delta *f-f\| _2\leq \delta \| Df\| _2$. Proof For smooth $f$, the fundamental theorem of calculus gives $f(x+h)-f(x)=\int _0^1 Df(x+sh)\cdot h\, ds$. Square, apply Cauchy–Schwarz in $s$, and integrate in $x$; translation invariance of Lebesgue measure gives the first estimate. For $H^1$ functions apply the calculation to their smooth mollifications and pass to the limit in $L^2$ for the functions and their weak derivatives. Approximation by mollifiers follows from translation continuity in $L^2$; it does not require any compactness theorem. Finally average the first estimate against $ho _\delta (h)$ and use the triangle inequality for the $L^2$ integral to obtain the second. $\square$ Theorem 7.18.2 (Strong L2 compactness on a closed manifold) . F7C78AA7EF28 On a smooth closed Riemannian manifold $(M^ n,g)$, every bounded sequence in $H^1(M)$ has a strongly $L^2(M)$ convergent subsequence. The same is true for an $H^1(\mathbb R^ n)$ bounded sequence whose members are supported in one fixed compact set. This is the compact embedding used in the fixed-parameter problem of [ ChAC ] , Exercise 4.4. Proof First take the Euclidean sequence with common compact support $K$. For fixed $\delta >0$, its convolutions have support in $K+\overline B_\delta $ and uniform bounds on values and first derivatives: \[  \| ho _\delta *f_ j\| _\infty \leq \| ho _\delta \| _2\| f_ j\| _2, \qquad \| Dho _\delta *f_ j\| _\infty \leq \| Dho _\delta \| _2\| f_ j\| _2.  \] Arzela–Ascoli makes this family precompact uniformly on the common compact set, hence in $L^2$. Lemma 7.18.1 bounds the $L^2$ distance from each original function to its convolution by $C\delta $. For each tolerance choose $\delta $ small and then a finite net for the convolutions. The same net, with the uniformly small smoothing error added, is a finite net for the original sequence. Total boundedness and completeness of $L^2$ yield a convergent subsequence. On $M$, choose finitely many coordinate charts and a smooth partition of unity with each cutoff supported compactly in its chart. The coordinate representations of the cutoff functions times $f_ j$, extended by zero, have a common compact support and uniform Euclidean $H^1$ bounds. This follows from the product rule and bounded comparability of the coordinate metric and volume density on the compact supports; zero extension creates no boundary jump there. Apply the Euclidean result in each chart and take a subsequence common to this finite collection. Since the cutoffs sum to one and their volume densities are uniformly comparable, the resulting sequence is Cauchy in $L^2(M)$. This proves the compactness statement without imposing a bound on the values of $f_ j$. $\square$ Corollary 7.18.3 (A positive Poincare constant on a connected closed manifold) . 92C2144D9701 If $M$ is additionally nonempty, connected and positive-dimensional, then \[  \lambda _1=\inf _{\substack {v\in H^1(M),\  \int _ Mv=0\ v
e 0}}  rac{\int _ M|
abla v|^2}{\int _ Mv^2}>0.  \] Consequently $\lambda _1\int _ M|f- ar f|^2\leq \int _ M|
abla f|^2$ for every $f\in H^1(M)$, where $ ar f$ is its average. Proof If the infimum were zero, choose mean-zero $v_ j$ of $L^2$ norm one with $\| 
abla v_ j\| _2	o 0$. Theorem 7.18.2 supplies a strongly $L^2$ convergent subsequence. Distributional testing in each chart shows that the limit has zero weak gradient. Lemma 6.5.1 makes it constant locally, and connectedness propagates that constant over the manifold. Its mean is zero, so it is zero, contradicting the limiting $L^2$ norm one. The inequality is then the Rayleigh definition applied to $f- ar f$. On a disconnected manifold, separate constants on different components show why a single global mean-zero condition would not suffice. $\square$

For fixed $\delta >0$, its convolutions have support in $K+\overline B_\delta $ and uniform bounds on values and first derivatives: \[  \| \rho _\delta *f_ j\| _\infty \leq \| \rho _\delta \| _2\| f_ j\| _2, \qquad \| D\rho _\delta *f_ j\| _\infty \leq \| D\rho _\delta \| _2\| f_ j\| _2.  \] Arzela–Ascoli makes this family precompact uniformly on the common compact set, hence in $L^2$. Lemma 7.18.1 bounds the $L^2$ distance from each original function to its convolution by $C\delta $. For each tolerance choose $\delta $ small and then a finite net for the convolutions. The same net, with the uniformly small smoothing error added, is a finite net for the original sequence. Total boundedness and completeness of $L^2$ yield a convergent subsequence. On $M$, choose finitely many coordinate charts and a smooth partition of unity with each cutoff supported compactly in its chart. The coordinate representations of the cutoff functions times $f_ j$, extended by zero, have a common compact support and uniform Euclidean $H^1$ bounds. This follows from the product rule and bounded comparability of the coordinate metric and volume density on the compact supports; zero extension creates no boundary jump there. Apply the Euclidean result in each chart and take a subsequence common to this finite collection. Since the cutoffs sum to one and their volume densities are uniformly comparable, the resulting sequence is Cauchy in $L^2(M)$. This proves the compactness statement without imposing a bound on the values of $f_ j$. $\square$

With upward normal and $A=D
u $, the signed principal curvature of the curve is $-u_{xx}/(1+u_ x^2)^{3/2}=-\cos x$. Multiplication by $v$ makes it $-1$. In dimension one this is a constant multiple of the identity tensor, hence parallel. For its product with a flat factor, the product connection preserves the curve and flat tangent factors, and $vA$ is minus the projection onto the curve factor, again parallel. The displayed identities follow. The slope tends to infinity at both strip edges, so the finite starting supremum used in the smoothing proof is unavailable. This example checks the exact square without extending a compact maximum principle to an unbounded domain. $\square$

The graphical equation then gives $u_ t=0$. The uniform slope bound is used for all past times, not merely separately on each time slice. $\square$

text: Example 14.19.6 (Why the grim reaper does not violate ancient rigidity) . A7AD2D7C46AE For the grim-reaper graph $u(x,t)=-\log \cos x+t$ on $(-\pi /2,\pi /2)$, and for its products with Euclidean factors, \[  v=\sec x,\qquad |A|=\cos x,\qquad v^2|A|^2=1.  \] The tensor $vA$ is parallel along each time slice. Thus it realizes the zero right-hand side of Proposition 14.19.1 , even though its curvature is not zero. Its unbounded slope and its strip domain exclude both the periodic smoothing conclusion with finite $V_ s$ and Corollary 14.19.5 . Proof The derivatives are $u_ x=\tan x$ and $u_{xx}=\sec ^2x$. With upward normal and $A=D\nu $, the signed principal curvature of the curve is $-u_{xx}/(1+u_ x^2)^{3/2}=-\cos x$. Multiplication by $v$ makes it $-1$. In dimension one this is a constant multiple of the identity tensor, hence parallel. For its product with a flat factor, the product connection preserves the curve and flat tangent factors, and $vA$ is minus the projection onto the curve factor, again parallel. The displayed identities follow. The slope tends to infinity at both strip edges, so the finite starting supremum used in the smoothing proof is unavailable. This example checks the exact square without extending a compact maximum principle to an unbounded domain. $\square$

text:
The curvature estimate from [ EH89 ] , Proposition 4.4, gives a useful compact-domain consequence. Throughout this section, the flow is assumed smooth for every $t\geq 0$ on a fixed flat torus $\mathbb T^ n$. We prove its convergence, including quantitative area decay. These conclusions do not replace a proof of global existence. Lemma 14.20.1 (Converting graph curvature to Euclidean Hessian bounds) . DC18B9C427CF For a smooth graph with $v=\sqrt{1+|Du|^2}$, its metric and scalar second fundamental form satisfy \[  g_{ij}=\delta _{ij}+u_ i u_ j,\qquad h_{ij}=-v^{-1}u_{ij},\qquad v^{-6}|D^2u|^2\leq |A|^2\leq v^{-2}|D^2u|^2.  \] The Hessian norm on the outer terms is Euclidean. In particular $|D^2u|\leq v^3|A|$. Proof The metric follows by differentiating the graph map. Differentiating $\langle 
u ,F_ jangle =0$ gives $h_{ij}=-\langle 
u ,F_{ij}angle =-u_{ij}/v$. In a Euclidean orthonormal basis diagonalizing $g^{-1}$, its eigenvalues lie between $v^{-2}$ and one. The squared tensor norm is $v^{-2}\sum _{i,j}\gamma _ i\gamma _ j u_{ij}^2$, where $\gamma _ i$ are these eigenvalues. Bound each product between $v^{-4}$ and one to obtain both inequalities. This proves the comparison without treating the coordinate Hessian as an intrinsic curvature tensor. $\square$ Lemma 14.20.2 (Periodicity controls slope and oscillation by the Hessian) . DC81EF33765D Let $d$ be the diameter of the flat torus. For $u\in C^2(\mathbb T^ n)$, \[  \| Du\| _\infty \leq d\| D^2u\| _\infty ,\qquad \max u-\min u\leq d\| Du\| _\infty \leq d^2\| D^2u\| _\infty .  \] Here the global parallel frame identifies tangent vectors at different points. Proof Every component of $Du$ has zero integral on the torus, by periodic integration by parts against a constant parallel vector. For points $x,y$, integrate the derivative of this vector-valued gradient along a shortest torus geodesic to get $|Du(x)-Du(y)|\leq d\| D^2u\| _\infty $. Average in $y$ and use the zero vector average to obtain the first estimate. Integrate $Du$ along a shortest geodesic between a maximum and a minimum for the second. A constant nonzero gradient on the Euclidean lift would not be periodic, which is precisely the obstruction removed by the averaging step. $\square$ Proposition 14.20.3 (Height intervals are nested) . 120F6F89BEF2 For a smooth periodic graphical flow, $\max _ xu(x,t)$ is nonincreasing and $\min _ xu(x,t)$ is nondecreasing. Hence its height remains in the initial interval at every smooth time. Proof At a spatial maximum, the graph equation has $Du=0$ and gives $u_ t=\Delta u\leq 0$. For a fully time-dependent argument, apply the first-interior-maximum test to $u-\max u(\cdot ,s)-\eta (t-s)$ on a compact time slab, using the positive definite graph coefficient matrix, and send $\eta \downarrow 0$. Apply the same reasoning to $-u$. Starting at any time $s$ proves nesting, not only a bound by the initial interval. This is the compact analogue of the height estimates in [ EH89 ] , Section 2. $\square$ Theorem 14.20.4 (Conditional convergence to one horizontal slice) . 033EF6B85768 Let a periodic graphical mean curvature flow be smooth for all $t\geq 0$, and put $V_0=\max \sqrt{1+|Du(\cdot ,0)|^2}$. There is a constant $c_\infty $ between its initial minimum and maximum such that \[  \| u(\cdot ,t)-c_\infty \| _\infty + \| Du(\cdot ,t)\| _\infty +\| D^2u(\cdot ,t)\| _\infty \leq C t^{-1/2}\quad (t>0).  \] The constant depends only on $V_0$ and the flat torus. This is a consequence of the slope-based curvature estimate of [ EH89 ] , Proposition 4.4, with periodicity used to control the height oscillation. Proof Proposition 14.18.4 bounds $v$ by $V_0$. Theorem 14.19.4 and Lemma 14.20.1 give \[  \| D^2u(\cdot ,t)\| _\infty \leq V_0^3\sqrt{ rac{V_0^2-1}{2t}}.  \] Lemma 14.20.2 gives the same rate for the gradient and oscillation. The nested closed height intervals in Proposition 14.20.3 are nonempty, bounded, and have length tending to zero. Their intersection is therefore one number $c_\infty $. At each time the distance of any height to this number is at most that interval's length. Combining these estimates proves the assertion. If $V_0=1$, the solution is already a constant and the estimates have zero right-hand side. The proof needs no conservation of the ordinary spatial average. $\square$ Proposition 14.20.5 (Graphical flow is an area gradient flow with variable mobility) . 87BC139616A5 For a smooth periodic function define its graph area $\mathcal A(u)=\int _{\mathbb T^ n}\sqrt{1+|Du|^2}\, dx$. Its first variation and the graphical flow equation are \[  D\mathcal A(u)[\phi ]=\int H\phi \, dx, \qquad u_ t=-vH.  \] Thus the flow is the negative gradient for the positive inner product $\langle \phi ,\eta angle _ u=\int \phi \eta /v\, dx$. Along it, \[   rac d{dt}\mathcal A(u(t))=-\int H^2v\, dx =-\int u_ t^2/v\, dx.  \] Proof Differentiate under the area integral and integrate by parts on the torus: $D\mathcal A(u)[\phi ]=\int Du\cdot D\phi /v=-\int \operatorname {div}(Du/v)\phi =\int H\phi $. The gradient with respect to the stated inner product is $vH$. Its negative is exactly the graphical equation. Substitution of $u_ t=-vH$ in the first variation proves the dissipation identity; it agrees with Proposition 14.1.2 because $d\mu =v\, dx$. The variable factor $v$ explains why an ordinary unweighted spatial mean is not automatically conserved. $\square$ Lemma 14.20.6 (An area-excess dissipation inequality) . 3D1A546B94E7 Let $u$ be any smooth function on the flat torus with $1\leq v\leq V$, and set \[  \mathcal F(u)=\mathcal A(u)-\operatorname {Vol}(\mathbb T^ n),\qquad \lambda _1=\inf _{\substack {f\in H^1,\  \int f=0\ f
e 0}}  rac{\int |Df|^2}{\int f^2}>0.  \] Then \[   rac1{V+1}\int |Du|^2\leq \mathcal F(u)\leq  rac12\int |Du|^2, \qquad \int H^2v\, dx\geq  rac{2\lambda _1}{V^2}\mathcal F(u).  \] Proof Use $v-1=|Du|^2/(v+1)$ to obtain the two-sided area comparison. If $Du=0$, the final estimate is immediate. Otherwise integration by parts gives \[  \int H(u- ar u)\, dx=\int  rac{|Du|^2}{v}\, dx \geq V^{-1}\int |Du|^2.  \] Cauchy–Schwarz and Corollary 7.18.3 bound its square above by $\lambda _1^{-1}\int H^2\int |Du|^2$. Cancel the positive gradient integral to get $\int H^2\geq \lambda _1V^{-2}\int |Du|^2$. Since $v\geq 1$ and $\int |Du|^2\geq 2\mathcal F$, this proves the dissipation bound. No critical-point assumption was made for this inequality. $\square$ Theorem 14.20.7 (Exponential decay of periodic graph area and gradient energy) . DFA20B22D3F3 Under Theorem 14.20.4 , put $\gamma =2\lambda _1/V_0^2$. Then \[  \mathcal F(u(t))\leq \mathcal F(u(0))e^{-\gamma t},\qquad \int |Du(\cdot ,t)|^2\leq (V_0+1)\mathcal F(u(0))e^{-\gamma t}.  \] The curvature estimate of [ EH89 ] supplies the slope-controlled setting; the quantitative energy decay follows here from the graph variation and the torus Poincare inequality. Proof The slope bound permits $V=V_0$ in Lemma 14.20.6 at every time. Proposition 14.20.5 gives $\mathcal F'(t)\leq -\gamma \mathcal F(t)$. Multiplication by $e^{\gamma t}$ and integration prove the first inequality. The lower area comparison from the lemma yields the second. Both inequalities hold on every existing smooth time interval; the all-time hypothesis is needed only when taking a large-time limit. $\square$ Lemma 14.20.8 (A Lipschitz-to-uniform interpolation estimate on the torus) . 0DA0D08FCC08 There is a constant $C$ depending only on the flat torus such that every vector-valued Lipschitz function $f$ with Lipschitz constant at most $L\geq 0$ satisfies \[  \| f\| _\infty \leq C\left(\| f\| _2+ L^{n/(n+2)}\| f\| _2^{2/(n+2)}ight).  \] The Euclidean norm is used in the target; $C$ does not depend on its dimension. Proof Choose a fixed $r_0>0$ smaller than the injectivity radius, so every ball of radius $r\leq r_0$ has volume $\omega _ nr^ n$. Let $M=\max |f|$, attained at $x_0$. If $M=0$ there is nothing to prove. If $L=0$, the function is constant and the first term suffices. Otherwise set $r=\min \{ r_0,M/(2L)\} $. The triangle inequality and the Lipschitz bound give $|f|\geq M/2$ on $B_ r(x_0)$. Hence $\| f\| _2^2\geq (\omega _ n/4)M^2r^ n$. If $r=r_0$, this bounds $M$ by a fixed multiple of $\| f\| _2$. In the other case it gives $M^{n+2}\leq C L^ n\| f\| _2^2$. Taking the appropriate root in each case proves the claim. Only the norm triangle inequality was used in the target, so the dimension of that target does not enter the constant. $\square$ Corollary 14.20.9 (Exponential convergence of height and slope) . A9521FCD1263 In the setting of Theorem 14.20.4 , with the same $c_\infty $ and $\gamma $, there is $C$ depending on the initial slope, area excess and torus such that \[  \| u(\cdot ,t)-c_\infty \| _\infty +\| Du(\cdot ,t)\| _\infty \leq C e^{-\gamma t/(n+2)}\qquad (t\geq 1).  \] The argument here gives exponential convergence in $C^1$ and the preceding polynomial bound in $C^2$; it does not assert uniform estimates of all derivatives without further parabolic input. Proof The Hessian estimate in the proof of Theorem 14.20.4 gives one uniform bound $L$ for the Lipschitz constant of $Du$ for $t\geq 1$. Theorem 14.20.7 gives $\| Du\| _2\leq C e^{-\gamma t/2}$. Apply Lemma 14.20.8 to this vector-valued gradient. Its two terms decay at rates $\gamma /2$ and $\gamma /(n+2)$, respectively, so the slower rate bounds their sum. The height interval contains $c_\infty $, and its length is at most $d\| Du\| _\infty $ by Lemma 14.20.2 . This gives the height estimate. When the initial area excess is zero, the solution is a constant and the conclusion is immediate. $\square$ Corollary 14.20.10 (The total curvature dissipation equals the initial area excess) . D29C250B9C03 For an all-time smooth periodic graphical flow, \[  \int _0^\infty \int _{M_ t}H^2\, d\mu _ t\, dt =\mathcal A(u(0))-\operatorname {Vol}(\mathbb T^ n).  \] More generally, the remaining dissipation after a time $s$ is exactly $\mathcal F(u(s))$ and is bounded by $\mathcal F(u(0))e^{-\gamma s}$. Proof Integrate Proposition 14.20.5 from $s$ to a finite $T$. The right-hand side is $\mathcal A(u(s))-\mathcal A(u(T))$. Theorem 14.20.7 implies that the latter area tends to the base torus volume as $T	o \infty $. Monotone convergence for the nonnegative time integrand gives the exact identity. The exponential bound is the same theorem evaluated at $s$. This is a finite total dissipation statement, not a pointwise estimate for $H$ at every late time. $\square$

section: 14.21 Maximum principles and entire graphical flows
text:
The periodic estimates avoid spatial infinity. We now give an explicit maximum principle sufficient for entire graphs with controlled growth, then identify the additional existence input from [ EH89 ] , Theorem 4.6. Smoothness on a noncompact time slice alone is not a global bound. Lemma 14.21.1 (Normal material heat equals the graph nondivergence operator) . DBBE715C49A2 For an entire graphical mean curvature flow, let \[  a^{ij}=\delta _{ij}- rac{u_ i u_ j}{1+|Du|^2}.  \] For any geometric scalar $f$ written in graph coordinates, \[  (\partial _ t^\perp -\Delta _ M)f =\partial _ t^{m graph}f-a^{ij}\partial _ i\partial _ j f.  \] The cancellation uses the graph equation and does not assert equality of the two time derivatives separately. Proof The graph metric has Christoffel symbols $\Gamma ^ k_{ij}=u_{ij}u_ k/v^2$, as follows by projecting $F_{ij}=u_{ij}e$ onto the tangent frame. Thus $\Delta _ M f=a^{ij}f_{ij}-a^{ij}u_{ij}u_ kf_ k/v^2$. The graph equation gives $a^{ij}u_{ij}=u_ t$. Meanwhile the tangential velocity in Lemma 14.18.3 has coordinate components $T^ k=u_ tu_ k/v^2$, since the projection of $e$ has components $u_ k/v^2$. Subtract the Laplacian from $\partial _ t^\perp f=\partial _ t^{m graph}f-T^ kf_ k$. The two first-order terms cancel. All statements are local, so the same calculation holds on a torus as well. $\square$ Lemma 14.21.2 (A maximum principle with an explicit polynomial growth condition) . 2C31DF28D132 On $\mathbb R^ n	imes [s,T]$, let $a(x,t)$ be symmetric with $0\leq a\leq A_0 I$, and let $|b(x,t)|\leq B_0$. Suppose $f$ is continuous up to $t=s$, twice differentiable in space and once in time for $t>s$, and satisfies \[  f_ t-a^{ij}f_{ij}-b^ if_ i\leq 0,\qquad f(x,s)\leq M, \qquad f(x,t)\leq C_0(1+|x|^2)^ m  \] for some finite $A_0,B_0,C_0,m\geq 0$, uniformly on the slab. Then $f\leq M$ throughout. Strict uniform ellipticity is not needed for this upper bound. Proof Choose $q>\max \{ m,1\} $ and put $\psi =(1+|x|^2)^ q$. Direct differentiation gives $|D\psi |\leq q\psi $ and $|D^2\psi |\leq 4q^2\psi $ in operator norm. For $K=1+4nA_0q^2+B_0q$, the function $B(x,t)=e^{K(t-s)}\psi (x)$ satisfies $B_ t-a^{ij}B_{ij}-b^ iB_ i\geq B>0$. For each $\eta >0$, the function $f-M-\eta B$ is negative initially and tends to minus infinity at spatial infinity uniformly in time, because $q>m$. If it were positive somewhere, it would have a positive maximum on a compact space-time cylinder, at a time later than $s$. section: 16.23 Mean values and model checks for graphical flow
text:
These examples test the conclusions of Sections 14.19 and 14.20 . They use the graphical equation studied in [ EH89 ] , Section 3, but the periodic mean-value computations below are direct calculations. Example 16.23.1 (Curve graphs preserve their ordinary spatial average) . 16419E95AD1A Let $u(x,t)$ be a smooth periodic curve graph with spatial period $\ell $. Then \[  u_ t= rac{u_{xx}}{1+u_ x^2}=\partial _ x\arctan u_ x, \qquad  rac d{dt}\int _0^\ell u(x,t)\, dx=0.  \] If the solution is smooth for all positive time, its limiting height is exactly $\ell ^{-1}\int _0^\ell u(x,0)dx$. Proof In dimension one Proposition 14.3.13 has the displayed coefficient. Differentiating $\arctan u_ x$ gives the divergence expression. Integration over the period has no endpoint term because $u_ x$ is periodic. If the flow is all-time smooth, Theorem 14.20.4 gives uniform convergence to a constant, so its conserved integral identifies that constant. This conservation law comes from the one-dimensional equation; it is not a consequence merely of the area being translation invariant in height. $\square$ Example 16.23.2 (A two-dimensional graph changes its spatial average) . A90A63365A59 On the square torus with side length $2\pi $, set \[  f(x,y)=\cos x+\cos y+\alpha \cos (x+y),\qquad u(x,y,0)=\delta f(x,y),  \] where $\alpha 
e 0$ is fixed. For any smooth graphical solution with this initial value, its normalized average $ ar u(t)$ satisfies \[   ar u'(0)=- rac\alpha 2\delta ^3+O(\delta ^5) \quad 	ext{as }\delta 	o 0.  \] Thus it is nonzero for sufficiently small nonzero $\delta $. The construction also gives examples in every dimension at least two by making the height independent of the extra variables. Proof All averages in this proof are normalized by $(2\pi )^{-2}$. At the initial time the equation gives \[   ar u'(0)=-\delta ^3\operatorname {avg}  rac{f_ i f_ j f_{ij}}{1+\delta ^2|Df|^2},  \] with summation over $i,j\in \{ 1,2\} $, since the average of $\Delta f$ is zero. The bounded trigonometric derivatives justify replacing the denominator by one with an $O(\delta ^2)$ error inside this average. Periodic integration by parts gives $\operatorname {avg}(f_ i f_ j f_{ij})=-	frac 12\operatorname {avg}(|Df|^2\Delta f)$. Writing $s=x+y$, one has \[  |Df|^2=\sin ^2x+\sin ^2y+2\alpha ^2\sin ^2s +2\alpha \sin s(\sin x+\sin y), \quad \Delta f=-\cos x-\cos y-2\alpha \cos s.  \] Every product has zero average except $-2\alpha \sin s\sin x\cos y$ and $-2\alpha \sin s\sin y\cos x$. Each has average $-\alpha /2$, using $\sin (x+y)=\sin x\cos y+\cos x\sin y$ and the averages of squared sines and cosines. Therefore $\operatorname {avg}(|Df|^2\Delta f)=-\alpha $ and the contracted Hessian average is $\alpha /2$. This gives the formula and its nonvanishing conclusion. In higher dimensions the zero extra derivatives leave the same normalized calculation. This computes the prescribed initial velocity of any smooth solution; existence itself is a separate parabolic input. $\square$ Example 16.23.3 (A single Fourier mode is not an exact nonlinear flow) . F41C1B96CB07 On a circle of length $2\pi $, the ansatz $u(x,t)=a(t)\cos x$ satisfies graphical mean curvature flow on a time interval only if $a$ vanishes identically. The linear heat ansatz $a(t)=a_0e^{-t}$ is an approximation at small amplitude, with exact residual \[  u_ t- rac{u_{xx}}{1+u_ x^2} =- rac{a(t)^3\cos x\sin ^2x}{1+a(t)^2\sin ^2x}.  \] Its uniform residual is at most $|a(t)|^3$. Proof For the general ansatz the equation reads $a'\cos x=-a\cos x/(1+a^2\sin ^2x)$. At $x=0$ it requires $a'=-a$. At any point where $\cos x
e 0$ and $\sin x
e 0$, the same equation, together with $a'=-a$, forces $a=0$. Thus at every time in the interval the amplitude vanishes. For $a'=-a$ without requiring an exact solution, subtraction gives the stated residual. Its bound follows from $|\cos x|,|\sin x|\leq 1$ and the denominator being at least one. Exponential linear decay therefore does not furnish an exact nonlinear solution by itself. $\square$

text:
An entire graphical self-shrinker is more rigid than a general entire minimal graph. We develop the argument of [ Wang09 ] , Theorem 1.1 and Lemmas 2.1–2.3, in the normalization $H=\langle X,
u angle /2$. For an upward graph this equation is \[  \left(\delta _{ij}- rac{u_ i u_ j}{1+|Du|^2}ight)u_{ij} = rac{x\cdot Du-u}{2}.  \] The weighted argument, the height estimate and the area estimate are separate steps. The area estimate below uses a cylinder divergence calculation, so it does not require the intersection with a sphere to have a prescribed topology. Expanding the square shows \[  |
abla \phi |^2-w^2|
abla z|^2 =z^2|

If $\langle 
u ,eangle >0$ everywhere for some constant vector $e$, then its image is a hyperplane through the origin. This extends the cutoff step of [ Wang09 ] , Lemma 2.1, to the stated immersed setting. Proof Use intrinsic distance cutoffs $\eta _ R$, equal to one on the radius-$R$ intrinsic ball about a fixed point, supported in the radius-$2R$ ball and with $|
abla \eta _ R|\leq 2/R$. Completeness makes their supports compact by Hopf–Rinow. u angle |/2\leq \sqrt{R^2+M_ R^2}/2$, where $M_ R=\max _{B_ R^ n}|u|\leq C_1R$. Insert $M=C_1R$ and $K=\sqrt{1+C_1^2}\, R/2$ in Proposition 14.22.5 . E47F718ACB71 If $u:\mathbb R^ n	o \mathbb R$, $n\geq 1$, is smooth and its graph satisfies $H=\langle X,
u angle /2$, then $u(x)=p\cdot x$ for a constant vector $p\in \mathbb R^ n$. No height, slope, curvature or volume-growth bound is assumed. It is complete: a Cauchy sequence for its induced metric projects to a Euclidean Cauchy sequence because the metric dominates the base metric. The base limit is finite; smoothness of $u$ makes the induced and base metrics uniformly comparable on a small neighborhood there, so the original sequence converges on the graph. Because it is an entire graph, this plane is the graph of a linear function. Alternatively $A=0$ gives $D^2u=0$, so $u=p\cdot x+b$, and the graph shrinker equation gives $b=0$. FFAD885D1136 The graph \[  u(x)=\sqrt{2n-|x|^2},\qquad |x|<\sqrt{2n},  \] is the upper hemisphere of the round self-shrinker. Its $n$ principal curvatures equal $1/\sqrt{2n}$, so their squared sum is $1/2$. Its area and Gaussian weight are finite. A meridian reaches the omitted equator in finite intrinsic length, proving incompleteness. In particular one cannot insert intrinsic exhaustion cutoffs with compact support and gradient tending uniformly to zero as in the complete proof. $\square$

text:
The round-sphere spectrum enters both constrained CMC stability and Gaussian stability. Here the harmonic-polynomial decomposition is proved algebraically before passing to the Sobolev energy. The reference is [ ABR01 ] , second edition, author PDF dated July 17, 2020, Chapter 5, especially Proposition 5.5, Theorem 5.7, Proposition 5.8 and Theorem 5.12. Our sphere has dimension $n$, so the ambient dimension in that source is $n+1$. Uniform polynomial approximation on a compact sphere (Stone–Weierstrass), density of continuous functions in $L^2$ for its finite Radon measure, and completeness of $H^1$ remain background inputs. Definition 7.19.1 (Homogeneous and harmonic polynomial spaces) . EEE6F4DCD817 For $n\geq 1$ and $k\geq 0$, let $\mathcal P_ k$ be the real homogeneous polynomials of degree $k$ on $\mathbb R^{n+1}$, and let $\mathcal H_ k=\ker (\Delta :\mathcal P_ k	o \mathcal P_{k-2})$. Set $\mathcal P_ j=\{ 0\} $ for $j<0$. The spherical harmonic space $\mathcal Y_ k$ consists of restrictions of elements of $\mathcal H_ k$ to the unit sphere $S^ n$. Restriction is injective by homogeneity. On polynomial coefficients define the positive inner product \[  (p,q)_ F=\sum _\alpha \alpha !p_\alpha q_\alpha , \qquad p(x)=\sum _\alpha p_\alpha x^\alpha .  \] This coefficient inner product is not the surface $L^2$ inner product; it is an algebraic tool for the next decomposition. Lemma 7.19.2 (Algebraic harmonic decomposition and dimensions) . 1C67A786BB08 For $k\geq 0$ one has \[  \mathcal P_ k=\mathcal H_ k\mathbin {\oplus }|x|^2\mathcal P_{k-2}, \qquad \dim \mathcal Y_ k= inom {n+k}{k}- inom {n+k-2}{k-2},  \] where the second binomial term is zero for $k<2$. Iteration gives the unique expression $p=\sum _{j=0}^{\lfloor k/2floor }|x|^{2j}h_{k-2j}$ with $h_{k-2j}\in \mathcal H_{k-2j}$. Compare [ ABR01 ] , Proposition 5.5, Theorem 5.7 and Proposition 5.8, pp. 76–78. Proof For monomials, multiplication by $x_ i$ is adjoint to $\partial _ i$ in the coefficient inner products: the factorial at index $\alpha +e_ i$ is $(\alpha _ i+1)\alpha !$. Thus multiplication by $|x|^2$ is adjoint to $\Delta $ between the indicated homogeneous spaces. Its range is therefore the orthogonal complement of $\ker \Delta =\mathcal H_ k$ inside the finite-dimensional space $\mathcal P_ k$. This proves the direct sum. Multiplication by $|x|^2$ is injective since the polynomial ring has no zero divisors, and $\dim \mathcal P_ k= inom {n+k}{k}$ by counting monomials. Subtraction gives the dimension formula. Repeatedly apply the unique direct-sum decomposition to the polynomial of degree $k-2$; the iteration stops at degree zero or one. This argument does not require a prior solution of a Dirichlet problem. $\square$ Proposition 7.19.3 (Eigenvalues and orthogonality of harmonic restrictions) . E224C5AACDBB Every $Y\in \mathcal Y_ k$ satisfies $-\Delta _{S^ n}Y=\lambda _ kY$, where $\lambda _ k=k(k+n-1)$. Spaces with distinct degrees are orthogonal both in $L^2(S^ n)$ and in the Dirichlet energy pairing. Proof In polar coordinates the Euclidean metric is $dr^2+r^2g_{S^ n}$ and its volume element is $r^ n\, dr\, d\sigma $. The divergence formula gives \[  \Delta _{\mathbb R^{n+1}}=\partial _ r^2+ rac nr\partial _ r+ rac1{r^2}\Delta _{S^ n}.  \] For a homogeneous polynomial $p(r	heta )=r^ kY(	heta )$ this yields $\Delta p=r^{k-2}(k(k+n-1)Y+\Delta _{S^ n}Y)$. Harmonicity gives the equation. Integration by parts on the closed sphere then gives $(\lambda _ k-\lambda _ j)\int Y_ kY_ j=0$ and $\int \langle 
abla Y_ k,
abla Y_ jangle =\lambda _ j\int Y_ kY_ j$. Since $\lambda _{k+1}-\lambda _ k=2k+n>0$, both pairings vanish when $j
e k$. This is the eigenfunction version of the orthogonality in [ ABR01 ] , Proposition 5.9, pp. 79–80. $\square$ Theorem 7.19.4 (Complete spherical harmonic expansion in L2) . text: Definition 7.19.1 (Homogeneous and harmonic polynomial spaces) . EEE6F4DCD817 For $n\geq 1$ and $k\geq 0$, let $\mathcal P_ k$ be the real homogeneous polynomials of degree $k$ on $\mathbb R^{n+1}$, and let $\mathcal H_ k=\ker (\Delta :\mathcal P_ k\to \mathcal P_{k-2})$. Set $\mathcal P_ j=\{ 0\} $ for $j<0$. The spherical harmonic space $\mathcal Y_ k$ consists of restrictions of elements of $\mathcal H_ k$ to the unit sphere $S^ n$. Restriction is injective by homogeneity. On polynomial coefficients define the positive inner product \[  (p,q)_ F=\sum _\alpha \alpha !p_\alpha q_\alpha , \qquad p(x)=\sum _\alpha p_\alpha x^\alpha .  \] This coefficient inner product is not the surface $L^2$ inner product; it is an algebraic tool for the next decomposition.

section: 7.19 Spherical harmonics and higher spectral gaps
text: Lemma 7.19.2 (Algebraic harmonic decomposition and dimensions) . 1C67A786BB08 For $k\geq 0$ one has \[  \mathcal P_ k=\mathcal H_ k\mathbin {\oplus }|x|^2\mathcal P_{k-2}, \qquad \dim \mathcal Y_ k=\binom {n+k}{k}-\binom {n+k-2}{k-2},  \] where the second binomial term is zero for $k<2$. Iteration gives the unique expression $p=\sum _{j=0}^{\lfloor k/2\rfloor }|x|^{2j}h_{k-2j}$ with $h_{k-2j}\in \mathcal H_{k-2j}$. Compare [ ABR01 ] , Proposition 5.5, Theorem 5.7 and Proposition 5.8, pp. 76–78. Proof For monomials, multiplication by $x_ i$ is adjoint to $\partial _ i$ in the coefficient inner products: the factorial at index $\alpha +e_ i$ is $(\alpha _ i+1)\alpha !$. Thus multiplication by $|x|^2$ is adjoint to $\Delta $ between the indicated homogeneous spaces. Its range is therefore the orthogonal complement of $\ker \Delta =\mathcal H_ k$ inside the finite-dimensional space $\mathcal P_ k$. This proves the direct sum. Multiplication by $|x|^2$ is injective since the polynomial ring has no zero divisors, and $\dim \mathcal P_ k=\binom {n+k}{k}$ by counting monomials. Subtraction gives the dimension formula. Repeatedly apply the unique direct-sum decomposition to the polynomial of degree $k-2$; the iteration stops at degree zero or one. This argument does not require a prior solution of a Dirichlet problem. $\square$

We retain the flat hypersurface conventions, $n\geq 1$, of Definition 14.18.1 . In this section $\mathcal P=\partial _ t^\perp -\Delta $, $v=\sqrt{1+|Du|^2}$ and $a=|A|^2$. The local estimates follow the method of [ EH91 ] , Theorem 2.1 and Theorem 3.1, printed pp. 550 and 554–557. Compact support of a cutoff is the ingredient replacing a hypothesis at infinity. The rational curvature weight below has an exact tensor-square identity before its negative terms are discarded. Lemma 14.23.1 (Spatial cutoffs on an entire graphical flow) . 20F0F94E8D82 Let $F(x,t)=(x,u(x,t))$ be a smooth entire graph on a closed finite time slab $[0,T]$. For an ambient center $X_0$, set \[  \eta =R^2-|F-X_0|^2-2nt.  \] Then $\mathcal P\eta =0$ and $|
abla \eta |^2\leq 4R^2$ wherever $\eta >0$. The set of base coordinates on which $\eta \geq 0$, over all these times, lies in one compact base ball. For the base cutoff $\zeta =R^2-|x-y_0|^2$, one has instead \[  0\leq \mathcal P\zeta =2\operatorname {tr}(g^{-1})\leq 2n, \qquad |
abla \zeta |^2\leq 4R^2\quad (\zeta >0).  \] Proof The Euclidean position equation gives $\mathcal P|F-X_0|^2=-2n$, proving the first identity. The intrinsic gradient is twice the tangential projection of $F-X_0$, giving its bound. An ambient ball bounds the horizontal coordinate by its projection onto the base, uniformly in time. On that compact base ball, smoothness bounds all relevant derivatives on the entire finite slab, even if they are unbounded globally. For the base cutoff, Lemma 14.21.1 gives $\mathcal P|x-y_0|^2=-2\operatorname {tr}(g^{-1})$. The eigenvalues of $g^{-1}$ lie in $(0,1]$, and its quadratic form is at most the Euclidean one, proving both estimates. These are the two cutoffs used in [ EH91 ] , Corollary 3.2; no general sign assumption on the heat operator of an unspecified radius function is needed. $\square$ Theorem 14.23.2 (The localized reciprocal-angle estimate) . 60A54E588296 For a smooth entire graphical flow on $[0,T]$, every ambient center and every $R>0$ satisfy \[  v(x,t) igl (R^2-|F(x,t)-X_0|^2-2nt igr )_+ \leq \sup _ y v(y,0) igl (R^2-|F(y,0)-X_0|^2 igr )_+.  \] The right side is finite by compactness of the base support. This is [ EH91 ] , Theorem 2.1, p. 550, for an entire graph. No global curvature or slope bound is assumed. Proof On $\eta >0$ put $q=v\eta $. The angle equation and Lemma 14.23.1 give \[  \left(\mathcal P+2v^{-1}
abla v\cdot 
abla ight)q=-a q\leq 0.  \] Indeed the two cross-gradient terms and the term $-2\eta v^{-1}|
abla v|^2$ cancel after adding this drift. The function $v\eta _+$ is continuous and vanishes at the spatial boundary of its support. All of that support lies in a compact base set over a finite time interval. On its interior every coefficient is smooth and bounded. The graph-coordinate drift from Lemma 14.18.3 vanishes at a spatial maximum, so the usual first-positive-maximum argument applies to $v\eta _+-M-\epsilon t$, where $M$ is its initial supremum. text: Lemma 14.23.1 (Spatial cutoffs on an entire graphical flow) . 20F0F94E8D82 Let $F(x,t)=(x,u(x,t))$ be a smooth entire graph on a closed finite time slab $[0,T]$. For an ambient center $X_0$, set \[  \eta =R^2-|F-X_0|^2-2nt.  \] Then $\mathcal P\eta =0$ and $|\nabla \eta |^2\leq 4R^2$ wherever $\eta >0$. The set of base coordinates on which $\eta \geq 0$, over all these times, lies in one compact base ball. For the base cutoff $\zeta =R^2-|x-y_0|^2$, one has instead \[  0\leq \mathcal P\zeta =2\operatorname {tr}(g^{-1})\leq 2n, \qquad |\nabla \zeta |^2\leq 4R^2\quad (\zeta >0).  \] Proof The Euclidean position equation gives $\mathcal P|F-X_0|^2=-2n$, proving the first identity. The intrinsic gradient is twice the tangential projection of $F-X_0$, giving its bound. An ambient ball bounds the horizontal coordinate by its projection onto the base, uniformly in time. On that compact base ball, smoothness bounds all relevant derivatives on the entire finite slab, even if they are unbounded globally. For the base cutoff, Lemma 14.21.1 gives $\mathcal P|x-y_0|^2=-2\operatorname {tr}(g^{-1})$. The eigenvalues of $g^{-1}$ lie in $(0,1]$, and its quadratic form is at most the Euclidean one, proving both estimates. These are the two cutoffs used in [ EH91 ] , Corollary 3.2; no general sign assumption on the heat operator of an unspecified radius function is needed. $\square$

title: 14.24 Automatic curvature control and bounded-slope uniqueness
search_title: Automatic curvature control and bounded-slope uniqueness
section: 14.24 Automatic curvature control and bounded-slope uniqueness
text: The local cutoff estimates of [ EH91 ] , Section 3, remove some hypotheses previously imposed to justify a maximum principle at infinity. We record exactly which bounds become conclusions. Throughout, hypersurfaces are smooth Euclidean graphs, $n\geq 1$, with the conventions of Section 14.18 . Statements about arbitrary locally Lipschitz graphs with unbounded slope belong to a different existence theorem. Proposition 14.24.1 (Bounded slope gives automatic positive-time curvature control) . 7C534FE9C79D Let $u:\mathbb R^ n\times (0,T]\to \mathbb R$ be a smooth graphical flow with $v\leq V<\infty $ on the whole slab. Then \[  |A(x,t)|^2\leq C(n)V^4/t.  \] In fact its sharp slope-based estimate is \[  (1+2t|A(x,t)|^2)v(x,t)^2\leq V^2.  \] No curvature or spatial growth bound is assumed in either assertion. In particular they apply with $V=V_0$ to a smooth flow up to time zero with bounded initial slope, by Corollary 14.23.3 . Proof Fix $0<\epsilon <t$. Apply Theorem 14.23.5 on a base ball centered at the chosen point and on the time interval $[\epsilon ,t]$, using time elapsed from $\epsilon $. At its center the estimate is $a(x,t)\leq C(n)V^4((t-\epsilon )^{-1}+R^{-2})$. The graph is smooth on every such compact ball. Let $R\to \infty $ and then $\epsilon \downarrow 0$. This proves the first estimate, and hence uniform curvature control on every closed positive-time slab. Theorem 14.21.4 now applies on $[\epsilon ,t]$: its formerly assumed slab curvature bound has just been proved. Its starting slope supremum is at most $V$. Therefore $(1+2(t-\epsilon )a(x,t))v(x,t)^2\leq V^2$. Let $\epsilon \downarrow 0$ for the sharp form. No convergence of the curvature at time zero is needed. This is the local-to-global procedure discussed in [ EH91 ] , Remark 3.3(i), followed by the exact time-weighted identity already in the project. $\square$ Corollary 14.24.2 (Ancient bounded-slope graphs are affine without a curvature hypothesis) . F0843648ED91 Let $u:\mathbb R^ n\times (-\infty ,T)\to \mathbb R$ be a smooth entire graphical flow with one uniform bound for $v$ over all space and past times. Then $u(x,t)=p\cdot x+c$ for fixed $p,c$. The slab curvature assumption in Corollary 14.21.5 is unnecessary once the local curvature estimate is available. Proof Fix $t<T$ and a starting time $s<t$. Translate time in Proposition 14.24.1 . It gives $|A(x,t)|^2\leq C(n)V^4/(t-s)$, uniformly in $s$. Let $s\to -\infty $. Thus $A=0$ at every point and time. Lemma 14.20.1 gives $D^2u=0$, so $u=p(t)\cdot x+c(t)$. The graph equation has zero right-hand side, hence $p'=0$ and $c'=0$. An entire translator with a bounded slope is consequently a stationary affine graph; translators on strips or with unbounded slope are outside these assumptions. $\square$ Corollary 14.24.3 (A bounded-gradient entire minimal graph is affine in every dimension) . E506656B488A If a smooth solution $u:\mathbb R^ n\to \mathbb R$ of the minimal graph equation has $\sup |Du|<\infty $, then $u$ is affine, for every $n\geq 1$. This is a bounded-gradient conclusion, not the unrestricted Bernstein theorem. The stationary use of graphical-flow estimates is explained in [ EH91 ] , Remark 3.6(iii). Proof Regard the graph as the time-independent solution $u(x,t)=u(x)$ for all $t\in \mathbb R$. The graphical flow equation is satisfied because its mean curvature is zero. Its slope bound is uniform for every past time. Corollary 14.24.2 therefore gives the affine conclusion. The argument leaves open the unrestricted entire minimal-graph problem when the slope is unbounded; no dimension threshold is being removed from that different statement. $\square$ Lemma 14.24.4 (A maximum principle with a time-integrable drift bound) . 2F5B0A379ED2 Suppose $0\leq a(x,t)\leq A_0I$ and $|b(x,t)|\leq B(t)$ on $\mathbb R^ n\times (0,T]$, where $B$ is continuous, nonnegative and integrable on $(0,T]$. Let $f$ be continuous on $\mathbb R^ n\times [0,T]$, smooth enough for the following inequality at positive time, and satisfy \[  f_ t-a^{ij}f_{ij}-b^ if_ i\leq 0,\quad f(x,0)\leq M, \quad f(x,t)\leq C(1+|x|^2)^ m  \] uniformly on the slab for some $C,m\geq 0$. Then $f\leq M$. Continuity at time zero is local; a uniform spatial rate of initial convergence is not assumed. Proof Repeat the barrier proof of Lemma 14.21.2 with $q>\max \{ m,1\} $ and \[  E(x,t)=(1+|x|^2)^ q \exp \left((1+4nA_0q^2)t+q\int _0^ t B(s)\, ds\right).  \] The spatial derivative bounds in that lemma give $E_ t-a^{ij}E_{ij}-b^ iE_ i\geq E>0$ for $t>0$. Integrability of $B$ makes $E$ finite and continuous at time zero. For fixed $\eta >0$, the uniform polynomial upper bound confines every possible positive maximum of $f-M-\eta E$ to a fixed compact base ball, uniformly in time. Initial values there are strictly negative. Continuity and the strict parabolic inequality exclude a positive maximum at later time exactly as before. Let $\eta \downarrow 0$ at each point. The argument allows $B(t)=Ct^{-1/2}$, but not a nonintegrable coefficient merely by ignoring its singularity. $\square$ Theorem 14.24.5 (Comparison and uniqueness in the bounded-slope entire class) . F14A47368365 Let $u_1,u_2$ be smooth entire graphical flows for $0<t\leq T$, continuous locally up to $t=0$, with one finite bound for both slopes on the whole positive-time slab. If $u_1(x,0)\leq u_2(x,0)$ for every $x$, then $u_1\leq u_2$ for every time. Thus equal initial functions give equal flows in this class, without an assumed initial or slab curvature bound. The curvature input is the locally proved estimate based on [ EH91 ] , Theorem 3.1. Proof Put $w=u_1-u_2$. Subtract the equations in the same way as Proposition 14.21.6 . Then \[  w_ t=a^{ij}(Du_1)w_{ij}+b^ kw_ k, \qquad b^ k=\int _0^1\partial _{p_ k}a^{ij}(Du_2+\theta Dw)\, d\theta \, (u_2)_{ij}.  \] The slope bounds control derivatives of the coefficient matrix on every interpolated gradient. Proposition 14.24.1 and Lemma 14.20.1 give $|D^2u_2|\leq C t^{-1/2}$, so $|b|\leq C t^{-1/2}$. This is integrable in time. The slope bounds and continuity of the two heights at the base origin give $|w(x,t)|\leq C_ T(1+|x|)$ uniformly for $0\leq t\leq T$. Apply Lemma 14.24.4 to $w$, whose initial value is nonpositive. This proves comparison. Applying it in both orders proves uniqueness. No differentiability of the initial function enters this argument. $\square$ Corollary 14.24.6 (Uniqueness of the globally Lipschitz-data construction) . A53230A383ED For every globally Lipschitz entire initial function, the Ecker–Huisken solution from Theorem 14.21.7 is unique among smooth positive-time entire graphical flows converging locally continuously to that function and having bounded slope on each finite positive-time slab, uniformly down to time zero. Ordered initial functions produce ordered solutions. Proof The cited existence theorem supplies such a solution and its slope bound. On any finite time interval, another flow in the stated class satisfies the hypotheses of Theorem 14.24.5 . Equal initial values give equality on that interval. Since the interval is arbitrary, uniqueness holds for all time. The same theorem applied to two constructed solutions proves order preservation. Existence remains the external parabolic theorem; the comparison and uniqueness argument is local to this section. This does not assert uniqueness for unrestricted entire graphs with unbounded slopes. $\square$ Proposition 14.24.7 (Convex initial data give upward motion) . E7087D5665CF Let $f:\mathbb R^ n\to \mathbb R$ be convex and globally Lipschitz, and let $u$ be its solution from Corollary 14.24.6 . Then \[  u(x,t)\geq f(x),\qquad u(x,t+s)\geq u(x,t)\quad (s,t\geq 0), \qquad u_ t\geq 0\quad (t>0).  \] If $f$ is not affine, then $u_ t>0$ everywhere at positive time, and $u(x,t)>f(x)$. Thus the scalar mean curvature with the upward orientation satisfies $H<0$. This assertion concerns the sign of motion and mean curvature; it does not establish preservation of convexity of the whole second fundamental form. Proof A finite convex function on $\mathbb R^ n$ is the supremum of its supporting affine functions, with a supporting function attaining the value at every point. We use this finite-dimensional supporting-hyperplane fact as convex-analysis background. If $f$ is $L$-Lipschitz, the slopes of these supporting functions have norm at most $L$: testing their defining inequality along each unit direction gives that bound. Each affine function defines a stationary bounded-slope graphical flow. Theorem 14.24.5 compares it with $u$, proving $u(\cdot ,t)\geq f$ after taking the supremum over supports. Fix $s>0$. The flow $u(x,t+s)$ has initial value $u(x,s)\geq f(x)$, remains bounded in slope on finite slabs and is smooth at $t=0$. Comparison with $u(x,t)$ proves time monotonicity. Smoothness then gives $q=u_ t\geq 0$ for positive time. Differentiating the graphical equation gives \[  q_ t=a^{ij}(Du)q_{ij} +\partial _{p_ k}a^{ij}(Du)u_{ij}q_ k.  \] On every positive-time compact cylinder this is a smooth uniformly parabolic linear equation. If $q$ vanished at an interior point at time $t_0>0$, the classical local strong maximum principle, propagated through overlapping bounded cylinders, would give $q=0$ throughout $\mathbb R^ n\times (0,t_0]$. Thus $u$ would be stationary on that interval, and its locally uniform initial trace $f$ would equal this smooth stationary graph. Since $f$ is convex, $D^2f$ is positive semidefinite; the minimal graph equation $a^{ij}(Df)f_{ij}=0$ with positive definite $a$ forces $D^2f=0$. Hence $f$ would be affine. For nonaffine $f$ this contradiction proves $u_ t>0$. Integrating on any closed positive-time subinterval and using $u\geq f$ gives $u(x,t)>f(x)$. Finally $u_ t=-Hv$ with $v>0$ gives $H<0$. The external input for existence remains [ EH89 ] , Theorem 4.6; the local strong maximum principle and convex supporting-hyperplane fact are the background used here. $\square$

Apply Theorem 14.23.5 on a base ball centered at the chosen point and on the time interval $[\epsilon ,t]$, using time elapsed from $\epsilon $. At its center the estimate is $a(x,t)\leq C(n)V^4((t-\epsilon )^{-1}+R^{-2})$. The graph is smooth on every such compact ball. Let $R\to \infty $ and then $\epsilon \downarrow 0$. This proves the first estimate, and hence uniform curvature control on every closed positive-time slab. Theorem 14.21.4 now applies on $[\epsilon ,t]$: its formerly assumed slab curvature bound has just been proved. Its starting slope supremum is at most $V$. Therefore $(1+2(t-\epsilon )a(x,t))v(x,t)^2\leq V^2$. Let $\epsilon \downarrow 0$ for the sharp form. No convergence of the curvature at time zero is needed. This is the local-to-global procedure discussed in [ EH91 ] , Remark 3.3(i), followed by the exact time-weighted identity already in the project. $\square$

F0843648ED91 Let $u:\mathbb R^ n\times (-\infty ,T)\to \mathbb R$ be a smooth entire graphical flow with one uniform bound for $v$ over all space and past times. Then $u(x,t)=p\cdot x+c$ for fixed $p,c$. The slab curvature assumption in Corollary 14.21.5 is unnecessary once the local curvature estimate is available. Proof Fix $t<T$ and a starting time $s<t$. Translate time in Proposition 14.24.1 . It gives $|A(x,t)|^2\leq C(n)V^4/(t-s)$, uniformly in $s$. Let $s\to -\infty $. Thus $A=0$ at every point and time. Lemma 14.20.1 gives $D^2u=0$, so $u=p(t)\cdot x+c(t)$. The graph equation has zero right-hand side, hence $p'=0$ and $c'=0$. An entire translator with a bounded slope is consequently a stationary affine graph; translators on strips or with unbounded slope are outside these assumptions. $\square$

text: Corollary 14.24.3 (A bounded-gradient entire minimal graph is affine in every dimension) . E506656B488A If a smooth solution $u:\mathbb R^ n\to \mathbb R$ of the minimal graph equation has $\sup |Du|<\infty $, then $u$ is affine, for every $n\geq 1$. This is a bounded-gradient conclusion, not the unrestricted Bernstein theorem. The stationary use of graphical-flow estimates is explained in [ EH91 ] , Remark 3.6(iii). Proof Regard the graph as the time-independent solution $u(x,t)=u(x)$ for all $t\in \mathbb R$. The graphical flow equation is satisfied because its mean curvature is zero. Its slope bound is uniform for every past time. Corollary 14.24.2 therefore gives the affine conclusion. The argument leaves open the unrestricted entire minimal-graph problem when the slope is unbounded; no dimension threshold is being removed from that different statement. $\square$

text: Lemma 14.24.4 (A maximum principle with a time-integrable drift bound) . 2F5B0A379ED2 Suppose $0\leq a(x,t)\leq A_0I$ and $|b(x,t)|\leq B(t)$ on $\mathbb R^ n\times (0,T]$, where $B$ is continuous, nonnegative and integrable on $(0,T]$. Let $f$ be continuous on $\mathbb R^ n\times [0,T]$, smooth enough for the following inequality at positive time, and satisfy \[  f_ t-a^{ij}f_{ij}-b^ if_ i\leq 0,\quad f(x,0)\leq M, \quad f(x,t)\leq C(1+|x|^2)^ m  \] uniformly on the slab for some $C,m\geq 0$. Then $f\leq M$. Continuity at time zero is local; a uniform spatial rate of initial convergence is not assumed. Proof Repeat the barrier proof of Lemma 14.21.2 with $q>\max \{ m,1\} $ and \[  E(x,t)=(1+|x|^2)^ q \exp \left((1+4nA_0q^2)t+q\int _0^ t B(s)\, ds\right).  \] The spatial derivative bounds in that lemma give $E_ t-a^{ij}E_{ij}-b^ iE_ i\geq E>0$ for $t>0$. Integrability of $B$ makes $E$ finite and continuous at time zero. For fixed $\eta >0$, the uniform polynomial upper bound confines every possible positive maximum of $f-M-\eta E$ to a fixed compact base ball, uniformly in time. Initial values there are strictly negative. Continuity and the strict parabolic inequality exclude a positive maximum at later time exactly as before. Let $\eta \downarrow 0$ at each point. The argument allows $B(t)=Ct^{-1/2}$, but not a nonintegrable coefficient merely by ignoring its singularity. $\square$

section: 14.24 Automatic curvature control and bounded-slope uniqueness
text: Theorem 14.24.5 (Comparison and uniqueness in the bounded-slope entire class) . F14A47368365 Let $u_1,u_2$ be smooth entire graphical flows for $0<t\leq T$, continuous locally up to $t=0$, with one finite bound for both slopes on the whole positive-time slab. If $u_1(x,0)\leq u_2(x,0)$ for every $x$, then $u_1\leq u_2$ for every time. Thus equal initial functions give equal flows in this class, without an assumed initial or slab curvature bound. The curvature input is the locally proved estimate based on [ EH91 ] , Theorem 3.1. Proof Put $w=u_1-u_2$. Subtract the equations in the same way as Proposition 14.21.6 . Then \[  w_ t=a^{ij}(Du_1)w_{ij}+b^ kw_ k, \qquad b^ k=\int _0^1\partial _{p_ k}a^{ij}(Du_2+\theta Dw)\, d\theta \, (u_2)_{ij}.  \] The slope bounds control derivatives of the coefficient matrix on every interpolated gradient. Proposition 14.24.1 and Lemma 14.20.1 give $|D^2u_2|\leq C t^{-1/2}$, so $|b|\leq C t^{-1/2}$. This is integrable in time. The slope bounds and continuity of the two heights at the base origin give $|w(x,t)|\leq C_ T(1+|x|)$ uniformly for $0\leq t\leq T$. Apply Lemma 14.24.4 to $w$, whose initial value is nonpositive. This proves comparison. Applying it in both orders proves uniqueness. No differentiability of the initial function enters this argument. $\square$

text: Corollary 14.24.6 (Uniqueness of the globally Lipschitz-data construction) . A53230A383ED For every globally Lipschitz entire initial function, the Ecker–Huisken solution from Theorem 14.21.7 is unique among smooth positive-time entire graphical flows converging locally continuously to that function and having bounded slope on each finite positive-time slab, uniformly down to time zero. Ordered initial functions produce ordered solutions. Proof The cited existence theorem supplies such a solution and its slope bound. On any finite time interval, another flow in the stated class satisfies the hypotheses of Theorem 14.24.5 . Equal initial values give equality on that interval. Since the interval is arbitrary, uniqueness holds for all time. The same theorem applied to two constructed solutions proves order preservation. Existence remains the external parabolic theorem; the comparison and uniqueness argument is local to this section. This does not assert uniqueness for unrestricted entire graphs with unbounded slopes. $\square$

title: Proposition 14.24.7 (Convex initial data give upward motion)
search_title: Convex initial data give upward motion
section: 14.24 Automatic curvature control and bounded-slope uniqueness
text: Proposition 14.24.7 (Convex initial data give upward motion) . E7087D5665CF Let $f:\mathbb R^ n\to \mathbb R$ be convex and globally Lipschitz, and let $u$ be its solution from Corollary 14.24.6 . Then \[  u(x,t)\geq f(x),\qquad u(x,t+s)\geq u(x,t)\quad (s,t\geq 0), \qquad u_ t\geq 0\quad (t>0).  \] If $f$ is not affine, then $u_ t>0$ everywhere at positive time, and $u(x,t)>f(x)$. Thus the scalar mean curvature with the upward orientation satisfies $H<0$. This assertion concerns the sign of motion and mean curvature; it does not establish preservation of convexity of the whole second fundamental form. Proof A finite convex function on $\mathbb R^ n$ is the supremum of its supporting affine functions, with a supporting function attaining the value at every point. We use this finite-dimensional supporting-hyperplane fact as convex-analysis background. If $f$ is $L$-Lipschitz, the slopes of these supporting functions have norm at most $L$: testing their defining inequality along each unit direction gives that bound. Each affine function defines a stationary bounded-slope graphical flow. Theorem 14.24.5 compares it with $u$, proving $u(\cdot ,t)\geq f$ after taking the supremum over supports. Fix $s>0$. The flow $u(x,t+s)$ has initial value $u(x,s)\geq f(x)$, remains bounded in slope on finite slabs and is smooth at $t=0$. Comparison with $u(x,t)$ proves time monotonicity. Smoothness then gives $q=u_ t\geq 0$ for positive time. Differentiating the graphical equation gives \[  q_ t=a^{ij}(Du)q_{ij} +\partial _{p_ k}a^{ij}(Du)u_{ij}q_ k.  \] On every positive-time compact cylinder this is a smooth uniformly parabolic linear equation. If $q$ vanished at an interior point at time $t_0>0$, the classical local strong maximum principle, propagated through overlapping bounded cylinders, would give $q=0$ throughout $\mathbb R^ n\times (0,t_0]$. Thus $u$ would be stationary on that interval, and its locally uniform initial trace $f$ would equal this smooth stationary graph. Since $f$ is convex, $D^2f$ is positive semidefinite; the minimal graph equation $a^{ij}(Df)f_{ij}=0$ with positive definite $a$ forces $D^2f=0$. Hence $f$ would be affine. For nonaffine $f$ this contradiction proves $u_ t>0$. Integrating on any closed positive-time subinterval and using $u\geq f$ gives $u(x,t)>f(x)$. Finally $u_ t=-Hv$ with $v>0$ gives $H<0$. The external input for existence remains [ EH89 ] , Theorem 4.6; the local strong maximum principle and convex supporting-hyperplane fact are the background used here. $\square$

title: 14.25 Height barriers and entire graphs of arbitrary growth
search_title: Height barriers and entire graphs of arbitrary growth
section: 14.25 Height barriers and entire graphs of arbitrary growth
text: Shrinking spheres give height control without differentiating the initial graph. We use the avoidance argument of [ EH91 ] , Section 5, pp. 567–568, and keep the subsequent parabolic existence theorem explicitly external. The assumptions for bounded-slope comparison are not silently transferred to arbitrary growth. Lemma 14.25.1 (Avoidance from a locally continuous initial graph) . 33446AAE0706 Let an entire graphical mean curvature flow be smooth for $0<t\leq T$ and converge locally uniformly as $t\downarrow 0$ to a continuous graph. Let $N_ t$ be a compact smooth hypersurface flow on $[0,T]$, whose initial image is disjoint from that graph. Then the two positive-time images remain disjoint, and their distance is at least their strictly positive initial distance. Proof The initial distance is attained and positive: a compact hypersurface and a closed entire graph are disjoint, and graph points with large base coordinate cannot minimize their distance. Over the whole time interval the compact flow has bounded image. Testing distances against a fixed base point bounds the minimum distance above uniformly, since the graph heights there extend continuously to time zero. Thus all minimizing graph base points lie in one compact ball. Locally uniform initial convergence makes the minimum distances converge to the initial positive distance as $t\downarrow 0$. On $[\epsilon ,T]$, Lemma 14.22.3 makes the distance nondecreasing. Let $\epsilon \downarrow 0$ to obtain the asserted lower bound. No tangent plane or curvature for the initial graph was used. $\square$ Proposition 14.25.2 (Local heights are controlled by a larger initial ball) . 0D43F66B768D In the preceding smooth positive-time, locally continuous initial-trace class, fix a base point $y$, $r\geq 0$, $T>0$, and $R$ with $R^2>r^2+2nT$. If $|u(x,0)|\leq M$ for $|x-y|\leq R$, then for $|x-y|\leq r$ and $0\leq t\leq T$, \[  |u(x,t)|\leq M+R-\sqrt{R^2-2nt-|x-y|^2}.  \] In particular this is a finite bound determined by the initial graph on a compact base ball. This is a quantitative form of the sphere barriers in [ EH91 ] , proof of Theorem 5.1. Proof Place a sphere of radius $R$ with center $(y,M+R+\epsilon )$, for $\epsilon >0$. Its entire ball lies strictly above the initial graph over its base projection, because its lowest height is $M+\epsilon $. Outside that projection the graph cannot meet the ball. The sphere shrinks to radius $\sqrt{R^2-2nt}$ and stays smooth through $T$. Lemma 14.25.1 prevents contact. At each fixed base point in $B_ r(y)$ its lower sheet exists throughout the interval, and the graph begins below that sheet. Continuity prevents crossing. The resulting upper bound is the displayed expression with an added $\epsilon $; let $\epsilon \downarrow 0$. Reflect the construction for the lower bound. A bound on the initial height outside $B_ R(y)$ is unnecessary because the initial comparison sphere has that bounded base projection. $\square$ Theorem 14.25.3 (A quantitative half-Hölder bound from Lipschitz initial data) . 33DD4BC0E6D3 Let a smooth positive-time entire graphical flow converge locally uniformly to a globally $L$-Lipschitz initial function $u_0$, with $L\geq 0$. Then \[  |u(x,t)-u_0(x)|\leq L\sqrt{2nt} \qquad (x\in \mathbb R^ n,\  t>0)  \] at every time of smooth existence. A slope or curvature bound for the later flow is not an additional hypothesis. The sphere-barrier method is [ EH91 ] , Section 5; the optimized constant is derived here. Proof Fix $x=y$ and $t>0$. For $R>\sqrt{2nt}$, place a sphere of radius $R$ with center at height $u_0(y)+R\sqrt{1+L^2}+\epsilon $ over $y$. Its lower sheet lies above the whole initial graph in its projected ball, since for $0\leq r\leq R$, \[  Lr+\sqrt{R^2-r^2}\leq R\sqrt{1+L^2}.  \] This is Cauchy–Schwarz applied to $(L,1)$ and $(r,\sqrt{R^2-r^2})$. The initial Lipschitz bound gives $u_0(x)\leq u_0(y)+L|x-y|$, so the vertical gap is at least $\epsilon $. Avoidance and continuity below the lower sheet, as in Proposition 14.25.2 , imply \[  u(y,t)-u_0(y)\leq R\sqrt{1+L^2}-\sqrt{R^2-2nt}  \] after letting $\epsilon \downarrow 0$. For $L>0$, choose $R=\sqrt{2nt}\sqrt{1+L^2}/L$; substitution makes the right side $L\sqrt{2nt}$. For $L=0$, let $R\to \infty $ to obtain zero. A reflected sphere gives the lower estimate. Since $y$ was arbitrary, the conclusion is uniform in space although initial heights themselves may be unbounded. $\square$ Proposition 14.25.4 (Uniform contraction and a time modulus for bounded-slope solutions) . A80F3D97491F For the globally Lipschitz-data solutions of Corollary 14.24.6 , \[  \sup _ x|u(x,t)-\widetilde u(x,t)| \leq \sup _ x|u(x,0)-\widetilde u(x,0)|  \] whenever the right side is finite. If the initial Lipschitz constant is at most $L$, then \[  \sup _ x|u(x,t)-u(x,s)|\leq L\sqrt{2n(t-s)}\qquad (0\leq s<t).  \] Proof If the initial difference is bounded by $\delta $, the functions $\widetilde u\pm \delta $ are also graphical solutions. Theorem 14.24.5 traps $u$ between them, proving contraction. The existence theorem gives $|Du|\leq L$ at all positive times. Start Theorem 14.25.3 at time $s$ with the function $u(\cdot ,s)$; the same Lipschitz constant applies. This proves the second estimate, with $s=0$ directly covered by that theorem. The height modulus uses compact sphere barriers; it is not obtained by integrating a nonexistent uniform initial curvature bound. $\square$ Theorem 14.25.5 (Ecker–Huisken existence for entire locally Lipschitz graphs) . 8E39161717CC Every locally Lipschitz function $u_0:\mathbb R^ n\to \mathbb R$, $n\geq 1$, is the initial value of an entire graphical mean curvature flow that is smooth for all $t>0$ and converges locally uniformly to $u_0$ at time zero. No global slope, height-growth or curvature bound is required. This is [ EH91 ] , Theorem 5.1 and Remark 5.2(i), printed p. 567, with its exhaustion and approximation argument on p. 568. The existence proof remains external: it uses graphical boundary-value existence, height-dependent local gradient estimates, higher derivative estimates and compact exhaustion. The local height and curvature estimates here and the height-dependent gradient proof in Theorem 14.26.2 explain parts of that argument but do not replace its remaining steps. Uniqueness in the unrestricted unbounded-slope class is not asserted by this statement. Example 14.25.6 (A rapidly growing graph and the divergent heat-kernel integral) . 6A6EB891C64F The smooth initial graph $u_0(x)=e^{|x|^4}$ admits an all-time positive-time smooth entire graphical mean curvature flow by Theorem 14.25.5 . In contrast, for every $t>0$ and fixed $x$, the Euclidean heat-kernel integral \[  (4\pi t)^{-n/2}\int _{\mathbb R^ n}e^{-|x-y|^2/(4t)}e^{|y|^4}\, dy  \] is infinite. This comparison concerns the heat-kernel construction, not a classification of all possible sign-changing heat-equation solutions without growth restrictions. Proof The initial function is smooth and hence locally Lipschitz, so it meets the cited graphical existence theorem despite its unbounded slope and rapid growth. For large $|y|$ with $x,t$ fixed, the exponent $|y|^4-|x-y|^2/(4t)$ is at least $|y|^4/2$. The integral over the exterior of that ball therefore diverges. The graph theorem and the heat-kernel computation make different assertions, and neither is deduced from a formal linearization at a graph with unbounded gradient. Local finite-height bounds for the nonlinear flow are consistent with Proposition 14.25.2 , which only asks for initial heights on a finite larger ball. $\square$

An ambient-ball cutoff controls angle only while the surface remains inside that ambient ball. A height-dependent cutoff instead gives a gradient estimate on a fixed base ball. We develop the maximum-principle argument of [ EH91 ] , Theorem 2.3, printed pp. 551–553, with explicit, nonoptimal constants. Lemma 14.26.1 (The height-dependent cutoff at a large-angle maximum) . 15ECD7CEFB78 Work on the unit base ball, suppose the graph height $h<0$ throughout a finite time slab, and let $ eta \geq 1$.
