title: 16.24 Corners and the scales in graphical estimates
search_title: Corners and the scales in graphical estimates
section: 16.24 Corners and the scales in graphical estimates
text: These examples connect the local estimates of [ EH91 ] with the explicit expanding curves constructed in Section 16.5 . They distinguish a sharp scaling exponent from a claim that every numerical constant in an estimate is optimal. Example 16.24.1 (The time exponent one half cannot be improved for Lipschitz graphs) . D3370A33F891 For the expanding curve $U(x,t)=\sqrt t\, u_ a(x/\sqrt t)$ of Proposition 16.5.4 , the initial trace is $\ell _ a|x|$ and \[  U(0,t)-U(0,0)=a\sqrt t.  \] Consequently a uniform time estimate with exponent $\alpha >1/2$ at zero cannot hold for all Lipschitz initial graphs, even for a single such nontrivial flow with its own finite constant. The curvature satisfies $|A|(0,t)=a/(2\sqrt t)$, so the positive-time curvature scale also occurs in an exact solution. Proof The profile has $u_ a(0)=a>0$, giving the height identity. Dividing it by $t^\alpha $ gives $a t^{1/2-\alpha }\to \infty $, excluding a finite constant for an estimate of that exponent near zero. Proposition 16.5.5 gives the curvature identity. These examples have bounded slope at all positive times by Lemma 16.5.2 ; the singular initial corner is why an initial curvature bound is unavailable. Products with Euclidean factors give the same height and curvature exponents in every hypersurface dimension. $\square$ Lemma 16.24.2 (The tip height parametrizes all positive symmetric cone slopes) . 6200E72780B0 For the even convex expander profiles, the map $a\mapsto \ell _ a$ is a continuous strictly increasing bijection from $(0,\infty )$ to $(0,\infty )$. Moreover \[  \frac{a}{\sqrt2}\leq \ell _ a, \qquad \arctan \ell _ a\leq \frac{\sqrt\pi }{2}a.  \] Proof The time estimate in Theorem 14.25.3 , applied at the tip to the explicit expander with initial Lipschitz constant $\ell _ a$ and $n=1$, gives $a\leq \sqrt2\ell _ a$. For the upper angle estimate, the defect equation of Proposition 16.5.1 gives \[  (\arctan p)'=q/2\leq (a/2)e^{-x^2/4}.  \] Integrate from zero to infinity and use $p(0)=0$, $p(\infty )=\ell _ a$ and $\int _0^\infty e^{-x^2/4}\, dx=\sqrt\pi $. If $a<b$ but $\ell _ a\geq \ell _ b$, their expanding flows have ordered initial traces in the opposite order. Theorem 14.24.5 gives $U_ b\leq U_ a$, hence $b\leq a$ at the tip at time one, a contradiction. Thus the slope is strictly increasing. To check continuity rather than assuming it from monotonicity, fix a compact interval of positive parameters. Smooth ODE dependence makes $p_ a(1)$ and $q_ a(1)$ bounded and continuous there. Lemma 16.5.2 bounds $p_ a(x)$ uniformly for $x\geq 1$. The defect bound therefore gives $p_ a'(x)\leq C e^{-x^2/4}$ uniformly over those parameters. Hence $p_ a(R)$ converges uniformly to $\ell _ a$ as $R\to \infty $. Every finite-$R$ value is continuous by ODE dependence, so its uniform limit is continuous. The angle bound implies $\ell _ a\to 0$ as $a\downarrow 0$, and the lower bound implies $\ell _ a\to \infty $ as $a\to \infty $. Continuity and strict increase finish the bijection proof. $\square$ Theorem 16.24.3 (The unique bounded-slope graphical expander for a symmetric corner) . 88EC1DC4D011 For every $\ell >0$ there is a unique smooth entire graphical self-expander whose slope is bounded and whose dilation flow converges locally uniformly to $\ell |x|$ at time zero. It is the even strictly convex profile $u_ a$ with $\ell _ a=\ell $. Uniqueness here is in this graphical bounded-slope class, not among arbitrary immersed networks or weak flows. The planar expander setting is studied in [ Hal12 ] , Section 6; the uniqueness proof here uses graphical comparison. Proof Lemma 16.24.2 supplies one parameter $a$. Theorem 16.5.3 and Proposition 16.5.4 supply the profile and its uniform initial trace. Any other profile in the stated class has a dilation flow smooth for positive time with the same locally uniform initial trace; dilation preserves the bound on its graph slope. Theorem 14.24.5 gives equality of the two flows. Their time-one slices are the profiles themselves. Evenness and strict convexity are therefore conclusions for every profile in this class, rather than extra assumptions imposed to prove uniqueness. $\square$ Example 16.24.4 (The spatial-radius term in local curvature estimates is necessary) . 87E95B631E65 For $\lambda >0$, consider the rescaled Scherk graph \[  u_\lambda (x,y)=\lambda \bigl (\log \cos (y/\lambda )-\log \cos (x/\lambda )\bigr ).  \] It is a stationary graphical flow on $|x|,|y|<\pi \lambda /2$. On the base ball $B_\lambda (0)$ its slope is bounded independently of $\lambda $, whereas $|A|^2(0)=2/\lambda ^2$ at every time. Thus the $R^{-2}$ term in Theorem 14.23.5 cannot be omitted when $R$ is finite, and its power agrees with scaling. Proof Example 7.2.14 verifies the minimal graph equation at scale one. Euclidean dilation preserves minimality, hence stationarity under flow. On $B_\lambda $, both dimensionless coordinates have magnitude at most one, so $|Du_\lambda |^2\leq 2\tan ^2(1)$. At the origin the gradient is zero and the Hessian is $\operatorname {diag}(1/\lambda ,-1/\lambda )$. The graph metric is Euclidean there, giving $|A|^2=2/\lambda ^2$. If the local curvature bound involved only $C(V)/t$, sending $t\to \infty $ along this stationary flow would force its curvature to vanish, a contradiction. The ball lies strictly inside the graph domain, so failure is not due to a lack of smoothness on its closure. $\square$

section: 16.25 Graphical expanders from homogeneous cones
text: The one-dimensional corner construction has a counterpart in every dimension. Global existence for Lipschitz graphs is the external input from [ EH89 ] , Theorem 4.6. Scaling and the bounded-slope comparison theorem then give the expander and its uniqueness. This argument concerns entire graphical hypersurfaces; it makes no assertion about the number of nongraphical expanders asymptotic to the same geometric cone. Theorem 16.25.1 (A unique bounded-slope graphical expander for a Lipschitz cone) . 9EC09394BFF2 Let $f:\mathbb R^ n\to \mathbb R$, $n\geq 1$, be globally $L$-Lipschitz and positively homogeneous of degree one: $f(\lambda x)=\lambda f(x)$ for every $\lambda >0$. There is a unique smooth entire graph $U$ with bounded slope whose dilation flow $\sqrt t\, U(x/\sqrt t)$ converges locally uniformly to $f$ as $t\downarrow 0$ and solves graphical mean curvature flow. It satisfies \[  \left(\delta _{ij}-\frac{U_ iU_ j}{1+|DU|^2}\right)U_{ij} =\frac{U-x\cdot DU}{2},\qquad |DU|\leq L, \qquad |U(x)-f(x)|\leq L\sqrt{2n}.  \] Its graph is properly embedded and complete. The existence input is [ EH89 ] , Theorem 4.6; the self-similarity and the stated uniqueness follow from the local comparison argument in this project. Proof Use Theorem 14.21.7 to obtain a smooth positive-time entire flow $u$ with initial trace $f$ and $|Du|\leq L$. For every $\lambda >0$ the parabolic rescaling \[  u_\lambda (x,t)=\lambda ^{-1}u(\lambda x,\lambda ^2t)  \] solves the same graph equation, has the same slope bound, and has initial trace $\lambda ^{-1}f(\lambda x)=f(x)$. On each finite common time interval, Theorem 14.24.5 gives $u_\lambda =u$. Taking $U=u(\cdot ,1)$ therefore yields $u(x,t)=\sqrt t\, U(x/\sqrt t)$. Differentiate this identity and substitute into the graph equation to obtain the displayed elliptic equation with the positive expander sign. The slope estimate is inherited from the flow, and Theorem 14.25.3 at time one gives the height estimate. An entire smooth graph is properly embedded: a compact ambient set bounds the base variable, and the graph is closed. Its induced metric dominates the Euclidean base metric. An intrinsic Cauchy sequence thus converges in the base; smoothness on a compact base neighborhood gives convergence in the graph metric. Hence the graph is complete. Finally, another profile in the stated class has a positive-time dilation flow with bounded slope and the same initial trace. Theorem 14.24.5 identifies the flows, hence their time-one profiles. Existence is not being reconstructed from the elliptic equation alone. $\square$ Proposition 16.25.2 (Order, symmetries and blow-down of cone expanders) . 35C79DC18B68 Write $U_ f$ for the profile in Theorem 16.25.1 . If $f\leq g$, then $U_ f\leq U_ g$. For $Q\in O(n)$ one has $U_{f\circ Q}=U_ f\circ Q$, and $U_{-f}=-U_ f$. In particular all orthogonal symmetries of the cone are inherited. The quantitative blow-down estimate is \[  \sup _{x\in \mathbb R^ n}|R^{-1}U_ f(Rx)-f(x)| \leq L\sqrt{2n}/R\qquad (R>0).  \] If $f(x)=p\cdot x$, then $U_ f(x)=p\cdot x$. Proof Order follows by applying Theorem 14.24.5 to the flows from the two cones. Orthogonal changes of the base and reflection in the height coordinate preserve the graph equation, and give the indicated initial traces. Uniqueness identifies the transformed flows with the corresponding constructed ones. Divide the uniform height estimate in Theorem 16.25.1 at $Rx$ by $R$ and use homogeneity to prove the blow-down estimate. Finally the linear function is a stationary graphical flow and solves the expander equation because both its Hessian and $U-x\cdot DU$ vanish. Uniqueness gives the last assertion. A vertical translate of a linear profile would not satisfy this origin-centered expander equation unless the added constant were zero. $\square$ Example 16.25.3 (Rotational expanders from circular graphical cones) . E19F15FD3062 For $\ell >0$, the cone $f(x)=\ell |x|$ produces a radial profile $U(x)=w(r)$, $r=|x|$. For $r>0$, \[  \frac{w''}{1+(w')^2}+\frac{n-1}{r}w' =\frac{w-rw'}2.  \] At its smooth center, $w'(0)=0$ and, writing $c=w(0)$, \[  0<c\leq \ell \sqrt{2n},\qquad w''(0)=\frac{c}{2n}, \qquad |A|(0)=\frac{c}{2\sqrt n}.  \] The dilation flow has tip height $c\sqrt t$ and curvature $c/(2\sqrt{nt})$ at its tip. Thus the one-half time scale occurs in radial hypersurface examples in every dimension. Proof Orthogonal symmetry in Proposition 16.25.2 makes $U$ radial. At $r>0$ its Hessian has eigenvalues $w''$ in the radial direction and $w'/r$ in the $n-1$ orthogonal directions, while the coefficient matrix has radial eigenvalue $(1+(w')^2)^{-1}$ and tangential eigenvalues one. This gives the equation. Smooth radial symmetry gives $DU(0)=0$ and $D^2U(0)=\alpha I$. The equation at the origin gives $n\alpha =c/2$. Comparison with the zero cone gives $u\geq 0$. Its initial trace is positive away from the origin. At any fixed positive time the solution is strictly positive by the classical local strong maximum principle: on positive-time cylinders the graph equation is a smooth uniformly parabolic scalar equation, and an interior zero would force zero at earlier positive times in the connected domain. Chaining overlapping bounded cylinders contradicts locally uniform convergence to the nonzero initial trace. This standard parabolic principle is used as background, not proved here. Hence $c>0$. The height bound at the origin gives $c\leq \ell \sqrt{2n}$. Since the graph metric at the origin is Euclidean, the second fundamental form has $n$ equal principal curvatures in absolute value $c/(2n)$; its norm is $c/(2\sqrt n)$. No global convexity or classification of all rotational immersions is needed for these conclusions. $\square$ Example 16.25.4 (A nonconvex cone with an expander of changing height sign) . AB32BF435231 In dimension two take $f(x_1,x_2)=|x_1|-|x_2|$. Its unique bounded-slope expander is even in each coordinate and satisfies \[  U(x_2,x_1)=-U(x_1,x_2).  \] It vanishes on both diagonals, is not affine, and takes both positive and negative values. At the origin $U=0$, $DU=0$, $H=0$ and $D^2U=\operatorname {diag}(a,-a)$ for some real $a$. No value or nonvanishing assertion for $a$ is required. They force the stated vanishing on the diagonals and the values of $U$, its gradient, and the shape of its Hessian at the origin. The expander equation gives zero mean curvature there. The uniform height estimate gives $|U-f|\leq 2\sqrt2$, so $U(R,0)>0$ and $U(0,R)<0$ for large $R$. If $U$ were affine, its blow-down would be a linear function, contradicting the explicit nonaffine cone. Moreover its scalar mean curvature with the upward orientation satisfies $H(x_2,x_1)=-H(x_1,x_2)$, by the formula $H=-\operatorname {div}(DU/v)$. If $H$ had one sign it would vanish identically. The expander equation would then give $U=x\cdot DU$, making $U$ homogeneous of degree one; smoothness at the origin forces such a function to be linear, a contradiction. Proof Proposition 14.24.7 gives strict height increase and $u_ t>0$ for the constructed flow. Its self-similar expression gives $2u_ t(x,1)=U_ f(x)-x\cdot DU_ f(x)$. This proves the defect inequality and the sign of $H=-u_ t/v$. A positively one-homogeneous continuous function has $f(0)=0$, so the strict height inequality yields $U_ f(0)>0$. The proof does not require a separate convexity-preservation theorem for the flow. $\square$

title: Theorem 16.25.1 (A unique bounded-slope graphical expander for a Lipschitz cone)

text: Theorem 16.25.1 (A unique bounded-slope graphical expander for a Lipschitz cone) . 9EC09394BFF2 Let $f:\mathbb R^ n\to \mathbb R$, $n\geq 1$, be globally $L$-Lipschitz and positively homogeneous of degree one: $f(\lambda x)=\lambda f(x)$ for every $\lambda >0$. There is a unique smooth entire graph $U$ with bounded slope whose dilation flow $\sqrt t\, U(x/\sqrt t)$ converges locally uniformly to $f$ as $t\downarrow 0$ and solves graphical mean curvature flow. It satisfies \[  \left(\delta _{ij}-\frac{U_ iU_ j}{1+|DU|^2}\right)U_{ij} =\frac{U-x\cdot DU}{2},\qquad |DU|\leq L, \qquad |U(x)-f(x)|\leq L\sqrt{2n}.  \] Its graph is properly embedded and complete. The existence input is [ EH89 ] , Theorem 4.6; the self-similarity and the stated uniqueness follow from the local comparison argument in this project. Proof Use Theorem 14.21.7 to obtain a smooth positive-time entire flow $u$ with initial trace $f$ and $|Du|\leq L$. For every $\lambda >0$ the parabolic rescaling \[  u_\lambda (x,t)=\lambda ^{-1}u(\lambda x,\lambda ^2t)  \] solves the same graph equation, has the same slope bound, and has initial trace $\lambda ^{-1}f(\lambda x)=f(x)$. On each finite common time interval, Theorem 14.24.5 gives $u_\lambda =u$. Taking $U=u(\cdot ,1)$ therefore yields $u(x,t)=\sqrt t\, U(x/\sqrt t)$. Differentiate this identity and substitute into the graph equation to obtain the displayed elliptic equation with the positive expander sign. The slope estimate is inherited from the flow, and Theorem 14.25.3 at time one gives the height estimate. An entire smooth graph is properly embedded: a compact ambient set bounds the base variable, and the graph is closed. Its induced metric dominates the Euclidean base metric. An intrinsic Cauchy sequence thus converges in the base; smoothness on a compact base neighborhood gives convergence in the graph metric. Hence the graph is complete. Finally, another profile in the stated class has a positive-time dilation flow with bounded slope and the same initial trace. Theorem 14.24.5 identifies the flows, hence their time-one profiles. Existence is not being reconstructed from the elliptic equation alone. $\square$

title: Proposition 16.25.2 (Order, symmetries and blow-down of cone expanders)
search_title: Order, symmetries and blow-down of cone expanders
section: 16.25 Graphical expanders from homogeneous cones
text: Proposition 16.25.2 (Order, symmetries and blow-down of cone expanders) . 35C79DC18B68 Write $U_ f$ for the profile in Theorem 16.25.1 . If $f\leq g$, then $U_ f\leq U_ g$. For $Q\in O(n)$ one has $U_{f\circ Q}=U_ f\circ Q$, and $U_{-f}=-U_ f$. In particular all orthogonal symmetries of the cone are inherited. The quantitative blow-down estimate is \[  \sup _{x\in \mathbb R^ n}|R^{-1}U_ f(Rx)-f(x)| \leq L\sqrt{2n}/R\qquad (R>0).  \] If $f(x)=p\cdot x$, then $U_ f(x)=p\cdot x$. Proof Order follows by applying Theorem 14.24.5 to the flows from the two cones. Orthogonal changes of the base and reflection in the height coordinate preserve the graph equation, and give the indicated initial traces. Uniqueness identifies the transformed flows with the corresponding constructed ones. Divide the uniform height estimate in Theorem 16.25.1 at $Rx$ by $R$ and use homogeneity to prove the blow-down estimate. Finally the linear function is a stationary graphical flow and solves the expander equation because both its Hessian and $U-x\cdot DU$ vanish. Uniqueness gives the last assertion. A vertical translate of a linear profile would not satisfy this origin-centered expander equation unless the added constant were zero. $\square$

text: Example 16.25.3 (Rotational expanders from circular graphical cones) . E19F15FD3062 For $\ell >0$, the cone $f(x)=\ell |x|$ produces a radial profile $U(x)=w(r)$, $r=|x|$. For $r>0$, \[  \frac{w''}{1+(w')^2}+\frac{n-1}{r}w' =\frac{w-rw'}2.  \] At its smooth center, $w'(0)=0$ and, writing $c=w(0)$, \[  0<c\leq \ell \sqrt{2n},\qquad w''(0)=\frac{c}{2n}, \qquad |A|(0)=\frac{c}{2\sqrt n}.  \] The dilation flow has tip height $c\sqrt t$ and curvature $c/(2\sqrt{nt})$ at its tip. Thus the one-half time scale occurs in radial hypersurface examples in every dimension. Proof Orthogonal symmetry in Proposition 16.25.2 makes $U$ radial. At $r>0$ its Hessian has eigenvalues $w''$ in the radial direction and $w'/r$ in the $n-1$ orthogonal directions, while the coefficient matrix has radial eigenvalue $(1+(w')^2)^{-1}$ and tangential eigenvalues one. This gives the equation. Smooth radial symmetry gives $DU(0)=0$ and $D^2U(0)=\alpha I$. The equation at the origin gives $n\alpha =c/2$. Comparison with the zero cone gives $u\geq 0$. Its initial trace is positive away from the origin. At any fixed positive time the solution is strictly positive by the classical local strong maximum principle: on positive-time cylinders the graph equation is a smooth uniformly parabolic scalar equation, and an interior zero would force zero at earlier positive times in the connected domain. Chaining overlapping bounded cylinders contradicts locally uniform convergence to the nonzero initial trace. This standard parabolic principle is used as background, not proved here. Hence $c>0$. The height bound at the origin gives $c\leq \ell \sqrt{2n}$. Since the graph metric at the origin is Euclidean, the second fundamental form has $n$ equal principal curvatures in absolute value $c/(2n)$; its norm is $c/(2\sqrt n)$. Dilation by $\sqrt t$ proves both time formulas. No global convexity or classification of all rotational immersions is needed for these conclusions. $\square$

title: 5.8 Countable tests for distributional currents
search_title: Countable tests for distributional currents
section: 5.8 Countable tests for distributional currents
text: Slicing produces order-one currents before the finite-mass estimate is known. Countable tests must therefore approximate first derivatives as well as coefficients. The following functional-analytic step expands the density argument used in [ Sim18 ] , Chapter 6, p. 183. Lemma 5.8.1 (Countable tests in the first-derivative topology) . 2CA69E1442BF For every open $W\subset \mathbb R^ N$ and form degree $q\geq 0$, there is a countable set of smooth compactly supported $q$-forms in $W$ such that every smooth test is approximated in the $C^1$ norm by a sequence from this set, with all sequence supports in one compact subset of $W$. There is also such a countable set within the comass unit ball which is dense among tests with comass at most one. See the countable-density step in [ Sim18 ] , Lemma 4.5. Proof Fix a nonnegative smooth compactly supported scalar convolution kernel. Extend each test coefficient by zero to $\mathbb R^ N$ and convolve at rational positive scales tending to zero. A smooth compactly supported function and its first derivatives converge uniformly under this operation; for sufficiently small scales all supports remain in a fixed compact subset of $W$. For a fixed scale, approximate the convolution integral and all its first derivatives by finite Riemann sums with rational centers. Uniform continuity of the kernel and its first derivatives, together with compact integration support, justifies both approximations simultaneously. Replace the finitely many real coefficients of the sums by rational numbers, changing the $C^1$ error by an arbitrarily small amount. Finite rational combinations of rational-scale kernels centered at rational points form a countable collection. Retain only combinations supported in $W$, and apply this to each component of the form. For the unit-comass assertion, also allow division by positive rational constants. Given an approximant $\eta _ j$ to a unit-comass test, uniform convergence implies $\sup _ x\| \eta _ j(x)\| _*\leq 1+o(1)$. Choose a rational divisor $r_ j\geq \max \{ 1,\sup _ x\| \eta _ j(x)\| _*\} $ with $r_ j\to 1$. Then $\eta _ j/r_ j$ has comass at most one and still converges in $C^1$ on the common compact support. This preserves countability. Add zero and negatives if needed. $\square$ Proposition 5.8.2 (Mass as a countable supremum for order-one currents) . 470B6DE01C14 Let $B$ be a $q$-current on $W$ satisfying, for each compact $K\subset W$, an estimate $|B(\omega )|\leq C_ K\| \omega \| _{C^1}$ for tests supported in $K$. For the countable unit-comass family $\{ \omega _ j\} $ of Lemma 5.8.1 , chosen to include zero and negatives, \[  \mathbf M_ W(B)=\sup _ j B(\omega _ j),  \] allowing infinite mass. If $t\mapsto B_ t(\omega )$ is measurable for every test and each $B_ t$ has this order-one property, then $t\mapsto \mathbf M_ W(B_ t)$ is measurable. This formalizes the testing step in the slicing estimates of [ Sim18 ] , Section 4. Proof Every chosen test is admissible in the definition of mass, giving one inequality. Conversely approximate any unit-comass test by the family in $C^1$ with common compact support. The assumed estimate implies convergence of its evaluations, so its value is bounded by the countable supremum. Taking the supremum over all tests proves the reverse inequality. The supremum of countably many measurable functions is measurable, which proves the last assertion. No uniformity in the constants $C_ K$ as $t$ varies is required. $\square$

The passage from a smooth cutoff to a Lipschitz slicing function requires convergence on the rectifiable support, which can have zero ambient volume. We make this step explicit. The source is [ Sim18 ] , Chapter 6, Lemma 4.5, pp. 182–183; the countable $C^1$ decomposition of rectifiable sets and the Euclidean area formula remain background inputs. Proposition 5.9.1 (Scalar coarea on a rectifiable curve) . 36CCCA6345A8 Let $M\subset U\subset \mathbb R^ N$ be a measurable countably one-rectifiable set of locally finite $\mathcal H^1$ measure, and let $f:U	o \mathbb R$ be locally Lipschitz. Define $
abla ^ Mf$ by differentiating on $C^1$ curve pieces. For every nonnegative measurable $g$, \[  \int _ M g|
abla ^ Mf|\, d\mathcal H^1 =\int _{\mathbb R}\sum _{x\in M\cap f^{-1}(t)}g(x)\, dt.  \] The formula is understood with measurable representatives; exceptional null subsets of $M$ contribute zero for almost every $t$. In particular the critical part $\{ 
abla ^ Mf=0\} $ contributes no points to almost every fiber. This is the counting-measure endpoint of the scalar coarea identity used in [ Sim18 ] , Chapter 6, Lemma 4.1. Proof Use the countable $C^1$ decomposition to partition $M$, up to an $\mathcal H^1$-null set, into disjoint measurable pieces contained in injective regular curve charts $\gamma :I	o \mathbb R^ N$. Subdivide the charts so that they and their inverses on their images are Lipschitz on the relevant relatively compact intervals. The weighted area formula, Proposition 3.3.1 , first gives arclength integration with factor $|\gamma '|$. The ordinary chain rule for the Lipschitz function $f\circ \gamma $ gives \[  |(f\circ \gamma )'|=|
abla ^ Mf|\, |\gamma '|  \] almost everywhere on each piece. Apply the one-dimensional weighted area formula to $f\circ \gamma $, inserting the indicator of that piece and the weight $g\circ \gamma $. The resulting sum counts exactly its points at level $t$, since $\gamma $ is injective. Sum over the disjoint pieces by Tonelli. The omitted null set has an $\mathcal L^1$-null image under the locally Lipschitz scalar map, by the Hausdorff-measure Lipschitz bound on a countable compact cover. Thus it affects no almost-everywhere assertion. Setting $g$ equal to the critical-set indicator proves the final assertion. This endpoint does not require applying the strict inequality $k<m$ in Theorem 3.3.3 with $k=m=1$. $\square$ Lemma 5.9.2 (Weak tangential convergence of ambient mollifications) . 4AAAD381706B Let $M$ be countably $m$-rectifiable with locally finite $\mathcal H^ m$ measure, and let $d\mu =	heta \, d\mathcal H^ m\llcorner M$ be locally finite, where $	heta \geq 0$ is measurable. Suppose $h$ is locally Lipschitz in an ambient open neighborhood. On a fixed compact subset, let $h_\varepsilon $ be smooth ambient mollifications of $h$. If $v$ is a $\mu $-integrable tangent vector field supported in that compact set, then \[  \lim _{\varepsilon \downarrow 0}\int _ M v\cdot 
abla ^ Mh_\varepsilon \, d\mu =\int _ M v\cdot 
abla ^ Mh\, d\mu .  \] This is a weak convergence statement against fixed $L^1(\mu )$ fields. It does not assert pointwise convergence of ambient derivatives on $M$. See [ Sim18 ] , p. 182, equation (1) in the proof of Lemma 4.5. Proof Localize to a slightly larger compact neighborhood on which $h$ has a finite Lipschitz constant $L$. A cutoff and an extension can be used before convolution; sufficiently small convolution radii give uniform convergence to $h$ and a uniform gradient bound on the compact set being tested. First work in a relatively compact regular $C^1$ chart $F:V\subset \mathbb R^ m	o M_ j$, with $DF$ and the inverse metric bounded. The functions $h_\varepsilon \circ F$ converge uniformly to $h\circ F$, while their first derivatives are uniformly bounded. For a smooth compactly supported scalar test $a$, integration by parts gives \[  \int _ V a\, \partial _ i(h_\varepsilon \circ F) =-\int _ V(\partial _ i a)(h_\varepsilon \circ F) \longrightarrow \int _ V a\, \partial _ i(h\circ F).  \] Approximation of an $L^1$ test by smooth tests, together with the uniform derivative bound, extends this convergence to every fixed $L^1$ coefficient. Expressing $v\cdot 
abla ^ Mh_\varepsilon $ in chart coordinates introduces only bounded coefficients from $DF$ and the inverse metric. The factor $	heta $ and the chart area density are absorbed into the $L^1$ test; the indicator of a measurable rectifiable piece is absorbed there as well. No derivative of a merely continuous chart metric is taken. Partition $M$ into disjoint measurable pieces covered by such charts, using the countable $C^1$ decomposition. A finite number of compact chart pieces captures all but an arbitrarily small amount of $\int |v|\, d\mu $. On that remainder both tangential gradients have the same uniform bound, so the difference of the integrals is bounded by a constant times this small tail. First pass to the limit on the finite union, then let the tail tend to zero. This proves the assertion for the original field. $\square$ Lemma 5.9.3 (Smooth scalar chain rule on a rectifiable support) . 15EB78009E28 Under the preceding rectifiability hypotheses, let $f$ be locally Lipschitz and $Q\in C^1(\mathbb R)$. Then \[  
abla ^ M(Q\circ f)=Q'(f)
abla ^ Mf \quad \mathcal H^ m	ext{-almost everywhere on }M.  \] On each compact set where $f$ and $Q'$ are bounded, the composition is Lipschitz. This is the smooth-outer-function case of the chain rule in [ Sim18 ] , Chapter 6, p. 183, equation (4). Proof In each $C^1$ chart the Lipschitz function $f\circ F$ is differentiable almost everywhere by Theorem 3.1.2 . The ordinary chain rule there gives $D(Q\circ f\circ F)=Q'(f\circ F)D(f\circ F)$. Passing from coordinate differentials to the tangential gradient proves the identity on that chart. The countable decomposition removes a single $\mathcal H^ m$-null set. The mean value theorem bounds the Lipschitz constant of the composition on each relevant compact neighborhood. $\square$ Definition 5.9.4 (Tangential contraction of a rectifiable current) . 058A5F0F3915 Let $T=\llbracket M,	heta ,	au rbracket $ be an integer rectifiable $m$-current of locally finite mass, $m\geq 1$, and let $h$ be locally Lipschitz. Set \[  (T\llcorner d^ Mh)(\omega ) =\int _ M\langle 	au ,d^ Mh\wedge \omega angle 	heta \, d\mathcal H^ m.  \] Here $d^ Mh$ can be extended to the ambient cotangent space by zero on the normal space; any extension gives the same evaluation on $	au $. Its mass measure is bounded by $|
abla ^ Mh|\, \| T\| $. This convention extends the smooth contraction in Definition 5.3.4 ; compare [ Sim18 ] , Chapter 6, equation (4.3) and the proof of Lemma 4.5. Proposition 5.9.5 (Boundary of a Lipschitz scalar restriction) . 79C5D9AEC72E Let $T=\llbracket M,	heta ,	au rbracket $ be locally integer rectifiable and locally normal, with $m\geq 1$, and let $h$ be locally Lipschitz. Then \[  \partial (T\llcorner h)=(\partial T)\llcorner h-T\llcorner d^ Mh.  \] Thus $T\llcorner h$ is locally normal, although its multiplicities need not be integers, and \[  \| \partial (T\llcorner h)\|  \leq |h|\, \| \partial T\| +|
abla ^ Mh|\, \| T\| .  \] These are measure inequalities on relatively compact sets. The argument expands the Lipschitz approximation step in [ Sim18 ] , Lemma 4.5, pp. 182–183. Proof Fix a smooth compactly supported $(m-1)$-form $\omega $. Apply Proposition 5.3.5 to ambient mollifications $h_\varepsilon $. Uniform convergence on the support of the tests gives convergence of $(T\llcorner h_\varepsilon )(d\omega )$ and $((\partial T)\llcorner h_\varepsilon )(\omega )$, since both currents have locally finite mass. The remaining term is \[  \int _ M\langle 	au ,d^ Mh_\varepsilon \wedge \omega angle \, d\| T\| .  \] Its integrand is the pairing of $
abla ^ Mh_\varepsilon $ with a fixed bounded measurable tangent field determined by $	au $ and $\omega $. Lemma 5.9.2 gives its limit. This proves the current identity. Contraction of a unit simple $m$-vector with a covector of norm $a$ has mass norm at most $a$; the integral representation therefore gives the stated bound on every Borel set by domination of vector-measure variation. The right side is locally finite. Integer multiplicity of $T$ also ensures locally finite $\mathcal H^ m$ on its nonzero multiplicity support, as required in the tangential-calculus lemmas. $\square$

Lemma 5.9.2 (Weak tangential convergence of ambient mollifications) . 4AAAD381706B Let $M$ be countably $m$-rectifiable with locally finite $\mathcal H^ m$ measure, and let $d\mu =	heta \, d\mathcal H^ m\llcorner M$ be locally finite, where $	heta \geq 0$ is measurable. Suppose $h$ is locally Lipschitz in an ambient open neighborhood. On a fixed compact subset, let $h_\varepsilon $ be smooth ambient mollifications of $h$. If $v$ is a $\mu $-integrable tangent vector field supported in that compact set, then \[  \lim _{\varepsilon \downarrow 0}\int _ M v\cdot 
abla ^ Mh_\varepsilon \, d\mu =\int _ M v\cdot 
abla ^ Mh\, d\mu .  \] This is a weak convergence statement against fixed $L^1(\mu )$ fields. It does not assert pointwise convergence of ambient derivatives on $M$. See [ Sim18 ] , p. 182, equation (1) in the proof of Lemma 4.5. Proof Localize to a slightly larger compact neighborhood on which $h$ has a finite Lipschitz constant $L$. A cutoff and an extension can be used before convolution; sufficiently small convolution radii give uniform convergence to $h$ and a uniform gradient bound on the compact set being tested. First work in a relatively compact regular $C^1$ chart $F:V\subset \mathbb R^ m	o M_ j$, with $DF$ and the inverse metric bounded. The functions $h_\varepsilon \circ F$ converge uniformly to $h\circ F$, while their first derivatives are uniformly bounded. For a smooth compactly supported scalar test $a$, integration by parts gives \[  \int _ V a\, \partial _ i(h_\varepsilon \circ F) =-\int _ V(\partial _ i a)(h_\varepsilon \circ F) \longrightarrow \int _ V a\, \partial _ i(h\circ F).  \] Approximation of an $L^1$ test by smooth tests, together with the uniform derivative bound, extends this convergence to every fixed $L^1$ coefficient. Expressing $v\cdot 
abla ^ Mh_\varepsilon $ in chart coordinates introduces only bounded coefficients from $DF$ and the inverse metric. The factor $	heta $ and the chart area density are absorbed into the $L^1$ test; the indicator of a measurable rectifiable piece is absorbed there as well. No derivative of a merely continuous chart metric is taken. Partition $M$ into disjoint measurable pieces covered by such charts, using the countable $C^1$ decomposition. A finite number of compact chart pieces captures all but an arbitrarily small amount of $\int |v|\, d\mu $. On that remainder both tangential gradients have the same uniform bound, so the difference of the integrals is bounded by a constant times this small tail. First pass to the limit on the finite union, then let the tail tend to zero. This proves the assertion for the original field. $\square$

text: Lemma 5.9.3 (Smooth scalar chain rule on a rectifiable support) . 15EB78009E28 Under the preceding rectifiability hypotheses, let $f$ be locally Lipschitz and $Q\in C^1(\mathbb R)$. Then \[  \nabla ^ M(Q\circ f)=Q'(f)\nabla ^ Mf \quad \mathcal H^ m\text{-almost everywhere on }M.  \] On each compact set where $f$ and $Q'$ are bounded, the composition is Lipschitz. This is the smooth-outer-function case of the chain rule in [ Sim18 ] , Chapter 6, p. 183, equation (4). Proof In each $C^1$ chart the Lipschitz function $f\circ F$ is differentiable almost everywhere by Theorem 3.1.2 . The ordinary chain rule there gives $D(Q\circ f\circ F)=Q'(f\circ F)D(f\circ F)$. Passing from coordinate differentials to the tangential gradient proves the identity on that chart. The countable decomposition removes a single $\mathcal H^ m$-null set. The mean value theorem bounds the Lipschitz constant of the composition on each relevant compact neighborhood. $\square$

text: Definition 5.9.4 (Tangential contraction of a rectifiable current) . 058A5F0F3915 Let $T=\llbracket M,\theta ,\tau \rrbracket $ be an integer rectifiable $m$-current of locally finite mass, $m\geq 1$, and let $h$ be locally Lipschitz. Set \[  (T\llcorner d^ Mh)(\omega ) =\int _ M\langle \tau ,d^ Mh\wedge \omega \rangle \theta \, d\mathcal H^ m.  \] Here $d^ Mh$ can be extended to the ambient cotangent space by zero on the normal space; any extension gives the same evaluation on $\tau $. Its mass measure is bounded by $|\nabla ^ Mh|\, \| T\| $. This convention extends the smooth contraction in Definition 5.3.4 ; compare [ Sim18 ] , Chapter 6, equation (4.3) and the proof of Lemma 4.5.

title: Proposition 5.9.5 (Boundary of a Lipschitz scalar restriction)
search_title: Boundary of a Lipschitz scalar restriction
section: 5.9 Tangential Lipschitz calculus for currents
text: Proposition 5.9.5 (Boundary of a Lipschitz scalar restriction) . 79C5D9AEC72E Let $T=\llbracket M,\theta ,\tau \rrbracket $ be locally integer rectifiable and locally normal, with $m\geq 1$, and let $h$ be locally Lipschitz. Then \[  \partial (T\llcorner h)=(\partial T)\llcorner h-T\llcorner d^ Mh.  \] Thus $T\llcorner h$ is locally normal, although its multiplicities need not be integers, and \[  \| \partial (T\llcorner h)\|  \leq |h|\, \| \partial T\| +|\nabla ^ Mh|\, \| T\| .  \] These are measure inequalities on relatively compact sets. The argument expands the Lipschitz approximation step in [ Sim18 ] , Lemma 4.5, pp. 182–183. Proof Fix a smooth compactly supported $(m-1)$-form $\omega $. Apply Proposition 5.3.5 to ambient mollifications $h_\varepsilon $. Uniform convergence on the support of the tests gives convergence of $(T\llcorner h_\varepsilon )(d\omega )$ and $((\partial T)\llcorner h_\varepsilon )(\omega )$, since both currents have locally finite mass. The remaining term is \[  \int _ M\langle \tau ,d^ Mh_\varepsilon \wedge \omega \rangle \, d\| T\| .  \] Its integrand is the pairing of $\nabla ^ Mh_\varepsilon $ with a fixed bounded measurable tangent field determined by $\tau $ and $\omega $. Lemma 5.9.2 gives its limit. This proves the current identity. Contraction of a unit simple $m$-vector with a covector of norm $a$ has mass norm at most $a$; the integral representation therefore gives the stated bound on every Borel set by domination of vector-measure variation. The right side is locally finite. Integer multiplicity of $T$ also ensures locally finite $\mathcal H^ m$ on its nonzero multiplicity support, as required in the tangential-calculus lemmas. $\square$

section: 5.10 Geometric slices and their boundary identity
text:
We separate the geometric level set, the distributional boundary, and the argument identifying them outside one null set. This supplies the boundary-identification argument used in Theorem 5.4.2 . Rectifiable coarea, the countable $C^1$ decomposition, and the almost-everywhere fiber tangent assertion are now developed locally, with locally proved Euclidean area/coarea and Whitney extension retained as inputs. These are the geometric ingredients in [ Sim18 ] , Chapter 6, Lemmas 4.1 and 4.5, pp. 180–183. Lemma 5.10.1 (Orientation of a codimension-one fiber) . BD53F1D000B3 Let $P$ be an oriented $m$-plane, $m\geq 1$, with unit simple orientation $	au $, and let $v\in P$ be a unit vector. Define $	au \mathbin {\lrcorner }v$ by \[  \langle 	au \mathbin {\lrcorner }v,\omega angle =\langle 	au ,v^ lat \wedge \omega angle .  \] It is the unit simple orientation of $P\cap v^\perp $ characterized by $v\wedge (	au \mathbin {\lrcorner }v)=	au $. When $m=1$, it is the signed unit zero-vector. This is the linear algebra in [ Sim18 ] , equation (4.3). Proof For $m\geq 2$, choose an oriented orthonormal basis $(v,e_2,\ldots ,e_ m)$ of $P$. Then $	au =v\wedge e_2\wedge \cdots \wedge e_ m$, and evaluation on basis forms shows that contraction is $e_2\wedge \cdots \wedge e_ m$. For $m=1$, write $	au =\sigma v$ with $\sigma \in \{ 1,-1\} $. The contraction is the scalar $\sigma \in \Lambda ^0P$, which gives the same identity and unit norm. These formulas give simplicity, norm one, the tangent plane, and the asserted orientation identity. $\square$ Definition 5.10.2 (The geometric level current) . E6A04ADFDFCA Let $T=\llbracket M,	heta ,	au rbracket $ be a locally integer rectifiable $m$-current of locally finite mass in an open set $U$, $m\geq 1$, and let $f:U	o \mathbb R$ be locally Lipschitz. Write \[  M_ t=\{ x\in M:f(x)=t,\  |
abla ^ Mf(x)|>0\} ,\qquad S_ t=\llbracket M_ t,	heta ,	au \mathbin {\lrcorner } (
abla ^ Mf/|
abla ^ Mf|)rbracket .  \] This is defined at the almost-everywhere levels where the fiber is rectifiable, its tangent plane is $T_ xM\cap \ker d^ Mf_ x$, and its weighted mass is locally finite. Values on the exceptional levels are not specified by this definition. See [ Sim18 ] , Lemma 4.1 and Definition 4.4. Proposition 5.10.3 (Mass and integration of geometric slices) . 39945FA00011 The geometric level currents exist for almost every $t$. For every Borel $E\subset U$, \[  \int _{\mathbb R}\| S_ t\| (E)\, dt =\int _ E|
abla ^ Mf|\, d\| T\| .  \] For a smooth compactly supported $(m-1)$-form $\omega $ and $\psi \in C_ c^\infty (\mathbb R)$, \[  \int _{\mathbb R}\psi (t)S_ t(\omega )\, dt =\int _ M\psi (f)\langle 	au ,d^ Mf\wedge \omega angle \, d\| T\| .  \] These are the mass and signed coarea identities underlying [ Sim18 ] , Lemma 4.5(1). Proof For $m\geq 2$, use weighted rectifiable coarea, Corollary 3.3.4 . For $m=1$, use Proposition 5.9.1 . For $m\geq 2$, the almost-everywhere tangent-plane assertion is proved in Theorem 3.10.6 , corresponding to the fiber input in [ Sim18 ] , Lemma 4.1. In dimension one a locally finite fiber consists of isolated points and has the zero-dimensional tangent. Lemma 5.10.1 makes the prescribed orientation unit and simple. The multiplicity is the positive integer $	heta $, so the mass measure is exactly $	heta \mathcal H^{m-1}\llcorner M_ t$. Coarea with weight $	heta \chi _ E$ proves the mass identity, including infinite values. With $E$ in a compact exhaustion, local Lipschitz bounds and local mass finiteness show that the slice has locally finite mass for almost every $t$, simultaneously on all compact subsets. For the signed identity, insert the weight \[  	heta \psi (f)\left\langle 	au \mathbin {\lrcorner }  rac{
abla ^ Mf}{|
abla ^ Mf|},\omega ightangle  \] on the noncritical part and set it to zero elsewhere. Its absolute value after multiplication by $|
abla ^ Mf|$ is integrable on the compact support of $\omega $. Signed coarea and the contraction identity therefore give the formula. Critical points contribute zero almost everywhere in the level, so this convention causes no missing term. $\square$ Lemma 5.10.4 (An integrated identity for the distributional slice) . 4D3D3D80B610 Assume also that $T$ is locally normal, and put $B_ t=\partial (T\llcorner \{ f<t\} )-(\partial T)\llcorner \{ f<t\} $. For every test $(m-1)$-form $\omega $ and $\psi \in C_ c^\infty (\mathbb R)$, \[  \int _{\mathbb R}\psi (t)B_ t(\omega )\, dt =\int _{\mathbb R}\psi (t)S_ t(\omega )\, dt.  \] The left-hand side exists without assuming finite mass of $B_ t$. This is an integrated version of the approximation argument in [ Sim18 ] , Lemma 4.5(2). Proof Set $Q(s)=\int _ s^\infty \psi (t)\, dt$. Fubini, applied to the locally finite measures representing $T$ and $\partial T$ on the test support, gives \[  \int \psi (t)B_ t(\omega )\, dt =(T\llcorner Q(f))(d\omega ) -((\partial T)\llcorner Q(f))(\omega ).  \] The composition $Q(f)$ is locally Lipschitz. Proposition 5.9.5 identifies this difference with $-(T\llcorner d^ M(Q(f)))(\omega )$. Since $Q'=-\psi $, Lemma 5.9.3 changes the negative sign to a positive one and gives \[  \int _ M\psi (f)\langle 	au ,d^ Mf\wedge \omega angle \, d\| T\| .  \] Proposition 5.10.3 identifies this with the required integral of $S_ t$. The two scalar functions of $t$ are measurable and locally integrable: the first is bounded by the local masses times the $C^1$ norm of $\omega $, and the second is locally integrable by coarea. $\square$ Proposition 5.10.5 (A single exceptional null set for all test forms) . 38E741B69B67 Under the preceding assumptions there is a Lebesgue-null set $N\subset \mathbb R$ such that \[  B_ t=S_ t\quad 	ext{as currents for every }t
otin N.  \] Thus equality is not merely an almost-everywhere assertion with a different exceptional set for each test form. This expands the countable-density step in [ Sim18 ] , p. 183. Proof For a fixed test form $\omega $, Lemma 5.10.4 says that the locally integrable function $B_ t(\omega )-S_ t(\omega )$ has zero pairing with every smooth compactly supported scalar function. Lemma 3.4.4 makes it zero almost everywhere. Choose countable $C^1$-dense test families on a relatively compact exhaustion of $U$ using Lemma 5.8.1 . The approximants have a common slightly larger compact support. Remove the null exceptional set for each member of all these countable families, together with the set where $S_ t$ fails to have locally finite mass. For each remaining $t$, a test supported in a compact $K$ satisfies \[  |B_ t(\omega )|\leq \| T\| (K)\| d\omega \| _{*,\infty } +\| \partial T\| (K)\| \omega \| _{*,\infty }, \qquad |S_ t(\omega )|\leq \| S_ t\| (K)\| \omega \| _{*,\infty }.  \] Use the slightly larger compact set for the same estimates on approximating forms. $C^1$ convergence therefore extends equality from the chosen countable family to every test. The removed set is countable union of null sets, proving the claim. The $C^1$ topology is necessary here because the distributional expression for $B_ t$ contains $d\omega $ before its finite-mass representation is established. $\square$ Proposition 5.10.6 (Integral restrictions and integral slice boundaries) . 8D661A656C0A If $T$ is locally integral, then for almost every $t$ both $T\llcorner \{ f<t\} $ and $S_ t$ are locally integral. For $m\geq 2$, \[  \partial S_ t=-S_ t^{\partial T},  \] where $S_ t^{\partial T}$ denotes the geometric slice constructed from $\partial T$. For $m=1$ the boundary of the zero-current $S_ t$ is zero. See [ Sim18 ] , Lemma 4.5(2)–(3). Proof Apply Proposition 5.10.5 to $T$. If $m\geq 2$, also apply it to $\partial T$, which is locally integer rectifiable and locally normal because $\partial ^2T=0$. Intersect the two full-measure sets of good levels. Taking a distributional boundary in the identity for $S_ t$ gives \[  \partial S_ t=-\partial ((\partial T)\llcorner \{ f<t\} ) =-S_ t^{\partial T}.  \] The latter is integer rectifiable with locally finite mass. Thus $S_ t$ and its boundary are integer rectifiable and locally finite, which is precisely local integrality. In dimension one its boundary vanishes by convention, giving the same conclusion directly. The restriction $T\llcorner \{ f<t\} $ is integer rectifiable, and \[  \partial (T\llcorner \{ f<t\} )=(\partial T)\llcorner \{ f<t\} +S_ t  \] has the same properties and locally finite mass. Hence the restriction is locally integral. No compactness theorem is needed for these deductions. $\square$

section: 5.11 Flat continuity and exceptional slicing levels
text: The lower and upper slices are meaningful as distributional currents even at exceptional levels. Their flat norm is controlled by the mass in a thin slab. Throughout this section $T$ is a compactly supported normal $m$-current in $\mathbb R^ N$, $m\geq 1$, and $f$ is locally Lipschitz near its support. Flat norms are the real-current norms of Definition 5.3.14 . These deductions refine the distinction between the two one-sided slices in [ Sim18 ] , equations (4.6)–(4.10), pp. 184–185. Definition 5.11.1 (Lower and upper distributional slices) . 2303BA9586EA For every real $t$, set \[  B_ t^- =\partial (T\llcorner \{ f<t\} )-(\partial T)\llcorner \{ f<t\} , \qquad B_ t^+ =-\partial (T\llcorner \{ f>t\} )+(\partial T)\llcorner \{ f>t\} .  \] Since $\partial T=\partial (T\llcorner \mathbb R^ N)$, the upper slice can also be written \[  B_ t^+=\partial (T\llcorner \{ f\leq t\} )-(\partial T)\llcorner \{ f\leq t\} .  \] Neither formula alone guarantees finite mass at every level. They agree with the usual geometric slice at almost every level when $T$ is integral. The signs agree with [ Sim18 ] , equations (4.6)–(4.7). Proposition 5.11.2 (Support and finite flat norm at every level) . 775CD4FED890 Both $B_ t^-$ and $B_ t^+$ are compactly supported currents with \[  \operatorname {spt}B_ t^\pm \subset \operatorname {spt}T\cap \{ f=t\} , \qquad \mathcal F_{\mathbb R}(B_ t^\pm ) \leq \mathbf M(T)+\mathbf M(\partial T).  \] Finite flat norm here does not imply finite mass. Compare the support assertion in [ Sim18 ] , equation (4.8). Proof For the lower slice use the flat decomposition with filling $T\llcorner \{ f<t\} $ and residual $-(\partial T)\llcorner \{ f<t\} $. Both have finite mass and compact support in $\operatorname {spt}T$, since $\operatorname {spt}\partial T\subset \operatorname {spt}T$. This proves the norm bound. Use the sublevel formula with $\leq $ for the upper slice. On the open set $\{ f<t\} $, the lower slice acts as $\partial T-\partial T=0$; on $\{ f>t\} $, both terms vanish. These statements are local: every test compactly supported in either open set has that same property on the support of its derivative. A partition of unity for a compact test support disjoint from the level extends this to all tests off $\{ f=t\} $. The same argument applies to the upper slice. Tests off $\operatorname {spt}T$ vanish as well, proving the inclusion. $\square$ Proposition 5.11.3 (A slab controls the flat change of a slice) . 93AF8799FE31 For $s<t$, \[  B_ t^- -B_ s^- =\partial (T\llcorner \{ s\leq f<t\} ) -(\partial T)\llcorner \{ s\leq f<t\} ,  \] and hence, with $\mu =\| T\| +\| \partial T\| $, \[  \mathcal F_{\mathbb R}(B_ t^- -B_ s^-) \leq \mu (\{ s\leq f<t\} ).  \] The analogous upper-slice bound uses $\{ s<f\leq t\} $. This is a flat-norm consequence of the restriction identities in [ Sim18 ] , equations (4.6)–(4.7). Proof Subtract the two lower-sublevel definitions and use the exact indicator identity $\chi _{\{ f<t\} }-\chi _{\{ f<s\} }=\chi _{\{ s\leq f<t\} }$. The two resulting terms are an admissible real flat decomposition. Their mass sum is at most the displayed slab measure. Subtracting the closed-sublevel formulas for the upper slices gives the stated alternative. title: 5.12 Mass bounds for slices of normal currents

section: 5.12 Mass bounds for slices of normal currents
text: Normal currents need not have rectifiable supports, so one cannot define a tangential derivative on such a support by invoking rectifiable charts. We instead prove the slicing mass bound first for smooth functions and then pass to Lipschitz functions through non-atomic levels. The argument develops [ Sim18 ] , Chapter 6, equations (4.6)–(4.11), pp. 184–185. All currents in this section have compact support in $\mathbb R^ N$, and all flat norms have real coefficients. Lemma 5.12.1 (Integrated smooth slicing for a normal current) . C59EE864BFBB Let $T$ be a normal $m$-current, $m\geq 1$, and $f\in C^\infty (\mathbb R^ N)$. Write $B_ t=B_ t^-$ for its lower distributional slice. For every test $(m-1)$-form $\omega $ and every $\psi \in C_ c^\infty (\mathbb R)$, \[  \int \psi (t)B_ t(\omega )\, dt=T(\psi (f)\, df\wedge \omega ).  \] Consequently the signed measure \[  A\longmapsto T(\chi _{f^{-1}(A)}df\wedge \omega )  \] has Lebesgue density $B_ t(\omega )$. This is the integrated form of [ Sim18 ] , equation (4.11). Proof Put $Q(s)=\int _ s^\infty \psi (t)\, dt$. Fubini gives the difference $(T\llcorner Q(f))(d\omega )-((\partial T)\llcorner Q(f))(\omega )$. The smooth scalar product rule, Proposition 5.3.5 , identifies it with $-T(d(Q(f))\wedge \omega )=T(\psi (f)df\wedge \omega )$. The scalar function $B_ t(\omega )$ is measurable and bounded by a fixed multiple of the two finite masses. It vanishes outside a bounded interval containing $f(\operatorname {spt}T)$: below that interval the restrictions vanish, while above it the two terms cancel. Thus it defines a finite signed measure. The right side is also a finite signed measure of the level variable. Equality on all smooth scalar tests implies equality as measures, by uniform density in continuous compactly supported tests and uniqueness in Riesz representation. This proves the final assertion without assuming a mass bound for $B_ t$ in advance. $\square$ Proposition 5.12.2 (Smooth slicing bounds the integral of mass) . DB4040635707 Under the preceding assumptions, for every open $W\subset \mathbb R^ N$ and Borel $A\subset \mathbb R$, \[  \int _ A\mathbf M_ W(B_ t)\, dt \leq \int _{W\cap f^{-1}(A)}|Df|\, d\| T\| .  \] The integrand is measurable, with infinity allowed before the estimate is proved. In particular $B_ t$ has finite mass for almost every level. Compare [ Sim18 ] , equations (4.9)–(4.10). Proof Each $B_ t$ has order at most one on every compact support, directly from its definition in terms of $T(d\omega )$ and $\partial T(\omega )$. Proposition 5.8.2 therefore provides a countable family $\{ \omega _ j\} _{j\geq 1}$ of smooth $(m-1)$-forms compactly supported in $W$, each of comass at most one, with $\mathbf M_ W(B_ t)=\sup _ j B_ t(\omega _ j)$. Include zero as the first test and include negatives. This test-space construction is independent of rectifiability. For the first $k$ tests, partition $A$ into disjoint measurable sets $A_1,\ldots ,A_ k$ on which the corresponding test realizes their maximum, breaking ties by the smallest index. By Lemma 5.12.1 , \[  \int _ A\max _{1\leq j\leq k}B_ t(\omega _ j)\, dt =\sum _{j=1}^ k T(\chi _{f^{-1}(A_ j)}df\wedge \omega _ j) \leq \int _{W\cap f^{-1}(A)}|Df|\, d\| T\| .  \] Indeed the inverse images of the $A_ j$ are disjoint, and $df\wedge \omega _ j$ has comass at most $|Df|$. This bound holds for arbitrary polar $m$-vectors by mass/comass duality; simplicity is unnecessary. Ensure zero is the first test, so the maxima are nonnegative and increase. Monotone convergence as $k\to \infty $ gives the result and measurability. Taking $W=\mathbb R^ N$ makes the right side finite because $T$ has compact support and $Df$ is bounded there. $\square$ Lemma 5.12.3 (Continuity under uniform perturbation of the slicing function) . 945B4DB69E85 Let $T$ be compactly supported and normal, and suppose $f_ j,f$ are continuous near its support and $f_ j\to f$ uniformly there. If \[  (\| T\| +\| \partial T\| )(\{ f=t\} )=0,  \] then their lower distributional slices satisfy \[  \mathcal F_{\mathbb R}(B_ t^{f_ j}-B_ t^ f)\longrightarrow 0.  \] The lower slices are defined by their restrictions even when they have infinite mass. This justifies the approximation in the final paragraph of [ Sim18 ] , Chapter 6, Section 4. Proof Let $\delta _ j=\sup _{\operatorname {spt}T}|f_ j-f|$. The symmetric difference of the two strict sublevels is contained in $\{ |f-t|\leq \delta _ j\} $ on the current support. Subtraction of the defining formulas gives a flat decomposition with filling $T\llcorner (\chi _{\{ f_ j<t\} }-\chi _{\{ f<t\} })$ and residual the negative analogous restriction of $\partial T$. Their mass sum is at most \[  (\| T\| +\| \partial T\| )(\{ |f-t|\leq \delta _ j\} ).  \] This tends to zero by finiteness of the measure and the assumed zero mass on the level. The conclusion also holds when some $\delta _ j=0$, by equality of the restrictions. Uniform approximation is used with respect to the current's support, rather than almost everywhere in ambient volume. $\square$ Theorem 5.12.4 (Lipschitz slicing of compact normal currents) . A55702EC34C6 Let $T$ be a compactly supported normal $m$-current in $\mathbb R^ N$, $m\geq 1$, and let $f:\mathbb R^ N\to \mathbb R$ be $L$-Lipschitz. For almost every $t$, the common lower and upper slice $B_ t$ is a compactly supported normal $(m-1)$-current. For every open $W$, \[  \int _{\mathbb R}\mathbf M_ W(B_ t)\, dt\leq L\| T\| (W).  \] If $m\geq 2$, then $\partial B_ t=-B_ t^{\partial T}$ at almost every level and \[  \int _{\mathbb R}\mathbf M_ W(\partial B_ t)\, dt \leq L\| \partial T\| (W).  \] For $m=1$, the slice boundary is zero. No rectifiability or integer-multiplicity conclusion is asserted. These are the normal-current slicing estimates of [ Sim18 ] , equations (4.8)–(4.10), with compact support used to state global mass integrals. Proof Let $f_ j$ be standard smooth ambient mollifications with radii tending to zero. Proposition 3.4.7 gives uniform convergence to $f$ and $|Df_ j|\leq L$. The finite measure $f_\# (\| T\| +\| \partial T\| )$ has at most countably many atoms. At every other level, Lemma 5.12.3 gives flat, hence weak, convergence of the corresponding slices. For fixed open $W$, mass is lower semicontinuous under weak convergence: it is the supremum of the continuous evaluations on tests of comass at most one supported in $W$. Fatou and Proposition 5.12.2 yield \[  \int \mathbf M_ W(B_ t^ f)\, dt \leq \liminf _ j\int \mathbf M_ W(B_ t^{f_ j})\, dt \leq L\| T\| (W).  \] Measurability follows from the same countable test family as in that proposition, applied to the order-one restriction formula. Taking $W=\mathbb R^ N$ proves finite mass at almost every level. The support is compact by Proposition 5.11.2 . When $m\geq 2$, repeat the mass argument for the normal current $\partial T$, whose boundary is zero. At every level the distributional algebra gives $\partial B_ t^ T=-B_ t^{\partial T}$. On the intersection of the two full-measure finite-mass sets this proves normality and the boundary integral estimate. In dimension one a zero-current has zero boundary, so the first mass conclusion already proves normality. Finally the two one-sided slices agree off the at most countable atomic set by Theorem 5.11.4 . The quantitative measure inequality holds for each $W$; the full-measure set on which slices are normal is chosen once using their global masses. $\square$ Corollary 5.12.5 (Almost every restriction of a normal current is normal) . AF626DCD5933 Under Theorem 5.12.4 , $T\llcorner \{ f<t\} $ is normal for almost every $t$, with \[  \partial (T\llcorner \{ f<t\} )=(\partial T)\llcorner \{ f<t\} +B_ t.  \] For every finite interval $(a,b)$ and every $\varepsilon >0$, a good level can be chosen in that interval, outside any prescribed null set, with \[  \mathbf M(B_ t)\leq \frac{L\mathbf M(T)}{b-a}+\varepsilon .  \] This is the normal-current analogue of the radius selection used for integral currents; see [ Sim18 ] , equation (4.10). Proof The restriction always has mass at most $\mathbf M(T)$. At a level of finite slice mass, its defining boundary formula has two finite-mass terms and gives normality. The integral of slice mass over $(a,b)$ is no larger than its full integral $L\mathbf M(T)$. If every good level outside the prescribed null set violated the stated bound, integration over the interval would contradict this inequality. The assertion uses a convenient global bound; it makes no claim of optimality for the chosen interval. $\square$ Corollary 5.12.6 (The mass bound uses only the intervening slab) . E8DFE6BF543E Under Theorem 5.12.4 , for every open $W$ and $a<b$, \[  \int _ a^ b\mathbf M_ W(B_ t)\, dt \leq L\| T\| (W\cap \{ a<f<b\} ).  \] For $m\geq 2$, the corresponding boundary integral is at most $L\| \partial T\| (W\cap \{ a<f<b\} )$. Thus the good-level bound in Corollary 5.12.5 can be sharpened to $L\| T\| (\{ a<f<b\} )/(b-a)+\varepsilon $. This is the interval estimate in [ Sim18 ] , equation (4.10). Proof The set $W'=W\cap \{ a<f<b\} $ is open. Since $B_ t$ is supported on $f^{-1}(t)$, its mass in $W'$ equals its mass in $W$ for $a<t<b$, and vanishes otherwise. Apply Theorem 5.12.4 with $W'$ and integrate over all levels. The same support argument applies to the boundary slice. Averaging over $(a,b)$ proves the strengthened level-selection estimate. In particular the masses on the two endpoint levels are not added to the open-slab right side. $\square$ Proposition 5.12.7 (Smooth localization commutes with slicing) . EED6DE376EB8 Let $T$ be a locally normal $m$-current on $U$, $m\geq 1$, let $f$ be locally Lipschitz, and let $\chi \in C_ c^\infty (U)$. At every level, as distributional currents, \[  B_ t^{\chi T}=\chi B_ t^ T.  \] The same holds for upper slices. Here multiplication of an arbitrary distributional current by $\chi $ means evaluation on $\chi $ times the test form. This localization expands the local formulation of [ Sim18 ] , equations (4.6)–(4.10). Proof The Leibniz identity $\partial (\chi R)=\chi \partial R-R\llcorner d\chi $ holds distributionally by evaluating on a test form and expanding $d(\chi \omega )$; no finite mass of $\partial R$ is required. Apply it to $R=T\llcorner \{ f<t\} $. On subtracting the restriction of $\partial (\chi T)=\chi \partial T-T\llcorner d\chi $, the two contractions cancel, because smooth contraction and Borel restriction of the finite-mass current $T$ commute. What remains is exactly $\chi B_ t^ T$. Closed sublevels give the upper-slice formula. $\square$ Theorem 5.12.8 (Local slicing of locally normal currents) . 963FC6952BFC Let $T$ be a locally normal $m$-current on $U\subset \mathbb R^ N$, $m\geq 1$, and let $f:U\to \mathbb R$ be locally Lipschitz. Outside a single Lebesgue-null set of levels, its slice is locally normal, is supported in $\operatorname {spt}T\cap f^{-1}(t)$, and satisfies \[  \partial B_ t^ T=-B_ t^{\partial T}\quad (m\geq 2).  \] If $V\Subset U$ is open and $f$ is $L$-Lipschitz on an open neighborhood of $\overline V$, then \[  \int _{\mathbb R}\mathbf M_ V(B_ t^ T)\, dt\leq L\| T\| (V).  \] The analogous bound for its boundary holds with $\| \partial T\| $ when $m\geq 2$. This is the local normal-current setting of [ Sim18 ] , pp. 184–185. Proof First fix such a neighborhood and choose a smooth cutoff $0\leq \chi \leq 1$ supported there, equal to one near $\overline V$. The current $\chi T$, extended by zero to $\mathbb R^ N$, is compactly supported and normal by the smooth product rule. Proposition 3.4.2 extends the restriction of $f$ on that neighborhood to a globally $L$-Lipschitz function $\widetilde f$; explicitly one can take the infimum of $f(y)+L|x-y|$ over points $y$ in the neighborhood. It equals $f$ there by its Lipschitz inequality. Apply Theorem 5.12.4 to $(\chi T,\widetilde f)$. Proposition 5.12.7 identifies its slice with that of $T$ on $V$. On this open set $\| \chi T\| =\| T\| $ and $\| \partial (\chi T)\| =\| \partial T\| $, because $\chi =1$ on a neighborhood. This proves the stated local mass estimates and normality on $V$ at almost every level. Cover $U$ by countably many relatively compact balls on neighborhoods of which $f$ is Lipschitz. Remove the null sets furnished for those balls and, when needed, for $\partial T$. Local normality then holds simultaneously throughout $U$. The distributional boundary identity follows by $\partial ^2=0$ exactly as in the compact case. The support statement is local: on the open strict sublevel the two terms cancel, on the open strict superlevel they vanish, and tests off $\operatorname {spt}T$ vanish. This gives the conclusion even when neither $T$ nor its boundary has finite total mass in $U$. $\square$

This justifies the approximation in the final paragraph of [ Sim18 ] , Chapter 6, Section 4. Proof Let $\delta _ j=\sup _{\operatorname {spt}T}|f_ j-f|$. The symmetric difference of the two strict sublevels is contained in $\{ |f-t|\leq \delta _ j\} $ on the current support. Subtraction of the defining formulas gives a flat decomposition with filling $T\llcorner (\chi _{\{ f_ j<t\} }-\chi _{\{ f<t\} })$ and residual the negative analogous restriction of $\partial T$. Their mass sum is at most \[  (\| T\| +\| \partial T\| )(\{ |f-t|\leq \delta _ j\} ).  \] This tends to zero by finiteness of the measure and the assumed zero mass on the level. The conclusion also holds when some $\delta _ j=0$, by equality of the restrictions. Uniform approximation is used with respect to the current's support, rather than almost everywhere in ambient volume. $\square$

title: Theorem 5.12.4 (Lipschitz slicing of compact normal currents)
search_title: Lipschitz slicing of compact normal currents
section: 5.12 Mass bounds for slices of normal currents
text: Theorem 5.12.4 (Lipschitz slicing of compact normal currents) . A55702EC34C6 Let $T$ be a compactly supported normal $m$-current in $\mathbb R^ N$, $m\geq 1$, and let $f:\mathbb R^ N\to \mathbb R$ be $L$-Lipschitz. For almost every $t$, the common lower and upper slice $B_ t$ is a compactly supported normal $(m-1)$-current. For every open $W$, \[  \int _{\mathbb R}\mathbf M_ W(B_ t)\, dt\leq L\| T\| (W).  \] If $m\geq 2$, then $\partial B_ t=-B_ t^{\partial T}$ at almost every level and \[  \int _{\mathbb R}\mathbf M_ W(\partial B_ t)\, dt \leq L\| \partial T\| (W).  \] For $m=1$, the slice boundary is zero. No rectifiability or integer-multiplicity conclusion is asserted. These are the normal-current slicing estimates of [ Sim18 ] , equations (4.8)–(4.10), with compact support used to state global mass integrals. Proof Let $f_ j$ be standard smooth ambient mollifications with radii tending to zero. Proposition 3.4.7 gives uniform convergence to $f$ and $|Df_ j|\leq L$. The finite measure $f_\# (\| T\| +\| \partial T\| )$ has at most countably many atoms. At every other level, Lemma 5.12.3 gives flat, hence weak, convergence of the corresponding slices. For fixed open $W$, mass is lower semicontinuous under weak convergence: it is the supremum of the continuous evaluations on tests of comass at most one supported in $W$. Fatou and Proposition 5.12.2 yield \[  \int \mathbf M_ W(B_ t^ f)\, dt \leq \liminf _ j\int \mathbf M_ W(B_ t^{f_ j})\, dt \leq L\| T\| (W).  \] Measurability follows from the same countable test family as in that proposition, applied to the order-one restriction formula. Taking $W=\mathbb R^ N$ proves finite mass at almost every level. The support is compact by Proposition 5.11.2 . When $m\geq 2$, repeat the mass argument for the normal current $\partial T$, whose boundary is zero. At every level the distributional algebra gives $\partial B_ t^ T=-B_ t^{\partial T}$. On the intersection of the two full-measure finite-mass sets this proves normality and the boundary integral estimate. In dimension one a zero-current has zero boundary, so the first mass conclusion already proves normality. Finally the two one-sided slices agree off the at most countable atomic set by Theorem 5.11.4 . The quantitative measure inequality holds for each $W$; the full-measure set on which slices are normal is chosen once using their global masses. $\square$

title: Corollary 5.12.5 (Almost every restriction of a normal current is normal)

section: 5.12 Mass bounds for slices of normal currents
text: Corollary 5.12.5 (Almost every restriction of a normal current is normal) . AF626DCD5933 Under Theorem 5.12.4 , $T\llcorner \{ f<t\} $ is normal for almost every $t$, with \[  \partial (T\llcorner \{ f<t\} )=(\partial T)\llcorner \{ f<t\} +B_ t.  \] For every finite interval $(a,b)$ and every $\varepsilon >0$, a good level can be chosen in that interval, outside any prescribed null set, with \[  \mathbf M(B_ t)\leq \frac{L\mathbf M(T)}{b-a}+\varepsilon .  \] This is the normal-current analogue of the radius selection used for integral currents; see [ Sim18 ] , equation (4.10). Proof The restriction always has mass at most $\mathbf M(T)$. At a level of finite slice mass, its defining boundary formula has two finite-mass terms and gives normality. The integral of slice mass over $(a,b)$ is no larger than its full integral $L\mathbf M(T)$. If every good level outside the prescribed null set violated the stated bound, integration over the interval would contradict this inequality. The assertion uses a convenient global bound; it makes no claim of optimality for the chosen interval. $\square$

text: Corollary 5.12.6 (The mass bound uses only the intervening slab) . E8DFE6BF543E Under Theorem 5.12.4 , for every open $W$ and $a<b$, \[  \int _ a^ b\mathbf M_ W(B_ t)\, dt \leq L\| T\| (W\cap \{ a<f<b\} ).  \] For $m\geq 2$, the corresponding boundary integral is at most $L\| \partial T\| (W\cap \{ a<f<b\} )$. Thus the good-level bound in Corollary 5.12.5 can be sharpened to $L\| T\| (\{ a<f<b\} )/(b-a)+\varepsilon $. This is the interval estimate in [ Sim18 ] , equation (4.10). Proof The set $W'=W\cap \{ a<f<b\} $ is open. Since $B_ t$ is supported on $f^{-1}(t)$, its mass in $W'$ equals its mass in $W$ for $a<t<b$, and vanishes otherwise. Apply Theorem 5.12.4 with $W'$ and integrate over all levels. The same support argument applies to the boundary slice. Averaging over $(a,b)$ proves the strengthened level-selection estimate. In particular the masses on the two endpoint levels are not added to the open-slab right side. $\square$

title: Proposition 5.12.7 (Smooth localization commutes with slicing)
search_title: Smooth localization commutes with slicing
section: 5.12 Mass bounds for slices of normal currents
text: Proposition 5.12.7 (Smooth localization commutes with slicing) . EED6DE376EB8 Let $T$ be a locally normal $m$-current on $U$, $m\geq 1$, let $f$ be locally Lipschitz, and let $\chi \in C_ c^\infty (U)$. At every level, as distributional currents, \[  B_ t^{\chi T}=\chi B_ t^ T.  \] The same holds for upper slices. Here multiplication of an arbitrary distributional current by $\chi $ means evaluation on $\chi $ times the test form. This localization expands the local formulation of [ Sim18 ] , equations (4.6)–(4.10). Proof The Leibniz identity $\partial (\chi R)=\chi \partial R-R\llcorner d\chi $ holds distributionally by evaluating on a test form and expanding $d(\chi \omega )$; no finite mass of $\partial R$ is required. Apply it to $R=T\llcorner \{ f<t\} $. On subtracting the restriction of $\partial (\chi T)=\chi \partial T-T\llcorner d\chi $, the two contractions cancel, because smooth contraction and Borel restriction of the finite-mass current $T$ commute. What remains is exactly $\chi B_ t^ T$. Closed sublevels give the upper-slice formula. $\square$

text: Theorem 5.12.8 (Local slicing of locally normal currents) . 963FC6952BFC Let $T$ be a locally normal $m$-current on $U\subset \mathbb R^ N$, $m\geq 1$, and let $f:U\to \mathbb R$ be locally Lipschitz. Outside a single Lebesgue-null set of levels, its slice is locally normal, is supported in $\operatorname {spt}T\cap f^{-1}(t)$, and satisfies \[  \partial B_ t^ T=-B_ t^{\partial T}\quad (m\geq 2).  \] If $V\Subset U$ is open and $f$ is $L$-Lipschitz on an open neighborhood of $\overline V$, then \[  \int _{\mathbb R}\mathbf M_ V(B_ t^ T)\, dt\leq L\| T\| (V).  \] The analogous bound for its boundary holds with $\| \partial T\| $ when $m\geq 2$. This is the local normal-current setting of [ Sim18 ] , pp. 184–185. Proof First fix such a neighborhood and choose a smooth cutoff $0\leq \chi \leq 1$ supported there, equal to one near $\overline V$. The current $\chi T$, extended by zero to $\mathbb R^ N$, is compactly supported and normal by the smooth product rule. Proposition 3.4.2 extends the restriction of $f$ on that neighborhood to a globally $L$-Lipschitz function $\widetilde f$; explicitly one can take the infimum of $f(y)+L|x-y|$ over points $y$ in the neighborhood. It equals $f$ there by its Lipschitz inequality. Apply Theorem 5.12.4 to $(\chi T,\widetilde f)$. Proposition 5.12.7 identifies its slice with that of $T$ on $V$. On this open set $\| \chi T\| =\| T\| $ and $\| \partial (\chi T)\| =\| \partial T\| $, because $\chi =1$ on a neighborhood. This proves the stated local mass estimates and normality on $V$ at almost every level. Cover $U$ by countably many relatively compact balls on neighborhoods of which $f$ is Lipschitz. Remove the null sets furnished for those balls and, when needed, for $\partial T$. Local normality then holds simultaneously throughout $U$. The distributional boundary identity follows by $\partial ^2=0$ exactly as in the compact case. The support statement is local: on the open strict sublevel the two terms cancel, on the open strict superlevel they vanish, and tests off $\operatorname {spt}T$ vanish. This gives the conclusion even when neither $T$ nor its boundary has finite total mass in $U$. $\square$
