section: 16.26 Examples of slicing, jumps and cancellation
text: These calculations distinguish flat convergence from mass convergence and show why exceptional levels and integrality hypotheses cannot be omitted. They use the scalar slicing conventions of [ Sim18 ] , Chapter 6, Section 4. Example 16.26.1 (Endpoint jumps for the rectangle) . D3422C8E82DC Let $T=\llbracket [0,1]^2,e_1\wedge e_2\rrbracket $ and $f(x,y)=x$, as in Example 5.4.5 . Denote by $I_ t$ the upward-oriented segment $\{ t\} \times [0,1]$. At the two endpoints, \[  B_0^-=0,\qquad B_0^+=I_0,\qquad B_1^-=I_1,\qquad B_1^+=0.  \] Thus the lower slice jumps from the right at zero and is left continuous at one. The two jumps come entirely from boundary mass on the cutting level, since $\| T\| (\{ f=0\} )=\| T\| (\{ f=1\} )=0$. Proof At zero the open sublevel contains no mass of $T$ or $\partial T$, so $B_0^-=0$. The closed sublevel contains no two-dimensional mass, but the boundary restriction is the left edge with downward orientation, namely $-I_0$. Hence $B_0^+=I_0$. At one, the open restriction of $T$ is all of $T$, while the boundary restriction is $\partial T-I_1$, giving $B_1^-=I_1$. The closed sublevel contains both currents completely, so $B_1^+=0$. These direct computations agree with the jump identity in Theorem 5.11.4 . The interior values $B_ t^-=B_ t^+=I_ t$, $0<t<1$, were computed in Example 5.4.5 . $\square$ Example 16.26.2 (A closed current can jump at a flat cap) . 32A4AD5A3DA5 In $\mathbb R^3$, let $H$ be the outward-oriented upper unit hemisphere and let $D$ be the unit disk in $\{ z=0\} $ oriented by $e_1\wedge e_2$. The integral current $T=\llbracket H\rrbracket -\llbracket D\rrbracket $ is a cycle. For $f(x,y,z)=z$, its level-zero slices satisfy \[  B_0^-=0,\qquad B_0^+=-\llbracket \partial D\rrbracket .  \] Here $\partial T=0$, so the jump comes entirely from the positive mass $\| T\| (\{ f=0\} )=\pi $ of the flat cap. For $0<t<1$, the slice is the clockwise circle of radius $\sqrt{1-t^2}$ at height $t$, and its mass is $2\pi \sqrt{1-t^2}$. Proof Stokes' theorem gives $\partial \llbracket H\rrbracket =\partial \llbracket D\rrbracket $, with counterclockwise boundary orientation viewed from above. Thus $\partial T=0$. The strict sublevel at zero contains no current mass, while the closed sublevel restriction is $-\llbracket D\rrbracket $, giving the claimed two values. For $0<t<1$, the part above $t$ is an outward-oriented spherical cap, whose boundary is the counterclockwise horizontal circle. Since the full current is closed, the boundary of the sublevel restriction is its negative. This proves the orientation and the length formula. The flat-norm jump is nonzero because its current is nonzero, by Proposition 5.3.15 ; it is at most $\pi $, using the disk as a filling. The example shows why both $\| T\| $ and $\| \partial T\| $ occur in the exceptional-level measure. $\square$ Example 16.26.3 (An integral current with a dense set of slice jumps) . FAA366BBDAFD There exists a compactly supported integral two-current in $\mathbb R^2$, with finite mass and finite boundary mass, whose lower slices by the coordinate $f(x,y)=x$ have a dense set of discontinuities in $(0,1)$ in real flat norm. This is consistent with their one-sided continuity and bounded total flat variation. Proof Enumerate the rationals in $(0,1)$ without repetitions as $q_ j$, $j\geq 1$. Put $h_ j=2^{-j-2}$ and \[  Q_ j=[q_ j,q_ j+h_ j]\times [2^{-j},2^{-j}+h_ j],\qquad T=\sum _{j=1}^\infty \llbracket Q_ j,e_1\wedge e_2\rrbracket .  \] The vertical bands of the squares are disjoint. All squares lie in a fixed compact rectangle, and \[  \sum _ j\mathbf M(\llbracket Q_ j\rrbracket )=\sum _ j h_ j^2=1/48, \qquad \sum _ j\mathbf M(\partial \llbracket Q_ j\rrbracket )=4\sum _ jh_ j=1.  \] The series and its boundary therefore converge in mass. Their explicit disjoint oriented area and edge representations have integer multiplicity, so $T$ is integral and normal. The accumulation line $y=0$ contributes no mass to either representation and no extra boundary: evaluating on a test and its derivative commutes with the absolutely convergent series. For any $t$, $T\llcorner \{ x=t\} =0$ because a vertical line has zero two-dimensional area. At $t=q_ j$, the boundary restriction includes the downward left edge of $Q_ j$. All other vertical edges at the same level lie in disjoint vertical bands. The horizontal edges meet that level in sets of zero length. Hence $(\partial T)\llcorner \{ x=q_ j\} $ is a nonzero current: a test localized near an interior point of the indicated left edge detects it and avoids all other bands. The jump formula in Theorem 5.11.4 now gives a nonzero jump at every $q_ j$. Nondegeneracy of the real flat norm makes each an actual flat discontinuity. Their set is dense. Proposition 5.11.5 still bounds the sum of the flat jump sizes by the finite total mass and boundary mass. Thus countability of exceptional levels does not imply that they are isolated. $\square$ Proposition 16.26.4 (The exact flat norm of two opposite point masses) . A7B2C05EB916 For $p,q\in \mathbb R^ N$, \[  \mathcal F_{\mathbb R}(\delta _ p-\delta _ q)=\min \{ |p-q|,2\} .  \] The norm is the real-current flat norm of Definition 5.3.14 ; no identification with an integer-polyhedral completion is required. This is an elementary example of the flat estimates accompanying the current operations in [ Sim18 ] , Chapter 6, Section 2. Proof An oriented segment from $q$ to $p$ fills the difference with mass $|p-q|$. Alternatively take the difference itself as residual, with mass at most two. These decompositions prove the upper bound. If $p=q$, the conclusion follows immediately. For the lower bound, set $e=(p-q)/|p-q|$ and $c=(p+q)/2$. The function \[  a(x)=\max \{ -1,\min \{ 1,e\cdot (x-c)\} \}   \] has absolute value at most one, Lipschitz constant at most one, and $a(p)-a(q)=\min \{ |p-q|,2\} $. Mollification gives smooth functions with the same two bounds and uniform convergence to $a$. Multiply them by cutoffs equal to one on a large ball containing $p,q$, bounded by one, and with gradients tending uniformly to zero as the ball grows. The resulting compactly supported tests $a_ j$ satisfy $\| a_ j\| _\infty \leq 1$, $\| Da_ j\| _\infty \leq 1+o(1)$ and the desired limiting difference of values. Proposition 5.3.15 applied to $a_ j/(1+o(1))$ proves the lower bound. This argument uses only the test bound for flat decompositions, not a general dual representation theorem for the flat norm. $\square$ Example 16.26.5 (A circle loses slice mass continuously in flat norm) . 6964E8EEA7B9 Let $T$ be the counterclockwise integration current of the circle of radius $R>0$ in $\mathbb R^2$, and set $f(x,y)=x$. For $|t|<R$, put $h_ t=\sqrt{R^2-t^2}$. Then \[  S_ t=\delta _{(t,-h_ t)}-\delta _{(t,h_ t)},\qquad \mathbf M(S_ t)=2,\qquad \mathcal F_{\mathbb R}(S_ t)=\min \{ 2h_ t,2\} .  \] At $t=\pm R$ both one-sided distributional slices are zero. Therefore $S_ t\to 0$ in flat norm as $t\to R$ from below, while the masses remain two. The coarea identity reads \[  \int _{\mathbb R}\mathbf M(S_ t)\, dt=4R =\int _{\operatorname {spt}T}|\nabla ^ Tf|\, d\mathcal H^1.  \] This illustrates scalar current slicing and the lower semicontinuity, rather than continuity, of mass. Proof Parametrize the circle by $\gamma (\alpha )=(R\cos \alpha ,R\sin \alpha )$ with increasing $\alpha $. Its unit tangent is $(-\sin \alpha ,\cos \alpha )$. The tangential derivative of $f$ is positive at the bottom point and negative at the top point, giving the stated signs by Lemma 5.10.1 . The points are distinct for $|t|<R$, hence their total variation is two. Their distance is $2h_ t$, so Proposition 16.26.4 gives the exact flat norm. The boundary of the circle current vanishes. At $R$ the strict sublevel contains the whole circle except one zero-mass point, so its restriction equals $T$ and its boundary is zero. At $-R$ the strict sublevel restriction is zero. Closed sublevels give the same currents because the endpoint singletons have zero length. This proves the endpoint statements directly. Finally the mass integral is twice the interval length $2R$. In the angular parametrization the other side is $R\int _0^{2\pi }|\sin \alpha |\, d\alpha =4R$. No value assigned at the two endpoints affects this integral. $\square$ Example 16.26.6 (A level atom need not create a slice jump) . D7C0B5AAB701 Let $T$ be the rightward integration current of $[0,1]\times \{ 0\} $ and let $f(x,y)=y$. Then $B_ t^-=B_ t^+=0$ for every $t$, although \[  (\| T\| +\| \partial T\| )(\{ f=0\} )=3.  \] Thus the countable atomic set in Theorem 5.11.4 can be strictly larger than the actual jump set. Proof The mass of $T$ is one, and its boundary consists of two opposite endpoint masses with total variation two. Both measures are supported on $f=0$. Every strict or closed sublevel either includes the entire pair $T,\partial T$ or includes neither. In the former case the slice is $\partial T-\partial T=0$; in the latter it is zero as well. Equivalently the jump formula at zero is $\partial (T\llcorner \{ f=0\} )-(\partial T)\llcorner \{ f=0\} =0$. Tangentially, $f$ is constant on the segment and its derivative is zero. $\square$ Example 16.26.7 (Diffuse slices of a diffuse normal current) . B8C720A93B65 Let $T$ be the normal two-current on $[0,1]^4$ from Example 16.14.2 , and take $f(x)=x_1$. For $0<t<1$, its distributional slice is the one-current \[  B_ t(\eta )=\int _{[0,1]^3}\eta _2(t,x_2,x_3,x_4)\, dx_2dx_3dx_4.  \] Its mass is one and its boundary mass is two. It is normal but not a rectifiable one-current. Thus slicing a normal current does not in itself produce integral or rectifiable slices. Proof For $\eta =\sum _ i\eta _ i dx_ i$, evaluate $\partial (T\llcorner \{ x_1<t\} )(\eta )$ by integrating $\partial _1\eta _2-\partial _2\eta _1+\partial _3\eta _4-\partial _4\eta _3$ over $[0,t]\times [0,1]^3$. The fundamental theorem of calculus gives the new face at $x_1=t$ plus the old faces with their restricted ranges. Subtracting $(\partial T)\llcorner \{ x_1<t\} $ cancels exactly those old faces. The remaining term is the stated formula. Its polar vector is $e_2$ and its mass measure is three-dimensional Lebesgue measure on the slice cube, so the mass is one. Applying its boundary to a scalar test differentiates only in $x_2$, producing the difference of two unit two-dimensional face measures; these are disjoint, giving boundary mass two. A countably one-rectifiable subset of that three-dimensional affine hyperplane has zero three-dimensional volume, by Lemma 16.14.4 and the same null-set cover argument as in Proposition 16.14.5 . Its mass therefore cannot be concentrated on any such set. This is an explicit normal-current calculation, and it does not apply the geometric slicing theorem outside its integer-rectifiability hypotheses. $\square$

text: Example 16.26.5 (A circle loses slice mass continuously in flat norm) . 6964E8EEA7B9 Let $T$ be the counterclockwise integration current of the circle of radius $R>0$ in $\mathbb R^2$, and set $f(x,y)=x$. For $|t|<R$, put $h_ t=\sqrt{R^2-t^2}$. Then \[  S_ t=\delta _{(t,-h_ t)}-\delta _{(t,h_ t)},\qquad \mathbf M(S_ t)=2,\qquad \mathcal F_{\mathbb R}(S_ t)=\min \{ 2h_ t,2\} .  \] At $t=\pm R$ both one-sided distributional slices are zero. Therefore $S_ t\to 0$ in flat norm as $t\to R$ from below, while the masses remain two. The coarea identity reads \[  \int _{\mathbb R}\mathbf M(S_ t)\, dt=4R =\int _{\operatorname {spt}T}|\nabla ^ Tf|\, d\mathcal H^1.  \] This illustrates scalar current slicing and the lower semicontinuity, rather than continuity, of mass. Proof Parametrize the circle by $\gamma (\alpha )=(R\cos \alpha ,R\sin \alpha )$ with increasing $\alpha $. Its unit tangent is $(-\sin \alpha ,\cos \alpha )$. The tangential derivative of $f$ is positive at the bottom point and negative at the top point, giving the stated signs by Lemma 5.10.1 . The points are distinct for $|t|<R$, hence their total variation is two. Their distance is $2h_ t$, so Proposition 16.26.4 gives the exact flat norm. The boundary of the circle current vanishes. At $R$ the strict sublevel contains the whole circle except one zero-mass point, so its restriction equals $T$ and its boundary is zero. At $-R$ the strict sublevel restriction is zero. Closed sublevels give the same currents because the endpoint singletons have zero length. This proves the endpoint statements directly. Finally the mass integral is twice the interval length $2R$. In the angular parametrization the other side is $R\int _0^{2\pi }|\sin \alpha |\, d\alpha =4R$. No value assigned at the two endpoints affects this integral. $\square$

title: Example 16.26.6 (A level atom need not create a slice jump)
search_title: A level atom need not create a slice jump
section: 16.26 Examples of slicing, jumps and cancellation
text: Example 16.26.6 (A level atom need not create a slice jump) . D7C0B5AAB701 Let $T$ be the rightward integration current of $[0,1]\times \{ 0\} $ and let $f(x,y)=y$. Then $B_ t^-=B_ t^+=0$ for every $t$, although \[  (\| T\| +\| \partial T\| )(\{ f=0\} )=3.  \] Thus the countable atomic set in Theorem 5.11.4 can be strictly larger than the actual jump set. Proof The mass of $T$ is one, and its boundary consists of two opposite endpoint masses with total variation two. Both measures are supported on $f=0$. Every strict or closed sublevel either includes the entire pair $T,\partial T$ or includes neither. In the former case the slice is $\partial T-\partial T=0$; in the latter it is zero as well. Equivalently the jump formula at zero is $\partial (T\llcorner \{ f=0\} )-(\partial T)\llcorner \{ f=0\} =0$. Tangentially, $f$ is constant on the segment and its derivative is zero. $\square$

title: Example 16.26.7 (Diffuse slices of a diffuse normal current)

section: 16.26 Examples of slicing, jumps and cancellation
text: Example 16.26.7 (Diffuse slices of a diffuse normal current) . B8C720A93B65 Let $T$ be the normal two-current on $[0,1]^4$ from Example 16.14.2 , and take $f(x)=x_1$. For $0<t<1$, its distributional slice is the one-current \[  B_ t(\eta )=\int _{[0,1]^3}\eta _2(t,x_2,x_3,x_4)\, dx_2dx_3dx_4.  \] Its mass is one and its boundary mass is two. It is normal but not a rectifiable one-current. Thus slicing a normal current does not in itself produce integral or rectifiable slices. Proof For $\eta =\sum _ i\eta _ i dx_ i$, evaluate $\partial (T\llcorner \{ x_1<t\} )(\eta )$ by integrating $\partial _1\eta _2-\partial _2\eta _1+\partial _3\eta _4-\partial _4\eta _3$ over $[0,t]\times [0,1]^3$. The fundamental theorem of calculus gives the new face at $x_1=t$ plus the old faces with their restricted ranges. Subtracting $(\partial T)\llcorner \{ x_1<t\} $ cancels exactly those old faces. The remaining term is the stated formula. Its polar vector is $e_2$ and its mass measure is three-dimensional Lebesgue measure on the slice cube, so the mass is one. Applying its boundary to a scalar test differentiates only in $x_2$, producing the difference of two unit two-dimensional face measures; these are disjoint, giving boundary mass two. A countably one-rectifiable subset of that three-dimensional affine hyperplane has zero three-dimensional volume, by Lemma 16.14.4 and the same null-set cover argument as in Proposition 16.14.5 . Its mass therefore cannot be concentrated on any such set. This is an explicit normal-current calculation, and it does not apply the geometric slicing theorem outside its integer-rectifiability hypotheses. $\square$

title: 2.6 Differentiation for arbitrary Euclidean Radon measures
search_title: Differentiation for arbitrary Euclidean Radon measures
section: 2.6 Differentiation for arbitrary Euclidean Radon measures
text: For a singular Radon measure, a fivefold dilation of a ball may increase its mass without any fixed bound. The Euclidean differentiation theorem therefore needs a covering input stronger than the fivefold selection used for Lebesgue measure. We isolate that input and prove its analytic consequences. The source is [ Sim18 ] , Chapter 1, Lemma 4.5 and Corollary 4.10, printed pp. 21–24. In this section closed balls are used for the covering argument, and the final result is also stated for open balls. Theorem 2.6.1 (Besicovitch selection for Euclidean balls) . D6286EBDCB63 For each $n$ there is an integer $N_ n$ with the following property. Let $\mathcal B$ be a collection of closed balls of positive radii in $\mathbb R^ n$, with bounded centers and bounded radii, and let $A$ be their set of centers. There are at most $N_ n$ finite or countable subcollections $\mathcal B_1,\ldots ,\mathcal B_{N_ n}$ such that each $\mathcal B_ i$ consists of pairwise disjoint balls and \[  A\subset \bigcup _{i=1}^{N_ n}\bigcup _{B\in \mathcal B_ i}B.  \] This is a cited geometric input: [ Sim18 ] , Chapter 1, Lemma 4.5, p. 21, where the proof is referred to [ Fed69 ] . It is not proved by the fivefold covering lemma, and its proof remains external here. The dimension-dependent bound is essential; a bound independent of the number of balls is being asserted. Proposition 2.6.2 (A finite-measure fine cover has an almost-everywhere disjoint selection) . 954642522D63 Let $\lambda $ be a positive Radon measure on $\mathbb R^ n$, let $A$ be a bounded Borel set with $\lambda (A)<\infty $, and let $\mathcal B$ be a family of closed balls centered in $A$ which covers $A$ finely: for each $x\in A$ there are balls in the family centered at $x$ with arbitrarily small positive radii. Then there is a finite or countable pairwise disjoint subfamily $\{ B_ j\} $ such that \[  \lambda \bigl (A\setminus \bigcup _ jB_ j\bigr )=0.  \] This is the symmetric Vitali consequence proved in [ Sim18 ] , Remark 4.4(3), pp. 21–22, in the bounded-set form needed for local applications. Proof If $\lambda (A)=0$, the empty collection suffices. Otherwise restrict to radii at most one and apply Theorem 2.6.1 . Since the at most $N_ n$ unions cover $A$, at least one union of disjoint balls covers a subset of $A$ of measure at least $\lambda (A)/N_ n$. A finite subcollection of that union covers measure at least $\lambda (A)/(2N_ n)$, by continuity from below. Keep those finitely many balls. Their union is closed. For each point of $A$ outside this finite closed union, sufficiently small balls from its original fine cover miss the union. Apply the same argument to the remaining set using only such balls. The newly chosen finite family is disjoint both internally and from all previously chosen balls. At each stage the uncovered measure is multiplied by at most $1-1/(2N_ n)$. If it becomes zero, stop; otherwise continue. The total selected family is countable, is pairwise disjoint, and leaves measure at most $(1-1/(2N_ n))^ k\lambda (A)$ after $k$ stages. Letting $k\to \infty $ proves the result. Closedness of each finite previous union is the reason the next fine cover remains available. $\square$ Proposition 2.6.3 (A maximal estimate without a doubling hypothesis) . B0AF5D98AEEC For a positive Radon measure $\lambda $ on $\mathbb R^ n$ and $g\in L^1(\lambda )$, put \[  M_\lambda g(x)=\sup _{0<r\leq 1} \frac{\int _{\overline{B_ r(x)}}|g|\, d\lambda }{\lambda (\overline{B_ r(x)})},  \] assigning value zero to a ratio with zero denominator. Then $M_\lambda g$ is Borel for a Borel representative of $g$, and for every $t>0$, \[  \lambda (\{ M_\lambda g>t\} )\leq \frac{N_ n}{t}\| g\| _{L^1(\lambda )}.  \] No doubling bound for $\lambda $ is assumed. This is a maximal-function formulation of the covering method behind [ Sim18 ] , Chapter 1, Section 4. Proof For a fixed radius, both ball integrals are Borel functions of the center by integration of the joint Borel ball indicator. On a compact ball both measures are finite. For fixed center, continuity from above of closed balls makes a positive-denominator ratio right continuous in the radius. Thus the displayed supremum can be taken over rational radii in $(0,1)$ together with radius one; zero-denominator terms cannot increase a nonnegative supremum. This proves measurability. For each $x$ in the bounded set $\{ M_\lambda g>t\} \cap B_ R(0)$, take the family of all witness balls centered at $x$ for which the ratio is greater than $t$. Their radii are at most one. Theorem 2.6.1 selects at most $N_ n$ disjoint subfamilies covering these centers. Every selected ball $B$ satisfies $t\lambda (B)<\int _ B|g|\, d\lambda $. Sum this inequality within each disjoint family and then over the families. The measure of the covered centers is bounded above by the sum of the selected ball masses, while each family's integral sum is at most $\| g\| _1$. Therefore the desired bound holds on $B_ R(0)$. Let $R\to \infty $ and use continuity from below. The argument does not enlarge a selected ball, so no comparison between its mass and a dilated ball's mass is needed. $\square$ Theorem 2.6.4 (Absolute oscillation vanishes at almost every Radon-measure point) . 96707809DDCF If $\lambda $ is a positive Radon measure on $\mathbb R^ n$ and $g\in L^1(\lambda )$, then for $\lambda $-almost every $x$, \[  \lim _{r\downarrow 0}\frac{1}{\lambda (\overline{B_ r(x)})} \int _{\overline{B_ r(x)}}|g(y)-g(x)|\, d\lambda (y)=0.  \] This is an absolute-oscillation form of the differentiation conclusion in [ Sim18 ] , Corollary 4.10. Its covering input is the cited Besicovitch theorem above. Proof Almost every point lies in the support of $\lambda $ and has a finite value of $g$. At these points all the denominators are positive. Let $Dg(x)$ be the limsup on the left. It is measurable: the same joint-kernel argument and rational-radius reduction as in Proposition 2.6.3 apply to the locally integrable function $|g(y)-g(x)|$ for fixed $x$. For $\phi \in C_ c(\mathbb R^ n)$, the triangle inequality and continuity at $x$ give \[  Dg(x)\leq M_\lambda (g-\phi )(x)+|g(x)-\phi (x)|.  \] The average oscillation of $\phi $ tends to zero because it is bounded by its supremum oscillation on the shrinking ball, regardless of the measure of that ball. For $\varepsilon >0$, the maximal estimate and Chebyshev's inequality therefore give \[  \lambda (\{ Dg>2\varepsilon \} ) \leq \frac{N_ n+1}{\varepsilon }\| g-\phi \| _{L^1(\lambda )}.  \] Theorem 2.3.8 supplies continuous compactly supported approximants with arbitrarily small right side. Hence this exceptional set has measure zero. Taking a countable sequence $\varepsilon \downarrow 0$ proves $Dg=0$ almost everywhere. This proves the oscillation conclusion from the stated geometric covering input, rather than assuming a doubling property for a potentially singular measure. $\square$ Theorem 2.6.5 (Differentiation of functions relative to a Euclidean Radon measure) . E9D501868A2F Let $\lambda $ be a positive Radon measure on an open set $U\subset \mathbb R^ n$, and let $f\in L^1_{\mathrm{loc}}(\lambda )$. For $\lambda $-almost every $x\in U$, \[  \lim _{r\downarrow 0}\frac{1}{\lambda (B_ r(x))} \int _{B_ r(x)}|f(y)-f(x)|\, d\lambda (y)=0, \qquad \lim _{r\downarrow 0}\frac{1}{\lambda (B_ r(x))} \int _{B_ r(x)}f\, d\lambda =f(x).  \] The denominators are positive at almost every point for all sufficiently small radii. The average conclusion applies componentwise to a finite-dimensional vector-valued function. This is [ Sim18 ] , Chapter 1, Corollary 4.10, pp. 23–24, with the Euclidean covering input isolated in Theorem 2.6.1 . Proof First assume $U=\mathbb R^ n$ and $f\in L^1(\lambda )$. Theorem 2.6.4 gives the closed-ball conclusion. At a point where it holds, fix a sufficiently small open-ball radius $r$ and take radii $s_ k\uparrow r$. Their closed balls increase to $B_ r(x)$. Continuity from below for the denominator and the nonnegative oscillation integral shows that every uniform bound for closed-ball averages at radii below a given scale also holds for open balls below that scale. Therefore the open-ball absolute oscillation tends to zero. The absolute value of the difference between the average of $f$ and $f(x)$ is bounded by that oscillation. For the local statement, exhaust $U$ by relatively compact open sets $V_ j$ and choose larger relatively compact open sets $W_ j$ containing their closures. Restrict $\lambda $ to $W_ j$ and extend this finite Borel measure by zero to $\mathbb R^ n$; it is a Radon measure there. Restrict $f$ to $W_ j$ and set it to zero elsewhere. Local integrability makes this a globally integrable function for the restricted measure. The whole-space result applies. At each point of $V_ j$, all sufficiently small balls lie in $W_ j$, so both integrals and denominators agree with the original ones. A countable union of exceptional null sets finishes the proof. Intersect the finitely many componentwise full-measure sets for a vector-valued function. The unproved geometric input remains Besicovitch selection, not the subsequent analytic differentiation argument. $\square$

u \cdot

title: 4.10 Two phases persist under perimeter blow-up
search_title: Two phases persist under perimeter blow-up
section: 4.10 Two phases persist under perimeter blow-up
text: A compactness limit can lose an entire phase unless both phases have quantitative volume. We derive the needed bounds from the already proved first-power Sobolev inequality. This expands [ Sim18 ] , Chapter 3, Theorem 4.4, printed p. 99, and avoids using the De Giorgi structure theorem in its own blow-up proof. Here $n\geq 2$. Proposition 4.10.1 (The first-power inequality for compactly supported BV functions) . 5D94D6D39FA5 If $u\in BV(\mathbb R^ n)$ has compact support, then \[  \| u\| _{L^{n/(n-1)}(\mathbb R^ n)}\leq |Du|(\mathbb R^ n).  \] The constant is the convenient nonsharp constant in Theorem 7.14.2 . This is the BV version of the Sobolev input in [ Sim18 ] , p. 99. Proof The smooth mollifications with a nonnegative kernel from Lemma 4.2.3 have compact support, converge to $u$ in $L^1$ and have gradient integral at most $|Du|(\mathbb R^ n)$. Apply Theorem 7.14.2 to each mollification. Choose a sequence tending to $u$ almost everywhere and apply Fatou to the power $n/(n-1)$. Taking the appropriate root proves the assertion, including the conclusion that this higher-power norm is finite. $\square$ Corollary 4.10.2 (A cutoff Sobolev estimate for a phase) . 620C34C97991 If $E$ has locally finite perimeter in $U$ and $0\leq \phi \in C_ c^1(U)$, then \[  \left(\int _ E\phi ^{n/(n-1)}\, dx\right)^{(n-1)/n} \leq \int \phi \, d|D\chi _ E|+\int _ E|D\phi |\, dx.  \] No bound on the total volume of $E$ is required. This is the cutoff inequality before equation (10) in [ Sim18 ] , p. 99. Proof By Proposition 4.2.2 , $\phi \chi _ E$, extended by zero, is compactly supported and belongs to $BV(\mathbb R^ n)$. Its variation is at most the sum on the right. Proposition 4.10.1 applies, and $|\phi \chi _ E|^{n/(n-1)}=\phi ^{n/(n-1)}\chi _ E$. This proves the claim using only the distributional product rule. $\square$ Proposition 4.10.3 (A radial volume-perimeter inequality) . A8AC237B1A7E If $B_ R(x)\Subset U$ and $V(r)=|E\cap B_ r(x)|$, then for almost every $0<r<R$, \[  V(r)^{(n-1)/n}\leq |D\chi _ E|(B_ r(x))+V'(r).  \] The same inequality holds for $W(r)=|B_ r(x)\setminus E|$ with the same perimeter measure. This is the radial cutoff passage on printed p. 99 of [ Sim18 ] . Proof Use the smooth radial functions $\phi _\delta $ constructed in Lemma 4.9.4 in Corollary 4.10.2 . Their values lie between zero and one and tend to the indicator of the closed ball. Its sphere is volume-null, so dominated convergence makes the left side tend to $V(r)^{(n-1)/n}$. At radii whose spheres have zero perimeter measure, the first term on the right tends to the open-ball perimeter. At Lebesgue points of $V'$, the second tends to $V'(r)$ by the weighted radial differentiation in that lemma. Both conditions hold almost everywhere. Apply the same argument to the complement for the final assertion. $\square$ Lemma 4.10.4 (A perimeter-support point sees positive volume of both phases) . 863266B2B394 If $x\in \operatorname {supp}|D\chi _ E|$ and $B_ r(x)\Subset U$, then \[  |E\cap B_ r(x)|>0,\qquad |B_ r(x)\setminus E|>0.  \] This is a qualitative support assertion; it does not yet give a uniform density bound. Proof If the first volume were zero, $\chi _ E=0$ almost everywhere on the ball. Its distributional derivative would vanish there by testing the defining integral, contradicting membership in the support. If the second volume were zero, use $\chi _ E=1$ and the fact that the integral of the divergence of a compactly supported field is zero. In both cases the vector derivative and hence its total variation vanish on the ball, which is impossible. $\square$ Lemma 4.10.5 (Integrating a positive radial differential inequality) . CC9DD078E7CD Suppose $V:[0,R)\to [0,\infty )$ is absolutely continuous on compact subintervals, $V(0)=0$, $V(r)>0$ for $r>0$, and \[  V(r)^{(n-1)/n}\leq C V'(r)\quad \text{for almost every }r\in (0,R),  \] where $C>0$. Then $V(r)\geq (r/(nC))^ n$ for every $0<r<R$. Proof The assumed inequality makes $V'\geq 0$ almost everywhere, so $V$ is nondecreasing. On $[\delta ,r]$ with $0<\delta <r<R$, it is bounded away from zero. The absolutely continuous chain rule therefore gives \[  \frac{d}{ds}V(s)^{1/n}=\frac1n V(s)^{-(n-1)/n}V'(s)\geq \frac{1}{nC}  \] almost everywhere on that interval. Integrate, and let $\delta \downarrow 0$. Absolute continuity at zero gives $V(\delta )\to 0$; alternatively the nonnegative term can be discarded before taking this limit. Raising the resulting root inequality to the power $n$ proves the claim at every radius. $\square$ Theorem 4.10.6 (Two-sided phase volume at a reduced-boundary point) . C37DA08B0091 If $x\in \partial ^*E$, then for some $r_0>0$ and all $0<r<r_0$, \[  |E\cap B_ r(x)|\geq c_ n r^ n,\qquad |B_ r(x)\setminus E|\geq c_ n r^ n, \qquad c_ n=(3n)^{-n}.  \] The constant is not sharp. These are the two estimates (10)–(11) in [ Sim18 ] , p. 99; the limiting density $1/2$ requires the subsequent blow-up argument. Proof Use Proposition 4.9.5 and Proposition 4.10.3 to obtain $V^{(n-1)/n}\leq \mu (B_ r)+V'\leq 3V'$ for almost every small radius. Lemma 4.10.4 supplies positivity at every radius, and Lemma 4.9.3 supplies absolute continuity and $V(0)=0$. Apply Lemma 4.10.5 with $C=3$. The argument for $W$ uses the other flux bound and gives the same constant. The intersection of the full-measure sets of good radii suffices for the differential inequalities; their integrated conclusions hold for every small radius. $\square$

title: 4.11 Classifying the reduced-boundary blow-up
search_title: Classifying the reduced-boundary blow-up
section: 4.11 Classifying the reduced-boundary blow-up
text:
Throughout this section $n\geq 2$, and $E$ has locally finite perimeter in an open set $U\subset \mathbb R^ n$. We now classify every subsequential limit using distributional derivatives and the two-phase volume bound. The argument follows the blow-up part of [ Sim18 ] , Chapter 3, Theorem 4.4, printed pp. 98–99, with all signs derived from the project's outward convention $D\chi _ E=-
u \, |D\chi _ E|$. The limiting set will be $\{ y:y\cdot 
u _ E(x)<0\} $. Lemma 4.11.1 (Zero tangential derivatives imply one-dimensional dependence) . FABC4798AB51 Suppose $u\in L^\infty (\mathbb R^ n)$ and $D_ i u=0$ in distributions for $i=1,\ldots ,n-1$. Then there is $h\in L^\infty (\mathbb R)$ such that \[  u(x',s)=h(s)\quad 	ext{for almost every }(x',s)\in \mathbb R^{n-1}	imes \mathbb R.  \] If $u$ is a characteristic function, $h$ is zero or one almost everywhere. This makes explicit the cylindrical-limit step after equation (8) in [ Sim18 ] , p. 98. Proof Convolve $u$ with a standard smooth compactly supported approximate identity on $\mathbb R^ n$. Boundedness makes the convolution well defined even when $u$ is not globally integrable. Each smooth $u_\delta $ has zero derivative in every $x'$ direction, hence is constant on each connected horizontal plane: $u_\delta (x',s)=h_\delta (s)$. On any bounded product $Q	imes I$, with $0<|Q|<\infty $, local $L^1$ convergence of convolutions implies \[  |Q|\int _ I|h_\delta -h_\gamma |\, ds =\int _{Q	imes I}|u_\delta -u_\gamma |\, dx\longrightarrow 0.  \] Thus $h_\delta $ has an $L^1_{\mathrm{loc}}(\mathbb R)$ limit $h$. Limits on overlapping intervals agree, and the uniform bound passes to $h$ by almost-everywhere convergence along a sequence. On every product cylinder $u=h(s)$ in $L^1$, hence almost everywhere; a countable exhaustion gives the global assertion. If $u$ is zero or one almost everywhere, Fubini on any such product shows that $h$ has the same property. $\square$ Lemma 4.11.2 (A one-dimensional monotone phase is a half-space) . A77606036837 Suppose $F\subset \mathbb R^ n$ is measurable, $D_ i\chi _ F=0$ for $i<n$, and $D_ n\chi _ F\leq 0$ in the distributional sense. Then for some $\lambda \in [-\infty ,\infty ]$, \[  F=\{ (x',s):s<\lambda \} \quad 	ext{up to a volume-null set}.  \] The endpoint values mean the empty set and all of $\mathbb R^ n$. text: Lemma 4.11.1 (Zero tangential derivatives imply one-dimensional dependence) . FABC4798AB51 Suppose $u\in L^\infty (\mathbb R^ n)$ and $D_ i u=0$ in distributions for $i=1,\ldots ,n-1$. Then there is $h\in L^\infty (\mathbb R)$ such that \[  u(x',s)=h(s)\quad \text{for almost every }(x',s)\in \mathbb R^{n-1}\times \mathbb R.  \] If $u$ is a characteristic function, $h$ is zero or one almost everywhere. This makes explicit the cylindrical-limit step after equation (8) in [ Sim18 ] , p. 98. Proof Convolve $u$ with a standard smooth compactly supported approximate identity on $\mathbb R^ n$. Boundedness makes the convolution well defined even when $u$ is not globally integrable. Each smooth $u_\delta $ has zero derivative in every $x'$ direction, hence is constant on each connected horizontal plane: $u_\delta (x',s)=h_\delta (s)$. On any bounded product $Q\times I$, with $0<|Q|<\infty $, local $L^1$ convergence of convolutions implies \[  |Q|\int _ I|h_\delta -h_\gamma |\, ds =\int _{Q\times I}|u_\delta -u_\gamma |\, dx\longrightarrow 0.  \] Thus $h_\delta $ has an $L^1_{\mathrm{loc}}(\mathbb R)$ limit $h$. Limits on overlapping intervals agree, and the uniform bound passes to $h$ by almost-everywhere convergence along a sequence. On every product cylinder $u=h(s)$ in $L^1$, hence almost everywhere; a countable exhaustion gives the global assertion. If $u$ is zero or one almost everywhere, Fubini on any such product shows that $h$ has the same property. $\square$

Throughout this section $n\geq 2$, and $E$ has locally finite perimeter in an open set $U\subset \mathbb R^ n$. Weak convergence of derivative measures alone does not imply convergence of their total variations. At a reduced-boundary point, polar alignment prevents the cancellation responsible for that failure. The results below complete the measure and density part of Theorem 4.3.2 . They expand [ Sim18 ] , Chapter 3, Theorem 4.4, equations (12)–(13), printed pp. 99–100. Countable rectifiability of the entire reduced boundary is a further theorem. Lemma 4.12.1 (The distributional derivative of an oriented half-space) . D302EA7F7BB9 For a unit vector $e$ and $H=\{ y:y\cdot e<0\} $, \[  D\chi _ H=-e\, \mathcal H^{n-1}\llcorner e^\perp , \qquad |D\chi _ H|=\mathcal H^{n-1}\llcorner e^\perp .  \] These identities hold locally even though the half-space has infinite total volume and perimeter. Proof Rotate coordinates so $e=e_ n$. For a compactly supported smooth field $X$, Fubini makes every tangential derivative integral zero. In the last coordinate the fundamental theorem of calculus gives \[  \int _ H\operatorname {div}X\, dy =\int _{\mathbb R^{n-1}}X_ n(y',0)\, dy'.  \] The distributional sign convention therefore gives the first formula, using the Euclidean normalization of Hausdorff measure on a plane. Its density vector has unit norm, which gives the variation formula by the polar representation of vector measures. Orthogonal change of variables gives the formula for $e$. $\square$ Proposition 4.12.2 (Aligned polar vectors prevent loss of variation) . 48D884ABF86A Let $\mu _ j$ be positive Radon measures on an open set $V$ with uniformly bounded mass on each relatively compact open subset. Let $|
u _ j|=1$ $\mu _ j$-almost everywhere, fix a unit vector $e$, and suppose \[  \int _ K|
u _ j-e|\, d\mu _ j\longrightarrow 0  \] for every compact $K\subset V$. If the vector measures $-
u _ j\mu _ j$ converge weakly locally to $-e\sigma $, where $\sigma $ is a positive Radon measure, then $\mu _ jightharpoonup \sigma $ locally. This is the no-cancellation step implicit in [ Sim18 ] , equation (12). Proof For a continuous scalar test $\phi $ compactly supported in $K$, \[  \left|\int \phi \, d\mu _ j-\int \phi \, 
u _ j\cdot e\, d\mu _ jight| \leq \| \phi \| _\infty \int _ K|
u _ j-e|\, d\mu _ j\longrightarrow 0.  \] The second integral is the pairing of $-
u _ j\mu _ j$ with the vector test $-\phi e$, so it tends to $\int \phi \, d\sigma $ by the assumed vector convergence. This proves the scalar weak convergence. The explicit polar hypothesis is what rules out mutually cancelling vector directions; weak convergence by itself would not suffice. $\square$ Theorem 4.12.3 (The unique perimeter tangent measure at a reduced-boundary point) . 5B5E0ED1D82A Let $E$ have locally finite perimeter in $U$ and let $x\in \partial ^*E$. For $F_ r(y)=x+ry$, define \[  \mu _{x,r}=r^{1-n}(F_ r^{-1})_\# |D\chi _ E|  \] on the expanding domain $F_ r^{-1}(U)$. Then, locally on $\mathbb R^ n$ as $r\downarrow 0$, \[  \mu _{x,r}ightharpoonup \mathcal H^{n-1}\llcorner 
u _ E(x)^\perp .  \] The limit is for every vanishing scale, with the fixed normalization $r^{1-n}$. This is [ Sim18 ] , equation (12), in outward-normal notation. Proof Write $e=
u _ E(x)$. Theorem 4.11.6 gives local $L^1$ convergence to $\chi _{H_ x}$. The local perimeter bounds from Proposition 4.9.5 , after scaling, allow Proposition 4.2.9 to identify the weak limit of vector derivatives as $D\chi _{H_ x}=-e\mathcal H^{n-1}\llcorner e^\perp $ by Lemma 4.12.1 . On each ball $B_ R$, Lemmas 4.9.1 and 4.9.6 give \[  \int _{B_ R}|
u (x+ry)-e|\, d\mu _{x,r}(y) \leq \sqrt{\varepsilon (rR)}\, \mu _{x,r}(B_ R)\longrightarrow 0.  \] Apply Proposition 4.12.2 along any sequence $r_ j\downarrow 0$ to obtain the asserted scalar weak limit. A contradiction with a fixed continuous compactly supported test rules out failure for the full parameter $r\downarrow 0$. Expanding domains cause no difficulty: every such test and a compact neighborhood of its support lie in the domain for all sufficiently small $r$. $\square$ Corollary 4.12.4 (Exact phase and perimeter densities) . F29DEC9B2073 At each $x\in \partial ^*E$, \[  \lim _{r\downarrow 0} rac{|E\cap B_ r(x)|}{\omega _ n r^ n}= rac12, \qquad \lim _{r\downarrow 0} rac{|D\chi _ E|(B_ r(x))}{\omega _{n-1}r^{n-1}}=1.  \] The nonsharp preliminary two-phase lower bound is thereby improved to an exact limit. This is the density conclusion in [ Sim18 ] , equation (13). Proof Apply the local $L^1$ convergence in Theorem 4.11.6 on $B_1$: the limit half-space occupies exactly half that ball, by reflection. Change variables to obtain the first limit. For the second, Theorem 4.12.3 and the continuity-set consequence of weak Radon-measure convergence give $\mu _{x,r}(B_1)	o \mathcal H^{n-1}(B_1\cap e^\perp )=\omega _{n-1}$. Indeed the sphere $\partial B_1$ intersects $e^\perp $ in a set of zero $(n-1)$-dimensional measure. This argument can also be seen directly by sandwiching the ball indicator between continuous cutoffs of slightly smaller and larger concentric balls, then sending the radius difference to zero. Rescaling gives the displayed perimeter density. $\square$ Corollary 4.12.5 (Perimeter mass outside the tangent cone is negligible) . B79E0A9D9C47 For $x\in \partial ^*E$, put $e=
u _ E(x)$. For every $0<\alpha <1$, \[  \lim _{r\downarrow 0}r^{1-n}|D\chi _ E|  igl (\{ z\in B_ r(x):|(z-x)\cdot e|\geq \alpha |z-x|\}  igr )=0.  \] This is concentration of the perimeter measure about the tangent plane. It is not, by itself, a claim about every point in the topological boundary. Proof Under the change of variables $z=x+ry$, the set is contained in the fixed compact set \[  K=\{ y\in \overline{B_1}:|y\cdot e|\geq \alpha |y|\} .  \] Its intersection with $e^\perp $ is the single point zero. Because $n-1\geq 1$, that point has zero $(n-1)$-dimensional measure. The upper bound for compact sets under weak convergence, applied to Theorem 4.12.3 , therefore yields $\limsup \mu _{x,r}(K)\leq 0$. This proves the assertion. Compact-set upper bounds follow from nonnegative continuous cutoffs and outer regularity, so no boundary regularity of $K$ is being assumed. $\square$ Proposition 4.12.6 (The outward normal converges with the perimeter measure) . BC6FF44C4CE9 Under the same hypotheses, for every compactly supported continuous vector field $X$ on $\mathbb R^ n$, \[  \lim _{r\downarrow 0}r^{1-n} \int X igl ((z-x)/r igr )\cdot 
u (z)\, d|D\chi _ E|(z) =\int _{
u _ E(x)^\perp }X(y)\cdot 
u _ E(x)\, d\mathcal H^{n-1}(y).  \] For sufficiently small $r$ the support of the original test lies in $U$. The formula holds for any measurable unit polar representative $
u $. Proof Write $e=
u _ E(x)$ and use the rescaled variables. The difference between the left integral and $\int X\cdot e\, d\mu _{x,r}$ is bounded by $\| X\| _\infty \int _ K|
u (x+ry)-e|\, d\mu _{x,r}$ on a fixed compact neighborhood $K$ of its support. That error tends to zero by the excess estimate in the proof of Theorem 4.12.3 . The remaining integral converges by that theorem. Changes of the polar field on a perimeter-null set affect none of the integrals. $\square$

This is the density conclusion in [ Sim18 ] , equation (13). Proof Apply the local $L^1$ convergence in Theorem 4.11.6 on $B_1$: the limit half-space occupies exactly half that ball, by reflection. Change variables to obtain the first limit. For the second, Theorem 4.12.3 and the continuity-set consequence of weak Radon-measure convergence give $\mu _{x,r}(B_1)\to \mathcal H^{n-1}(B_1\cap e^\perp )=\omega _{n-1}$. Indeed the sphere $\partial B_1$ intersects $e^\perp $ in a set of zero $(n-1)$-dimensional measure. This argument can also be seen directly by sandwiching the ball indicator between continuous cutoffs of slightly smaller and larger concentric balls, then sending the radius difference to zero. Rescaling gives the displayed perimeter density. $\square$

text: Corollary 4.12.5 (Perimeter mass outside the tangent cone is negligible) . B79E0A9D9C47 For $x\in \partial ^*E$, put $e=\nu _ E(x)$. For every $0<\alpha <1$, \[  \lim _{r\downarrow 0}r^{1-n}|D\chi _ E| \bigl (\{ z\in B_ r(x):|(z-x)\cdot e|\geq \alpha |z-x|\} \bigr )=0.  \] This is concentration of the perimeter measure about the tangent plane. title: 4.13 From perimeter tangents to Lipschitz graphs
search_title: From perimeter tangents to Lipschitz graphs
section: 4.13 From perimeter tangents to Lipschitz graphs
text:
A tangent measure is a limiting statement at one point. To obtain rectifiability, one must compare nearby points on sets where the relevant scales are uniform. We give that covering argument in codimension one, following the mechanism of [ Sim18 ] , Chapter 3, Theorem 1.6, printed pp. 88–90, as invoked in the proof of Theorem 4.4 on p. 100. The constants below are chosen for transparency, not sharpness. This section proves countable rectifiability; it does not identify the perimeter measure with Hausdorff measure. Definition 4.13.1 (Mass outside a candidate tangent plane) . 1657E1668A52 For a unit vector $e\in \mathbb R^ n$, $x\in \mathbb R^ n$ and $0<\alpha <1$, write \[  C_\alpha (x,e)=\{ z:|(z-x)\cdot e|\geq \alpha |z-x|\} .  \] Thus $C_\alpha (x,e)$ is the union of the two closed cones about the normal line. Small mass in $C_\alpha (x,e)\cap B_ r(x)$ expresses concentration near the hyperplane $e^\perp $ through $x$. This notation uses the normal component directly; compare the cone notation in [ Sim18 ] , pp. 88–89. Lemma 4.13.2 (The reduced boundary and its normal are Borel) . 713ECED9181E For a locally finite-perimeter set $E$ in $U$, the set $\partial ^*E\cap U$ is Borel, and $x\mapsto 
u _ E(x)$ is Borel on it. In particular it is measurable for every Hausdorff measure. This supplies the measurability needed in the rectifiability statement, starting from [ Sim18 ] , equations (4.2)–(4.3), pp. 96–97. Proof Put $\mu =|D\chi _ E|$. For each fixed $r>0$, the functions $x\mapsto \mu (B_ r(x))$ and the coordinate functions of $x\mapsto D\chi _ E(B_ r(x))$ are Borel wherever the closed ball lies in $U$. Indeed the kernel $\chi _{\{ |y-x|<r\} }$ is Borel in $(x,y)$, and integration against the positive measure, or the positive and negative parts of each derivative component, preserves measurability. Localize to a countable compact exhaustion of $U$ so all relevant integrals are finite. Thus the normalized vector $A_ r(x)=D\chi _ E(B_ r(x))/\mu (B_ r(x))$ is Borel on the Borel set where its denominator is positive and finite. On $U\cap \operatorname {supp}\mu $, every sufficiently small denominator is positive. The existence of a limit of $A_ q(x)$ over positive rational $q\downarrow 0$ is a countable Cauchy condition; the assertion that the limiting norm is one is also Borel, using $q=1/k$ once those balls lie in $U$. These conditions are equivalent to the full-radius limit in Definition 4.1.4 . To see the nontrivial implication, for each fixed small $r$ take rational $q_ i\uparrow r$. Continuity from below for the finite measure and each signed component gives $A_{q_ i}(x)	o A_ r(x)$. Every uniform small-radius bound on rational averages therefore passes to the real radius $r$. The Cauchy limit over rational radii is consequently the limit over all radii. Intersecting the stated Borel conditions with the relatively closed support gives the Borel reduced boundary. Its outward normal is the negative pointwise limit of the Borel functions $A_{1/k}$, so is Borel there. $\square$ Lemma 4.13.3 (A pair of points in a normal direction forces cone mass) . 9E356A954D5F Let $x
e y$, put $d=|y-x|$, and let $e,e_ x$ be unit vectors with $|e-e_ x|\leq 1/8$. If \[  |(y-x)\cdot e|>	frac 12d,  \] then \[  B_{d/32}(y)\subset C_{1/4}(x,e_ x)\cap B_{2d}(x).  \] This is the geometric ball inclusion behind the contradiction argument in [ Sim18 ] , pp. 89–90. Proof First $|(y-x)\cdot e_ x|\geq |(y-x)\cdot e|-|y-x||e-e_ x|>3d/8$. For $z\in B_{d/32}(y)$, the triangle inequality gives \[  |(z-x)\cdot e_ x|>11d/32,\qquad |z-x|<33d/32<2d.  \] The ratio of the first bound to the second exceeds $1/3$, hence exceeds $1/4$. This proves both inclusions. The absolute values make the estimate valid for either normal direction. $\square$ Proposition 4.13.4 (Uniform density and cone bounds give one Lipschitz graph) . CF5202CEB133 Let $m=n-1\geq 1$, let $\mu $ be a positive Radon measure on an open set $U\subset \mathbb R^ n$, and let $S\subset U$. Suppose there are $c>0$, $ho >0$, a fixed unit vector $e$, and unit vectors $e_ x$ for $x\in S$ such that $|e_ x-e|\leq 1/8$, $B_ho (x)\subset U$, and for every $x\in S$ and $0<r<ho $, \[  \mu (B_ r(x))\geq c r^ m, \qquad \mu (C_{1/4}(x,e_ x)\cap B_ r(x))\leq \delta r^ m, \qquad \delta = rac{c}{2\cdot 64^ m}.  \] If $\operatorname {diam}S<ho /2$, then $S$ is contained in the graph of a real function on $e^\perp $ with Lipschitz constant at most $1/\sqrt3$. No measurability assumption on $S$ is required for this geometric containment. Proof Take distinct $x,y\in S$ and let $d=|y-x|<ho /2$. If their difference satisfied the hypothesis of Lemma 4.13.3 , the mass of the ball from that lemma would be bounded below and above by \[  c(d/32)^ m \leq \mu (B_{d/32}(y)) \leq \mu (C_{1/4}(x,e_ x)\cap B_{2d}(x)) \leq \delta (2d)^ m=	frac 12c(d/32)^ m,  \] which is impossible. Hence $|(y-x)\cdot e|\leq |y-x|/2$ for all pairs. With $p$ the orthogonal projection onto $e^\perp $, the Pythagorean identity gives \[  |p(y)-p(x)|\geq 	frac {\sqrt3}{2}|y-x|, \qquad |(y-x)\cdot e|\leq 	frac 1{\sqrt3}|p(y)-p(x)|.  \] In particular $p$ is injective on $S$, so the height function $h(p(x))=x\cdot e$ is well defined and $1/\sqrt3$-Lipschitz on $p(S)$. If $S$ is empty there is nothing to prove. Otherwise Proposition 3.4.2 , applied in the Euclidean hyperplane $e^\perp $, extends $h$ to the whole hyperplane with the same Lipschitz bound. Its graph contains $S$. $\square$ Theorem 4.13.5 (A pointwise density-and-cone criterion for a countable graph cover) . 8B6161F902E6 Let $\mu $ be a positive Radon measure on $U\subset \mathbb R^ n$, $m=n-1\geq 1$, and $S\subset U$. Suppose that for every $x\in S$ there is a unit vector $e_ x$ such that \[  \liminf _{r\downarrow 0} rac{\mu (B_ r(x))}{r^ m}>0, \qquad \lim _{r\downarrow 0} rac{\mu (C_{1/4}(x,e_ x)\cap B_ r(x))}{r^ m}=0.  \] Then $S$ is contained in a countable union of Lipschitz graphs over $(n-1)$-planes. This is the hypersurface version of the graph-cover mechanism in [ Sim18 ] , pp. 88–90. Proof For each positive integer $k$, set $c_ k=1/k$ and $\delta _ k=c_ k/(2\cdot 64^ m)$. For positive integers $k,j$, let $S_{k,j}$ contain those $x\in S$ for which $B_{1/j}(x)\subset U$ and both \[  \mu (B_ r(x))\geq c_ kr^ m,\qquad \mu (C_{1/4}(x,e_ x)\cap B_ r(x))\leq \delta _ kr^ m  \] hold for every $0<r<1/j$. The two pointwise limits ensure that every $x\in S$ belongs to at least one such set: first choose $k$ with $1/k$ strictly below the positive lower limit, then $j$ sufficiently large for both bounds and the domain inclusion. Thus $S= igcup _{k,j}S_{k,j}$. Choose finitely many unit vectors whose open $1/8$-balls cover the unit sphere. Split each $S_{k,j}$ according to which of these vectors is within $1/8$ of $e_ x$, allowing overlap. Intersect further with a countable cover of Euclidean space by balls of diameter less than $1/(2j)$. Each resulting piece satisfies Proposition 4.13.4 with $ho =1/j$ and $c=c_ k$, so lies in one whole Lipschitz graph. There are countably many pieces. Their covering property gives the conclusion. This direct partition uses uniform bounds on each piece and does not need to claim the convergence is uniform on all of $S$. $\square$ Theorem 4.13.6 (Countable rectifiability of the reduced boundary) . C02EADB4998C If $E$ has locally finite perimeter in $U\subset \mathbb R^ n$, $n\geq 2$, then $\partial ^*E\cap U$ is contained in a countable union of Lipschitz graphs over $(n-1)$-planes. In particular it is countably $(n-1)$-rectifiable. This proves the graph-cover conclusion in [ Sim18 ] , Chapter 3, Theorem 4.4, p. 100. The equality $|D\chi _ E|=\mathcal H^{n-1}\llcorner \partial ^*E$ is not used in this proof. Proof Take $\mu =|D\chi _ E|$, $S=\partial ^*E\cap U$, and $e_ x=
u _ E(x)$. Corollary 4.12.4 gives $\mu (B_ r(x))/r^{n-1}	o \omega _{n-1}>0$ at every point of $S$. Corollary 4.12.5 gives the required cone limit for $\alpha =1/4$. Apply Theorem 4.13.5 . Lemma 4.13.2 supplies Hausdorff measurability. The graph map $z\mapsto z+h(z)e$ is Lipschitz, so these are also countably many Lipschitz images in the sense of Definition 3.1.1 . The proof covers every reduced-boundary point, rather than introducing an unexamined exceptional subset. Identification of the boundary measure remains a separate step in the full structure theorem. $\square$

Suppose there are $c>0$, $\rho >0$, a fixed unit vector $e$, and unit vectors $e_ x$ for $x\in S$ such that $|e_ x-e|\leq 1/8$, $B_\rho (x)\subset U$, and for every $x\in S$ and $0<r<\rho $, \[  \mu (B_ r(x))\geq c r^ m, \qquad \mu (C_{1/4}(x,e_ x)\cap B_ r(x))\leq \delta r^ m, \qquad \delta =\frac{c}{2\cdot 64^ m}.  \] If $\operatorname {diam}S<\rho /2$, then $S$ is contained in the graph of a real function on $e^\perp $ with Lipschitz constant at most $1/\sqrt3$. text:
The graph cover and the pointwise density limit still have to be connected to the perimeter measure. We separate the needed measure comparisons and state the remaining differentiation input explicitly. This completes the structure proof from [ Sim18 ] , Chapter 3, Theorem 4.4, printed pp. 97–100, relative to the Radon differentiation theorem proved from the cited Besicovitch covering input and the rectifiable-set density theorem proved through $C^1$ pieces. Corollary 4.14.1 (The perimeter measure is concentrated on the reduced boundary) . 4654F1F7DB1D For a locally finite-perimeter set $E$ in $U$, \[  |D\chi _ E|(U\setminus \partial ^*E)=0.  \] This is the concentration assertion at the beginning of the proof of [ Sim18 ] , Chapter 3, Theorem 4.4, p. 97. Proof Put $\mu =|D\chi _ E|$ and write $D\chi _ E=-
u \mu $ with $|
u |=1$ almost everywhere. The bounded polar field belongs locally to $L^1(\mu )$. Theorem 2.6.5 , applied to its finitely many components, gives \[   rac{D\chi _ E(B_ r(x))}{\mu (B_ r(x))}\longrightarrow -
u (x) \quad 	ext{for }\mu 	ext{-almost every }x.  \] The complement of the support of $\mu $ is a countable union of open balls with zero measure, so almost every such point also lies in that support. Since the limit has length one, these points belong to the reduced boundary by definition. Its Borel measurability follows from Lemma 4.13.2 , so the displayed measure statement is well defined. $\square$ Proposition 4.14.2 (A lower density bound controls Hausdorff measure) . 4AC44593129C Let $\mu $ be a positive Radon measure on $U\subset \mathbb R^ n$, let $m>0$, and let $S\subset U$ be Borel. Suppose that for each $x\in S$ and every sufficiently small $r>0$, \[  \mu (B_ r(x))\geq c r^ m  \] with a fixed $c>0$; the permitted scale may depend on $x$. Then for every Borel $A\subset S$, \[  \mathcal H^ m(A)\leq  rac{5^ m\omega _ m}{c}\mu (A).  \] Here $m$ is an integer between one and $n$ so that $\omega _ m$ has the normalization of Definition 2.2.1 . The bound is not sharp. Proof First suppose $A$ is bounded and lies in a compact subset of $U$. Take an open $O\subset U$ containing $A$ and a positive diameter scale $\delta $. For each $x\in A$ use all sufficiently small balls centered at $x$ that lie in $O$, have radius less than $\delta /10$, and satisfy the stated mass lower bound. This family covers $A$ and has bounded centers and radii. Lemma 2.5.1 provides disjoint selected balls $B_{r_ i}(x_ i)$ whose fivefold dilations cover $A$. Their diameters are less than $\delta $, so the normalized Hausdorff content satisfies \[  \mathcal H^ m_\delta (A) \leq \sum _ i\omega _ m(5r_ i)^ m \leq  rac{5^ m\omega _ m}{c}\sum _ i\mu (B_{r_ i}(x_ i)) \leq  rac{5^ m\omega _ m}{c}\mu (O).  \] Let $\delta \downarrow 0$ and then use outer regularity of $\mu $ to take the infimum over $O$. It is enough to use open sets inside a fixed relatively compact neighborhood of $A$, so their measures are finite in this step. Finally exhaust $U$ by compact sets and apply the result to their intersections with $A$. These sets increase to $A$, and both Borel measures are continuous from below, proving the general assertion. The constants come from fivefold dilation and the normalized diameter definition, not a sharp density comparison theorem. $\square$ Proposition 4.14.3 (An upper density bound controls the restricted Radon measure) . 77C1DB68F24B Let $\mu $ be a positive Radon measure on $U$, and let $S\subset U$ be Borel. Suppose that for every $x\in S$ and all sufficiently small $r>0$, \[  \mu (B_ r(x))\leq C\omega _ m r^ m,  \] where $1\leq m\leq n$ and $C$ is fixed, but the permitted scale may depend on $x$. Then for every Borel $A\subset S$, \[  \mu (A)\leq C4^ m\mathcal H^ m(A).  \] This is the diameter-cover comparison used after equation (13) in [ Sim18 ] , p. 100, with a convenient enlarged radius. Proof Let $S_ j$ consist of points of $S$ for which $\operatorname {dist}(x,\mathbb R^ n\setminus U)>1/j$ and the stated upper bound holds for all $0<r<1/j$. These are Borel sets: it suffices to test positive rational radii, because continuity from below of open balls passes the bound to every real radius. They increase with $j$ and cover $S$. Fix $j$ and cover $A\cap S_ j$ by sets $Q_ i$ of diameters $d_ i<\delta <1/(2j)$, with total normalized cost within $\varepsilon $ of $\mathcal H^ m_\delta (A\cap S_ j)$. Discard sets missing $A\cap S_ j$, and choose $x_ i\in Q_ i\cap A\cap S_ j$ for the others. When $d_ i>0$, $Q_ i\subset B_{2d_ i}(x_ i)$, and \[  \mu (B_{2d_ i}(x_ i))\leq C\omega _ m(2d_ i)^ m =C4^ m\omega _ m(d_ i/2)^ m.  \] When $d_ i=0$, $Q_ i$ contains at most the single point $x_ i$, and $\mu (\{ x_ i\} )=0$ by the assumed upper bound and $m>0$. Corollary 4.14.1 (The perimeter measure is concentrated on the reduced boundary) . 4654F1F7DB1D For a locally finite-perimeter set $E$ in $U$, \[  |D\chi _ E|(U\setminus \partial ^*E)=0.  \] This is the concentration assertion at the beginning of the proof of [ Sim18 ] , Chapter 3, Theorem 4.4, p. 97. u \mu $ with $|
u |=1$ almost everywhere. The bounded polar field belongs locally to $L^1(\mu )$. Theorem 2.6.5 , applied to its finitely many components, gives \[   rac{D\chi _ E(B_ r(x))}{\mu (B_ r(x))}\longrightarrow -

title: Proposition 4.14.2 (A lower density bound controls Hausdorff measure)

text: Proposition 4.14.2 (A lower density bound controls Hausdorff measure) . 4AC44593129C Let $\mu $ be a positive Radon measure on $U\subset \mathbb R^ n$, let $m>0$, and let $S\subset U$ be Borel. Suppose that for each $x\in S$ and every sufficiently small $r>0$, \[  \mu (B_ r(x))\geq c r^ m  \] with a fixed $c>0$; the permitted scale may depend on $x$. Then for every Borel $A\subset S$, \[  \mathcal H^ m(A)\leq \frac{5^ m\omega _ m}{c}\mu (A).  \] Here $m$ is an integer between one and $n$ so that $\omega _ m$ has the normalization of Definition 2.2.1 . The bound is not sharp. Proof First suppose $A$ is bounded and lies in a compact subset of $U$. Take an open $O\subset U$ containing $A$ and a positive diameter scale $\delta $. For each $x\in A$ use all sufficiently small balls centered at $x$ that lie in $O$, have radius less than $\delta /10$, and satisfy the stated mass lower bound. This family covers $A$ and has bounded centers and radii. Lemma 2.5.1 provides disjoint selected balls $B_{r_ i}(x_ i)$ whose fivefold dilations cover $A$. Their diameters are less than $\delta $, so the normalized Hausdorff content satisfies \[  \mathcal H^ m_\delta (A) \leq \sum _ i\omega _ m(5r_ i)^ m \leq \frac{5^ m\omega _ m}{c}\sum _ i\mu (B_{r_ i}(x_ i)) \leq \frac{5^ m\omega _ m}{c}\mu (O).  \] Let $\delta \downarrow 0$ and then use outer regularity of $\mu $ to take the infimum over $O$. It is enough to use open sets inside a fixed relatively compact neighborhood of $A$, so their measures are finite in this step. Finally exhaust $U$ by compact sets and apply the result to their intersections with $A$. These sets increase to $A$, and both Borel measures are continuous from below, proving the general assertion. The constants come from fivefold dilation and the normalized diameter definition, not a sharp density comparison theorem. $\square$

text: Proposition 4.14.3 (An upper density bound controls the restricted Radon measure) . 77C1DB68F24B Let $\mu $ be a positive Radon measure on $U$, and let $S\subset U$ be Borel. Suppose that for every $x\in S$ and all sufficiently small $r>0$, \[  \mu (B_ r(x))\leq C\omega _ m r^ m,  \] where $1\leq m\leq n$ and $C$ is fixed, but the permitted scale may depend on $x$. Then for every Borel $A\subset S$, \[  \mu (A)\leq C4^ m\mathcal H^ m(A).  \] This is the diameter-cover comparison used after equation (13) in [ Sim18 ] , p. 100, with a convenient enlarged radius. Proof Let $S_ j$ consist of points of $S$ for which $\operatorname {dist}(x,\mathbb R^ n\setminus U)>1/j$ and the stated upper bound holds for all $0<r<1/j$. These are Borel sets: it suffices to test positive rational radii, because continuity from below of open balls passes the bound to every real radius. They increase with $j$ and cover $S$. Fix $j$ and cover $A\cap S_ j$ by sets $Q_ i$ of diameters $d_ i<\delta <1/(2j)$, with total normalized cost within $\varepsilon $ of $\mathcal H^ m_\delta (A\cap S_ j)$. Discard sets missing $A\cap S_ j$, and choose $x_ i\in Q_ i\cap A\cap S_ j$ for the others. When $d_ i>0$, $Q_ i\subset B_{2d_ i}(x_ i)$, and \[  \mu (B_{2d_ i}(x_ i))\leq C\omega _ m(2d_ i)^ m =C4^ m\omega _ m(d_ i/2)^ m.  \] When $d_ i=0$, $Q_ i$ contains at most the single point $x_ i$, and $\mu (\{ x_ i\} )=0$ by the assumed upper bound and $m>0$. Subadditivity gives \[  \mu (A\cap S_ j)\leq C4^ m \bigl (\mathcal H^ m_\delta (A\cap S_ j)+\varepsilon \bigr ) \leq C4^ m\bigl (\mathcal H^ m(A)+\varepsilon \bigr ).  \] If the Hausdorff measure on the right is infinite the result is immediate; otherwise such finite-cost covers exist. Let $\varepsilon \downarrow 0$ and then $j\to \infty $, using continuity from below of $\mu $. This proves the assertion without assuming a uniform radius on all of $A$. $\square$

title: 16.27 Examples of phase density and perimeter blow-ups
search_title: Examples of phase density and perimeter blow-ups
section: 16.27 Examples of phase density and perimeter blow-ups
text: These elementary examples separate the reduced boundary, phase density, topological boundary and perimeter tangent measures. They use the distributional framework of [ Sim18 ] , Chapter 3, Section 4, and the explicit blow-up results developed in the perimeter chapter. Their calculations do not use the general rectifiability theorem. Example 16.27.1 (A smooth subgraph has the expected oriented blow-up) . E5E731EAB307 Suppose $u\in C^1$ near $0\in \mathbb R^{n-1}$, $u(0)=0$, $Du(0)=0$, and locally $E=\{ (z,s):s<u(z)\} $. The origin belongs to $\partial ^*E$, its outward normal is $e_ n$, and $E_{0,r}\to \{ s<0\} $ locally in volume. Its rescaled perimeter measures converge to $\mathcal H^{n-1}\llcorner \{ s=0\} $. If $u$ is $C^2$, then for each fixed $R$, \[  |(E_{0,r}\mathbin {\triangle }\{ s<0\} )\cap B_ R|=O_ R(r), \qquad \frac{1}{|D\chi _ E|(B_ r)}\int _{B_ r}|\nu -e_ n|^2\, d|D\chi _ E|=O(r^2).  \] The constants depend on a local bound for $D^2u$. Proof The local smooth-domain calculation in Example 4.1.6 , or direct integration by parts in the subgraph, gives outward normal $(-Du,1)/\sqrt{1+|Du|^2}$ and perimeter density $\sqrt{1+|Du|^2}\, dz$ on its graph. This continuous normal tends to $e_ n$ and the graph meets every ball in positive surface measure, so its normalized polar average tends to $e_ n$, proving reduced-boundary membership. The dilated graph has height $u(rz)/r$ and gradient $Du(rz)$, both tending uniformly to zero on every fixed compact base set. The symmetric difference in $B_ R$ is bounded by \[  \int _{|z|<R}\frac{|u(rz)|}{r}\, dz\longrightarrow 0.  \] For any compactly supported continuous scalar test $\phi $, its rescaled perimeter integral is \[  \int \phi (z,u(rz)/r)\sqrt{1+|Du(rz)|^2}\, dz,  \] with integration confined to a fixed bounded projection of the test support. Dominated convergence gives the planar limit. When $|D^2u|\leq C$, Taylor's formula bounds $|u(rz)|/r$ by $Cr|z|^2/2$ and $|Du(z)|$ by $C|z|$. The first bound gives the stated volume rate. On the graph inside $B_ r$, $|\nu -e_ n|\leq C' r$; averaging its square gives the second rate. These are local rates for a smooth model, not uniform rates for an arbitrary finite-perimeter set. $\square$ Example 16.27.2 (A planar sector has unit perimeter density at every vertex angle) . 7CF1D190561A For $0<\theta <2\pi $, let \[  E_\theta =\{ \rho (\cos t,\sin t):\rho >0,\  -\theta /2<t<\theta /2\} \subset \mathbb R^2.  \] At the vertex, \[  |E_\theta \cap B_ r|=\tfrac 12\theta r^2,\qquad P(E_\theta ;B_ r)=2r,\qquad \frac{D\chi _{E_\theta }(B_ r)}{P(E_\theta ;B_ r)} =\sin (\theta /2)e_1.  \] Consequently the perimeter density normalized by $\omega _1r=2r$ is one for every angle, but the vertex is reduced-boundary exactly when $\theta =\pi $. Perimeter density one alone does not characterize the reduced boundary. Proof Polar integration gives the volume. On the upper ray the outward normal is $(-\sin (\theta /2),\cos (\theta /2))$; on the lower ray it is $(-\sin (\theta /2),-\cos (\theta /2))$. Integration by parts on the sector cut off between radii $\varepsilon $ and a large radius gives the derivative measure as minus these normals times length on the two rays. The test field is zero near the large boundary, and the small circular boundary term tends to zero with its length $\theta \varepsilon $. There is no vertex atom. Each ray has length $r$ inside $B_ r$, so its variation mass is $2r$ and its vector derivative has value $2r\sin (\theta /2)e_1$. The normalized vector has length one precisely at $\theta =\pi $. At every other angle the limiting average exists but has length less than one, so Definition 4.1.4 excludes the vertex. $\square$ Example 16.27.3 (Density one half does not characterize the reduced boundary) . 7708B31F27FA For $E=\{ (x,y):xy>0\} $, the origin has phase density $1/2$ and lies in the support of the perimeter measure, but does not belong to $\partial ^*E$. In fact \[  P(E;B_ r)=4r,\qquad D\chi _ E(B_ r)=0  \] for every $r>0$. Proof The two occupied quadrants have total angle $\pi $, so they occupy half of every centered ball. Applying the ray calculation in Example 16.27.2 separately to these two disjoint quadrants, or integrating by parts in each, gives one copy of length measure on each of the four axis rays. On opposite rays the outward normals are opposite, so the four vector contributions cancel in every centered ball. The positive variation is $4r$, whereas the averaged derivative vector is zero. This violates the unit-length condition in the reduced-boundary definition despite the exact phase density. The example is distinct from a smooth crossing immersion: it is a measurable phase whose distributional boundary has four rays. $\square$ Example 16.27.4 (A thin slab loses all phase volume but retains two sheets of perimeter) . C719FA3BCD61 For $E_ j=\{ y\in \mathbb R^ n:0<y_ n<1/j\} $, one has locally \[  \chi _{E_ j}\to 0\text{ in }L^1,\qquad D\chi _{E_ j}\rightharpoonup 0,\qquad |D\chi _{E_ j}|\rightharpoonup 2\mathcal H^{n-1}\llcorner \{ y_ n=0\} .  \] Thus local $L^1$ convergence and locally bounded perimeter do not ensure convergence of perimeter measures to the limit set's perimeter. Proof The volume on a fixed compact set is at most its bounded projection volume times $1/j$. By one-dimensional integration in $y_ n$, \[  D\chi _{E_ j}=e_ n\mathcal H^{n-1}\llcorner \{ y_ n=0\}  -e_ n\mathcal H^{n-1}\llcorner \{ y_ n=1/j\} .  \] The two planes are disjoint, so their positive measures add in the total variation. Continuous compactly supported test integrals on the translated plane converge to those on the original plane by uniform continuity and bounded projection. Consequently the vector measures cancel in the limit while their variations add. The missing hypothesis of Proposition 4.12.2 is alignment of the two opposite polar directions. $\square$ Example 16.27.5 (A quadratic cusp has a double-line perimeter tangent and an empty phase tangent) . 490DFC3EF874 Let $E=\{ (x,y)\in \mathbb R^2:|y|<x^2\} $. At the origin, \[  \chi _{E_{0,r}}\to 0\quad \text{in }L^1_{\mathrm{loc}},\qquad r^{-1}(F_ r^{-1})_\# |D\chi _ E| \rightharpoonup 2\mathcal H^1\llcorner \{ y=0\} .  \] The origin lies in the perimeter support and has phase density zero; it is not in the reduced boundary. In fact $D\chi _ E(B_ r)=0$ for every $r>0$. This is a phase-boundary example, distinct from the calibrated complex cusp in Example 5.6.4 . Proof For a compactly supported smooth field $X=(X_1,X_2)$, integrate first in $y$ over $(-x^2,x^2)$ and use the one-dimensional Leibniz rule in $x$. One obtains \[  \int _ E\operatorname {div}X =\int _{\mathbb R}\bigl [-2xX_1(x,x^2)+X_2(x,x^2) -2xX_1(x,-x^2)-X_2(x,-x^2)\bigr ]\, dx.  \] Thus the perimeter is arclength on the two parabolas, with outward normals $(-2x,1)/\sqrt{1+4x^2}$ above and $(-2x,-1)/\sqrt{1+4x^2}$ below. They meet only at one point, which has zero length measure. Symmetry in $x$ cancels the horizontal vector integral in a centered ball, and symmetry in $y$ cancels the vertical integral. Their positive lengths do not cancel and are positive in every centered ball. The rescaled phase is $\{ (X,Y):|Y|<rX^2\} $, whose volume in $B_ R$ is bounded by $2r\int _{-R}^ R X^2\, dX\to 0$. For a compactly supported continuous test $\phi $, its rescaled perimeter integral is \[  \int _{\mathbb R}\bigl [\phi (X,rX^2)+\phi (X,-rX^2)\bigr ] \sqrt{1+4r^2X^2}\, dX.  \] Dominated convergence on a bounded projection gives twice line measure. The empty phase tangent and double-line perimeter tangent demonstrate precisely the cancellation that polar alignment excludes at a reduced-boundary point. $\square$ Example 16.27.6 (A negligible dense modification preserves every perimeter blow-up) . DA161D3EEA56 Let $H=\{ y_ n<0\} $, and set \[  E=(H\setminus \mathbb Q^ n)\cup (\mathbb Q^ n\setminus H).  \] Then $E=H$ almost everywhere, $\partial ^*E=\{ y_ n=0\} $ and every reduced-boundary blow-up is the same oriented half-space as for $H$. Nevertheless the topological boundary of this representative is all of $\mathbb R^ n$. Proof The symmetric difference is contained in the countable null set $\mathbb Q^ n$. Characteristic functions, derivative measures and their polar averages are unchanged, so Lemma 4.12.1 gives the reduced boundary and its outward normal. At a point off the plane, some ball has zero perimeter measure, excluding it from the reduced boundary; on the plane the polar vector is constant of unit length. The set and its complement are both dense: every ball contains a smaller ball lying strictly in one of the two half-spaces, and within that smaller ball there are both rational and nonrational points, one type in $E$ and the other outside it. Hence every point is a topological boundary point. The result extends Example 4.3.3 to a nonzero perimeter measure with unchanged geometric blow-ups. $\square$

Consequently the vector measures cancel in the limit while their variations add. The missing hypothesis of Proposition 4.12.2 is alignment of the two opposite polar directions. $\square$

text: Example 16.27.5 (A quadratic cusp has a double-line perimeter tangent and an empty phase tangent) . 490DFC3EF874 Let $E=\{ (x,y)\in \mathbb R^2:|y|<x^2\} $. At the origin, \[  \chi _{E_{0,r}}\to 0\quad \text{in }L^1_{\mathrm{loc}},\qquad r^{-1}(F_ r^{-1})_\# |D\chi _ E| \rightharpoonup 2\mathcal H^1\llcorner \{ y=0\} .  \] The origin lies in the perimeter support and has phase density zero; it is not in the reduced boundary. In fact $D\chi _ E(B_ r)=0$ for every $r>0$. This is a phase-boundary example, distinct from the calibrated complex cusp in Example 5.6.4 . Proof For a compactly supported smooth field $X=(X_1,X_2)$, integrate first in $y$ over $(-x^2,x^2)$ and use the one-dimensional Leibniz rule in $x$. One obtains \[  \int _ E\operatorname {div}X =\int _{\mathbb R}\bigl [-2xX_1(x,x^2)+X_2(x,x^2) -2xX_1(x,-x^2)-X_2(x,-x^2)\bigr ]\, dx.  \] Thus the perimeter is arclength on the two parabolas, with outward normals $(-2x,1)/\sqrt{1+4x^2}$ above and $(-2x,-1)/\sqrt{1+4x^2}$ below. They meet only at one point, which has zero length measure. Symmetry in $x$ cancels the horizontal vector integral in a centered ball, and symmetry in $y$ cancels the vertical integral. Their positive lengths do not cancel and are positive in every centered ball. The rescaled phase is $\{ (X,Y):|Y|<rX^2\} $, whose volume in $B_ R$ is bounded by $2r\int _{-R}^ R X^2\, dX\to 0$. For a compactly supported continuous test $\phi $, its rescaled perimeter integral is \[  \int _{\mathbb R}\bigl [\phi (X,rX^2)+\phi (X,-rX^2)\bigr ] \sqrt{1+4r^2X^2}\, dX.  \] Dominated convergence on a bounded projection gives twice line measure. The empty phase tangent and double-line perimeter tangent demonstrate precisely the cancellation that polar alignment excludes at a reduced-boundary point. $\square$

title: Example 16.27.6 (A negligible dense modification preserves every perimeter blow-up)

text: Example 16.27.6 (A negligible dense modification preserves every perimeter blow-up) . DA161D3EEA56 Let $H=\{ y_ n<0\} $, and set \[  E=(H\setminus \mathbb Q^ n)\cup (\mathbb Q^ n\setminus H).  \] Then $E=H$ almost everywhere, $\partial ^*E=\{ y_ n=0\} $ and every reduced-boundary blow-up is the same oriented half-space as for $H$. Nevertheless the topological boundary of this representative is all of $\mathbb R^ n$. Proof The symmetric difference is contained in the countable null set $\mathbb Q^ n$. Characteristic functions, derivative measures and their polar averages are unchanged, so Lemma 4.12.1 gives the reduced boundary and its outward normal. At a point off the plane, some ball has zero perimeter measure, excluding it from the reduced boundary; on the plane the polar vector is constant of unit length. The set and its complement are both dense: every ball contains a smaller ball lying strictly in one of the two half-spaces, and within that smaller ball there are both rational and nonrational points, one type in $E$ and the other outside it. Hence every point is a topological boundary point. The result extends Example 4.3.3 to a nonzero perimeter measure with unchanged geometric blow-ups. $\square$
