section: 3.5 Continuously differentiable pieces of Lipschitz images
text:
The tangent theorem for a rectifiable set begins with a decomposition into smooth pieces, rather than with a separation assumption between those pieces. We expand [ Sim18 ] , Chapter 2, Theorems 1.5–1.6, printed pp. 46–48, and Chapter 3, Lemma 1.2 and Remark 1.3, pp. 85–86. Whitney extension remains external; the Euclidean area formula now has a local proof in Theorem 3.13.8 . The approximation concerns agreement outside a set of small measure, not uniform approximation of derivatives everywhere. Definition 3.5.1 (A compatible first-order jet on a closed set) . DA25DC227B60 Let $C\subset \mathbb R^ m$ be closed. A scalar first-order jet consists of continuous maps $h:C	o \mathbb R$ and $a:C	o \mathbb R^ m$. It is compatible if for each compact $K\subset C$, \[  \lim _{\delta \downarrow 0}\sup _{\substack {x,y\in K\ 0<|x-y|<\delta }}  rac{|h(y)-h(x)-a(x)\cdot (y-x)|}{|y-x|}=0.  \] The supremum over an empty set is zero. Uniformity over pairs in a compact set is part of the condition. This is the condition in [ Sim18 ] , Chapter 2, Theorem 1.6. Theorem 3.5.2 (Whitney extension for first-order jets) . 57E484726390 Every compatible jet in Definition 3.5.1 is the restriction of a function $g\in C^1(\mathbb R^ m)$: $g=h$ and $Dg=a$ on $C$. Conversely, the restriction of a $C^1$ function gives a compatible jet. The existence assertion is a cited theorem, [ Sim18 ] , Chapter 2, Theorem 1.6, pp. 46–47, where the proof is referred to [ Fed69 ] . Its extension construction is not proved here. For necessity, the segment formula for $g(y)-g(x)$ and uniform continuity of $Dg$ on the compact convex hull of $K$ give the displayed remainder estimate. Lemma 3.5.3 (Measurable differentiability defects) . 12007A5574B9 Let $f:\mathbb R^ m	o \mathbb R$ be Lipschitz and let $a(x)$ be its derivative at differentiability points, extended by zero on the exceptional set. It can be chosen Borel. Put \[  d_ k(x)=\sup _{0<|z|<1/k}  rac{|f(x+z)-f(x)-a(x)\cdot z|}{|z|}.  \] Then $d_ k$ is Borel, is bounded by twice the Lipschitz constant at differentiability points, and decreases to zero at every such point. This is the defect used in the proof of [ Sim18 ] , Theorem 1.5, p. 48. Proof Coordinate difference quotients are continuous functions of $x$, so the set where their limits exist is Borel and their limits there are Borel. Rademacher's theorem, Theorem 3.1.2 , supplies a full-measure differentiability set. The full differentiability condition can itself be expressed by the vanishing of the defects below using the coordinate limits, hence is Borel. Set $a=0$ off that set. At a fixed $x$ the quotient is continuous in $z
e 0$, so its supremum can be taken over nonzero rational vectors with length less than $1/k$. It is consequently a countable supremum of Borel functions. At a differentiability point $|a|\leq \operatorname {Lip}f$ and the defining differentiability limit proves the last two assertions. The shrinking domains of the suprema give monotonicity in $k$. $\square$ Lemma 3.5.4 (Compact subsets with continuous and uniform jets) . 5CF7F513FF12 For a Lipschitz scalar $f$, a bounded Lebesgue-measurable set $A\subset \mathbb R^ m$, and $\varepsilon >0$, there is a compact $C\subset A$ consisting of differentiability points with $|A\setminus C|<\varepsilon $, such that $Df|C$ is continuous and the defects in Lemma 3.5.3 tend uniformly to zero on $C$. The restricted jet $(f,Df)|C$ is compatible. Proof Discard the null nondifferentiability set. Egoroff's theorem on the finite-measure set $A$ gives a measurable subset with complement of measure less than $\varepsilon /2$ on which $d_ k	o 0$ uniformly. Lusin's theorem and inner regularity give a compact subset of it, with additional loss less than $\varepsilon /2$, on which $Df$ is continuous. These two elementary finite-measure theorems are the background inputs also used in [ Sim18 ] , p. 48. Continuity of $f$ is automatic. For $x,y\in C$ with $0<|x-y|<1/k$, the normalized jet remainder is at most $d_ k(x)$. Uniform convergence therefore gives the compatibility condition. This step needs neither an extension of the jet nor an area formula. $\square$ Theorem 3.5.5 (Lipschitz functions agree with a smooth function off a small set) . 23ACEA4A9DD0 If $f:\mathbb R^ m	o \mathbb R$ is Lipschitz and $\varepsilon >0$, there exists $g\in C^1(\mathbb R^ m)$ such that \[  \mathcal L^ m igl (\{ f
e g\} \cup \{ Df
e Dg\}  igr )<\varepsilon ,  \] where the derivative comparison ignores the null nondifferentiability set of $f$. This is [ Sim18 ] , Chapter 2, Theorem 1.5, with the Whitney extension step isolated above. Proof Partition space into the bounded shells $A_ j=\{ j-1\leq |x|<j\} $, $j\geq 1$. Apply Lemma 3.5.4 to obtain compact $C_ j\subset A_ j$ with loss less than $\varepsilon 2^{-j}$, continuous restricted derivative, and uniform differentiability defects. The family $\{ C_ j\} $ is locally finite: a bounded neighborhood meets only finitely many shells. Hence $C= igcup _ jC_ j$ is closed. The compact sets are disjoint. In any bounded neighborhood there are only finitely many of them, so their pairwise distances are positive whenever both are nonempty. Consequently $Df|C$ is continuous locally and the defects tend uniformly to zero on each compact subset of $C$, being the maximum of finitely many uniform defects. The jet is compatible. Theorem 3.5.2 supplies $g\in C^1$ with $g=f$ and $Dg=Df$ on $C$. The union of the two disagreement sets is contained, up to the stated null set, in $\mathbb R^ m\setminus C$. Its measure is less than $\sum _ j\varepsilon 2^{-j}=\varepsilon $. No finiteness of the total ambient measure or compact support of $f$ is assumed. $\square$ Corollary 3.5.6 (Vector-valued agreement on one common good set) . 7AC9CD6B4783 If $f:\mathbb R^ m	o \mathbb R^ n$ is Lipschitz and $\varepsilon >0$, there is $g\in C^1(\mathbb R^ m;\mathbb R^ n)$ such that $f=g$ and $Df=Dg$ outside a set of Lebesgue measure less than $\varepsilon $. Proof Apply Theorem 3.5.5 to each of the $n$ scalar components, with exceptional measure less than $\varepsilon /n$. Collect the resulting functions into $g$. Outside the union of their exceptional sets every component and every derivative agrees. Subadditivity gives the claimed measure bound. The common set is essential when using the rank of the vector-valued derivative. $\square$ Theorem 3.5.7 (Countable decomposition into embedded smooth manifolds) . E0F7CAFA3215 For $1\leq m\leq n$, an $\mathcal H^ m$-measurable $M\subset \mathbb R^ n$ is countably $m$-rectifiable if and only if it is contained, apart from an $\mathcal H^ m$-null set, in a countable union of embedded $m$-dimensional $C^1$ submanifolds. No local finiteness of $\mathcal H^ m\llcorner M$ is required for this equivalence. This is [ Sim18 ] , Chapter 3, Lemma 1.2, pp. 85–86. Proof First take a Lipschitz parametrization $f:\mathbb R^ m	o \mathbb R^ n$. For each positive integer $i$, Corollary 3.5.6 gives a $C^1$ map $g_ i$ agreeing with $f$ outside a set of measure less than $1/i$. The set $Z$ on which none of the equalities $f=g_ i$ holds has measure zero, since it is contained in each disagreement set. The elementary Hausdorff-measure Lipschitz bound gives $\mathcal H^ m(f(Z))=0$. Thus $f(\mathbb R^ m)$ is covered, apart from that null image, by the images $g_ i(\mathbb R^ m)$. For a fixed $g_ i$, its critical set $C_ i=\{ \operatorname {rank}Dg_ i<m\} $ has $\mathcal H^ m(g_ i(C_ i))=0$ by the locally proved area formula, Theorem 3.2.2 : its Jacobian vanishes, while the multiplicity is at least one on its image. To apply the Lipschitz version of that formula, exhaust the domain by bounded balls on whose closures $Dg_ i$ is bounded, apply it on each ball, and take the countable union of the null critical images. At every point outside $C_ i$, some $m$ coordinate functions have invertible derivative. The inverse function theorem writes the image of a sufficiently small neighborhood as an embedded $C^1$ graph over those coordinates; injectivity follows from that same coordinate inverse. A countable subcover of the open full-rank domain gives countably many such graphs. Apply this argument to every Lipschitz map in Definition 3.1.1 , and collect the countably many null sets and charts. Conversely each embedded $C^1$ manifold has a countable cover by chart images with bounded derivatives on relatively compact base balls. Each graph chart is Lipschitz there and extends coordinatewise to a Lipschitz map on all of $\mathbb R^ m$ by Proposition 3.4.2 . The vector extension may increase the constant by the square root of its target dimension, which does not affect countable rectifiability. Add the given exceptional null set. The proof uses Whitney extension, the inverse function theorem and the Euclidean area formula; it does not use the tangent-plane characterization it will help establish. $\square$ Lemma 3.5.8 (A countable cover by finite-area graph patches) . 9430ACAC50F7 An embedded $m$-dimensional $C^1$ submanifold of $\mathbb R^ n$ has a countable cover by relatively open graph patches $N_ j$ of finite $\mathcal H^ m$ measure. Every point of each patch is an interior point of its parametrization domain; the closed base ball of each patch lies inside a larger chart with bounded derivative. For a measurable rectifiable set $M$, these patches can be made into a disjoint measurable partition of $M$, apart from a null set, by assigning a point to the first patch containing it. Proof Use local graph charts from the inverse function theorem and choose smaller open base balls with closures inside their original domains. A countable subcover exists by the countable basis of the ambient space. The derivative is bounded on each closed base ball. The graph Jacobian is therefore bounded, and the area formula gives finite measure because the base ball has finite volume. The graph of a continuous map over an open domain is Borel. Number the patches, intersect them with $M$, and remove all preceding pieces to obtain disjoint measurable sets. The null exceptional set from Theorem 3.5.7 remains null. Artificial patch edges are excluded by using open base balls; every covered point is interior to at least one patch. This avoids assuming that an entire nonproper submanifold has locally finite ambient area. $\square$

title: 3.6 Tangent measures of rectifiable pieces
search_title: Tangent measures of rectifiable pieces
section: 3.6 Tangent measures of rectifiable pieces
text: We prove the forward implication of the tangent-plane characterization in [ Sim18 ] , Chapter 3, Theorem 1.6, printed pp. 87–88. The main issue is that other pieces of a rectifiable set can accumulate near the chosen piece. Differentiation with respect to the measure of their union controls this contribution without assuming a positive distance between pieces. Here $1\leq m\leq n$. Lemma 3.6.1 (Borel representatives for locally finite Hausdorff measure) . 3C9EA6CE752A If $M\subset U\subset \mathbb R^ n$ is $\mathcal H^ m$-measurable, $U$ is open, and $\mathcal H^ m(M\cap K)<\infty $ for every compact $K\subset U$, there is a Borel set $M\subset B\subset U$ with $\mathcal H^ m(B\setminus M)=0$. The Borel measure $\sigma (A)=\mathcal H^ m(M\cap A)$ on $U$ is locally finite and Radon, and is unchanged if $M$ is replaced by $B$. The measures obtained by translation and dilation are likewise unchanged. Proof Choose increasing compact sets $K_ j\subset U$ exhausting $U$. For each integer $j$, the set $M\cap K_ j$ has finite Hausdorff measure. Borel regularity of Hausdorff measure, recalled in Definition 2.2.1 , provides a Borel superset $B_ j$ with the same measure. Measurability and finite measure give $\mathcal H^ m(B_ j\setminus M)=0$ after subtracting $M\cap K_ j$. The union $B=\bigcup _ jB_ j$ contains $M$ and differs from it by a countable union of null sets. Restrictions agree on every Borel test set, proving the measure identity and local finiteness. Intersect the Borel hull with $U$ if necessary. A locally finite Borel measure on a Euclidean open set is Radon. Pushforwards preserve equality of measures, giving the last assertion. This supplies a Borel representative when applying the Radon differentiation theorem; it does not identify topological boundaries of representatives. $\square$ Proposition 3.6.2 (The tangent measure of a continuously differentiable graph) . 19A8BA237DE1 Let $V\subset \mathbb R^ m$ be open, let $u:V\to \mathbb R^{n-m}$ be $C^1$, and let $N=\{ (z,u(z)):z\in V\} $. At $x=(a,u(a))$ with $a\in V$, put $T=\{ (v,Du(a)v):v\in \mathbb R^ m\} $. For every $\phi \in C_ c(\mathbb R^ n)$, \[  \lim _{r\downarrow 0}r^{-m}\int _ N\phi ((y-x)/r)\, d\mathcal H^ m(y) =\int _ T\phi \, d\mathcal H^ m.  \] Only the portion of $N$ near $x$ enters this identity. This proves the smooth-patch limit used in [ Sim18 ] , p. 87, from the now locally proved Euclidean area formula. Proof Write $J(z)=\sqrt{\det (I+Du(z)^*Du(z))}$. The weighted area formula, Proposition 3.3.1 , and the substitution $z=a+rv$ express the integral on the left as \[  \int _{(V-a)/r}\phi \left(v,\frac{u(a+rv)-u(a)}r\right)J(a+rv)\, dv.  \] If the test is supported in $B_ R(0)$, a contributing $v$ has $|v|\leq R$. For all sufficiently small $r$, this whole closed base ball lies in $(V-a)/r$. The segment formula and continuity of $Du$ give uniform convergence of the scaled height to $Du(a)v$ on that ball, and $J(a+rv)\to J(a)$ uniformly. The integrands are uniformly bounded on a fixed finite-volume ball. Dominated convergence gives \[  J(a)\int _{\mathbb R^ m}\phi (v,Du(a)v)\, dv.  \] The linear area formula for the injective graph map $v\mapsto (v,Du(a)v)$ identifies this with the integral on $T$. A sufficiently small ambient ball projects into a compact subset of $V$, so no global area bound on the whole graph is needed. The case $m=n$ has zero-dimensional target and $J=1$. $\square$ Corollary 3.6.3 (Unit density at an interior point of a graph patch) . FA97E756FBFC Under Proposition 3.6.2 , \[  \lim _{r\downarrow 0}\frac{\mathcal H^ m(N\cap B_ r(x))}{\omega _ m r^ m}=1.  \] The assertion applies at every interior point of a finite-area patch from Lemma 3.5.8 . Proof The sphere $\partial B_1$ has zero $\mathcal H^ m\llcorner T$ measure: in the $m$-plane it is an $(m-1)$-sphere. Sandwich its ball indicator between continuous cutoffs supported in slightly larger balls and equal to one on slightly smaller balls. Proposition 3.6.2 then bounds the lower and upper limiting masses by $\omega _ m(1-\delta )^ m$ and $\omega _ m(1+\delta )^ m$. Let $\delta \downarrow 0$. This proves the ball-mass limit without treating the discontinuous indicator as a continuous test. $\square$ Lemma 3.6.4 (Differentiation on the union of two measurable sets) . 8A605F7E5FCD Let $M,N\subset U\subset \mathbb R^ n$ be Borel, with $U$ open, and have locally finite $\mathcal H^ m$ measure in $U$, and put $\lambda =\mathcal H^ m\llcorner (M\cup N)$. At $\mathcal H^ m$-almost every $x\in M\cap N$, \[  \frac{\mathcal H^ m(M\cap B_ r(x))}{\lambda (B_ r(x))}\to 1, \qquad \frac{\mathcal H^ m(N\cap B_ r(x))}{\lambda (B_ r(x))}\to 1, \qquad \frac{\mathcal H^ m((M\mathbin {\triangle }N)\cap B_ r(x))}{\lambda (B_ r(x))}\to 0.  \] If also $\mathcal H^ m(N\cap B_ r(x))/(\omega _ mr^ m)\to 1$ at such a point, then the symmetric-difference numerator is $o(r^ m)$ and $\lambda (B_ r(x))/(\omega _ mr^ m)\to 1$. Proof The union measure is locally finite and Radon. Theorem 2.6.5 applies to the bounded functions $\chi _ M$ and $\chi _ N$. At almost every point of their common part, both values are one and both averages tend to one. Their missing portions have relative measure tending to zero, and their sum is exactly the relative measure of $M\mathbin {\triangle }N$ within the union. This proves the first three limits. If the additional unit-density hypothesis holds, divide $\mathcal H^ m(N\cap B_ r)/(\omega _ mr^ m)$ by $\mathcal H^ m(N\cap B_ r)/\lambda (B_ r)$ to obtain the limit for $\lambda $. Multiplication gives the $o(r^ m)$ estimate. The union, rather than the sum of two restricted measures, avoids double-counting $M\cap N$. $\square$ Proposition 3.6.5 (Transfer of a tangent across an almost-full common part) . E0BE88808391 Let $M\subset U$ be Borel with locally finite $\mathcal H^ m$ measure in the open set $U$, and let $N\subset U$ be a finite-area $C^1$ graph patch. Then for $\mathcal H^ m$-almost every $x\in M\cap N$, the set $M$ has the approximate tangent $T_ xN$ in Definition 3.1.3 . At these points, \[  \mathcal H^ m((M\mathbin {\triangle }N)\cap B_ r(x))=o(r^ m).  \] This accounts for the accumulating other pieces in the forward proof of [ Sim18 ] , Theorem 1.6. Proof Every point of $N$ is interior to its base domain. Corollary 3.6.3 and Lemma 3.6.4 give the stated small symmetric-difference mass outside an $\mathcal H^ m$-null subset of $M\cap N$. Fix any such point. For a continuous test supported in $B_ R(0)$, the absolute difference between the scaled $M$ and $N$ integrals is at most \[  \| \phi \| _\infty r^{-m} \mathcal H^ m((M\mathbin {\triangle }N)\cap B_{Rr}(x))\longrightarrow 0.  \] The graph integral tends to the integral on $T_ xN$ by Proposition 3.6.2 . Therefore the $M$ integral has the same limit. The chosen exceptional set depends only on the symmetric-difference estimate, so one full-measure set works for every test and every fixed $R$, with no uncountable intersection of test-dependent null sets. $\square$ Theorem 3.6.6 (Rectifiable sets have approximate tangent planes) . 508BF16A8066 Let $M\subset U\subset \mathbb R^ n$, with $U$ open, be $\mathcal H^ m$-measurable, countably $m$-rectifiable and locally finite in $\mathcal H^ m$ measure in $U$. Then the approximate tangent $T_ xM$ exists at $\mathcal H^ m$-almost every point of $M$. On each $C^1$ patch $N$ of a countable covering it equals $T_ xN$ at almost every point of $M\cap N$. This is the forward direction of [ Sim18 ] , Chapter 3, Theorem 1.6 and Remark 1.5(2), pp. 87–88. Proof Replace $M$ by its Borel hull from Lemma 3.6.1 ; this changes no restricted or scaled measure and preserves rectifiability up to a null set. Theorem 3.5.7 and Lemma 3.5.8 cover the set up to a null subset by countably many Borel finite-area patches. Apply Proposition 3.6.5 to each patch. The union of the exceptional subsets is still $\mathcal H^ m$-null. At every other covered point the tangent exists and equals that of each patch containing it outside its exceptional subset. This proves both assertions. Local finiteness is used to make the union measure Radon; countable rectifiability alone does not supply it. $\square$ Corollary 3.6.7 (Density one on a locally finite rectifiable set) . FA919827E4FB Under Theorem 3.6.6 , \[  \lim _{r\downarrow 0}\frac{\mathcal H^ m(M\cap B_ r(x))}{\omega _ mr^ m}=1 \quad \text{for }\mathcal H^ m\text{-almost every }x\in M.  \] The proof depends on Whitney extension, Euclidean area, and the Besicovitch input to Radon differentiation; it does not assume the full rectifiable-set tangent characterization. Proof At every point with a tangent, apply the continuous-cutoff argument of Corollary 3.6.3 to the limit in Definition 3.1.3 . The plane has unit normalized ball mass and does not charge the unit sphere. Theorem 3.6.6 makes such points a full-measure set. This is the exact constant needed in the final perimeter measure-identification argument. $\square$ Corollary 3.6.8 (Tangent agreement on intersections) . 4E4D4F977258 If $M_1,M_2\subset U$ are measurable, countably $m$-rectifiable and locally finite in $\mathcal H^ m$ measure in an open set $U\subset \mathbb R^ n$, then \[  T_ xM_1=T_ xM_2 \quad \text{for }\mathcal H^ m\text{-almost every }x\in M_1\cap M_2.  \] Their union is locally finite and countably rectifiable; it has the same tangent at almost every point of the intersection. Proof Use Borel representatives and let $\lambda $ be the Hausdorff measure restricted to their union. At almost every point of the intersection, both restricted measures have unit density by Corollary 3.6.7 , and the symmetric-difference mass is $o(r^ m)$ by Lemma 3.6.4 . The scaled test integrals therefore have the same limits by the estimate in Proposition 3.6.5 . The plane measures in these limits have supports equal to their planes, so equal limits imply equal planes. The mass of the union minus either set is bounded by the symmetric-difference mass, proving the final assertion by the same estimate. Intersecting the finitely many full-measure sets is legitimate. $\square$

text: Lemma 3.6.1 (Borel representatives for locally finite Hausdorff measure) . 3C9EA6CE752A If $M\subset U\subset \mathbb R^ n$ is $\mathcal H^ m$-measurable, $U$ is open, and $\mathcal H^ m(M\cap K)<\infty $ for every compact $K\subset U$, there is a Borel set $M\subset B\subset U$ with $\mathcal H^ m(B\setminus M)=0$. The Borel measure $\sigma (A)=\mathcal H^ m(M\cap A)$ on $U$ is locally finite and Radon, and is unchanged if $M$ is replaced by $B$. The measures obtained by translation and dilation are likewise unchanged. Proof Choose increasing compact sets $K_ j\subset U$ exhausting $U$. For each integer $j$, the set $M\cap K_ j$ has finite Hausdorff measure. Borel regularity of Hausdorff measure, recalled in Definition 2.2.1 , provides a Borel superset $B_ j$ with the same measure. Measurability and finite measure give $\mathcal H^ m(B_ j\setminus M)=0$ after subtracting $M\cap K_ j$. The union $B=\bigcup _ jB_ j$ contains $M$ and differs from it by a countable union of null sets. Restrictions agree on every Borel test set, proving the measure identity and local finiteness. Intersect the Borel hull with $U$ if necessary. A locally finite Borel measure on a Euclidean open set is Radon. Pushforwards preserve equality of measures, giving the last assertion. This supplies a Borel representative when applying the Radon differentiation theorem; it does not identify topological boundaries of representatives. $\square$

title: Proposition 3.6.2 (The tangent measure of a continuously differentiable graph)
search_title: The tangent measure of a continuously differentiable graph
section: 3.6 Tangent measures of rectifiable pieces
text: Proposition 3.6.2 (The tangent measure of a continuously differentiable graph) . 19A8BA237DE1 Let $V\subset \mathbb R^ m$ be open, let $u:V\to \mathbb R^{n-m}$ be $C^1$, and let $N=\{ (z,u(z)):z\in V\} $. At $x=(a,u(a))$ with $a\in V$, put $T=\{ (v,Du(a)v):v\in \mathbb R^ m\} $. For every $\phi \in C_ c(\mathbb R^ n)$, \[  \lim _{r\downarrow 0}r^{-m}\int _ N\phi ((y-x)/r)\, d\mathcal H^ m(y) =\int _ T\phi \, d\mathcal H^ m.  \] Only the portion of $N$ near $x$ enters this identity. This proves the smooth-patch limit used in [ Sim18 ] , p. 87, from the now locally proved Euclidean area formula. Proof Write $J(z)=\sqrt{\det (I+Du(z)^*Du(z))}$. The weighted area formula, Proposition 3.3.1 , and the substitution $z=a+rv$ express the integral on the left as \[  \int _{(V-a)/r}\phi \left(v,\frac{u(a+rv)-u(a)}r\right)J(a+rv)\, dv.  \] If the test is supported in $B_ R(0)$, a contributing $v$ has $|v|\leq R$. For all sufficiently small $r$, this whole closed base ball lies in $(V-a)/r$. The segment formula and continuity of $Du$ give uniform convergence of the scaled height to $Du(a)v$ on that ball, and $J(a+rv)\to J(a)$ uniformly. The integrands are uniformly bounded on a fixed finite-volume ball. Dominated convergence gives \[  J(a)\int _{\mathbb R^ m}\phi (v,Du(a)v)\, dv.  \] The linear area formula for the injective graph map $v\mapsto (v,Du(a)v)$ identifies this with the integral on $T$. A sufficiently small ambient ball projects into a compact subset of $V$, so no global area bound on the whole graph is needed. The case $m=n$ has zero-dimensional target and $J=1$. $\square$

title: 3.7 Cone criteria in arbitrary codimension
search_title: Cone criteria in arbitrary codimension
section: 3.7 Cone criteria in arbitrary codimension
text: The reduced-boundary graph argument has a version for an $m$-plane in $\mathbb R^ n$, with $1\leq m<n$. The normal component is now a vector in an $(n-m)$-dimensional space. We supply the details needed for the converse implication in [ Sim18 ] , Chapter 3, Theorem 1.6, printed pp. 88–90. A coordinatewise scalar extension is sufficient; an optimal vector-valued extension theorem is not needed. Definition 3.7.1 (Projection distance and the cone outside a plane) . FC9C64E80FA4 For an $m$-dimensional linear plane $P\subset \mathbb R^ n$, let $p_ P$ be its orthogonal projection and $q_ P=I-p_ P$. Put \[  d(P,Q)=\| p_ P-p_ Q\| _{\mathrm{op}},\qquad C_\alpha (x,P)=\{ z:|q_ P(z-x)|\geq \alpha |z-x|\} ,\quad 0<\alpha <1.  \] The cone consists of directions whose angle from the plane is bounded below. This is equivalent to the complementary-plane convention in [ Sim18 ] , equations (1)–(3), p. 88. For codimension one it agrees with Definition 4.13.1 after choosing a unit normal. Lemma 3.7.2 (Finite nets of planes) . 286A09C1E40A The $m$-dimensional planes form a compact metric space under $d$. In particular, for each $\eta >0$ finitely many open $d$-balls of radius $\eta $ cover all of them. Also $\| q_ P-q_ Q\| _{\mathrm{op}}=d(P,Q)$. Proof Identify a plane with its real $n\times n$ orthogonal projection matrix. Such matrices are exactly those satisfying $A^*=A$, $A^2=A$ and $\operatorname {tr}A=m$. These polynomial conditions are closed. A real symmetric idempotent has eigenvalues zero or one, so these matrices are bounded and the trace condition makes their rank exactly $m$. They form a compact subset of the finite-dimensional matrix space. The operator norm induces its usual topology, and compactness gives a finite subcover of the cover by all open balls of radius $\eta $. The equality for complementary projections follows from $q_ P-q_ Q=-(p_ P-p_ Q)$. This justifies the finite orientation selection in the cone proof. $\square$ Lemma 3.7.3 (A ball forced outside a nearby plane) . 78A96A322A6D Let $x\ne y$, $d_0=|y-x|$, and let $P,P_ x$ be $m$-planes with $d(P,P_ x)\leq 1/8$. If $|q_ P(y-x)|>d_0/2$, then \[  B_{d_0/32}(y)\subset C_{1/4}(x,P_ x)\cap B_{2d_0}(x).  \] This is the vector-normal version of Lemma 4.13.3 . Proof The projection estimate gives $|q_{P_ x}(y-x)|>3d_0/8$. For $|z-y|<d_0/32$, use $\| q_{P_ x}\| _{\mathrm{op}}=1$ to obtain $|q_{P_ x}(z-x)|>11d_0/32$, while $|z-x|<33d_0/32<2d_0$. Their ratio exceeds $1/3$ and hence $1/4$. No sign choice for a normal vector is involved, so the calculation works in every codimension. $\square$ Proposition 3.7.4 (Uniform plane-cone bounds imply a vector-valued graph) . 3D34669B9F06 Let $\mu $ be Radon on an open $U\subset \mathbb R^ n$ and $S\subset U$. Suppose $c,\rho >0$, an $m$-plane $P$, and $m$-planes $P_ x$ for $x\in S$ satisfy $d(P_ x,P)\leq 1/8$, $B_\rho (x)\subset U$, and, for every $0<r<\rho $, \[  \mu (B_ r(x))\geq cr^ m,\qquad \mu (C_{1/4}(x,P_ x)\cap B_ r(x))\leq \delta r^ m, \qquad \delta =\frac{c}{2\cdot 64^ m}.  \] If $\operatorname {diam}S<\rho /2$, then $S$ lies on the graph over $P$ of a map $h:P\to P^\perp $ with Lipschitz constant at most $\sqrt{(n-m)/3}$. On the projected subset $p_ P(S)$ the original height map has the sharper bound $1/\sqrt3$. Proof If a pair $x,y\in S$ had $|q_ P(y-x)|>|y-x|/2$, Lemma 3.7.3 would give \[  c(d_0/32)^ m\leq \mu (B_{d_0/32}(y)) \leq \mu (C_{1/4}(x,P_ x)\cap B_{2d_0}(x)) \leq \delta (2d_0)^ m=\tfrac 12c(d_0/32)^ m,  \] where $d_0=|y-x|<\rho /2$. This is impossible. Hence every pair satisfies $|q_ P(y-x)|\leq |y-x|/2$. Orthogonality gives $|p_ P(y-x)|\geq \sqrt3|y-x|/2$ and $|q_ P(y-x)|\leq |p_ P(y-x)|/\sqrt3$. Projection is injective, and the height map on its image is $h_0(p_ Px)=q_ Px$ with the claimed bound. Choose an orthonormal basis of $P^\perp $. Each of the $n-m$ components of $h_0$ is scalar $1/\sqrt3$-Lipschitz. Proposition 3.4.2 extends it to all of $P$ with that bound. The Euclidean norm of the vector of component differences is at most $\sqrt{(n-m)/3}$ times the base distance. These extensions form $h$. If $S$ is empty take $h=0$. The resulting whole graph is a Lipschitz image of $\mathbb R^ m$; the possibly enlarged extension constant has no effect on containment or rectifiability. $\square$ Theorem 3.7.5 (Pointwise plane-cone bounds give a countable graph cover) . 0535AECAFAE7 Let $\mu $ be Radon on an open $U\subset \mathbb R^ n$, and let $S\subset U$. Suppose that for each $x\in S$ there is an $m$-plane $P_ x$ for which \[  \liminf _{r\downarrow 0}\frac{\mu (B_ r(x))}{r^ m}>0,\qquad \lim _{r\downarrow 0}\frac{\mu (C_{1/4}(x,P_ x)\cap B_ r(x))}{r^ m}=0.  \] Then $S$ is contained in countably many whole Lipschitz graphs over $m$-planes. No measurability of the plane selection is needed for this containment assertion. Proof For positive integers $k,j$, retain those points for which $B_{1/j}(x)\subset U$ and the lower bound with $c=1/k$ and cone upper bound with $\delta =c/(2\cdot 64^ m)$ both hold for all $0<r<1/j$. The two limits imply that these countably many classes cover $S$: first choose a smaller positive lower constant, then a sufficiently small common scale at the given point. Split each class using the finite $1/8$-net of planes from Lemma 3.7.2 , allowing overlap. Intersect with a countable cover of space by balls of diameter less than $1/(2j)$. Each resulting piece satisfies Proposition 3.7.4 . There are countably many pieces and hence countably many graphs. This construction uses uniform inequalities only on the defined pieces, not an unsupported uniform convergence assertion on $S$ itself. $\square$ Lemma 3.7.6 (A plane tangent supplies density and cone decay) . 487ED9476A1A Let $\mu $ be Radon on an open $U\subset \mathbb R^ n$, let $x\in U$, and suppose \[  r^{-m}(\eta _{x,r})_\# \mu \rightharpoonup \mathcal H^ m\llcorner P, \qquad \eta _{x,r}(y)=(y-x)/r,  \] locally as $r\downarrow 0$, where $m\geq 1$. Then $\mu (B_ r(x))/(\omega _ mr^ m)\to 1$ and, for every $0<\alpha <1$, \[  r^{-m}\mu (C_\alpha (x,P)\cap B_ r(x))\to 0.  \] This is the content of [ Sim18 ] , Chapter 3, Remark 1.5(3), p. 87. Proof The ball mass follows by continuous cutoffs as in Corollary 3.6.3 . For the cone, its rescaling inside $B_1$ lies in the compact set $K=\{ |q_ Pz|\geq \alpha |z|\} \cap \overline B_1$. Its intersection with $P$ is only the origin, which has zero $\mathcal H^ m$ measure for $m\geq 1$. The upper bound for compact sets under weak Radon convergence gives a limiting upper mass of zero. These two arguments use different continuity facts: the unit sphere has zero plane measure, whereas the closed cone compact set itself has zero plane measure. $\square$ Theorem 3.7.7 (Almost-everywhere plane tangents imply rectifiability) . 1C1255DA63AF Let $M\subset \mathbb R^ n$ be $\mathcal H^ m$-measurable and locally finite in $\mathcal H^ m$ measure, with $1\leq m<n$. If $T_ xM$ in Definition 3.1.3 exists at almost every point of $M$, then $M$ is countably $m$-rectifiable. This proves the converse in [ Sim18 ] , Chapter 3, Theorem 1.6, pp. 88–90. Proof Use Lemma 3.6.1 to regard $\mu =\mathcal H^ m\llcorner M$ as a locally finite Radon measure. Let $S\subset M$ be the full-measure set on which the tangent exists, and assign $P_ x=T_ xM$. Lemma 3.7.6 supplies both hypotheses of Theorem 3.7.5 , with positive density $\omega _ m$. Thus $S$ lies in countably many Lipschitz graphs, each a Lipschitz image of $\mathbb R^ m$. The remaining subset of $M$ has zero $\mathcal H^ m$ measure, exactly the allowed exception in Definition 3.1.1 . Nothing in this argument identifies a merely positive finite density with a plane tangent; the directional cone decay is also required. $\square$

section: 3.7 Cone criteria in arbitrary codimension
text: Lemma 3.7.2 (Finite nets of planes) . 286A09C1E40A The $m$-dimensional planes form a compact metric space under $d$. In particular, for each $\eta >0$ finitely many open $d$-balls of radius $\eta $ cover all of them. Also $\| q_ P-q_ Q\| _{\mathrm{op}}=d(P,Q)$. Proof Identify a plane with its real $n\times n$ orthogonal projection matrix. Such matrices are exactly those satisfying $A^*=A$, $A^2=A$ and $\operatorname {tr}A=m$. These polynomial conditions are closed. A real symmetric idempotent has eigenvalues zero or one, so these matrices are bounded and the trace condition makes their rank exactly $m$. They form a compact subset of the finite-dimensional matrix space. The operator norm induces its usual topology, and compactness gives a finite subcover of the cover by all open balls of radius $\eta $. The equality for complementary projections follows from $q_ P-q_ Q=-(p_ P-p_ Q)$. This justifies the finite orientation selection in the cone proof. $\square$

title: Lemma 3.7.3 (A ball forced outside a nearby plane)
search_title: A ball forced outside a nearby plane
section: 3.7 Cone criteria in arbitrary codimension
text: Lemma 3.7.3 (A ball forced outside a nearby plane) . 78A96A322A6D Let $x\ne y$, $d_0=|y-x|$, and let $P,P_ x$ be $m$-planes with $d(P,P_ x)\leq 1/8$. If $|q_ P(y-x)|>d_0/2$, then \[  B_{d_0/32}(y)\subset C_{1/4}(x,P_ x)\cap B_{2d_0}(x).  \] This is the vector-normal version of Lemma 4.13.3 . Proof The projection estimate gives $|q_{P_ x}(y-x)|>3d_0/8$. For $|z-y|<d_0/32$, use $\| q_{P_ x}\| _{\mathrm{op}}=1$ to obtain $|q_{P_ x}(z-x)|>11d_0/32$, while $|z-x|<33d_0/32<2d_0$. Their ratio exceeds $1/3$ and hence $1/4$. No sign choice for a normal vector is involved, so the calculation works in every codimension. $\square$

title: Proposition 3.7.4 (Uniform plane-cone bounds imply a vector-valued graph)
search_title: Uniform plane-cone bounds imply a vector-valued graph
section: 3.7 Cone criteria in arbitrary codimension
text: Proposition 3.7.4 (Uniform plane-cone bounds imply a vector-valued graph) . 3D34669B9F06 Let $\mu $ be Radon on an open $U\subset \mathbb R^ n$ and $S\subset U$. Suppose $c,\rho >0$, an $m$-plane $P$, and $m$-planes $P_ x$ for $x\in S$ satisfy $d(P_ x,P)\leq 1/8$, $B_\rho (x)\subset U$, and, for every $0<r<\rho $, \[  \mu (B_ r(x))\geq cr^ m,\qquad \mu (C_{1/4}(x,P_ x)\cap B_ r(x))\leq \delta r^ m, \qquad \delta =\frac{c}{2\cdot 64^ m}.  \] If $\operatorname {diam}S<\rho /2$, then $S$ lies on the graph over $P$ of a map $h:P\to P^\perp $ with Lipschitz constant at most $\sqrt{(n-m)/3}$. On the projected subset $p_ P(S)$ the original height map has the sharper bound $1/\sqrt3$. Proof If a pair $x,y\in S$ had $|q_ P(y-x)|>|y-x|/2$, Lemma 3.7.3 would give \[  c(d_0/32)^ m\leq \mu (B_{d_0/32}(y)) \leq \mu (C_{1/4}(x,P_ x)\cap B_{2d_0}(x)) \leq \delta (2d_0)^ m=\tfrac 12c(d_0/32)^ m,  \] where $d_0=|y-x|<\rho /2$. This is impossible. Hence every pair satisfies $|q_ P(y-x)|\leq |y-x|/2$. Orthogonality gives $|p_ P(y-x)|\geq \sqrt3|y-x|/2$ and $|q_ P(y-x)|\leq |p_ P(y-x)|/\sqrt3$. Projection is injective, and the height map on its image is $h_0(p_ Px)=q_ Px$ with the claimed bound. Choose an orthonormal basis of $P^\perp $. Each of the $n-m$ components of $h_0$ is scalar $1/\sqrt3$-Lipschitz. Proposition 3.4.2 extends it to all of $P$ with that bound. The Euclidean norm of the vector of component differences is at most $\sqrt{(n-m)/3}$ times the base distance. These extensions form $h$. If $S$ is empty take $h=0$. The resulting whole graph is a Lipschitz image of $\mathbb R^ m$; the possibly enlarged extension constant has no effect on containment or rectifiability. $\square$

title: Theorem 3.7.5 (Pointwise plane-cone bounds give a countable graph cover)
search_title: Pointwise plane-cone bounds give a countable graph cover
section: 3.7 Cone criteria in arbitrary codimension
text: Theorem 3.7.5 (Pointwise plane-cone bounds give a countable graph cover) . 0535AECAFAE7 Let $\mu $ be Radon on an open $U\subset \mathbb R^ n$, and let $S\subset U$. Suppose that for each $x\in S$ there is an $m$-plane $P_ x$ for which \[  \liminf _{r\downarrow 0}\frac{\mu (B_ r(x))}{r^ m}>0,\qquad \lim _{r\downarrow 0}\frac{\mu (C_{1/4}(x,P_ x)\cap B_ r(x))}{r^ m}=0.  \] Then $S$ is contained in countably many whole Lipschitz graphs over $m$-planes. No measurability of the plane selection is needed for this containment assertion. Proof For positive integers $k,j$, retain those points for which $B_{1/j}(x)\subset U$ and the lower bound with $c=1/k$ and cone upper bound with $\delta =c/(2\cdot 64^ m)$ both hold for all $0<r<1/j$. The two limits imply that these countably many classes cover $S$: first choose a smaller positive lower constant, then a sufficiently small common scale at the given point. Split each class using the finite $1/8$-net of planes from Lemma 3.7.2 , allowing overlap. Intersect with a countable cover of space by balls of diameter less than $1/(2j)$. Each resulting piece satisfies Proposition 3.7.4 . There are countably many pieces and hence countably many graphs. This construction uses uniform inequalities only on the defined pieces, not an unsupported uniform convergence assertion on $S$ itself. $\square$

title: Lemma 3.7.6 (A plane tangent supplies density and cone decay)
search_title: A plane tangent supplies density and cone decay
section: 3.7 Cone criteria in arbitrary codimension
text: Lemma 3.7.6 (A plane tangent supplies density and cone decay) . 487ED9476A1A Let $\mu $ be Radon on an open $U\subset \mathbb R^ n$, let $x\in U$, and suppose \[  r^{-m}(\eta _{x,r})_\# \mu \rightharpoonup \mathcal H^ m\llcorner P, \qquad \eta _{x,r}(y)=(y-x)/r,  \] locally as $r\downarrow 0$, where $m\geq 1$. Then $\mu (B_ r(x))/(\omega _ mr^ m)\to 1$ and, for every $0<\alpha <1$, \[  r^{-m}\mu (C_\alpha (x,P)\cap B_ r(x))\to 0.  \] This is the content of [ Sim18 ] , Chapter 3, Remark 1.5(3), p. 87. Proof The ball mass follows by continuous cutoffs as in Corollary 3.6.3 . For the cone, its rescaling inside $B_1$ lies in the compact set $K=\{ |q_ Pz|\geq \alpha |z|\} \cap \overline B_1$. Its intersection with $P$ is only the origin, which has zero $\mathcal H^ m$ measure for $m\geq 1$. The upper bound for compact sets under weak Radon convergence gives a limiting upper mass of zero. These two arguments use different continuity facts: the unit sphere has zero plane measure, whereas the closed cone compact set itself has zero plane measure. $\square$

title: Theorem 3.7.7 (Almost-everywhere plane tangents imply rectifiability)
search_title: Almost-everywhere plane tangents imply rectifiability
section: 3.7 Cone criteria in arbitrary codimension
text: Theorem 3.7.7 (Almost-everywhere plane tangents imply rectifiability) . 1C1255DA63AF Let $M\subset \mathbb R^ n$ be $\mathcal H^ m$-measurable and locally finite in $\mathcal H^ m$ measure, with $1\leq m<n$. If $T_ xM$ in Definition 3.1.3 exists at almost every point of $M$, then $M$ is countably $m$-rectifiable. This proves the converse in [ Sim18 ] , Chapter 3, Theorem 1.6, pp. 88–90. Proof Use Lemma 3.6.1 to regard $\mu =\mathcal H^ m\llcorner M$ as a locally finite Radon measure. Let $S\subset M$ be the full-measure set on which the tangent exists, and assign $P_ x=T_ xM$. Lemma 3.7.6 supplies both hypotheses of Theorem 3.7.5 , with positive density $\omega _ m$. Thus $S$ lies in countably many Lipschitz graphs, each a Lipschitz image of $\mathbb R^ m$. The remaining subset of $M$ has zero $\mathcal H^ m$ measure, exactly the allowed exception in Definition 3.1.1 . Nothing in this argument identifies a merely positive finite density with a plane tangent; the directional cone decay is also required. $\square$

title: 3.8 Weights and tangent measures
search_title: Weights and tangent measures
section: 3.8 Weights and tangent measures
text: An integrable weight can make a rectifiable surface measure locally finite even when its unweighted area is not. We prove the weighted tangent statement by exhausting the surface with subsets where the weight has a positive lower bound. This expands [ Sim18 ] , Chapter 3, Definition 1.7 and Theorem 1.9, printed pp. 90–92. Here $1\leq m<n$ and $U\subset \mathbb R^ n$ is open. We write $\eta _{x,r}(y)=(y-x)/r$. Proposition 3.8.1 (Multiplying a unit-density tangent by an integrable weight) . D3D6B64F4764 Let $M\subset U$ be measurable, countably $m$-rectifiable and locally finite in $\mathcal H^ m$ measure. Put $\sigma =\mathcal H^ m\llcorner M$. For $f\in L^1_{\mathrm{loc}}(\sigma )$, at $\sigma $-almost every $x$ and for every $\phi \in C_ c(\mathbb R^ n)$, \[  \lim _{r\downarrow 0}r^{-m}\int _ M\phi ((y-x)/r)f(y)\, d\mathcal H^ m(y) =f(x)\int _{T_ xM}\phi \, d\mathcal H^ m.  \] The weight may be signed. All integrals are local to $U$ for small enough $r$. Proof Choose a point where Theorem 3.6.6 , Corollary 3.6.7 , and the absolute-oscillation conclusion of Theorem 2.6.5 for $f$ all hold. Their simultaneous set has full $\sigma $ measure. For a test supported in $B_ R$, the difference between the scaled integral with $f(y)$ and that with the constant $f(x)$ has absolute value at most \[  \| \phi \| _\infty r^{-m}\int _{B_{Rr}(x)}|f(y)-f(x)|\, d\sigma (y).  \] The oscillation integral is $o(\sigma (B_{Rr}(x)))$, and the density limit gives $\sigma (B_{Rr}(x))=O(r^ m)$. Thus the error tends to zero. The remaining constant-weight integral converges by the tangent theorem. The same full-measure set works for every compactly supported test, since the oscillation and density estimates hold at all small radii. A countable compact exhaustion proves the local-domain version. $\square$ Definition 3.8.2 (A tangent plane with respect to a positive weight) . 8AE36515BAA5 Let $M\subset U$ be $\mathcal H^ m$-measurable, and let $\theta :M\to (0,\infty )$ be measurable and finite, with $\mu =\theta \mathcal H^ m\llcorner M$ locally finite. An $m$-plane $P$ is a weighted approximate tangent at $x\in M$ if \[  \lim _{r\downarrow 0}r^{-m}\int _ M\phi ((y-x)/r)\theta (y)\, d\mathcal H^ m(y) =\theta (x)\int _ P\phi \, d\mathcal H^ m \quad (\phi \in C_ c(\mathbb R^ n)).  \] This is the convention of [ Sim18 ] , Definition 1.7, p. 91. Positivity and finiteness of $\theta (x)$ make the plane unique when it exists. The definition does not require locally finite unweighted area. Lemma 3.8.3 (Positive weights give finite-area pieces and the same null sets) . 21236CD2BB9C Under Definition 3.8.2 , there are increasing measurable sets $M_ j\subset M$ covering $M$, such that $M_ j$ is bounded and has finite $\mathcal H^ m$ measure, and $1/j\leq \theta \leq j$ on $M_ j$. Further, $\mu (A)=0$ for a measurable $A\subset M$ if and only if $\mathcal H^ m(A)=0$. Borel representatives can be chosen for $M$ and its restricted weighted measure. Proof Choose increasing compact sets $K_ j\subset U$ whose union is $U$, and put $M_ j=M\cap K_ j\cap \{ 1/j\leq \theta \leq j\} $. They increase and cover $M$ because the weight is positive and finite. The bound $\mathcal H^ m(M_ j)\leq j\mu (K_ j)<\infty $ proves finite area. For a measurable $A$, a zero Hausdorff measure gives a zero weighted integral; conversely $\mathcal H^ m(A\cap M_ j)\leq j\mu (A)$ and continuity from below show that a zero weighted integral forces $\mathcal H^ m(A)=0$. Each $M_ j$ has a Borel hull with null Hausdorff difference, by the argument in Lemma 3.6.1 . Their union is a Borel representative of $M$ modulo an $\mathcal H^ m$-null set. On this sigma-finite Hausdorff measure space, a measurable finite function has a Borel representative modulo a null set, by approximation with simple functions and Borel representatives of their level sets. Its weighted restriction is a locally finite Borel measure, hence Radon. Such changes do not change any integral or almost-everywhere assertion. $\square$ Lemma 3.8.4 (Recovering a tangent from a full-density restriction) . 173F37205E7D Let $\mu $ be Radon, $A$ Borel, $x\in A$, and suppose \[  \frac{(\mu \llcorner A)(B_ r(x))}{\mu (B_ r(x))}\to 1, \qquad r^{-m}(\eta _{x,r})_\# (\mu \llcorner A) \rightharpoonup q\mathcal H^ m\llcorner P  \] for $q\in (0,\infty )$ and an $m$-plane $P$. Then $r^{-m}(\eta _{x,r})_\# \mu $ has the same limit, and \[  \mu (B_ r(x)\setminus A)=o(r^ m).  \] Proof The plane-tangent ball calculation gives $(\mu \llcorner A)(B_ r)/(\omega _ mr^ m)\to q$. Dividing by the first assumed ratio gives $\mu (B_ r)/(\omega _ mr^ m)\to q$. Subtracting the two expressions gives the stated small mass outside $A$. The difference of the two scaled integrals against a test supported in $B_ R$ is bounded by its supremum norm times $r^{-m}\mu (B_{Rr}(x)\setminus A)$, which tends to zero. Thus the unrestricted tangent is the same. This conclusion needs the positive finite density of the restricted tangent as well as relative density one. $\square$ Theorem 3.8.5 (Weighted tangents without locally finite unweighted area) . 97F1676D4605 Suppose $M$ is countably $m$-rectifiable and satisfies Definition 3.8.2 . Then the weighted approximate tangent exists at $\mathcal H^ m$-almost every point of $M$, and \[  \lim _{r\downarrow 0}\frac{\mu (B_ r(x))}{\omega _ mr^ m}=\theta (x)  \] at almost every such point. This proves the forward direction of [ Sim18 ] , Theorem 1.9, p. 91. Proof Use the Borel representatives and pieces $M_ j$ in Lemma 3.8.3 . Each piece is rectifiable with finite unweighted area. Proposition 3.8.1 , applied to its restricted weight, gives the tangent $\theta (x)\mathcal H^ m\llcorner T_ xM_ j$ for $\mu _ j=\mu \llcorner M_ j$ at $\mathcal H^ m$-almost every $x\in M_ j$. By Theorem 2.6.5 for $\chi _{M_ j}$ with respect to $\mu $, one also has $\mu _ j(B_ r)/\mu (B_ r)\to 1$ at $\mu $-almost every point of $M_ j$. The null-set equivalence makes both conclusions simultaneous outside an $\mathcal H^ m$-null subset of $M_ j$. Lemma 3.8.4 transfers the tangent to $\mu $. A countable union of exceptional subsets covers the only exclusions in $M$. The ball-density assertion follows either from that lemma or by continuous approximation of the unit-ball indicator. Positivity of $\theta $ is used when transferring relative density to absolute scale $r^ m$. $\square$ Theorem 3.8.6 (Positive weighted plane tangents imply rectifiability) . BC73C8D035CF Under Definition 3.8.2 , suppose the weighted approximate tangent exists at $\mathcal H^ m$-almost every point of $M$. Then $M$ is countably $m$-rectifiable. Together with Theorem 3.8.5 , this gives the weighted characterization in [ Sim18 ] , Theorem 1.9. Proof At a point with tangent $\theta (x)\mathcal H^ m\llcorner P_ x$, the continuous-cutoff and compact-cone arguments in Lemma 3.7.6 give positive lower density $\theta (x)\omega _ m$ for $\mu $ and zero normalized mass in $C_{1/4}(x,P_ x)\cap B_ r(x)$. Apply Theorem 3.7.5 to the full-measure set of such points, using the Radon measure from Lemma 3.8.3 . The result is a countable graph cover; the omitted subset is Hausdorff-null by hypothesis. This proves rectifiability without asserting locally finite unweighted area. The positive density constant may vary with $x$, as allowed by the pointwise cone theorem. $\square$ Corollary 3.8.7 (The tangent plane is independent of a positive weight) . EC2DBE512FEA Suppose a rectifiable $M$ carries two positive finite measurable weights $\theta ,\rho $ whose weighted measures are locally finite. Their weighted approximate tangent planes agree at $\mathcal H^ m$-almost every point of $M$, although their limiting plane measures have coefficients $\theta (x)$ and $\rho (x)$. Proof Exhaust $M$ by compactly located measurable pieces where both weights lie between $1/j$ and $j$. Each piece has finite unweighted area. On each piece Proposition 3.8.1 gives the same ordinary tangent plane for both weights, with their respective coefficients. Radon differentiation of the piece's indicator and Lemma 3.8.4 transfer each limit to its full weighted measure. Remove the countable union of exceptional Hausdorff-null subsets. The limiting planes coincide there because both were obtained from the same piece. This proof compares planes, not the unequal scalar multiplicities. $\square$

title: 6.13 Almost-everywhere varifold blow-ups
search_title: Almost-everywhere varifold blow-ups
section: 6.13 Almost-everywhere varifold blow-ups
text: A rectifiable varifold carries both a weighted measure and a tangent-plane field. Scalar convergence of the weight does not by itself control the plane coordinate. We prove the needed approximate continuity and obtain the full varifold blow-up at almost every point. The conventions are those of [ Sim18 ] , Chapter 3, pp. 90–92, and Chapter 8, Section 1, pp. 235–236. In this section $1\leq m<n$, $M\subset U\subset \mathbb R^ n$ is measurable and countably $m$-rectifiable with locally finite unweighted area, and $0<\theta <\infty $ is measurable with $\mu =\theta \mathcal H^ m\llcorner M$ locally finite. Lemma 6.13.1 (A Borel representative of the tangent-plane field) . A187938F7549 There is a Borel matrix field $A:U\to \mathbb R^{n\times n}$ which equals the orthogonal projection onto $T_ xM$ at $\mathcal H^ m$-almost every $x\in M$. It can be chosen to be a rank-$m$ orthogonal projection at every point of $U$. Any two such representatives agree $\mu $-almost everywhere on $M$. Proof Use the Borel representative of $M$ and the countable $C^1$ patch cover from Theorem 3.5.7 and Lemma 3.5.8 . Assign each point to the first patch containing it. On a patch with regular derivative matrix $DF$, projection onto its tangent is \[  DF\bigl ((DF)^*DF\bigr )^{-1}(DF)^*.  \] This is continuous in chart coordinates; the inverse chart is continuous, so it is a Borel field on the patch. The first-patch assignment gives a Borel field on the covered part of $M$. Put any fixed rank-$m$ projection on its complement. title: 3.9 Tangential derivatives on overlapping pieces
search_title: Tangential derivatives on overlapping pieces
section: 3.9 Tangential derivatives on overlapping pieces
text: The tangential derivative of an ambient Lipschitz function is defined by restricting to smooth pieces. We prove that these definitions agree almost everywhere on overlaps. The source is [ Sim18 ] , Chapter 3, Section 2, printed p. 92, together with the chart differentiability discussion in Chapter 2, Section 4. We use the already proved tangent agreement and Rademacher theorem, and keep the area formula as a recorded input. Throughout, $U\subset \mathbb R^ n$ is open and $1\leq m\leq n$. Lemma 3.9.1 (A density-one set approaches every direction) . 2296D505996A Let $A\subset \mathbb R^ m$ be measurable and have Lebesgue density one at $a$. For every fixed $v\in \mathbb R^ m$, \[  \operatorname {dist}(a+tv,A)=o(|t|)\quad \text{as }t\to 0.  \] Consequently, for any sequence $t_ j\to 0$ of nonzero numbers, there are $a_ j\in A$ with $a_ j=a+t_ jv+o(|t_ j|)$. Proof If the distance estimate failed, some $\varepsilon >0$ and sequence $t_ j\to 0$ would have $B_{\varepsilon |t_ j|/2}(a+t_ jv)$ disjoint from $A$. These balls lie in $B_{(|v|+\varepsilon )|t_ j|}(a)$ and have volume $\omega _ m(\varepsilon |t_ j|/2)^ m$. The fraction of missing volume in the latter balls would be bounded below by the positive number $(\varepsilon /(2(|v|+\varepsilon )))^ m$, contradicting density one. This also covers $v=0$. To choose $a_ j$, approximate the infimum defining the distance within $|t_ j|/j$; density one ensures $A$ is nonempty near $a$. These points give the displayed expansion. The lemma provides points of the set approaching a direction, not a whole line segment contained in it. $\square$ Proposition 3.9.2 (Differentiable functions agreeing on a measurable set have the same derivative there) . B495767E329D Let $V\subset \mathbb R^ m$ be open and $f,g:V\to \mathbb R^ k$ be locally Lipschitz and let $A\subset V$ be measurable with $f=g$ on $A$. Then $Df=Dg$ at almost every point of $A$. More precisely this holds at every density-one point $a\in A$ where both functions are differentiable. Proof At such a point fix $v$ and use Lemma 3.9.1 to choose $a_ j\in A$ with $a_ j=a+t_ jv+o(|t_ j|)$. Because $f(a)=g(a)$ and $f(a_ j)=g(a_ j)$, their differentiability expansions give \[  0=(Df(a)-Dg(a))(a_ j-a)+o(|a_ j-a|) =t_ j(Df(a)-Dg(a))v+o(|t_ j|).  \] Divide by $t_ j$ and pass to the limit. The difference vanishes on every $v$, so the derivatives agree. Rademacher and Lebesgue differentiation make the indicated differentiability and density conditions hold at almost every point of $A$. This argument applies componentwise to vector targets and does not require that $A$ have interior. $\square$ Lemma 3.9.3 (Restriction to a regular chart defines a tangential differential) . 5A50F9921DE6 Let $F:V\subset \mathbb R^ m\to N\subset U\subset \mathbb R^ n$ be an injective regular $C^1$ chart of an embedded manifold, and let $f:U\to \mathbb R^ k$ be locally Lipschitz. At almost every chart point $a$, the derivative $D(f\circ F)(a)$ exists and defines a linear map on $T_{F(a)}N$ by \[  L_{F(a)}(DF(a)v)=D(f\circ F)(a)v.  \] On a neighborhood where $f$ has Lipschitz constant $L$, this map has operator norm at most $L$. Changing regular $C^1$ coordinates gives the same map at points where the derivatives exist. Proof On relatively compact base balls $F$ has bounded derivative, so $f\circ F$ is Lipschitz. Rademacher gives its derivative almost everywhere; a countable exhaustion covers the chart. Regularity makes $DF(a)$ an isomorphism onto its tangent image, giving a well-defined linear map. For each $v$, the Lipschitz bound for $f$ gives \[  |D(f\circ F)(a)v| =\lim _{t\to 0}\frac{|f(F(a+tv))-f(F(a))|}{|t|} \leq L|DF(a)v|.  \] The chain rule for composition with a $C^1$ coordinate diffeomorphism proves coordinate independence. Its derivative and inverse derivative are locally bounded, so null sets are preserved under such coordinate changes. The area formula, with the strictly positive chart Jacobian, identifies coordinate-null exceptional sets with $\mathcal H^ m$-null exceptional subsets of $N$. An ambient derivative of $f$ need not exist at these surface points; only derivatives of its chart restriction are used. $\square$ Proposition 3.9.4 (Tangential differentials agree on two overlapping manifolds) . 2ED1B228648C Let $N_1,N_2\subset U\subset \mathbb R^ n$ be embedded $m$-dimensional $C^1$ manifolds and $f:U\to \mathbb R^ k$ locally Lipschitz. At $\mathcal H^ m$-almost every $x\in N_1\cap N_2$, their tangent planes coincide and the two tangential differentials of $f$ agree on that common plane. No open overlap of the manifolds is required. Proof Cover both manifolds by countably many finite-area graph patches and consider one pair of patches with charts $F_ i$. The tangent agreement follows from Corollary 3.6.8 . The set $A=F_1^{-1}(N_1\cap N_2)$ is measurable in the first chart. Lebesgue differentiation makes almost every point of $A$ a density-one point. The positive Jacobian in the area formula transfers this conclusion to almost every point of the intersection. Lemma 3.9.3 removes further null sets so both chart restrictions are differentiable. At a remaining point $x=F_1(a)$ and for $v\in T_ xN_1=T_ xN_2$, choose $w$ with $DF_1(a)w=v$. Lemma 3.9.1 gives $a_ j\in A$ with $a_ j=a+t_ jw+o(|t_ j|)$. Put $x_ j=F_1(a_ j)$; then $x_ j\in N_1\cap N_2$ and $x_ j=x+t_ jv+o(|t_ j|)$. Use graph coordinates for the second patch. Its inverse is the restriction of a linear orthogonal projection $p_2$ onto its base plane, after translation. Thus its inverse coordinates satisfy $b_ j=b+t_ jp_2v+o(|t_ j|)$, and $DF_2(b)p_2v=v$ because $v$ belongs to its tangent plane. Expand $f\circ F_ i$ along these points. Both expansions evaluate the same quantity $f(x_ j)-f(x)$, and they give respectively $t_ jL_1(v)+o(|t_ j|)$ and $t_ jL_2(v)+o(|t_ j|)$. Dividing and passing to the limit gives $L_1(v)=L_2(v)$. The finite-dimensional argument applies to each direction at the same good point. A countable union over the pairs of patches completes the proof. $\square$ Theorem 3.9.5 (An intrinsic tangential differential on a rectifiable set) . 20072C3F5DC1 Let $M\subset U$ be measurable, countably $m$-rectifiable and locally finite in $\mathcal H^ m$ measure, and let $f:U\to \mathbb R^ k$ be locally Lipschitz. Differentiation on any countable $C^1$ decomposition defines a measurable linear map \[  d^ Mf_ x:T_ xM\to \mathbb R^ k \quad \text{for }\mathcal H^ m\text{-almost every }x\in M,  \] independent of the decomposition up to a null set. Its norm is at most the local Lipschitz constant of $f$. Where the ambient derivative exists, $d^ Mf_ x=Df(x)|_{T_ xM}$ at the almost-everywhere points under consideration. For scalar $f$, its Euclidean dual is the tangential gradient $\nabla ^ Mf$. Proof Use Theorem 3.5.7 and Lemma 3.5.8 to partition $M$ into countably many measurable chart pieces modulo a null set. Lemma 3.9.3 defines the maps on each piece and bounds their norms. The derivative of a Lipschitz chart function is measurable as a limit of difference quotients. In a chart with $g=f\circ F$, the ambient representative is the matrix \[  Dg\bigl ((DF)^*DF\bigr )^{-1}(DF)^*.  \] It restricts to the required map on the tangent plane and is zero on its orthogonal complement. The inverse chart metric is continuous, so this matrix field is measurable. Thus the resulting field is measurable on the pieces and on their countable union. For two decompositions, compare every pair of patches by Proposition 3.9.4 . The countable union of its exceptional sets is null. The maps therefore agree on one full-measure subset of $M$; tangent identification there is Theorem 3.6.6 . If $f$ is ambient differentiable at such a point, its expansion along a $C^1$ chart immediately gives $D(f\circ F)=Df\circ DF$, proving the restriction formula. For a scalar target, the Euclidean inner product on the tangent plane identifies a linear functional with a unique vector. This proves the independence assertion used in Definition 3.3.2 ; it does not prove the coarea formula or its almost-everywhere fiber geometry. $\square$

text: The tangent theorems describe almost-everywhere measure geometry, with precise normalization and hypotheses. The following examples explain why uniform jet conditions, local area bounds, positive weights and the mode of convergence matter. The framework is [ Sim18 ] , Chapter 2, Remark 1.7, pp. 47–48, and Chapter 3, pp. 85–92. Example 16.28.1 (Pointwise jet remainders do not suffice for a smooth extension) . 1314ED4D7847 Let $C=\{ 0\} \cup \{ 1/k:k\geq 1\} $, set $h(0)=0$, $h(1/k)=(-1)^ k k^{-3/2}$ and $a=0$ on $C$. Both $h$ and $a$ are continuous. At every fixed $x\in C$ the first-order remainder tends to zero as $y\to x$ within $C$, but the jet has no $C^1(\mathbb R)$ extension. This is the example in [ Sim18 ] , Chapter 2, Remark 1.7(1), p. 47. Proof Every nonzero point of $C$ is isolated, so its pointwise condition is vacuous at sufficiently small distances. At zero the normalized remainder is $|h(1/k)|/(1/k)=k^{-1/2}\to 0$. These values also prove continuity of $h$ at zero. However the absolute slope between adjacent points is \[  \frac{k^{-3/2}+(k+1)^{-3/2}}{1/k-1/(k+1)} =k(k+1)\bigl (k^{-3/2}+(k+1)^{-3/2}\bigr )\longrightarrow \infty .  \] If a $C^1$ extension existed, the ordinary mean value theorem on each adjacent interval would produce a derivative of this absolute size at a point tending to zero. Continuity of the derivative near zero would make those values bounded, a contradiction. Equivalently the supremum in Definition 3.5.1 fails to tend to zero on the compact set $C$. The missing hypothesis is uniformity over nearby pairs, not continuity of the prescribed gradient alone. $\square$ Example 16.28.2 (A parabola converges weakly to its tangent but not in variation) . 6C1B14714CC2 Let $M=\{ (s,s^2):s\in \mathbb R\} $ and $\sigma _ r=r^{-1}(\eta _{0,r})_\# (\mathcal H^1\llcorner M)$. Then $\sigma _ r\rightharpoonup \mathcal H^1\llcorner P$ for $P=\{ y=0\} $. Nevertheless, writing $|\alpha |$ for the total variation measure of a signed measure, \[  \left|\sigma _ r-\mathcal H^1\llcorner P\right|(B_1(0))\longrightarrow 4.  \] Thus the tangent limit is not convergence in total variation, even for a smooth embedded curve. Proof The rescaled curve is $y=rs^2$, and the graph area formula gives $d\sigma _ r=\sqrt{1+4r^2s^2}\, ds$ on it. Proposition 3.6.2 gives weak convergence; its ball version gives $\sigma _ r(B_1)\to 2$. For every $r>0$, the parabola and $P$ meet only at zero, a point of zero length for both measures. Their restrictions to $B_1$ are mutually singular. Therefore the total variation of their difference on this ball is the sum of their masses, $\sigma _ r(B_1)+\mathcal H^1(P\cap B_1)=\sigma _ r(B_1)+2\to 4$. This uses the full signed-measure variation convention, with no probability-theory factor of one half. $\square$ Example 16.28.3 (Weighted circles with infinite unweighted area near their limit) . 688BAE194A4B In $\mathbb R^3$ let \[  C_ j=\{ (\cos t,\sin t,1/j):0\leq t<2\pi \} ,\qquad M=\bigcup _{j\geq 1}C_ j,\qquad \theta |_{C_ j}=2^{-j}.  \] The measure $\mu =\theta \mathcal H^1\llcorner M$ has total mass $2\pi $. The set $M$ is countably one-rectifiable but its unweighted length is infinite in every neighborhood of any point of the limiting circle $C_\infty =\{ (\cos t,\sin t,0)\} $. Every point of $C_ j$ has weighted tangent $2^{-j}\mathcal H^1$ on its tangent line. Every point of $C_\infty $ belongs to $\operatorname {supp}\mu $ but has one-dimensional density zero. Proof The circles are disjoint smooth curves, and summing $2\pi 2^{-j}$ gives the total mass. At any point on a fixed $C_ j$, its height is a positive distance from the heights of all other circles, so a sufficiently small neighborhood meets only this circle. Its weighted tangent follows from Proposition 3.6.2 or the local smooth curve calculation. By rotation take $q=(1,0,0)$ on the limiting circle. In each fixed ball about $q$, all sufficiently large $j$ contribute an arc of length bounded below by a positive constant depending only on that ball. There are infinitely many such circles, proving infinite unweighted length there. Every ball has positive weighted mass as well, so $q$ belongs to the support. For $0<r<1/2$, only circles with $j>1/r$ can meet $B_ r(q)$. The projection of a contributing arc onto its horizontal unit circle lies in the chordal ball of radius $r$ about $(1,0)$, whose arc length is $4\arcsin (r/2)\leq \pi r$. Thus \[  0\leq \frac{\mu (B_ r(q))}{2r} \leq \frac\pi 2\sum _{j>1/r}2^{-j}\longrightarrow 0.  \] The limiting circle is absent from $M$. This example illustrates both the usefulness of weighted tangents without locally finite unweighted area and the distinction between almost-everywhere density and density at every support point. No stationarity is asserted. $\square$ Example 16.28.4 (A finite rectifiable length measure can have a two-dimensional support) . 266B0CFDCAC6 There is a Borel countably one-rectifiable set $M\subset (0,1)^2$ with $0<\mathcal H^1(M)<\infty $ such that \[  \operatorname {supp}(\mathcal H^1\llcorner M)=[0,1]^2.  \] Nevertheless $M$ has an approximate tangent line and unit one-dimensional density at $\mathcal H^1$-almost every point. Therefore an almost-everywhere tangent theorem is not a smoothness theorem for the topological support. Proof Enumerate the rational points $q_ j$ of $(0,1)^2$ without repetitions. Choose $0<r_ j<\min \{ 2^{-j},\tfrac 12\operatorname {dist}(q_ j,\partial (0,1)^2)\} $, and let $C_ j$ be the circle of radius $r_ j$ centered at $q_ j$. Put $M=\bigcup _ jC_ j$. This is a countable union of compact smooth curves, contained in the open square, and $\mathcal H^1(M)\leq 2\pi \sum _ jr_ j<\infty $. Its measure is positive because it contains a circle of positive length. Every open ball contained in the square contains some whole circle: choose infinitely many rational centers in a smaller concentric ball, and then one with sufficiently large index that its radius bound $2^{-j}$ is smaller than the remaining distance to the ball's edge. Thus every such ball has positive restricted length. Every neighborhood of a boundary point of the closed square contains an interior ball of this type. Outside the closed square the measure vanishes on a neighborhood. These observations prove the exact support identity. Countable rectifiability and finite area permit Theorem 3.6.6 and Corollary 3.6.7 to be applied, proving the almost-everywhere conclusions despite the dense accumulation of other circles. $\square$ Example 16.28.5 (A zero weight can hide an unrectifiable component) . 6133EE47A2AE Let $P$ be the horizontal axis and let $K'=K+(0,2)$, where $K$ is the four-corner set of Definition 16.12.1 . Set $M=P\cup K'$, with weight $\theta =1$ on $P$ and $\theta =0$ on $K'$. Then $\mu =\theta \mathcal H^1\llcorner M$ is line measure on $P$, although $M$ is not countably one-rectifiable. If zero weights were allowed in the equality defining a weighted tangent, every line would satisfy that equality at every point of $K'$. Positivity in Definition 3.8.2 is therefore necessary for both uniqueness and the characterization. Proof The weighted measure identity is immediate. The translated dust has finite positive length and is purely one-unrectifiable by Theorem 16.12.7 ; if $M$ were rectifiable, its measurable subset $K'$ would be rectifiable, contradicting that result. The dust is a positive distance from $P$. At a point of $K'$, a compactly supported scaled test therefore sees no weighted mass for all sufficiently small radii, so its limiting integral is zero. The putative right side $\theta (x)\int _ L\phi $ is also zero for every line $L$. At a point of $P$ the usual line tangent holds. Thus simply removing the positive-weight hypothesis would make the purported tangent condition compatible with the unrectifiable dust. The dust result follows the example in [ Mor16 ] , pp. 36–37. $\square$ Example 16.28.6 (Changing one value of a weight changes a pointwise tangent formula) . F80607FDF014 On an $m$-plane $P$, let $\theta =1$ except that $\theta (0)=7$, where $m\geq 1$. The measure $\theta \mathcal H^ m\llcorner P$ is still $\mathcal H^ m\llcorner P$. Its normalized tangent at zero has coefficient one, not seven. The weighted tangent formula with the specified pointwise value $\theta (0)$ therefore fails there, while holding at every other point. Proof A singleton has zero $\mathcal H^ m$ measure for $m\geq 1$, so the measures are equal. Dilation centered at zero leaves normalized plane measure unchanged. For a nonnegative continuous compactly supported test with positive integral on $P$, multiplying that integral by seven gives a different value; no change of plane can repair the coefficient, as the unit-ball mass would still be seven times $\omega _ m$. At a nonzero point the prescribed value is one and the same plane calculation applies. This is why theorems about a measurable weight and its density are almost-everywhere assertions and must not depend on arbitrarily reassigned exceptional values. $\square$ Example 16.28.7 (An artificial patch edge has half the plane density) . 68876AF1BB63 Let $P$ be an $m$-plane, $m\geq 1$, and let $e\in P$ be a unit vector. For $N=\{ z\in P:z\cdot e\geq 0\} $, every point of its edge $\{ z\in P:z\cdot e=0\} $ has density $1/2$ with respect to $\mathcal H^ m\llcorner N$, and its normalized tangent measure is a half-plane measure. It is not the full-plane tangent of Definition 3.1.3 . The edge is $\mathcal H^ m$-null. Proof Translation by an edge point and dilation preserve the half-plane and its normalized measure. Reflection in the edge exchanges the two halves of the plane ball and preserves Hausdorff measure, so its ball mass is exactly $\omega _ mr^ m/2$. The measure limit is therefore the same half-plane measure at every scale, whose ball mass excludes any unit full-plane limit. The edge is an $(m-1)$-plane and has zero $\mathcal H^ m$ measure, directly from diameter covers on bounded pieces. This explains why the finite-area patch arguments use interior points of open base domains: an artificial truncation edge should not be treated as an interior smooth tangent point. $\square$

title: 3.10 Chart proofs of rectifiable area and coarea
search_title: Chart proofs of rectifiable area and coarea
section: 3.10 Chart proofs of rectifiable area and coarea
text: This section develops the chart mechanism behind [ Sim18 ] , Chapter 3, equations (2.4)–(2.9) and Remark 2.10, printed pp. 92–94. The Euclidean area and coarea formulas used here now have local proofs in Theorems 3.13.8 and 3.2.4 . The tangential differential and its independence, the $C^1$ decomposition, and the tangent theorem are supplied by the preceding development. Throughout, $U\subset \mathbb R^ n$ and the coordinate domains are open, and $1\leq m\leq n$. Unless otherwise specified, all weights are nonnegative and all integrals may be infinite. Lemma 3.10.1 (Area Jacobians under a change of tangent coordinates) . 29B22C797308 Let $A:\mathbb R^ m\to \mathbb R^ n$ be injective and linear, let $T=A(\mathbb R^ m)$, and let $L:T\to \mathbb R^ q$ be linear with $q\geq m$. Then \[  J_ m(LA)=J_ mL\, J_ mA.  \] Here $J_ mL$ uses the Euclidean metric restricted to $T$; either side can vanish if $L$ loses rank. Proof Choose an isometry $Q:\mathbb R^ m\to T$, and write $A=QR$ with an invertible $m\times m$ matrix $R$. The Gram matrix of $LA$ is $R^*(LQ)^*(LQ)R$, whose determinant is $\det (R)^2\det ((LQ)^*(LQ))$. Also $J_ mA=|\det R|$ and $J_ mL=\sqrt{\det ((LQ)^*(LQ))}$. Taking square roots proves the identity, including a zero Gram determinant. Orthogonal choice of $Q$ does not change any of these quantities. $\square$ Theorem 3.10.2 (Weighted area on a rectifiable domain) . 1AFF9641C00C Let $M\subset U\subset \mathbb R^ n$ be measurable, countably $m$-rectifiable and locally finite in $\mathcal H^ m$ measure, let $f:U\to \mathbb R^ q$ be locally Lipschitz with $q\geq m$, and let $h:M\to [0,\infty ]$ be measurable. Then \[  \int _ M h(x)J_ m(d^ Mf_ x)\, d\mathcal H^ m(x) =\int _{\mathbb R^ q}\sum _{x\in M\cap f^{-1}(y)}h(x)\, d\mathcal H^ m(y).  \] The fiber sum has a measurable representative. This is [ Sim18 ] , equations (2.4)–(2.6), derived here from the Euclidean weighted area formula. Products with a zero Jacobian use the convention $0\cdot \infty =0$. Proof Choose a Borel representative for $M$ and a Borel representative for $h$ relative to its sigma-finite restricted Hausdorff measure. This changes them only on an $\mathcal H^ m$-null subset; the image of that subset is null by the Lipschitz bound. Partition this representative of $M$, apart from an $\mathcal H^ m$-null set, into disjoint Borel pieces $M_ i$ lying in injective regular $C^1$ charts $F_ i:V_ i\to U$ as in Lemma 3.5.8 . Subdivide so the chart and the relevant restrictions of $f$ are Lipschitz on each piece's neighborhood. Put $A_ i=F_ i^{-1}(M_ i)$ and $g_ i=f\circ F_ i$. At almost every point of $A_ i$, Theorem 3.9.5 gives $Dg_ i=d^ Mf\circ DF_ i$. Lemma 3.10.1 therefore gives \[  J_ mDg_ i=J_ m(d^ Mf)J_ mDF_ i.  \] Apply Proposition 3.3.1 to $g_ i$ with weight $\chi _{A_ i}(h\circ F_ i)$. Apply the same formula to the injective chart $F_ i$ to change the left integral to integration on $M_ i$. The resulting right sum is over precisely the points of $M_ i\cap f^{-1}(y)$, because $F_ i$ is injective. Sum over $i$ using monotone convergence; the pieces are disjoint, so each point is counted once. This construction also gives measurability of the resulting sum modulo null sets. The omitted Hausdorff-null set has Hausdorff-null image under $f$, by the elementary Lipschitz bound on a countable local cover. Its fiber contribution therefore vanishes for almost every target point. On the left it contributes zero as well. This completes the formula on $M$ and permits infinite values by monotone approximation of $h$. $\square$ Lemma 3.10.3 (A Hausdorff-null set has null lower-dimensional fibers) . 1250D3393B38 Let $1\leq k<m$, let $f:U\subset \mathbb R^ n\to \mathbb R^ k$ be locally Lipschitz, and let $Z\subset U$ have $\mathcal H^ m(Z)=0$. Then \[  \mathcal H^{m-k}(Z\cap f^{-1}(y))=0 \quad \text{for }\mathcal L^ k\text{-almost every }y.  \] No rectifiability of $Z$ is assumed. This is the null-set part of the Lipschitz slicing estimate in [ Sim18 ] , Chapter 2, Theorem 1.10, pp. 49–51, proved directly by diameter covers. Proof Localize to $Z$ in a compact subset of a ball where $f$ has Lipschitz constant $L$ and whose closure lies in $U$. A countable such localization covers the original set. Put $d=m-k>0$. For each integer $l$, Hausdorff-nullness gives a cover by closed balls $Q_{li}$ of positive radii $r_{li}<2^{-l}$, all in the chosen neighborhood, with $\sum _ i r_{li}^ m<2^{-l}$. One obtains such balls from diameter covers by choosing centers in $Z$ and enlarging radii by a fixed factor; countably many zero-diameter cover members may be discarded, since their intersections with every fiber have zero $\mathcal H^ d$ measure. The sets $f(Q_{li})$ are compact, so \[  F_ l(y)=\sum _ i\omega _ d r_{li}^ d\chi _{f(Q_{li})}(y)  \] is measurable. Each image is contained in a $k$-ball of radius $Lr_{li}$ about the image of its center. Hence \[  \int F_ l\, dy\leq \omega _ d\omega _ kL^ k\sum _ i r_{li}^{d+k} <\omega _ d\omega _ kL^ k2^{-l}.  \] Tonelli implies $\sum _ lF_ l(y)<\infty $ for almost every $y$, so $F_ l(y)\to 0$ there. The corresponding selected balls cover $Z\cap f^{-1}(y)$ and have diameters less than $2^{1-l}$. Their normalized Hausdorff cost is at most $F_ l(y)$. Thus $\mathcal H^ d_{2^{1-l}}(Z\cap f^{-1}(y))\leq F_ l(y)$, and sending $l\to \infty $ gives zero outer Hausdorff measure. The countable exceptional sets from localization and the discarded countable cover members cause no additional problem. This proof also avoids presupposing measurability of an arbitrary fiber measure function. $\square$ Theorem 3.10.4 (Regular geometry of almost every Euclidean Lipschitz fiber) . 04B518A13580 Let $V\subset \mathbb R^ m$ be open and $g:V\to \mathbb R^ k$ be locally Lipschitz, with $1\leq k<m$. For almost every $y\in \mathbb R^ k$, the fiber $N_ y=g^{-1}(y)$ is countably $(m-k)$-rectifiable and locally finite in $\mathcal H^{m-k}$ measure in $V$. At $\mathcal H^{m-k}$-almost every point of each such fiber, $g$ is differentiable, has derivative of rank $k$, and \[  T_ xN_ y=\ker Dg(x).  \] The proof uses the locally proved Euclidean coarea formula and the local $C^1$ approximation theorem. Proof On a countable family of relatively compact balls covering $V$, extend the restriction of each component of $g$ to a global Lipschitz function by Proposition 3.4.2 . Corollary 3.5.6 , with exceptional measures tending to zero, supplies countably many $C^1$ maps $G_ i$ which agree with $g$ and $Dg$ on sets whose union covers each ball up to a Lebesgue-null set. Collect those null sets and the nondifferentiability set into $Z$. The Euclidean coarea formula, Theorem 3.2.4 , implies that $Z$ meets almost every fiber in an $\mathcal H^{m-k}$-null set. The same formula applied to the set where $\operatorname {rank}Dg<k$ gives a null contribution to almost every fiber, since its $k$-Jacobian is zero. At every remaining point where $g=G_ i$ and $Dg=DG_ i$, the derivative has rank $k$. The implicit function theorem makes the regular level $G_ i^{-1}(y)$ a $C^1$ submanifold of dimension $m-k$ near that point, with tangent $\ker DG_ i$. These regular level manifolds admit countably many charts. For a fixed good $y$, they cover the actual fiber up to a null set, proving countable rectifiability. The Euclidean coarea formula on a countable compact exhaustion gives local finite fiber measure for almost every $y$, because $J_ kg$ is bounded on each compact neighborhood and that neighborhood has finite volume. At almost every point of the common part of the fiber and each regular level patch, the tangent agreement in Theorem 3.6.6 identifies the fiber tangent with the patch tangent. On the agreement subset under consideration $DG_ i=Dg$, so that tangent is $\ker Dg$. Remove the countable union of all exceptional subsets. This proves the simultaneous geometry assertion. The coarea input is a scalar integral identity here; the fiber rectifiability and tangent identification have been derived from it and the $C^1$ approximation. $\square$ Lemma 3.10.5 (The Jacobian identity separating a fiber from its normal directions) . 5D79F192098C Let $A:\mathbb R^ m\to \mathbb R^ n$ be injective and linear, and let $B:\mathbb R^ m\to \mathbb R^ k$ be linear of rank $k$, where $1\leq k<m$. Set $T=A(\mathbb R^ m)$ and define $L:T\to \mathbb R^ k$ by $LA=B$. With $K=\ker B$, \[  J_ mA\, J_ kL=J_ kB\, J_{m-k}(A|_ K).  \] The $k$-Jacobians use the coarea convention $J_ kL=\sqrt{\det (LL^*)}$. The $m$- and $(m-k)$-Jacobians use the area convention. This is the coordinate identity behind [ Sim18 ] , equation (2.8). Proof Choose orthonormal coordinates on $\mathbb R^ m=K\oplus K^\perp $. Then $B=(0,C)$ with invertible $k\times k$ matrix $C$. The tangential coarea matrix is $BG^{-1}B^*=C(G^{-1})_{22}C^*$, because $A$ identifies $T$ with this metric on the domain. The block inverse formula and the Schur determinant formula give \[  \det G\, \det ((G^{-1})_{22})=\det G_{11}.  \] Indeed both formulas use the positive definite Schur complement $G_{22}-G_{21}G_{11}^{-1}G_{12}$. Taking positive square roots proves the identity. The proof makes explicit which metric enters the tangential coarea Jacobian; replacing it by $BB^*$ before accounting for the chart metric would be incorrect. $\square$ Theorem 3.10.6 (Rectifiable coarea and the tangent of almost every fiber) . 8318DBBE96A5 Let $M\subset U\subset \mathbb R^ n$ be measurable, countably $m$-rectifiable and locally finite in $\mathcal H^ m$ measure. Let $f:U\to \mathbb R^ k$ be locally Lipschitz, $1\leq k<m$, and let $h:M\to [0,\infty ]$ be measurable. Then \[  \int _ M hJ_ k(d^ Mf)\, d\mathcal H^ m =\int _{\mathbb R^ k}\int _{M\cap f^{-1}(y)}h\, d\mathcal H^{m-k}\, dy.  \] For almost every $y$, the fiber is countably $(m-k)$-rectifiable and locally finite in $\mathcal H^{m-k}$ measure. At almost every point of such a fiber, $d^ Mf$ has rank $k$ and \[  T_ x(M\cap f^{-1}(y))=\ker d^ Mf_ x\subset T_ xM.  \] This is the content of [ Sim18 ] , Chapter 3, equation (2.8), its weighted extension (2.9), and Remark 2.10(2), pp. 93–94, with the fiber tangent step supplied explicitly. The Borel choice makes every coordinate piece and its intersections with the closed fibers measurable for the relevant Hausdorff measures. Theorem 3.10.4 gives a rectifiable, locally finite fiber of $g_ i$ at almost every level, with tangent $\ker Dg_ i$ almost everywhere. Its measurable subset $A_ i\cap g_ i^{-1}(y)$ has the same tangent almost everywhere on that subset by Corollary 3.6.8 . It transforms the fiber integral into \[  \int _{A_ i\cap g_ i^{-1}(y)} (h\circ F_ i)\, J_{m-k}(DF_ i|_{\ker Dg_ i})\, d\mathcal H^{m-k}.  \] The kernel expression is set to zero on the rank-deficient or nondifferentiable set, which has null fiber measure for almost every level. The ambient-null set where $Dg_ i=d^ Mf\circ DF_ i$ or the prescribed tangential representative fails is also removed: Euclidean coarea makes its intersection with almost every base fiber null. It is measurable on the full-rank set: the orthogonal kernel projection is $I-(Dg_ i)^*(Dg_ i(Dg_ i)^*)^{-1}Dg_ i$, a continuous matrix expression in a full-rank derivative. Integrate the last display in $y$ and apply the Euclidean coarea formula, extended to nonnegative weights by simple functions and monotone convergence.
