Thus the fiber measures are locally finite for almost every level. Finally each regular base fiber is covered modulo null sets by the $C^1$ regular level pieces used in Theorem 3.10.4 . Their images under the injective regular chart are $C^1$ submanifolds with tangent $DF_ i(\ker Dg_ i)=\ker d^ Mf$. The tangent transfer theorem identifies the actual fiber's tangent with these piece tangents at almost every point. The countable union of exceptional subsets is null. text: Lemma 3.10.1 (Area Jacobians under a change of tangent coordinates) . 29B22C797308 Let $A:\mathbb R^ m\to \mathbb R^ n$ be injective and linear, let $T=A(\mathbb R^ m)$, and let $L:T\to \mathbb R^ q$ be linear with $q\geq m$. Then \[  J_ m(LA)=J_ mL\, J_ mA.  \] Here $J_ mL$ uses the Euclidean metric restricted to $T$; either side can vanish if $L$ loses rank. Proof Choose an isometry $Q:\mathbb R^ m\to T$, and write $A=QR$ with an invertible $m\times m$ matrix $R$. The Gram matrix of $LA$ is $R^*(LQ)^*(LQ)R$, whose determinant is $\det (R)^2\det ((LQ)^*(LQ))$. Also $J_ mA=|\det R|$ and $J_ mL=\sqrt{\det ((LQ)^*(LQ))}$. Taking square roots proves the identity, including a zero Gram determinant. Orthogonal choice of $Q$ does not change any of these quantities. $\square$

section: 3.10 Chart proofs of rectifiable area and coarea
text: Theorem 3.10.2 (Weighted area on a rectifiable domain) . 1AFF9641C00C Let $M\subset U\subset \mathbb R^ n$ be measurable, countably $m$-rectifiable and locally finite in $\mathcal H^ m$ measure, let $f:U\to \mathbb R^ q$ be locally Lipschitz with $q\geq m$, and let $h:M\to [0,\infty ]$ be measurable. Then \[  \int _ M h(x)J_ m(d^ Mf_ x)\, d\mathcal H^ m(x) =\int _{\mathbb R^ q}\sum _{x\in M\cap f^{-1}(y)}h(x)\, d\mathcal H^ m(y).  \] The fiber sum has a measurable representative. This is [ Sim18 ] , equations (2.4)–(2.6), derived here from the Euclidean weighted area formula. Products with a zero Jacobian use the convention $0\cdot \infty =0$. Proof Choose a Borel representative for $M$ and a Borel representative for $h$ relative to its sigma-finite restricted Hausdorff measure. This changes them only on an $\mathcal H^ m$-null subset; the image of that subset is null by the Lipschitz bound. Partition this representative of $M$, apart from an $\mathcal H^ m$-null set, into disjoint Borel pieces $M_ i$ lying in injective regular $C^1$ charts $F_ i:V_ i\to U$ as in Lemma 3.5.8 . Subdivide so the chart and the relevant restrictions of $f$ are Lipschitz on each piece's neighborhood. Put $A_ i=F_ i^{-1}(M_ i)$ and $g_ i=f\circ F_ i$. At almost every point of $A_ i$, Theorem 3.9.5 gives $Dg_ i=d^ Mf\circ DF_ i$. Lemma 3.10.1 therefore gives \[  J_ mDg_ i=J_ m(d^ Mf)J_ mDF_ i.  \] Apply Proposition 3.3.1 to $g_ i$ with weight $\chi _{A_ i}(h\circ F_ i)$. Apply the same formula to the injective chart $F_ i$ to change the left integral to integration on $M_ i$. The resulting right sum is over precisely the points of $M_ i\cap f^{-1}(y)$, because $F_ i$ is injective. Sum over $i$ using monotone convergence; the pieces are disjoint, so each point is counted once. This construction also gives measurability of the resulting sum modulo null sets. The omitted Hausdorff-null set has Hausdorff-null image under $f$, by the elementary Lipschitz bound on a countable local cover. Its fiber contribution therefore vanishes for almost every target point. On the left it contributes zero as well. This completes the formula on $M$ and permits infinite values by monotone approximation of $h$. $\square$

title: Lemma 3.10.3 (A Hausdorff-null set has null lower-dimensional fibers)

text: Lemma 3.10.3 (A Hausdorff-null set has null lower-dimensional fibers) . 1250D3393B38 Let $1\leq k<m$, let $f:U\subset \mathbb R^ n\to \mathbb R^ k$ be locally Lipschitz, and let $Z\subset U$ have $\mathcal H^ m(Z)=0$. Then \[  \mathcal H^{m-k}(Z\cap f^{-1}(y))=0 \quad \text{for }\mathcal L^ k\text{-almost every }y.  \] No rectifiability of $Z$ is assumed. This is the null-set part of the Lipschitz slicing estimate in [ Sim18 ] , Chapter 2, Theorem 1.10, pp. 49–51, proved directly by diameter covers. Proof Localize to $Z$ in a compact subset of a ball where $f$ has Lipschitz constant $L$ and whose closure lies in $U$. A countable such localization covers the original set. Put $d=m-k>0$. For each integer $l$, Hausdorff-nullness gives a cover by closed balls $Q_{li}$ of positive radii $r_{li}<2^{-l}$, all in the chosen neighborhood, with $\sum _ i r_{li}^ m<2^{-l}$. One obtains such balls from diameter covers by choosing centers in $Z$ and enlarging radii by a fixed factor; countably many zero-diameter cover members may be discarded, since their intersections with every fiber have zero $\mathcal H^ d$ measure. The sets $f(Q_{li})$ are compact, so \[  F_ l(y)=\sum _ i\omega _ d r_{li}^ d\chi _{f(Q_{li})}(y)  \] is measurable. Each image is contained in a $k$-ball of radius $Lr_{li}$ about the image of its center. Hence \[  \int F_ l\, dy\leq \omega _ d\omega _ kL^ k\sum _ i r_{li}^{d+k} <\omega _ d\omega _ kL^ k2^{-l}.  \] Tonelli implies $\sum _ lF_ l(y)<\infty $ for almost every $y$, so $F_ l(y)\to 0$ there. The corresponding selected balls cover $Z\cap f^{-1}(y)$ and have diameters less than $2^{1-l}$. Their normalized Hausdorff cost is at most $F_ l(y)$. Thus $\mathcal H^ d_{2^{1-l}}(Z\cap f^{-1}(y))\leq F_ l(y)$, and sending $l\to \infty $ gives zero outer Hausdorff measure. The countable exceptional sets from localization and the discarded countable cover members cause no additional problem. This proof also avoids presupposing measurability of an arbitrary fiber measure function. $\square$

text: Theorem 3.10.4 (Regular geometry of almost every Euclidean Lipschitz fiber) . 04B518A13580 Let $V\subset \mathbb R^ m$ be open and $g:V\to \mathbb R^ k$ be locally Lipschitz, with $1\leq k<m$. For almost every $y\in \mathbb R^ k$, the fiber $N_ y=g^{-1}(y)$ is countably $(m-k)$-rectifiable and locally finite in $\mathcal H^{m-k}$ measure in $V$. At $\mathcal H^{m-k}$-almost every point of each such fiber, $g$ is differentiable, has derivative of rank $k$, and \[  T_ xN_ y=\ker Dg(x).  \] The proof uses the locally proved Euclidean coarea formula and the local $C^1$ approximation theorem. At almost every point of the common part of the fiber and each regular level patch, the tangent agreement in Theorem 3.6.6 identifies the fiber tangent with the patch tangent. On the agreement subset under consideration $DG_ i=Dg$, so that tangent is $\ker Dg$. Remove the countable union of all exceptional subsets. This proves the simultaneous geometry assertion. The coarea input is a scalar integral identity here; the fiber rectifiability and tangent identification have been derived from it and the $C^1$ approximation. $\square$

title: 3.11 Rectifiable parts and projection tests
search_title: Rectifiable parts and projection tests
section: 3.11 Rectifiable parts and projection tests
text: A set can contain both smooth pieces and a part that meets every smooth piece in zero measure. This section develops the measurable decomposition and elementary projection tests in [ Sim18 ] , Chapter 3, Definition 3.1 and Lemmas 3.2–3.3, printed pp. 94–95. We assume $1\leq m<n$. The almost-everywhere projection theorem of Besicovitch and Federer is a deeper result and is not used in these proofs. Definition 3.11.1 (Pure unrectifiability) . 89B12245E801 An $\mathcal H^ m$-measurable set $P\subset \mathbb R^ n$ is purely $m$-unrectifiable if $\mathcal H^ m(P\cap R)=0$ for every measurable countably $m$-rectifiable set $R$. Equivalently, $P$ contains no measurable countably $m$-rectifiable subset of positive $\mathcal H^ m$ measure. The equivalence uses the fact that measurable subsets of a countably rectifiable set are countably rectifiable, directly from Definition 3.1.1 . This is the measurable-set convention for [ Sim18 ] , Definition 3.1. Lemma 3.11.2 (Borel cores for a sigma-finite Hausdorff measure) . 515E86DC0050 If $A\subset \mathbb R^ n$ is $\mathcal H^ m$-measurable and sigma-finite for that measure, then there are Borel sets $C\subset A\subset B$ with $\mathcal H^ m(B\setminus C)=0$. If $A$ is countably $m$-rectifiable, both $B$ and $C$ are countably $m$-rectifiable as well. Proof Write $A$ as a countable union of measurable finite-measure sets $A_ j$. Borel regularity gives a Borel hull $B_ j\supset A_ j$ with the same finite measure. Since $A_ j$ is measurable, $\mathcal H^ m(B_ j\setminus A_ j)=0$. Apply Borel regularity again to obtain a Borel null set $Z_ j$ containing $B_ j\setminus A_ j$. Then $C_ j=B_ j\setminus Z_ j$ is Borel, lies in $A_ j$, and differs from it by a null set. Put $C=\bigcup _ j C_ j$ and $B=\bigcup _ j B_ j$. These have the required inclusions and null difference. A subset of a countably rectifiable set is covered by the same Lipschitz images up to the inherited null set; adding a Hausdorff-null set also preserves rectifiability. Thus the last assertion follows from the definition. This argument does not require local finiteness of the unweighted area of $A$. $\square$ Proposition 3.11.3 (Testing pure unrectifiability on smooth patches) . 6C6ABE5BBDD1 An $\mathcal H^ m$-measurable set $P$ is purely $m$-unrectifiable if and only if $\mathcal H^ m(P\cap N)=0$ for every finite-area embedded $C^1$ graph patch $N$ of dimension $m$. Proof Every such patch is countably rectifiable, so the forward implication is part of Definition 3.11.1 . Conversely let $R$ be countably rectifiable. Theorem 3.5.7 and Lemma 3.5.8 cover $R$, apart from a Hausdorff-null subset, by countably many finite-area smooth patches $N_ j$. Their intersections with $P$ are null by assumption. Their countable union and the exceptional null set still have zero measure, proving $\mathcal H^ m(P\cap R)=0$. Local finiteness of $P$ is not needed for this implication. $\square$ Proposition 3.11.4 (A maximal rectifiable part of a finite-measure set) . 252D1E4D029C Let $A$ be a Borel set with $\mathcal H^ m(A)<\infty $. There exists a Borel countably $m$-rectifiable subset $R\subset A$ such that $P=A\setminus R$ is purely $m$-unrectifiable. Its measure is \[  \mathcal H^ m(R)=\sup \{ \mathcal H^ m(S):S\subset A\text{ Borel and countably }m\text{-rectifiable}\} .  \] This is the finite-measure step in [ Sim18 ] , Lemma 3.2. Proof Call the supremum $\alpha \in [0,\mathcal H^ m(A)]$. Choose Borel rectifiable $S_ j\subset A$ with $\mathcal H^ m(S_ j)>\alpha -1/j$, allowing $S_ j=\varnothing $ when $\alpha =0$. Their union $R$ is Borel and countably rectifiable. It contains every $S_ j$, so $\mathcal H^ m(R)\geq \alpha $; by its own admissibility it has measure at most $\alpha $. Hence equality holds. If the residual set contained a measurable rectifiable subset $E$ of positive measure, Lemma 3.11.2 would give a Borel rectifiable core $E'\subset E$ of the same positive measure. The disjoint union $R\cup E'$ would be an admissible Borel rectifiable subset of $A$ with measure greater than $\alpha $, a contradiction. By Definition 3.11.1 , the residual is purely unrectifiable. Finiteness of $\alpha $ is the reason for doing this step on finite-measure pieces. $\square$ Theorem 3.11.5 (Decomposition into rectifiable and purely unrectifiable parts) . 3DEAC4B1091B Every $\mathcal H^ m$-measurable sigma-finite set $A\subset \mathbb R^ n$ admits a disjoint decomposition $A=R\cup P$, where $R$ is Borel and countably $m$-rectifiable, and $P$ is measurable and purely $m$-unrectifiable. The decomposition is unique modulo $\mathcal H^ m$-null sets. This is the measurable form of [ Sim18 ] , Lemma 3.2, with uniqueness made explicit. Proof Use Lemma 3.11.2 to choose a Borel core of $A$ with null remainder. Partition that core into countably many Borel sets $A_ j$ of finite measure. To see this partition exists, first use finite-measure Borel hulls of a sigma-finite measurable cover and intersect them with the core, then remove preceding sets. Apply Proposition 3.11.4 to each $A_ j$, obtaining $A_ j=R_ j\cup P_ j$. Set $R=\bigcup _ jR_ j$ and $P=A\setminus R$. The union $R$ is Borel and rectifiable. For every rectifiable set $S$, each $S\cap P_ j$ is null, and the omitted core remainder is null. Thus $S\cap P$ is null, proving pure unrectifiability. For uniqueness, suppose also $A=\widetilde R\cup \widetilde P$ with the same properties. The measurable set $R\setminus \widetilde R$ lies in $R\cap \widetilde P$, which is null because $R$ is rectifiable and $\widetilde P$ is purely unrectifiable. Interchanging the decompositions gives $\mathcal H^ m(\widetilde R\setminus R)=0$. Hence $R\mathbin \triangle \widetilde R$ and consequently $P\mathbin \triangle \widetilde P$ are null. Uniqueness is a measure assertion and does not assert equality of topological supports. $\square$ Corollary 3.11.6 (The rectifiable part captures every rectifiable subset) . D3E05BFEA686 For the decomposition in Theorem 3.11.5 , every measurable countably $m$-rectifiable subset $S\subset A$ satisfies $\mathcal H^ m(S\setminus R)=0$. More generally, the rectifiable part of a measurable subset $B\subset A$ is $B\cap R$ modulo a null set. Proof The first difference is contained in $S\cap P$, which is null by pure unrectifiability. For the second assertion, $B\cap R$ is rectifiable, and $B\cap P$ remains purely unrectifiable by the definition. The two form a decomposition of $B$. Choosing a Borel core of $B\cap R$ changes it only by a null set, so the uniqueness statement of Theorem 3.11.5 applies. Thus restriction commutes with the decomposition at the measure level, even if the chosen set representatives change. $\square$ Lemma 3.11.7 (A regular coordinate projection detects positive area locally) . 42BE02CF01D1 Let $N$ be an embedded $m$-dimensional $C^1$ manifold in $\mathbb R^ n$, and let $E\subset N$ be measurable with positive $\mathcal H^ m$ measure. Then there are $m$ coordinate axes and a graph patch $N_0\subset N$ such that the corresponding orthogonal projection $p_ I$ is injective on $N_0$, has a Lipschitz inverse on its image, and \[  \mathcal H^ m(p_ I(E\cap N_0))>0.  \] This is the local inverse-function argument in [ Sim18 ] , Lemma 3.3, p. 95. Proof A regular chart has an $n\times m$ derivative matrix of rank $m$, so at every point some $m\times m$ coordinate minor is invertible. The inverse function theorem writes a neighborhood in $N$ as a graph over those coordinate axes. Shrink to an open base ball with compact closure in the graph domain. Its graph inverse has bounded derivative and is Lipschitz on that convex ball. These neighborhoods give a countable cover of $N$, allowing different coordinate projections for different neighborhoods. Since $E$ has positive measure, one covered piece $E\cap N_0$ has positive measure. If its projection were null, the Hausdorff-measure Lipschitz bound for the inverse graph map would make the piece itself null, a contradiction. Measurability of the projected set follows by taking a Borel representative of the piece and a null remainder: the graph projection is a homeomorphism on its patch and maps the remainder to a null set. No global injectivity of the projection on all of $N$ is claimed. $\square$ Theorem 3.11.8 (Null coordinate projections imply pure unrectifiability) . 56DDB002413B Let $S\subset \mathbb R^ n$ be $\mathcal H^ m$-measurable. If \[  \mathcal H^ m(p_ I(S))=0 \quad \text{for every }I\subset \{ 1,\ldots ,n\} ,\quad |I|=m,  \] then $S$ is purely $m$-unrectifiable. Here $p_ I$ is projection onto the coordinate $m$-plane indexed by $I$, and the zero-measure assertion may be read in the outer-measure sense. This is [ Sim18 ] , Lemma 3.3. Proof If $S$ were not purely unrectifiable, Proposition 3.11.3 would supply a finite-area smooth patch $N$ with $\mathcal H^ m(S\cap N)>0$. Lemma 3.11.7 , applied to that common part, would then give a coordinate projection with positive projected measure. Its image lies inside $p_ I(S)$, contradicting the assumed null outer measure. A single null projection does not suffice, as an $m$-plane with a rank-deficient projection can have that property. $\square$ Proposition 3.11.9 (Coordinate projection Jacobians control rectifiable area with multiplicity) . 7C39343F0486 Let $M\subset \mathbb R^ n$ be measurable, countably $m$-rectifiable and locally finite in $\mathcal H^ m$ measure, and put $q=\binom nm$. For each coordinate $m$-plane let $N_ I(y)=\mathcal H^0(M\cap p_ I^{-1}(y))$. Then \[  \mathcal H^ m(M)\leq \sum _{|I|=m}\int _{p_ I(\mathbb R^ n)}N_ I(y)\, d\mathcal H^ m(y) \leq \sqrt q\, \mathcal H^ m(M).  \] Infinite values are allowed. The area Jacobian $J_ I$ of $p_ I$ restricted to this tangent is the absolute value of the $I$-minor of $Q$. The Cauchy–Binet identity gives $\sum _ IJ_ I^2=\det (Q^*Q)=1$. The finite sum commutes with the integral, proving both bounds. If every multiplicity is at most an integer $N$ almost everywhere, the first bound in particular gives $\mathcal H^ m(M)\leq N\sum _ I\mathcal H^ m(p_ I(M))$. $\square$

title: Definition 3.11.1 (Pure unrectifiability)
search_title: Pure unrectifiability
section: 3.11 Rectifiable parts and projection tests
text: Definition 3.11.1 (Pure unrectifiability) . 89B12245E801 An $\mathcal H^ m$-measurable set $P\subset \mathbb R^ n$ is purely $m$-unrectifiable if $\mathcal H^ m(P\cap R)=0$ for every measurable countably $m$-rectifiable set $R$. Equivalently, $P$ contains no measurable countably $m$-rectifiable subset of positive $\mathcal H^ m$ measure. The equivalence uses the fact that measurable subsets of a countably rectifiable set are countably rectifiable, directly from Definition 3.1.1 . This is the measurable-set convention for [ Sim18 ] , Definition 3.1.

title: Lemma 3.11.2 (Borel cores for a sigma-finite Hausdorff measure)
search_title: Borel cores for a sigma-finite Hausdorff measure
section: 3.11 Rectifiable parts and projection tests
text: Lemma 3.11.2 (Borel cores for a sigma-finite Hausdorff measure) . 515E86DC0050 If $A\subset \mathbb R^ n$ is $\mathcal H^ m$-measurable and sigma-finite for that measure, then there are Borel sets $C\subset A\subset B$ with $\mathcal H^ m(B\setminus C)=0$. If $A$ is countably $m$-rectifiable, both $B$ and $C$ are countably $m$-rectifiable as well. Proof Write $A$ as a countable union of measurable finite-measure sets $A_ j$. Borel regularity gives a Borel hull $B_ j\supset A_ j$ with the same finite measure. Since $A_ j$ is measurable, $\mathcal H^ m(B_ j\setminus A_ j)=0$. Apply Borel regularity again to obtain a Borel null set $Z_ j$ containing $B_ j\setminus A_ j$. Then $C_ j=B_ j\setminus Z_ j$ is Borel, lies in $A_ j$, and differs from it by a null set. Put $C=\bigcup _ j C_ j$ and $B=\bigcup _ j B_ j$. These have the required inclusions and null difference. A subset of a countably rectifiable set is covered by the same Lipschitz images up to the inherited null set; adding a Hausdorff-null set also preserves rectifiability. Thus the last assertion follows from the definition. This argument does not require local finiteness of the unweighted area of $A$. $\square$

title: Proposition 3.11.3 (Testing pure unrectifiability on smooth patches)
search_title: Testing pure unrectifiability on smooth patches
section: 3.11 Rectifiable parts and projection tests
text: Proposition 3.11.3 (Testing pure unrectifiability on smooth patches) . 6C6ABE5BBDD1 An $\mathcal H^ m$-measurable set $P$ is purely $m$-unrectifiable if and only if $\mathcal H^ m(P\cap N)=0$ for every finite-area embedded $C^1$ graph patch $N$ of dimension $m$. Proof Every such patch is countably rectifiable, so the forward implication is part of Definition 3.11.1 . Conversely let $R$ be countably rectifiable. Theorem 3.5.7 and Lemma 3.5.8 cover $R$, apart from a Hausdorff-null subset, by countably many finite-area smooth patches $N_ j$. Their intersections with $P$ are null by assumption. Their countable union and the exceptional null set still have zero measure, proving $\mathcal H^ m(P\cap R)=0$. Local finiteness of $P$ is not needed for this implication. $\square$

title: Proposition 3.11.4 (A maximal rectifiable part of a finite-measure set)
search_title: A maximal rectifiable part of a finite-measure set
section: 3.11 Rectifiable parts and projection tests
text: Proposition 3.11.4 (A maximal rectifiable part of a finite-measure set) . 252D1E4D029C Let $A$ be a Borel set with $\mathcal H^ m(A)<\infty $. There exists a Borel countably $m$-rectifiable subset $R\subset A$ such that $P=A\setminus R$ is purely $m$-unrectifiable. Its measure is \[  \mathcal H^ m(R)=\sup \{ \mathcal H^ m(S):S\subset A\text{ Borel and countably }m\text{-rectifiable}\} .  \] This is the finite-measure step in [ Sim18 ] , Lemma 3.2. Proof Call the supremum $\alpha \in [0,\mathcal H^ m(A)]$. Choose Borel rectifiable $S_ j\subset A$ with $\mathcal H^ m(S_ j)>\alpha -1/j$, allowing $S_ j=\varnothing $ when $\alpha =0$. Their union $R$ is Borel and countably rectifiable. It contains every $S_ j$, so $\mathcal H^ m(R)\geq \alpha $; by its own admissibility it has measure at most $\alpha $. Hence equality holds. If the residual set contained a measurable rectifiable subset $E$ of positive measure, Lemma 3.11.2 would give a Borel rectifiable core $E'\subset E$ of the same positive measure. The disjoint union $R\cup E'$ would be an admissible Borel rectifiable subset of $A$ with measure greater than $\alpha $, a contradiction. By Definition 3.11.1 , the residual is purely unrectifiable. Finiteness of $\alpha $ is the reason for doing this step on finite-measure pieces. $\square$

title: Theorem 3.11.5 (Decomposition into rectifiable and purely unrectifiable parts)
search_title: Decomposition into rectifiable and purely unrectifiable parts
section: 3.11 Rectifiable parts and projection tests
text: Theorem 3.11.5 (Decomposition into rectifiable and purely unrectifiable parts) . 3DEAC4B1091B Every $\mathcal H^ m$-measurable sigma-finite set $A\subset \mathbb R^ n$ admits a disjoint decomposition $A=R\cup P$, where $R$ is Borel and countably $m$-rectifiable, and $P$ is measurable and purely $m$-unrectifiable. The decomposition is unique modulo $\mathcal H^ m$-null sets. This is the measurable form of [ Sim18 ] , Lemma 3.2, with uniqueness made explicit. Proof Use Lemma 3.11.2 to choose a Borel core of $A$ with null remainder. Partition that core into countably many Borel sets $A_ j$ of finite measure. To see this partition exists, first use finite-measure Borel hulls of a sigma-finite measurable cover and intersect them with the core, then remove preceding sets. Apply Proposition 3.11.4 to each $A_ j$, obtaining $A_ j=R_ j\cup P_ j$. Set $R=\bigcup _ jR_ j$ and $P=A\setminus R$. The union $R$ is Borel and rectifiable. For every rectifiable set $S$, each $S\cap P_ j$ is null, and the omitted core remainder is null. Thus $S\cap P$ is null, proving pure unrectifiability. For uniqueness, suppose also $A=\widetilde R\cup \widetilde P$ with the same properties. The measurable set $R\setminus \widetilde R$ lies in $R\cap \widetilde P$, which is null because $R$ is rectifiable and $\widetilde P$ is purely unrectifiable. Interchanging the decompositions gives $\mathcal H^ m(\widetilde R\setminus R)=0$. Hence $R\mathbin \triangle \widetilde R$ and consequently $P\mathbin \triangle \widetilde P$ are null. Uniqueness is a measure assertion and does not assert equality of topological supports. $\square$

title: 3.12 Fiber integration and selecting useful levels
search_title: Fiber integration and selecting useful levels
section: 3.12 Fiber integration and selecting useful levels
text:
The coarea identity has consequences beyond a single integral formula. It identifies an absolutely continuous pushforward after weighting by the Jacobian, controls the regular part after dividing by the Jacobian, and permits simultaneous choices of levels. We expand [ Sim18 ] , Chapter 2, Theorem 7.5 and Remarks 7.7, printed pp. 80–81, and Chapter 3, equation (2.9), p. 93. Throughout $M\subset U\subset \mathbb R^ n$ is measurable, countably $m$-rectifiable and locally finite in $\mathcal H^ m$, $U$ is open, $f:U	o \mathbb R^ k$ is locally Lipschitz, and $1\leq k<m$. Write $J=J_ k(d^ Mf)$ and $M_ y=M\cap f^{-1}(y)$. Proposition 3.12.1 (The pushforward of Jacobian-weighted area) . F0DB5F917E61 For every nonnegative measurable $h$ on $M$, the Borel pushforward satisfies \[  f_\# (hJ\mathcal H^ m\llcorner M)=F\mathcal L^ k, \qquad F(y)=\int _{M_ y}h\, d\mathcal H^{m-k} \quad 	ext{almost everywhere}.  \] The fiber integral has a measurable representative. Both measures may have infinite mass; this formula does not itself assert local finiteness of the pushforward. Proof Choose Borel representatives modulo the relevant Hausdorff-null sets, using the representative and null-fiber steps in Theorem 3.10.6 . Apply that theorem to the weight $h\chi _{f^{-1}(B)}$, where $B\subset \mathbb R^ k$ is Borel. On the fiber at $y$ the extra indicator is exactly $\chi _ B(y)$, so the identity becomes \[  \int _{M\cap f^{-1}(B)}hJ\, d\mathcal H^ m =\int _ BF(y)\, dy.  \] This is equality of the indicated Borel measures. The choices of representatives do not alter either side: their differences lie in a Hausdorff-null set and almost every fiber meets that set in lower-dimensional Hausdorff measure zero. The convention $0\cdot \infty =0$ is inherited from coarea. Global finite mass, when imposed, makes the density integrable; it is not required for the equality. $\square$ Proposition 3.12.2 (Dividing by the Jacobian on the regular part) . 3CECBDFC419F Put $R=\{ x\in M:J(x)>0\} $ and $C=M\setminus R$, with $J=0$ on its exceptional undefined set. For any nonnegative measurable $a$, \[  f_\# (a\mathcal H^ m\llcorner R)=G\mathcal L^ k, \qquad G(y)=\int _{R\cap M_ y} rac{a}{J}\, d\mathcal H^{m-k}.  \] Consequently \[  f_\# (a\mathcal H^ m\llcorner M)=G\mathcal L^ k+f_\# (a\mathcal H^ m\llcorner C).  \] The second summand is a critical-set contribution; it is not asserted to be singular with respect to Lebesgue measure. If $\int _ Ra\, d\mathcal H^ m<\infty $, then $G\in L^1(\mathbb R^ k)$ and is finite almost everywhere. Proof Use Proposition 3.12.1 with $h=a/J$ on $R$ and zero on $C$. This is a nonnegative measurable weight, and $hJ=a\chi _ R$ with the stated zero convention. The resulting density is exactly $G$. Add the pushforward of the complementary measure to obtain the second formula. The total integral of $G$ equals the regular mass by the same identity, proving the last assertion. Although the critical set has zero lower-dimensional measure in almost every fiber by coarea, its $m$-dimensional measure can be positive. Thus its unweighted pushforward cannot simply be deleted. Example 16.29.4 gives a nonzero critical contribution explicitly. $\square$ Theorem 3.12.3 (The fiberwise Sard conclusion at C1 regularity) . 2626EBF3C6FC Let $N\subset U$ be an embedded $m$-dimensional $C^1$ manifold and let $f|N$ be $C^1$. Put $C=\{ x\in N:\operatorname {rank}d^ Nf_ x<k\} $. For almost every $y$, $N\cap f^{-1}(y)$ is the union of a possibly empty $(m-k)$-dimensional $C^1$ manifold and a relatively closed subset of that fiber with zero $\mathcal H^{m-k}$ measure. The manifold is its regular part, and its tangent at $x$ is $\ker d^ Nf_ x$. This is [ Sim18 ] , Chapter 2, Theorem 7.5, p. 80. Proof The rank-deficient set $C$ is relatively closed in $N$ because the tangential derivative is continuous and all $k	imes k$ minors vanish on it. At a point of $N\setminus C$, the implicit function theorem makes the level set a $C^1$ manifold of dimension $m-k$, with tangent equal to the kernel. These local descriptions form the regular part of the level set as an embedded manifold. Cover $N$ by the finite-area patches of Lemma 3.5.8 . On each patch apply Theorem 3.10.6 to the indicator of $C$. Its tangential Jacobian is zero, so the integral of the critical fiber measure is zero. This measure is therefore zero at almost every level. The countable union of exceptional level sets is null, proving the assertion on all of $N$, without assuming the entire nonproper manifold has locally finite ambient area. The result says that the critical part of almost every fiber is negligible; it does not say that this part is empty. The stronger critical-value conclusion requires additional smoothness hypotheses, as distinguished in [ Sim18 ] , Remark 7.6. $\square$ Proposition 3.12.4 (Selecting levels that satisfy finitely many bounds) . AB01DD7A7444 Let $Y\subset \mathbb R^ k$ be measurable with $0<v=\mathcal L^ k(Y)<\infty $. Let $h_1,\ldots ,h_ s$ be nonnegative measurable weights with \[  E_ i=\int _{M\cap f^{-1}(Y)}h_ iJ\, d\mathcal H^ m<\infty .  \] Choose $\varepsilon _ i>0$ with $\sum _ i\varepsilon _ i<1$. Outside any prescribed null set of levels, there is a measurable set $S\subset Y$ of measure at least $(1-\sum _ i\varepsilon _ i)v$ on which all the estimates \[  \int _{M_ y}h_ i\, d\mathcal H^{m-k}\leq  rac{E_ i}{\varepsilon _ i v} \quad (i=1,\ldots ,s)  \] hold. If $E_ i=0$, the corresponding bound is zero. Proof Coarea makes each fiber cost $F_ i(y)$ measurable, with $\int _ YF_ i=E_ i$. If $E_ i>0$, Markov's inequality gives measure at most $\varepsilon _ i v$ to the set $\{ F_ i>E_ i/(\varepsilon _ i v)\} $. If $E_ i=0$, nonnegativity gives $F_ i=0$ almost everywhere, so its positive set is null. Remove the finite union of these bad sets and the prescribed null set. Subadditivity gives the asserted measure lower bound, and every remaining point satisfies every inequality. The strict positivity of this lower bound ensures that an admissible level exists. This quantifies the good-level principle of [ Sim18 ] , Remark 7.7(1), and makes explicit how several requirements can be imposed at once. $\square$ Proposition 3.12.5 (Good levels along a level-dependent subsequence) . DC9B0DCFE731 Let $Y$ and $v$ be as above, and let $F_ j:Y	o [0,\infty ]$ be measurable with $E_ j=\int _ YF_ j<\infty $. For any $0<\varepsilon <1$, there is a measurable set $S\subset Y$ of measure at least $(1-\varepsilon )v$ such that for each $y\in S$ an infinite subsequence $j_ l=j_ l(y)$ satisfies \[  F_{j_ l}(y)\leq  rac{E_{j_ l}}{\varepsilon v}.  \] In coarea applications, $F_ j$ may be the weighted fiber costs for different rectifiable sets. The subsequence is allowed to depend on $y$. This is the selection content of [ Sim18 ] , Remark 7.7(2), pp. 80–81. Proof After removing the countable union of null sets associated with any zero $E_ j$, define $G_ j=\{ F_ j\leq E_ j/(\varepsilon v)\} $. Markov's inequality gives $|G_ j|\geq (1-\varepsilon )v$. For each $N$, the union $H_ N= igcup _{j\geq N}G_ j$ therefore has at least this measure. The sets $H_ N$ decrease and lie in the finite-measure set $Y$, so continuity from above gives $| igcap _ NH_ N|\geq (1-\varepsilon )v$. This intersection is the limsup of the good sets: each of its points lies in infinitely many $G_ j$. Listing those indices in increasing order gives the required subsequence. Nothing in this argument selects one subsequence that works for every level simultaneously. $\square$ Proposition 3.12.6 (Summable errors vanish on almost every fiber) . 3F1F6A59BCFB Let $F_ j:Y	o [0,\infty ]$ be measurable with $\sum _ j\int _ YF_ j<\infty $. Then $\sum _ jF_ j(y)<\infty $ and $F_ j(y)	o 0$ for almost every $y$. In particular, if coarea gives fiber costs with $\int _ YF_ j	o 0$, one can choose a subsequence of indices, independent of the level, along which the costs tend to zero almost everywhere. Proof Tonelli's theorem gives $\int _ Y\sum _ jF_ j=\sum _ j\int _ YF_ j<\infty $. The nonnegative sum is finite almost everywhere, and its terms tend to zero there. For the last assertion choose increasing indices $j_ l$ with $\int _ YF_{j_ l}\leq 2^{-l}$; the first assertion then applies to this subsequence. Here the conclusion is almost-everywhere convergence along one common subsequence, under the stronger vanishing-integral hypothesis. It should not be confused with the bounded normalized-cost subsequences in Proposition 3.12.5 . $\square$ Proposition 3.12.7 (The distance-volume function is absolutely continuous off its critical part) . DE97D6ADACDB Let $a\in \mathbb R^ n$ and $0<\alpha < eta $ with $\overline{B_ eta (a)}\subset U$. Put $ho (x)=|x-a|$, $J=|
abla ^ Mho |$, $R=\{ x\in M:J(x)>0\} $, and \[  V_ R(t)=\mathcal H^ m(R\cap \{ \alpha <ho <t\} ),\qquad \alpha \leq t\leq  eta .  \] Then $V_ R$ is absolutely continuous and for almost every $t$, \[  V_ R'(t)=\int _{R\cap \partial B_ t(a)} rac1{|
abla ^ Mho |}\, d\mathcal H^{m-1} \geq \mathcal H^{m-1}(M\cap \partial B_ t(a)).  \] The inequality holds at almost every $t\in (\alpha , eta )$; coarea discards the critical part of the fiber at these levels. This statement concerns the regular part of the distance function and does not assert absolute continuity of the full volume function. Proof The restricted area in the compact annulus is finite. Proposition 3.12.2 , applied to $f=ho $ and its regular part, gives an integrable density \[  G(t)=\int _{R\cap \partial B_ t(a)}J^{-1}\, d\mathcal H^{m-1}  \] on $(\alpha , eta )$. Thus $V_ R(t)=\int _\alpha ^ tG(s)\, ds$. The fundamental theorem for Lebesgue integrals proves absolute continuity and the derivative formula. Since $|
abla ^ Mho |\leq 1$, its reciprocal on $R$ is at least one. The critical-fiber measure vanishes for almost every radius by coarea with the indicator of $\{ J=0\} $; this proves the final comparison with the whole fiber. A surface lying on one sphere has a nonzero critical contribution and a jump in the full volume function, as illustrated in Example 16.29.5 . $\square$

On the fiber at $y$ the extra indicator is exactly $\chi _ B(y)$, so the identity becomes \[  \int _{M\cap f^{-1}(B)}hJ\, d\mathcal H^ m =\int _ BF(y)\, dy.  \] This is equality of the indicated Borel measures. The convention $0\cdot \infty =0$ is inherited from coarea. Global finite mass, when imposed, makes the density integrable; it is not required for the equality. $\square$

text: Proposition 3.12.2 (Dividing by the Jacobian on the regular part) . 3CECBDFC419F Put $R=\{ x\in M:J(x)>0\} $ and $C=M\setminus R$, with $J=0$ on its exceptional undefined set. For any nonnegative measurable $a$, \[  f_\# (a\mathcal H^ m\llcorner R)=G\mathcal L^ k, \qquad G(y)=\int _{R\cap M_ y}\frac{a}{J}\, d\mathcal H^{m-k}.  \] Consequently \[  f_\# (a\mathcal H^ m\llcorner M)=G\mathcal L^ k+f_\# (a\mathcal H^ m\llcorner C).  \] The second summand is a critical-set contribution; it is not asserted to be singular with respect to Lebesgue measure. If $\int _ Ra\, d\mathcal H^ m<\infty $, then $G\in L^1(\mathbb R^ k)$ and is finite almost everywhere. Proof Use Proposition 3.12.1 with $h=a/J$ on $R$ and zero on $C$. This is a nonnegative measurable weight, and $hJ=a\chi _ R$ with the stated zero convention. The resulting density is exactly $G$. Add the pushforward of the complementary measure to obtain the second formula. The total integral of $G$ equals the regular mass by the same identity, proving the last assertion. Although the critical set has zero lower-dimensional measure in almost every fiber by coarea, its $m$-dimensional measure can be positive. Thus its unweighted pushforward cannot simply be deleted. Example 16.29.4 gives a nonzero critical contribution explicitly. $\square$

title: Theorem 3.12.3 (The fiberwise Sard conclusion at C1 regularity)
search_title: The fiberwise Sard conclusion at C1 regularity
section: 3.12 Fiber integration and selecting useful levels
text: Theorem 3.12.3 (The fiberwise Sard conclusion at C1 regularity) . 2626EBF3C6FC Let $N\subset U$ be an embedded $m$-dimensional $C^1$ manifold and let $f|N$ be $C^1$. Put $C=\{ x\in N:\operatorname {rank}d^ Nf_ x<k\} $. For almost every $y$, $N\cap f^{-1}(y)$ is the union of a possibly empty $(m-k)$-dimensional $C^1$ manifold and a relatively closed subset of that fiber with zero $\mathcal H^{m-k}$ measure. The manifold is its regular part, and its tangent at $x$ is $\ker d^ Nf_ x$. This is [ Sim18 ] , Chapter 2, Theorem 7.5, p. 80. Proof The rank-deficient set $C$ is relatively closed in $N$ because the tangential derivative is continuous and all $k\times k$ minors vanish on it. At a point of $N\setminus C$, the implicit function theorem makes the level set a $C^1$ manifold of dimension $m-k$, with tangent equal to the kernel. These local descriptions form the regular part of the level set as an embedded manifold. Cover $N$ by the finite-area patches of Lemma 3.5.8 . On each patch apply Theorem 3.10.6 to the indicator of $C$. Its tangential Jacobian is zero, so the integral of the critical fiber measure is zero. This measure is therefore zero at almost every level. The countable union of exceptional level sets is null, proving the assertion on all of $N$, without assuming the entire nonproper manifold has locally finite ambient area. The result says that the critical part of almost every fiber is negligible; it does not say that this part is empty. The stronger critical-value conclusion requires additional smoothness hypotheses, as distinguished in [ Sim18 ] , Remark 7.6. $\square$

title: Proposition 3.12.4 (Selecting levels that satisfy finitely many bounds)
search_title: Selecting levels that satisfy finitely many bounds
section: 3.12 Fiber integration and selecting useful levels
text: Proposition 3.12.4 (Selecting levels that satisfy finitely many bounds) . AB01DD7A7444 Let $Y\subset \mathbb R^ k$ be measurable with $0<v=\mathcal L^ k(Y)<\infty $. Let $h_1,\ldots ,h_ s$ be nonnegative measurable weights with \[  E_ i=\int _{M\cap f^{-1}(Y)}h_ iJ\, d\mathcal H^ m<\infty .  \] Choose $\varepsilon _ i>0$ with $\sum _ i\varepsilon _ i<1$. Outside any prescribed null set of levels, there is a measurable set $S\subset Y$ of measure at least $(1-\sum _ i\varepsilon _ i)v$ on which all the estimates \[  \int _{M_ y}h_ i\, d\mathcal H^{m-k}\leq \frac{E_ i}{\varepsilon _ i v} \quad (i=1,\ldots ,s)  \] hold. If $E_ i=0$, the corresponding bound is zero. Proof Coarea makes each fiber cost $F_ i(y)$ measurable, with $\int _ YF_ i=E_ i$. If $E_ i>0$, Markov's inequality gives measure at most $\varepsilon _ i v$ to the set $\{ F_ i>E_ i/(\varepsilon _ i v)\} $. If $E_ i=0$, nonnegativity gives $F_ i=0$ almost everywhere, so its positive set is null. Remove the finite union of these bad sets and the prescribed null set. Subadditivity gives the asserted measure lower bound, and every remaining point satisfies every inequality. The strict positivity of this lower bound ensures that an admissible level exists. This quantifies the good-level principle of [ Sim18 ] , Remark 7.7(1), and makes explicit how several requirements can be imposed at once. $\square$

title: Proposition 3.12.5 (Good levels along a level-dependent subsequence)
search_title: Good levels along a level-dependent subsequence
section: 3.12 Fiber integration and selecting useful levels
text: Proposition 3.12.5 (Good levels along a level-dependent subsequence) . DC9B0DCFE731 Let $Y$ and $v$ be as above, and let $F_ j:Y\to [0,\infty ]$ be measurable with $E_ j=\int _ YF_ j<\infty $. For any $0<\varepsilon <1$, there is a measurable set $S\subset Y$ of measure at least $(1-\varepsilon )v$ such that for each $y\in S$ an infinite subsequence $j_ l=j_ l(y)$ satisfies \[  F_{j_ l}(y)\leq \frac{E_{j_ l}}{\varepsilon v}.  \] In coarea applications, $F_ j$ may be the weighted fiber costs for different rectifiable sets. The subsequence is allowed to depend on $y$. This is the selection content of [ Sim18 ] , Remark 7.7(2), pp. 80–81. Proof After removing the countable union of null sets associated with any zero $E_ j$, define $G_ j=\{ F_ j\leq E_ j/(\varepsilon v)\} $. Markov's inequality gives $|G_ j|\geq (1-\varepsilon )v$. For each $N$, the union $H_ N=\bigcup _{j\geq N}G_ j$ therefore has at least this measure. The sets $H_ N$ decrease and lie in the finite-measure set $Y$, so continuity from above gives $|\bigcap _ NH_ N|\geq (1-\varepsilon )v$. This intersection is the limsup of the good sets: each of its points lies in infinitely many $G_ j$. Listing those indices in increasing order gives the required subsequence. Nothing in this argument selects one subsequence that works for every level simultaneously. $\square$

title: Proposition 3.12.6 (Summable errors vanish on almost every fiber)
search_title: Summable errors vanish on almost every fiber
section: 3.12 Fiber integration and selecting useful levels
text: Proposition 3.12.6 (Summable errors vanish on almost every fiber) . 3F1F6A59BCFB Let $F_ j:Y\to [0,\infty ]$ be measurable with $\sum _ j\int _ YF_ j<\infty $. Then $\sum _ jF_ j(y)<\infty $ and $F_ j(y)\to 0$ for almost every $y$. In particular, if coarea gives fiber costs with $\int _ YF_ j\to 0$, one can choose a subsequence of indices, independent of the level, along which the costs tend to zero almost everywhere. Proof Tonelli's theorem gives $\int _ Y\sum _ jF_ j=\sum _ j\int _ YF_ j<\infty $. The nonnegative sum is finite almost everywhere, and its terms tend to zero there. For the last assertion choose increasing indices $j_ l$ with $\int _ YF_{j_ l}\leq 2^{-l}$; the first assertion then applies to this subsequence. Here the conclusion is almost-everywhere convergence along one common subsequence, under the stronger vanishing-integral hypothesis. It should not be confused with the bounded normalized-cost subsequences in Proposition 3.12.5 . $\square$

Proposition 3.12.7 (The distance-volume function is absolutely continuous off its critical part) . DE97D6ADACDB Let $a\in \mathbb R^ n$ and $0<\alpha < eta $ with $\overline{B_ eta (a)}\subset U$. Put $ho (x)=|x-a|$, $J=|
abla ^ Mho |$, $R=\{ x\in M:J(x)>0\} $, and \[  V_ R(t)=\mathcal H^ m(R\cap \{ \alpha <ho <t\} ),\qquad \alpha \leq t\leq  eta .  \] Then $V_ R$ is absolutely continuous and for almost every $t$, \[  V_ R'(t)=\int _{R\cap \partial B_ t(a)} rac1{|
abla ^ Mho |}\, d\mathcal H^{m-1} \geq \mathcal H^{m-1}(M\cap \partial B_ t(a)).  \] The inequality holds at almost every $t\in (\alpha , eta )$; coarea discards the critical part of the fiber at these levels. title: 16.29 Examples of coarea, multiplicity and projection
search_title: Examples of coarea, multiplicity and projection
section: 16.29 Examples of coarea, multiplicity and projection
text:
These calculations illustrate the area and coarea conventions in [ Sim18 ] , Chapter 2, Sections 3 and 7, and Chapter 3, Sections 2–3. Each example specifies whether it counts points, measures a positive-dimensional fiber, or pushes an unweighted surface measure forward. Exceptional levels can carry large fibers even when every almost-everywhere conclusion is valid. Example 16.29.1 (A tilted plane checks the coarea metric factor) . 49CF1B83DAE5 Let $M_ a=\{ (s,t,as):(s,t)\in (0,1)^2\} \subset \mathbb R^3$ and $f(x,y,z)=x$, with $a\in \mathbb R$. Then \[  d\mathcal H^2\llcorner M_ a=\sqrt{1+a^2}\, ds\, dt, \qquad J_1(d^{M_ a}f)= rac1{\sqrt{1+a^2}}.  \] For $0<u<1$, the fiber $M_ a\cap f^{-1}(u)$ has length one. Thus coarea gives $\int _{M_ a}J_1(d^{M_ a}f)\, d\mathcal H^2=1$, whereas the unweighted area is $\sqrt{1+a^2}$. Proof The graph derivative has tangent columns $(1,0,a)$ and $(0,1,0)$, which are orthogonal with squared lengths $1+a^2$ and one. Its area Jacobian is therefore $\sqrt{1+a^2}$. In the corresponding orthonormal tangent basis, the derivative of $f$ is the row $(1/\sqrt{1+a^2},0)$, giving the stated coarea Jacobian. A fiber has fixed $s=u$ and varies only in $t$, with unit speed and length one. Integrating either side of coarea gives one. Replacing the tangential Jacobian by the ambient gradient norm $|Df|=1$ would incorrectly give the larger unweighted area when $a
e 0$. $\square$ Example 16.29.2 (Height on a round two-sphere has a constant area density) . E66117D1B5C1 Let $R>0$ and let $z$ denote height on the sphere $S_ R^2\subset \mathbb R^3$. Away from its poles, \[  |
abla ^{S_ R^2}z|= rac{\sqrt{R^2-z^2}}R, \qquad \mathcal H^1(S_ R^2\cap \{ z=t\} )=2\pi \sqrt{R^2-t^2} \quad (-R<t<R).  \] The pushforward of area by height is $2\pi R\, \chi _{(-R,R)}\mathcal L^1$. In particular the sphere has area $4\pi R^2$, and \[  \int _{S_ R^2}|
abla ^{S_ R^2}z|\, dA=\pi ^2R^2.  \] Proof The unit normal is $x/R$. Projection of $e_3$ onto the tangent plane has norm $\sqrt{1-(z/R)^2}$, proving the gradient formula. The fiber is a horizontal circle of the indicated radius. The inverse-Jacobian formula in Proposition 3.12.2 gives the area pushforward density as the fiber length divided by this gradient norm, namely $2\pi R$. The two poles have zero area and contribute no critical pushforward mass. Integrating the constant density over $(-R,R)$ gives the area. Ordinary coarea gives the last integral as \[  2\pi \int _{-R}^ R\sqrt{R^2-t^2}\, dt=\pi ^2R^2,  \] since the integral is the area of a semicircle. Equivalently the parametrization $(\sqrt{R^2-t^2}\cos 	heta ,\sqrt{R^2-t^2}\sin 	heta ,t)$ has orthogonal derivatives with lengths $\sqrt{R^2-t^2}$ and $R/\sqrt{R^2-t^2}$, and hence constant area Jacobian $R$. The divergent reciprocal near the poles cancels the shrinking fiber length. $\square$ Example 16.29.3 (Squared radius on a disk gives a uniform pushforward) . 0D4EEA37173E Let $R>0$, $D_ R=\{ x\in \mathbb R^2:|x|<R\} $ and $f(x)=|x|^2$. Then \[  f_\# (\mathcal L^2\llcorner D_ R)=\pi \chi _{(0,R^2)}\mathcal L^1.  \] For $0<t<R^2$, the fiber length is $2\pi \sqrt t$ and $|Df|=2\sqrt t$ on the fiber. The origin is critical but has zero area. Proof The derivative is $2x$, so the only critical point is the origin. Each positive fiber in the range is a circle of radius $\sqrt t$. Proposition 3.12.2 gives density $(2\pi \sqrt t)/(2\sqrt t)=\pi $ for the unweighted pushforward. There is no atom from the critical point because it has zero two-dimensional measure. Independently, the sublevel set $\{ f<t\} $ has area $\pi t$ for $0<t<R^2$, whose derivative is the same constant. Coarea with its Jacobian weight instead gives density $2\pi \sqrt t$; the two pushforwards must not be conflated. $\square$ Example 16.29.4 (A flat plateau produces a critical atom) . EB1FFD21A1B7 On $D=(-1,1)	imes (0,1)\subset \mathbb R^2$, let $f(x,y)=\max \{ x,0\} $. Its unweighted area pushforward is \[  f_\# (\mathcal L^2\llcorner D)=\delta _0+\chi _{(0,1)}\mathcal L^1.  \] Its Jacobian-weighted pushforward is only $\chi _{(0,1)}\mathcal L^1$. The exceptional fiber $f^{-1}(0)$ has infinite $\mathcal H^1$ measure, although almost every fiber in the range has length one. Proof On $x<0$ the map is constant and its gradient is zero. This half-rectangle has area one and pushes to a unit atom at zero. On $x>0$ the gradient is $(1,0)$, and Fubini gives Lebesgue measure on $(0,1)$ as the pushforward. The line $x=0$ is a null set for area, so its nondifferentiability has no effect. Multiplication by the Jacobian removes the flat half-rectangle and yields the second pushforward. The fiber at zero contains a nonempty open rectangle. Its one-dimensional Hausdorff measure is infinite: if a bounded set had finite $\mathcal H^1$, diameter covers would give zero two-dimensional Lebesgue measure by multiplying their one-dimensional cost by the maximum diameter and letting that diameter tend to zero. This contradicts the positive area of the half-rectangle. For $t\in (0,1)$ the fiber is a vertical unit segment, and other nonzero levels have empty fibers. An infinite fiber value at one Lebesgue-null level does not affect the coarea integral. This example shows why the critical contribution in Proposition 3.12.2 must be retained. $\square$ Example 16.29.5 (Distance is constant on a sphere and its volume function jumps) . 812BD5E64F51 Let $R>0$, $M=S_ R^2\subset \mathbb R^3$ and $ho (x)=|x|$. Its tangential gradient vanishes everywhere, while \[  ho _\# (\mathcal H^2\llcorner M)=4\pi R^2\delta _ R.  \] The function $V(t)=\mathcal H^2(M\cap B_ t(0))$ equals zero for $t\leq R$ and $4\pi R^2$ for $t>R$. It is not absolutely continuous. Coarea nevertheless holds: all level intersections except the single level $R$ are empty. Proof The function $ho |M$ is the constant $R$, so its tangential derivative is zero and its unweighted pushforward is the claimed atom. The area is $4\pi R^2$ by Example 16.29.2 . The strict inequality in the open-ball definition accounts for $V(R)=0$. At the one nonempty level the fiber is the entire two-sphere and has infinite one-dimensional measure, by the same dimension comparison as in Example 16.29.4 , applied to a regular chart. That value occurs on a null set of radii, and the integral of the fiber length is zero, agreeing with the zero Jacobian integral. Proposition 3.12.7 concerns the empty regular part in this example and makes no incorrect absolute-continuity claim for $V$ itself. $\square$ Example 16.29.6 (A fold counts two preimages rather than one image) . 36E81AC368FB For $f:(-1,1)	o \mathbb R$, $f(s)=s^2$, the image has length one, but \[  \int _{-1}^1|f'(s)|\, ds=2 =\int _0^1\# f^{-1}(t)\, dt.  \] The unweighted pushforward of $ds$ has density $t^{-1/2}\chi _{(0,1)}(t)$, which is integrable despite its singularity at zero. This is an equal-dimensional area-formula example, not a positive-dimensional coarea fiber. Proof For $0<t<1$ there are two preimages $\pm \sqrt t$, and outside $[0,1)$ there are none. The unique preimage at zero does not affect the integral. Direct integration gives $\int _{-1}^1 2|s|\, ds=2$, matching the multiplicity integral. For the unweighted pushforward, apply the weighted area formula with weight $1/|f'|$ away from the null point zero. At each positive target value the two inverse derivative factors are each $1/(2\sqrt t)$, summing to $1/\sqrt t$. Its integral over $(0,1)$ is two, the original interval length. Thus counting the image once would lose one sheet, while omitting the inverse derivative would describe a different pushforward measure. $\square$ Example 16.29.7 (A segment and a separated dust realize both decomposition parts) . 508F24AC4E8F Let $L=[0,1]	imes \{ 0\} $ and let $K'=K+(0,2)$ be a translated four-corner set. For $A=L\cup K'$, its rectifiable part is $L$ and its purely one-unrectifiable part is $K'$, modulo $\mathcal H^1$-null sets. Both parts have positive finite length. Proof The segment is a compact Lipschitz image of an interval and has length one. The translated four-corner set has positive finite length and is purely one-unrectifiable by Theorem 16.12.7 . Translation preserves those properties. The two sets are disjoint by their height ranges, so they already give a decomposition of the required type. Uniqueness in Theorem 3.11.5 identifies them with the canonical measure classes of the two parts. In particular no positive-length portion of the dust can be absorbed into a different rectifiable part by changing the chosen representative. $\square$ Example 16.29.8 (One null coordinate projection does not imply pure unrectifiability) . 0B1ACA8FF719 For $1\leq m<n$, consider \[  M=\operatorname {span}\{ e_1,\ldots ,e_{m-1},e_{m+1}\} \subset \mathbb R^ n,  \] with the empty initial list allowed when $m=1$. Projection onto $\operatorname {span}\{ e_1,\ldots ,e_ m\} $ has $m$-dimensional image measure zero, although $M$ is a smooth rectifiable $m$-plane. Projection onto its own coordinate plane is the identity. Proof The first projection maps $M$ to the $(m-1)$-plane spanned by $e_1,\ldots ,e_{m-1}$. This lower-dimensional plane has zero $\mathcal H^ m$ measure, as follows from diameter covers of bounded pieces. Yet the plane $M$ itself has positive $m$-measure on every nonempty relative ball, and is countably rectifiable by its linear parametrization. It is therefore not purely $m$-unrectifiable. The second coordinate projection has Jacobian one on $M$. This explains why Theorem 3.11.8 requires all coordinate $m$-projections, including when $n<2m$ so a fully orthogonal $m$-plane would not exist. $\square$

text: Example 16.29.6 (A fold counts two preimages rather than one image) . 36E81AC368FB For $f:(-1,1)\to \mathbb R$, $f(s)=s^2$, the image has length one, but \[  \int _{-1}^1|f'(s)|\, ds=2 =\int _0^1\# f^{-1}(t)\, dt.  \] The unweighted pushforward of $ds$ has density $t^{-1/2}\chi _{(0,1)}(t)$, which is integrable despite its singularity at zero. This is an equal-dimensional area-formula example, not a positive-dimensional coarea fiber. Proof For $0<t<1$ there are two preimages $\pm \sqrt t$, and outside $[0,1)$ there are none. The unique preimage at zero does not affect the integral. Direct integration gives $\int _{-1}^1 2|s|\, ds=2$, matching the multiplicity integral. For the unweighted pushforward, apply the weighted area formula with weight $1/|f'|$ away from the null point zero. At each positive target value the two inverse derivative factors are each $1/(2\sqrt t)$, summing to $1/\sqrt t$. Its integral over $(0,1)$ is two, the original interval length. Thus counting the image once would lose one sheet, while omitting the inverse derivative would describe a different pushforward measure. $\square$

title: Example 16.29.7 (A segment and a separated dust realize both decomposition parts)
search_title: A segment and a separated dust realize both decomposition parts
section: 16.29 Examples of coarea, multiplicity and projection
text: Example 16.29.7 (A segment and a separated dust realize both decomposition parts) . 508F24AC4E8F Let $L=[0,1]\times \{ 0\} $ and let $K'=K+(0,2)$ be a translated four-corner set. For $A=L\cup K'$, its rectifiable part is $L$ and its purely one-unrectifiable part is $K'$, modulo $\mathcal H^1$-null sets. Both parts have positive finite length. Proof The segment is a compact Lipschitz image of an interval and has length one. The translated four-corner set has positive finite length and is purely one-unrectifiable by Theorem 16.12.7 . Translation preserves those properties. The two sets are disjoint by their height ranges, so they already give a decomposition of the required type. Uniqueness in Theorem 3.11.5 identifies them with the canonical measure classes of the two parts. In particular no positive-length portion of the dust can be absorbed into a different rectifiable part by changing the chosen representative. $\square$

title: Example 16.29.8 (One null coordinate projection does not imply pure unrectifiability)
search_title: One null coordinate projection does not imply pure unrectifiability
section: 16.29 Examples of coarea, multiplicity and projection
text: Example 16.29.8 (One null coordinate projection does not imply pure unrectifiability) . 0B1ACA8FF719 For $1\leq m<n$, consider \[  M=\operatorname {span}\{ e_1,\ldots ,e_{m-1},e_{m+1}\} \subset \mathbb R^ n,  \] with the empty initial list allowed when $m=1$. Projection onto $\operatorname {span}\{ e_1,\ldots ,e_ m\} $ has $m$-dimensional image measure zero, although $M$ is a smooth rectifiable $m$-plane. Projection onto its own coordinate plane is the identity. Proof The first projection maps $M$ to the $(m-1)$-plane spanned by $e_1,\ldots ,e_{m-1}$. This lower-dimensional plane has zero $\mathcal H^ m$ measure, as follows from diameter covers of bounded pieces. Yet the plane $M$ itself has positive $m$-measure on every nonempty relative ball, and is countably rectifiable by its linear parametrization. It is therefore not purely $m$-unrectifiable. The second coordinate projection has Jacobian one on $M$. This explains why Theorem 3.11.8 requires all coordinate $m$-projections, including when $n<2m$ so a fully orthogonal $m$-plane would not exist. $\square$

title: 3.13 The area formula from metric pieces
search_title: The area formula from metric pieces
section: 3.13 The area formula from metric pieces
text: We expand the three cases in [ Sim18 ] , Chapter 2, Theorem 3.3 and its proof, printed pp. 57–60. The proof uses differentiability, countably many pieces on which distances are close to a fixed linear metric, and an injective graph regularization of the critical set. It uses the normalization $\mathcal H^ m=\mathcal L^ m$ on $\mathbb R^ m$, the diameter-cover Lipschitz estimate and ordinary linear change of variables. It does not use rectifiable-set tangent theorems, Whitney extension, or coarea. Throughout $1\leq m\leq n$. Lemma 3.13.1 (An injective linear map determines a positive domain metric) . 249B82161066 Let $L:\mathbb R^ m\to \mathbb R^ n$ be injective and linear, and put $T=(L^*L)^{1/2}$. Then $T$ is positive definite, $|Tv|=|Lv|$ for every $v$, and $\det T=J_ mL$. For every Lebesgue-measurable $E\subset \mathbb R^ m$, \[  \mathcal H^ m(L(E))=\mathcal H^ m(T(E))=J_ mL\, \mathcal L^ m(E).  \] This is the linear normalization used in [ Sim18 ] , proof of Theorem 3.3, pp. 58–59. Proof The spectral theorem constructs the positive square root and gives $|Tv|^2=\langle L^*Lv,v\rangle =|Lv|^2$. Its determinant is the square root of $\det (L^*L)$. The map $LT^{-1}$ is an isometric linear embedding, so the diameter-cover definition gives invariance of Hausdorff measure under it. On the domain plane, the normalization recorded in Definition 2.2.1 identifies $\mathcal H^ m$ with Lebesgue measure; ordinary linear change of variables gives $\mathcal L^ m(T(E))=|\det T|\mathcal L^ m(E)$. This establishes the linear case without an area formula for nonlinear maps. Infinite values follow by increasing bounded pieces. $\square$ Lemma 3.13.2 (Measurability of a finite-volume Lipschitz image) . E5CA65543835 Let $f:\mathbb R^ m\to \mathbb R^ n$ be Lipschitz, and let $E\subset \mathbb R^ m$ be Lebesgue measurable with finite measure. Then $f(E)$ is $\mathcal H^ m$-measurable. If $|E|=0$, then $\mathcal H^ m(f(E))=0$. Proof Choose compact sets $K_ j\subset E$ with $|E\setminus \bigcup _ jK_ j|=0$ by inner regularity. Images of the compact sets are compact, so their union is Borel. Proposition 2.2.2 gives \[  \mathcal H^ m(f(Z))\leq (\operatorname {Lip}f)^ m\mathcal H^ m(Z)=0 \quad \text{when }|Z|=0.  \] Thus $f(E)$ differs from the Borel union $\bigcup _ jf(K_ j)$ by a Hausdorff-null set and is measurable for the complete Hausdorff measure. This also proves the null assertion. The argument extends to arbitrary measurable $E$ by a countable bounded exhaustion. It requires neither injectivity nor any assertion that every continuous image of a Borel set is Borel. $\square$ Proposition 3.13.3 (A countable partition with controlled linear metric) . 8A21EBE8AE53 Let $f:\mathbb R^ m\to \mathbb R^ n$ be Lipschitz, let $A$ be a measurable subset of its differentiability set on which $Df$ has rank $m$, and fix $0<\varepsilon <1$. There is a countable disjoint measurable partition $A=\bigcup _\ell E_\ell $ and positive definite symmetric maps $T_\ell :\mathbb R^ m\to \mathbb R^ m$ such that, for every $x,x'\in E_\ell $, \[  (1-\varepsilon )|T_\ell (x-x')| \leq |f(x)-f(x')| \leq (1+\varepsilon )|T_\ell (x-x')|,  \] and at every $x\in E_\ell $, \[  (1-\varepsilon )\det T_\ell \leq J_ mDf(x) \leq (1+\varepsilon )\det T_\ell .  \] In particular $f$ is injective on each piece. This is the quantified partition underlying [ Sim18 ] , pp. 58–59. Proof Choose a countable dense family of injective linear maps $L_ j:\mathbb R^ m\to \mathbb R^ n$ and put $T_ j=(L_ j^*L_ j)^{1/2}$. At a fixed full-rank differentiability point $x$, the smallest singular value of $Df(x)$ is positive. Differentiability makes $|f(x+v)-f(x)-Df(x)v|/|v|$ arbitrarily small for all sufficiently small nonzero $v$. Choose $L_ j$ close enough to $Df(x)$ in operator norm and its Jacobian close enough to $J_ mDf(x)$. These two facts give the displayed distance and Jacobian inequalities with $T_ j$, for all $0<|v|<1/i$ for some positive integer $i$. The positive least singular value converts the small error measured by $|v|$ into an error relative to $|L_ jv|=|T_ jv|$. For fixed $j,i$, the set of qualifying $x$ is measurable. The Jacobian condition uses a measurable derivative representative; the distance inequalities can be tested only on rational nonzero vectors $v$ of length less than $1/i$. Continuity in $v$ then supplies the inequalities for all such vectors. This is a countable family of inequalities between measurable functions of $x$. The union of these qualifying sets covers $A$. Assign a point to the first pair $(j,i)$ in a fixed enumeration, and then partition each assigned set by a countable disjoint grid of sets of diameter strictly less than $1/i$. Both distance inequalities now apply to every pair in the resulting piece. Use $T_\ell =T_ j$ for that piece. Empty pieces may be omitted. The lower bound and invertibility of $T_ j$ imply injectivity. No area estimate has been used to construct this partition. $\square$ Lemma 3.13.4 (Area bounds on one metric piece) . 36D6E8A409D9 Suppose $E$ has finite Lebesgue measure and the two bounds in Proposition 3.13.3 hold on $E$ with one positive definite $T$. Then \[  \frac{(1-\varepsilon )^ m}{1+\varepsilon }\int _ EJ_ mDf\, dx \leq \mathcal H^ m(f(E)) \leq \frac{(1+\varepsilon )^ m}{1-\varepsilon }\int _ EJ_ mDf\, dx.  \] Both comparison factors tend to one as $\varepsilon \downarrow 0$. Proof The map $h=f\circ T^{-1}:T(E)\to f(E)$ is injective and has Lipschitz constant at most $1+\varepsilon $; its inverse has Lipschitz constant at most $(1-\varepsilon )^{-1}$. Proposition 2.2.2 , applied separately to these two maps on their domains, gives \[  (1-\varepsilon )^ m\mathcal H^ m(T(E)) \leq \mathcal H^ m(f(E)) \leq (1+\varepsilon )^ m\mathcal H^ m(T(E)).  \] Lemma 3.13.1 identifies the domain measure as $\det T\, |E|$. Integrate the pointwise bounds $(1-\varepsilon )\det T\leq J_ mDf\leq (1+\varepsilon )\det T$. Substitution gives exactly the two displayed ratios. The image is measurable by Lemma 3.13.2 . Keeping the denominator factors explicit avoids reversing an inequality when comparing the Jacobian integral with $\det T\, |E|$. $\square$ Proposition 3.13.5 (The area identity on the full-rank differentiability set) . 64CD4DD34AB0 For Lipschitz $f:\mathbb R^ m\to \mathbb R^ n$ and a finite-volume measurable set $A$ of full-rank differentiability points, \[  \int _ AJ_ mDf\, dx =\int _{\mathbb R^ n}\# (A\cap f^{-1}(y))\, d\mathcal H^ m(y).  \] The multiplicity function is measurable and finite almost everywhere. This is the full-rank case of [ Sim18 ] , Theorem 3.3. Proof For a fixed $\varepsilon $, partition $A$ by Proposition 3.13.3 . Each restriction is injective, and each image is measurable by Lemma 3.13.2 . Therefore, at every target point, \[  \# (A\cap f^{-1}(y))=\sum _\ell \chi _{f(E_\ell )}(y).  \] This proves measurability, including the value infinity when infinitely many pieces contribute. Sum Lemma 3.13.4 over the disjoint domain pieces. Monotone convergence identifies the image-measure sum with the multiplicity integral, so the same two comparison factors bound it by $\int _ AJ_ mDf$. This last integral is finite because $J_ mDf\leq (\operatorname {Lip}f)^ m$ almost everywhere and $|A|<\infty $. Let $\varepsilon \downarrow 0$ to obtain equality. Finiteness of the integral gives finiteness of the multiplicity for almost every target point. The partitions may depend on $\varepsilon $; the function being integrated does not. $\square$ Lemma 3.13.6 (An injective graph regularization of a rank-deficient map) . 34F8CC476DF4 Let $f:\mathbb R^ m\to \mathbb R^ n$ be Lipschitz with constant $L$, and set $F_\varepsilon (x)=(f(x),\varepsilon x)$ for $0<\varepsilon \leq 1$. This map is injective and Lipschitz. At every differentiability point of $f$, its derivative has rank $m$ and \[  J_ mDF_\varepsilon =\sqrt{\det (Df^*Df+\varepsilon ^2I_ m)}.  \] If $\operatorname {rank}Df<m$, this is at most $\varepsilon (L^2+1)^{(m-1)/2}$. Proof The last coordinate block determines $x$, proving injectivity, and $\operatorname {Lip}F_\varepsilon \leq \sqrt{L^2+\varepsilon ^2}$. Its derivative has the vertical block $\varepsilon I_ m$, so is injective. Its Gram matrix is $Df^*Df+\varepsilon ^2I_ m$. At a rank-deficient point at least one eigenvalue of $Df^*Df$ is zero, and all eigenvalues are at most $L^2$. Thus one regularized eigenvalue is $\varepsilon ^2$, while the others are at most $L^2+1$. Taking the square root of their product gives the stated bound. Its order is $\varepsilon $ in the worst rank-$m-1$ case; a uniform quadratic error in $\varepsilon $ is unnecessary and generally false. $\square$ Proposition 3.13.7 (The critical differentiability set has a null image) . 0A1766CE1A05 Let $f:\mathbb R^ m\to \mathbb R^ n$ be Lipschitz and let $A$ be a measurable set of differentiability points with $\operatorname {rank}Df<m$. Then $\mathcal H^ m(f(A))=0$. Proof First assume $|A|<\infty $. Lemma 3.13.6 and Proposition 3.13.5 , now in target $\mathbb R^{n+m}$, give \[  \mathcal H^ m(F_\varepsilon (A)) =\int _ AJ_ mDF_\varepsilon \, dx \leq \varepsilon (L^2+1)^{(m-1)/2}|A|.  \] Here injectivity of $F_\varepsilon $ turns its multiplicity into the indicator of its image. Orthogonal projection onto the first $n$ coordinates is one-Lipschitz and maps $F_\varepsilon (A)$ onto $f(A)$. Consequently the same upper bound holds for $\mathcal H^ m(f(A))$. Let $\varepsilon \downarrow 0$. General $A$ is a countable union of finite-volume intersections with bounded balls, so its image is a countable union of null images. This proves the critical case using the already established full-rank case, rather than assuming the desired area formula on critical points. $\square$ Theorem 3.13.8 (Euclidean area with measurable multiplicity) . 6695035EB27D Let $V\subset \mathbb R^ m$ be open, let $f:V\to \mathbb R^ n$ be locally Lipschitz, and let $A\subset V$ be Lebesgue measurable. Then the counting function $N_ A(y)=\# (A\cap f^{-1}(y))$ is $\mathcal H^ m$-measurable, and \[  \int _ AJ_ mDf\, dx=\int _{\mathbb R^ n}N_ A(y)\, d\mathcal H^ m(y).  \] The Jacobian is assigned zero on the null set of nondifferentiability. Infinite values are permitted. This supplies the proof of [ Sim18 ] , Theorem 3.3, through its separate full-rank, critical and exceptional cases. Proof First let $f$ be globally Lipschitz and $|A|<\infty $. Partition $A$ into its full-rank differentiability part $R$, its rank-deficient differentiability part $C$, and its nondifferentiability part $Z$. Measurable derivative representatives make these measurable. Rademacher's theorem, Theorem 3.1.2 , gives $|Z|=0$, so Lemma 3.13.2 gives $\mathcal H^ m(f(Z))=0$. Proposition 3.13.7 gives the same conclusion for $f(C)$. Their multiplicity functions vanish outside those null images and are measurable for complete Hausdorff measure, regardless of possibly infinite values on the images. Their Jacobian integrals are zero. Proposition 3.13.5 treats $R$. Counts add on disjoint domain subsets, and this proves the identity on $A$. For the local case, cover $V$ by countably many bounded balls with closures in larger balls on which $f$ is Lipschitz. Extend its coordinate functions from each larger ball to all of $\mathbb R^ m$ by Proposition 3.4.2 . The vector extension is Lipschitz, possibly with a larger constant. On the smaller ball it agrees with $f$ on a neighborhood of every point, so its derivative agrees wherever that of $f$ exists. Partition $A$ disjointly among the smaller balls and apply the established finite-volume formula on each part. Sum by monotone convergence. This proves both the identity and the measurability of its counting function for arbitrary $A$, while preserving every local derivative. The proof uses neither Whitney extension nor rectifiable-set decomposition or coarea. $\square$ Corollary 3.13.9 (A null image is equivalent to a vanishing area Jacobian) . C5AE6A4945BD Under Theorem 3.13.8 , $\mathcal H^ m(f(A))=0$ if and only if $J_ mDf=0$ almost everywhere on $A$. In particular, a measurable positive-volume set on which the area Jacobian is positive almost everywhere has an image of positive $m$-dimensional measure. Proof The image is measurable by countable local versions of Lemma 3.13.2 . Its indicator is bounded above by $N_ A$, since every point of the image has at least one preimage. If the Jacobian vanishes almost everywhere, the area identity gives $\int N_ A=0$ and hence zero measure for the image. Conversely if the image is null, $N_ A$ vanishes off a null set, so its integral and the Jacobian integral are zero. Nonnegativity of the Jacobian gives its almost-everywhere vanishing. The final assertion is the contrapositive with a positive integral, which may be infinite. $\square$ Proposition 3.13.10 (Finite-volume domains have finite multiplicity almost everywhere) . 3AE746AD9F73 If $f:\mathbb R^ m\to \mathbb R^ n$ has Lipschitz constant $L$ and $A$ is measurable with finite volume, then \[  \int _{\mathbb R^ n}N_ A\, d\mathcal H^ m\leq L^ m|A|, \qquad \mathcal H^ m(\{ N_ A\geq q\} )\leq \frac{L^ m|A|}{q} \quad (q=1,2,\ldots ).  \] In particular almost every target point has finitely many preimages in $A$. This conclusion permits exceptional infinite fibers. Proof All singular values of $Df$ are at most $L$, so $J_ mDf\leq L^ m$ at differentiability points. Theorem 3.13.8 gives the integral bound. On $\{ N_ A\geq q\} $ the counting function is at least $q$, giving the second inequality by integration. The set where $N_ A=\infty $ is contained in every such superlevel set, so its measure is zero on letting $q\to \infty $. A constant map can still have an entire domain as the fiber at its one exceptional image point. $\square$

text: Theorem 3.13.8 (Euclidean area with measurable multiplicity) . 6695035EB27D Let $V\subset \mathbb R^ m$ be open, let $f:V\to \mathbb R^ n$ be locally Lipschitz, and let $A\subset V$ be Lebesgue measurable. Then the counting function $N_ A(y)=\# (A\cap f^{-1}(y))$ is $\mathcal H^ m$-measurable, and \[  \int _ AJ_ mDf\, dx=\int _{\mathbb R^ n}N_ A(y)\, d\mathcal H^ m(y).  \] The Jacobian is assigned zero on the null set of nondifferentiability. Infinite values are permitted. This supplies the proof of [ Sim18 ] , Theorem 3.3, through its separate full-rank, critical and exceptional cases. Proof First let $f$ be globally Lipschitz and $|A|<\infty $. Partition $A$ into its full-rank differentiability part $R$, its rank-deficient differentiability part $C$, and its nondifferentiability part $Z$. Measurable derivative representatives make these measurable. Rademacher's theorem, Theorem 3.1.2 , gives $|Z|=0$, so Lemma 3.13.2 gives $\mathcal H^ m(f(Z))=0$. Proposition 3.13.7 gives the same conclusion for $f(C)$. Their multiplicity functions vanish outside those null images and are measurable for complete Hausdorff measure, regardless of possibly infinite values on the images. Their Jacobian integrals are zero. Proposition 3.13.5 treats $R$. Counts add on disjoint domain subsets, and this proves the identity on $A$. For the local case, cover $V$ by countably many bounded balls with closures in larger balls on which $f$ is Lipschitz. Extend its coordinate functions from each larger ball to all of $\mathbb R^ m$ by Proposition 3.4.2 . The vector extension is Lipschitz, possibly with a larger constant. On the smaller ball it agrees with $f$ on a neighborhood of every point, so its derivative agrees wherever that of $f$ exists. Partition $A$ disjointly among the smaller balls and apply the established finite-volume formula on each part. Sum by monotone convergence. This proves both the identity and the measurability of its counting function for arbitrary $A$, while preserving every local derivative. The proof uses neither Whitney extension nor rectifiable-set decomposition or coarea. $\square$

title: Corollary 3.13.9 (A null image is equivalent to a vanishing area Jacobian)
search_title: A null image is equivalent to a vanishing area Jacobian
section: 3.13 The area formula from metric pieces
text: Corollary 3.13.9 (A null image is equivalent to a vanishing area Jacobian) . C5AE6A4945BD Under Theorem 3.13.8 , $\mathcal H^ m(f(A))=0$ if and only if $J_ mDf=0$ almost everywhere on $A$. In particular, a measurable positive-volume set on which the area Jacobian is positive almost everywhere has an image of positive $m$-dimensional measure. Proof The image is measurable by countable local versions of Lemma 3.13.2 . Its indicator is bounded above by $N_ A$, since every point of the image has at least one preimage. If the Jacobian vanishes almost everywhere, the area identity gives $\int N_ A=0$ and hence zero measure for the image. Conversely if the image is null, $N_ A$ vanishes off a null set, so its integral and the Jacobian integral are zero. Nonnegativity of the Jacobian gives its almost-everywhere vanishing. The final assertion is the contrapositive with a positive integral, which may be infinite. $\square$

title: Proposition 3.13.10 (Finite-volume domains have finite multiplicity almost everywhere)

text: Proposition 3.13.10 (Finite-volume domains have finite multiplicity almost everywhere) . 3AE746AD9F73 If $f:\mathbb R^ m\to \mathbb R^ n$ has Lipschitz constant $L$ and $A$ is measurable with finite volume, then \[  \int _{\mathbb R^ n}N_ A\, d\mathcal H^ m\leq L^ m|A|, \qquad \mathcal H^ m(\{ N_ A\geq q\} )\leq \frac{L^ m|A|}{q} \quad (q=1,2,\ldots ).  \] In particular almost every target point has finitely many preimages in $A$. This conclusion permits exceptional infinite fibers. Proof All singular values of $Df$ are at most $L$, so $J_ mDf\leq L^ m$ at differentiability points. Theorem 3.13.8 gives the integral bound. On $\{ N_ A\geq q\} $ the counting function is at least $q$, giving the second inequality by integration. The set where $N_ A=\infty $ is contained in every such superlevel set, so its measure is zero on letting $q\to \infty $. A constant map can still have an entire domain as the fiber at its one exceptional image point. $\square$
