section: 3.14 A proof of Euclidean coarea from area
text: We develop the regular-map and critical-map steps in [ Sim18 ] , Chapter 2, Theorem 7.3, printed pp. 76–79, and then pass to Lipschitz maps by the $C^1$ approximation theorem. The Euclidean area formula is now proved in Theorem 3.13.8 ; Whitney extension remains an external input. The preliminary slicing estimate is proved from diameter covers; in particular it does not use the coarea theorem being established. All Hausdorff measures use the normalization in Definition 2.2.1 . Lemma 3.14.1 (Measurability of the measure of a compact fiber) . A4D9D83AD84A Let $K\subset \mathbb R^ N$ be compact, let $f:K\to \mathbb R^ k$ be continuous, and let $d$ be an integer with $1\leq d\leq N$. Then \[  y\longmapsto \mathcal H^ d(K\cap f^{-1}(y))  \] is a Borel function with values in $[0,\infty ]$. Proof For each positive integer $j$, define $c_ j(y)$ as the infimum of $\sum _ i\omega _ d(\operatorname {diam}O_ i/2)^ d$ over finite covers of the compact fiber by open sets $O_ i$ of diameter less than $1/j$. Restrict to the countable family of finite unions of balls with rational centers and radii. There are countably many finite cover candidates. A candidate covers the fiber precisely when $y\notin f(K\setminus \bigcup _ iO_ i)$. The set on the right being excluded is compact, so the set of levels where the candidate is a cover is open. Consequently $\{ y:c_ j(y)<a\} $ is open for every $a$, and $c_ j$ is Borel. The family restrictions do not change the limit: $c_ j(y)\geq \mathcal H^ d_{1/j}(K\cap f^{-1}(y))$. Conversely, start with a diameter cover of the fiber by sets of diameter less than $1/(2j)$, with total cost within $\varepsilon $ of the corresponding Hausdorff content. Enlarge each set slightly to an open finite union of rational balls, increasing its cost by at most $\varepsilon 2^{-i}$ and keeping its diameter below $1/j$. Such an enlargement exists by a finite fine grid cover of each bounded set. Compactness of the fiber selects a finite subcover from these open sets. Thus $c_ j(y)\leq \mathcal H^ d_{1/(2j)}(K\cap f^{-1}(y))+2\varepsilon $ whenever the latter content is finite. Infinite content causes no upper-bound restriction. Sending $\varepsilon \downarrow 0$ and then $j\to \infty $ proves that the increasing functions $c_ j$ converge to the Hausdorff measure of the fiber. Their pointwise limit is Borel. Empty fibers have cost zero throughout. $\square$ Lemma 3.14.2 (Measurable fibers for a finite Hausdorff-measure set) . B3307B7EDAFF Let $1\leq k<m\leq N$, let $A\subset U\subset \mathbb R^ N$ be $\mathcal H^ m$-measurable with finite measure, with $U$ open, and let $f:U\to \mathbb R^ k$ be locally Lipschitz. Then $y\mapsto \mathcal H^{m-k}(A\cap f^{-1}(y))$, read as outer measure at exceptional levels if needed, is Lebesgue measurable. Almost every fiber is Hausdorff measurable. Proof Choose a Borel core of $A$ by Lemma 3.11.2 . Its finite restricted measure is Radon, so inner regularity gives increasing compact sets $K_ j\subset A$ with $\mathcal H^ m(A\setminus \bigcup _ jK_ j)=0$. Lemma 3.14.1 shows that each compact fiber measure is Borel. Continuity from below of Hausdorff measure on the increasing compact fibers gives a measurable fiber measure for $\bigcup _ jK_ j$. The omitted set has null fibers for almost every level by Lemma 3.10.3 . This lemma was proved directly by covers, without coarea. At the remaining levels the full fiber differs from a countable union of compact sets by a set of zero Hausdorff outer measure. It is therefore Hausdorff measurable and has the same measure as that union. Since Lebesgue measure is complete, modifying the measurable fiber function on the exceptional null set preserves measurability. The same conclusion holds for sigma-finite sets by disjoint finite-measure pieces and a countable union of exceptional level sets. $\square$ Proposition 3.14.3 (A coarse Lipschitz slicing estimate) . 34A5B7462AAA Let $1\leq k<m\leq N$, let $f:\mathbb R^ N\to \mathbb R^ k$ have Lipschitz constant $L$, and let $A$ be $\mathcal H^ m$-measurable with finite measure. Then \[  \int _{\mathbb R^ k}\mathcal H^{m-k}(A\cap f^{-1}(y))\, dy \leq \frac{2^ m\omega _ k\omega _{m-k}}{\omega _ m}L^ k\mathcal H^ m(A).  \] The constant is not sharp. This is a diameter-cover version of [ Sim18 ] , Chapter 2, Theorem 1.10, pp. 49–51; it is sufficient for the critical-set argument below. Proof Put $d=m-k>0$. Choose diameter covers $E_{li}$ of $A$ with positive diameters $s_{li}<1/l$ and normalized $m$-cost at most $\mathcal H^ m(A)+1/l$. Countably many zero-diameter members have zero $d$-measure in every fiber and can be discarded. For each remaining member meeting $A$, select $x_{li}\in A\cap E_{li}$ and replace it by the closed ball $Q_{li}=\overline B_{s_{li}}(x_{li})$. These balls still cover $A$ apart from the harmless countable set. Their images under $f$ are compact and lie in target balls of radius $Ls_{li}$. The measurable function \[  F_ l(y)=\sum _ i\omega _ d s_{li}^ d\chi _{f(Q_{li})}(y)  \] therefore satisfies \[  \int F_ l\, dy\leq \omega _ d\omega _ kL^ k\sum _ i s_{li}^{m} \leq \frac{2^ m\omega _ d\omega _ k}{\omega _ m}L^ k \bigl (\mathcal H^ m(A)+1/l\bigr ).  \] The balls contributing to $F_ l(y)$ cover the fiber and have diameter less than $2/l$, so its Hausdorff content at that scale is at most $F_ l(y)$. Hence the fiber measure is bounded by $\liminf _ lF_ l(y)$. It is measurable by Lemma 3.14.2 . Fatou's lemma gives the stated integral bound. The factor $2^ m$ records the passage from diameter sets to enclosing balls; no sharp isodiametric inequality is being asserted. For $L=0$, every image is a point of zero target Lebesgue measure and the same argument gives zero. $\square$ Proposition 3.14.4 (Coarea for a C1 map of full rank) . 487D5A52497A Let $U\subset \mathbb R^ n$ be open and let $f:U\to \mathbb R^ k$ be $C^1$, with $1\leq k<n$ and $\operatorname {rank}Df=k$ everywhere. For every Lebesgue-measurable $A\subset U$, \[  \int _ AJ_ kDf\, dx=\int _{\mathbb R^ k}\mathcal H^{n-k}(A\cap f^{-1}(y))\, dy.  \] This regular case uses only ordinary change of variables, Fubini, Euclidean area on the fibers and the linear Jacobian identity. Proof Near each point, choose $k$ input coordinates on which the corresponding minor of $Df$ is invertible. The map $g(x)=(f(x),p(x))$, with $p$ the remaining $n-k$ coordinates, is a $C^1$ diffeomorphism on a sufficiently small neighborhood. Write its inverse as $\psi (y,z)$ on an open set $W\subset \mathbb R^ k\times \mathbb R^{n-k}$. On a fixed level, $z\mapsto \psi (y,z)$ is injective and regular. The identity $f\circ \psi (y,z)=y$ and Lemma 3.10.5 give \[  J_ kDf(\psi (y,z))\, |\det D\psi (y,z)| =J_{n-k}(D_ z\psi (y,z)).  \] Indeed use $A=D\psi $, $B=(I_ k,0)$ and $\ker B=\{ 0\} \times \mathbb R^{n-k}$ in that lemma. Ordinary change of variables on the diffeomorphism and Fubini now give, for a Borel subset $A$ of this neighborhood, \[  \int _ AJ_ kDf\, dx =\int _{\mathbb R^ k}\int _{\{ z:(y,z)\in W\} } \chi _ A(\psi (y,z))J_{n-k}(D_ z\psi )\, dz\, dy.  \] The injective case of Theorem 3.2.2 identifies the inner integral with the fiber measure. Cover $U$ by countably many such neighborhoods and partition a Borel $A$ among them. Additivity on the disjoint pieces and monotone convergence prove the formula for Borel sets, allowing infinite values. For general Lebesgue-measurable $A$, choose a Borel representative modulo a null set on a countable bounded exhaustion. Lemma 3.10.3 removes the remainder on almost every fiber. This proves the general assertion without using a coarea theorem for the regular case. $\square$ Lemma 3.14.5 (Adding small target directions makes a critical map regular) . E4AAF448FD9F Let $U\subset \mathbb R^ n$ be open and let $f:U\to \mathbb R^ k$ be $C^1$, with $1\leq k<n$. For $0<\varepsilon \leq 1$, define \[  F_\varepsilon (x,z)=f(x)+\varepsilon z, \qquad (x,z)\in U\times (0,1)^ k.  \] This map has rank $k$ everywhere. If $\operatorname {rank}Df(x)<k$ and $\| Df(x)\| _{\mathrm{op}}\leq L$, then \[  J_ kDF_\varepsilon (x,z) =\sqrt{\det (Df(x)Df(x)^*+\varepsilon ^2I_ k)} \leq \varepsilon (L^2+1)^{(k-1)/2}.  \] This is the regularization in [ Sim18 ] , proof of Theorem 7.3, pp. 78–79. Proof The derivative matrix is $[Df,\varepsilon I_ k]$, so its row rank is $k$ and its Gram matrix is the one displayed. At a critical point the nonnegative eigenvalues of $DfDf^*$ lie in $[0,L^2]$ and at least one is zero. After adding $\varepsilon ^2I_ k$, at least one eigenvalue is exactly $\varepsilon ^2$ and the other $k-1$ eigenvalues are at most $L^2+1$. Their product and its square root give the bound. For $k=1$ the estimate is exactly $J_1DF_\varepsilon =\varepsilon $ on the critical set. $\square$ Proposition 3.14.6 (The critical set of a C1 map has null almost-everywhere fibers) . DAFD441F176A Let $f:U\subset \mathbb R^ n\to \mathbb R^ k$ be $C^1$, with $U$ open and $1\leq k<n$. Put $C=\{ x:\operatorname {rank}Df(x)<k\} $. Then \[  \mathcal H^{n-k}(C\cap f^{-1}(y))=0 \quad \text{for almost every }y\in \mathbb R^ k.  \] This conclusion is proved without assuming the Euclidean coarea formula for critical maps. Proof It suffices to prove the assertion for a Borel subset $A\subset C$ in a closed ball whose concentric larger closed ball lies in $U$; countably many such subsets cover $C$. The derivative has a finite bound $L$ on the larger ball. Integration along segments in that ball shows that $f$ is Lipschitz on the smaller ball, so the fiber-measurability lemma applies to $A$, and $|A|<\infty $. Apply Proposition 3.14.4 to $F_\varepsilon $ from Lemma 3.14.5 , on the measurable set $A\times (0,1)^ k$. Writing \[  B_ y=(A\times (0,1)^ k)\cap F_\varepsilon ^{-1}(y),  \] we obtain \[  \int _{\mathbb R^ k}\mathcal H^ n(B_ y)\, dy \leq \varepsilon (L^2+1)^{(k-1)/2}|A|.  \] In particular $B_ y$ is Borel and has finite $n$-measure at almost every level. Apply Proposition 3.14.3 on each such set to the one-Lipschitz projection $(x,z)\mapsto z$. Its fiber at $z\in (0,1)^ k$ is an isometric copy of $A\cap f^{-1}(y-\varepsilon z)$. Thus, with $C_{n,k}=2^ n\omega _ k\omega _{n-k}/\omega _ n$ and $H(v)=\mathcal H^{n-k}(A\cap f^{-1}(v))$, \[  \int _{(0,1)^ k}H(y-\varepsilon z)\, dz \leq C_{n,k}\mathcal H^ n(B_ y) \quad \text{for almost every }y.  \] The function $H$ is Lebesgue measurable by Lemma 3.14.2 . A Borel representative may be used in the double integral: contain its exceptional set in a Borel null set, whose translate is null on each fixed $z$ slice, and Tonelli shows that the joint exceptional set has product measure zero. Integrate the last inequality in $y$ and change variables $v=y-\varepsilon z$. Since the cube has volume one, this gives \[  \int _{\mathbb R^ k}H(v)\, dv \leq C_{n,k}\varepsilon (L^2+1)^{(k-1)/2}|A|.  \] The left side is independent of $\varepsilon $. Let it tend to zero; nonnegativity forces $H=0$ almost everywhere. Countable compact localization completes the proof. The coarse slicing estimate was proved for arbitrary finite-measure sets, so its use on $B_ y$ presupposes neither rectifiability of $A$ nor a critical coarea theorem. $\square$ Theorem 3.14.7 (Euclidean coarea for a C1 map) . 0D599A7625BD For a $C^1$ map $f:U\to \mathbb R^ k$ on an open $U\subset \mathbb R^ n$, $1\leq k<n$, and a Lebesgue-measurable $A\subset U$, \[  \int _ AJ_ kDf\, dx=\int _{\mathbb R^ k}\mathcal H^{n-k}(A\cap f^{-1}(y))\, dy.  \] Both sides can be infinite. The proof retains Euclidean area and ordinary Euclidean integration as inputs. Proof The regular set $U\setminus C$ is open, and Proposition 3.14.4 proves the formula on $A\setminus C$. On $A\cap C$, the Jacobian is zero. Proposition 3.14.6 gives zero fiber measure at almost every level, so both sides for this part vanish. The two pieces are disjoint; adding them proves the formula. Measurability on a countable bounded exhaustion is Lemma 3.14.2 . The decomposition does not claim that the critical values form a null set; only the relevant lower-dimensional measure of almost every critical fiber is zero. $\square$ Proposition 3.14.8 (C1 agreement reduces a Lipschitz map to smooth coarea) . 336B57437B6F Let $f:\mathbb R^ n\to \mathbb R^ k$ be globally Lipschitz, with $1\leq k<n$, and let $A\subset \mathbb R^ n$ be bounded and Lebesgue measurable. Then \[  \int _ AJ_ kDf\, dx=\int _{\mathbb R^ k}\mathcal H^{n-k}(A\cap f^{-1}(y))\, dy.  \] Here $Df$ is supplied by Rademacher and the Jacobian is zero on its exceptional set. The proof uses Whitney-based $C^1$ approximation and the preceding $C^1$ formula. Proof For every positive integer $j$, Corollary 3.5.6 gives a $C^1$ map $g_ j$ agreeing with both $f$ and its derivative off a set of measure less than $1/j$. Let $E_ j$ be the differentiability points where both equalities hold. Their union has full measure, since its complement lies in each exceptional set and thus has measure at most $1/j$ for every $j$. Make the $E_ j$ disjoint by assigning each point to the first qualifying index. These agreement sets are measurable because $f,g_ j$ and the derivative representatives are measurable. Apply Theorem 3.14.7 to $g_ j$ on $A\cap E_ j$. On this set $J_ kDg_ j=J_ kDf$, and its fiber under $g_ j$ is exactly its fiber under $f$. Sum the identities over $j$. Additivity of measure on the disjoint fiber pieces and monotone convergence identify the sum with the coarea identity for $A\cap \bigcup _ jE_ j$. The omitted subset has zero volume, and Lemma 3.10.3 gives zero lower-dimensional fiber measure at almost every level. It affects neither side. This proves the formula without using Euclidean coarea in the $C^1$ approximation or null-fiber steps. $\square$

If $\operatorname {rank}Df(x)<k$ and $\| Df(x)\| _{\mathrm{op}}\leq L$, then \[  J_ kDF_\varepsilon (x,z) =\sqrt{\det (Df(x)Df(x)^*+\varepsilon ^2I_ k)} \leq \varepsilon (L^2+1)^{(k-1)/2}.  \] This is the regularization in [ Sim18 ] , proof of Theorem 7.3, pp. 78–79. At a critical point the nonnegative eigenvalues of $DfDf^*$ lie in $[0,L^2]$ and at least one is zero. After adding $\varepsilon ^2I_ k$, at least one eigenvalue is exactly $\varepsilon ^2$ and the other $k-1$ eigenvalues are at most $L^2+1$. Their product and its square root give the bound. For $k=1$ the estimate is exactly $J_1DF_\varepsilon =\varepsilon $ on the critical set. $\square$

title: Proposition 3.14.6 (The critical set of a C1 map has null almost-everywhere fibers)
search_title: The critical set of a C1 map has null almost-everywhere fibers
section: 3.14 A proof of Euclidean coarea from area
text: Proposition 3.14.6 (The critical set of a C1 map has null almost-everywhere fibers) . DAFD441F176A Let $f:U\subset \mathbb R^ n\to \mathbb R^ k$ be $C^1$, with $U$ open and $1\leq k<n$. Put $C=\{ x:\operatorname {rank}Df(x)<k\} $. Then \[  \mathcal H^{n-k}(C\cap f^{-1}(y))=0 \quad \text{for almost every }y\in \mathbb R^ k.  \] This conclusion is proved without assuming the Euclidean coarea formula for critical maps. Proof It suffices to prove the assertion for a Borel subset $A\subset C$ in a closed ball whose concentric larger closed ball lies in $U$; countably many such subsets cover $C$. The derivative has a finite bound $L$ on the larger ball. Integration along segments in that ball shows that $f$ is Lipschitz on the smaller ball, so the fiber-measurability lemma applies to $A$, and $|A|<\infty $. Apply Proposition 3.14.4 to $F_\varepsilon $ from Lemma 3.14.5 , on the measurable set $A\times (0,1)^ k$. Writing \[  B_ y=(A\times (0,1)^ k)\cap F_\varepsilon ^{-1}(y),  \] we obtain \[  \int _{\mathbb R^ k}\mathcal H^ n(B_ y)\, dy \leq \varepsilon (L^2+1)^{(k-1)/2}|A|.  \] In particular $B_ y$ is Borel and has finite $n$-measure at almost every level. Apply Proposition 3.14.3 on each such set to the one-Lipschitz projection $(x,z)\mapsto z$. Its fiber at $z\in (0,1)^ k$ is an isometric copy of $A\cap f^{-1}(y-\varepsilon z)$. Thus, with $C_{n,k}=2^ n\omega _ k\omega _{n-k}/\omega _ n$ and $H(v)=\mathcal H^{n-k}(A\cap f^{-1}(v))$, \[  \int _{(0,1)^ k}H(y-\varepsilon z)\, dz \leq C_{n,k}\mathcal H^ n(B_ y) \quad \text{for almost every }y.  \] The function $H$ is Lebesgue measurable by Lemma 3.14.2 . A Borel representative may be used in the double integral: contain its exceptional set in a Borel null set, whose translate is null on each fixed $z$ slice, and Tonelli shows that the joint exceptional set has product measure zero. Integrate the last inequality in $y$ and change variables $v=y-\varepsilon z$. Since the cube has volume one, this gives \[  \int _{\mathbb R^ k}H(v)\, dv \leq C_{n,k}\varepsilon (L^2+1)^{(k-1)/2}|A|.  \] The left side is independent of $\varepsilon $. Let it tend to zero; nonnegativity forces $H=0$ almost everywhere. Countable compact localization completes the proof. The coarse slicing estimate was proved for arbitrary finite-measure sets, so its use on $B_ y$ presupposes neither rectifiability of $A$ nor a critical coarea theorem. $\square$

title: Theorem 3.14.7 (Euclidean coarea for a C1 map)
search_title: Euclidean coarea for a C1 map
section: 3.14 A proof of Euclidean coarea from area
text: Theorem 3.14.7 (Euclidean coarea for a C1 map) . 0D599A7625BD For a $C^1$ map $f:U\to \mathbb R^ k$ on an open $U\subset \mathbb R^ n$, $1\leq k<n$, and a Lebesgue-measurable $A\subset U$, \[  \int _ AJ_ kDf\, dx=\int _{\mathbb R^ k}\mathcal H^{n-k}(A\cap f^{-1}(y))\, dy.  \] Both sides can be infinite. The proof retains Euclidean area and ordinary Euclidean integration as inputs. Proof The regular set $U\setminus C$ is open, and Proposition 3.14.4 proves the formula on $A\setminus C$. On $A\cap C$, the Jacobian is zero. Proposition 3.14.6 gives zero fiber measure at almost every level, so both sides for this part vanish. The two pieces are disjoint; adding them proves the formula. Measurability on a countable bounded exhaustion is Lemma 3.14.2 . The decomposition does not claim that the critical values form a null set; only the relevant lower-dimensional measure of almost every critical fiber is zero. $\square$

title: Proposition 3.14.8 (C1 agreement reduces a Lipschitz map to smooth coarea)
search_title: C1 agreement reduces a Lipschitz map to smooth coarea
section: 3.14 A proof of Euclidean coarea from area
text: Proposition 3.14.8 (C1 agreement reduces a Lipschitz map to smooth coarea) . 336B57437B6F Let $f:\mathbb R^ n\to \mathbb R^ k$ be globally Lipschitz, with $1\leq k<n$, and let $A\subset \mathbb R^ n$ be bounded and Lebesgue measurable. Then \[  \int _ AJ_ kDf\, dx=\int _{\mathbb R^ k}\mathcal H^{n-k}(A\cap f^{-1}(y))\, dy.  \] Here $Df$ is supplied by Rademacher and the Jacobian is zero on its exceptional set. The proof uses Whitney-based $C^1$ approximation and the preceding $C^1$ formula. Proof For every positive integer $j$, Corollary 3.5.6 gives a $C^1$ map $g_ j$ agreeing with both $f$ and its derivative off a set of measure less than $1/j$. Let $E_ j$ be the differentiability points where both equalities hold. Their union has full measure, since its complement lies in each exceptional set and thus has measure at most $1/j$ for every $j$. Make the $E_ j$ disjoint by assigning each point to the first qualifying index. These agreement sets are measurable because $f,g_ j$ and the derivative representatives are measurable. Apply Theorem 3.14.7 to $g_ j$ on $A\cap E_ j$. On this set $J_ kDg_ j=J_ kDf$, and its fiber under $g_ j$ is exactly its fiber under $f$. Sum the identities over $j$. Additivity of measure on the disjoint fiber pieces and monotone convergence identify the sum with the coarea identity for $A\cap \bigcup _ jE_ j$. The omitted subset has zero volume, and Lemma 3.10.3 gives zero lower-dimensional fiber measure at almost every level. It affects neither side. This proves the formula without using Euclidean coarea in the $C^1$ approximation or null-fiber steps. $\square$

title: 16.30 Examples of area, critical sets and pushforward densities
search_title: Examples of area, critical sets and pushforward densities
section: 16.30 Examples of area, critical sets and pushforward densities
text:
The area and coarea formulas in [ Sim18 ] , Chapter 2, Sections 3 and 7, describe different measures even for elementary maps. These original calculations develop their metric factors, critical sets, exceptional fibers and multiplicities. The fat Cantor construction is the one already given in Definition 16.11.1 ; no new existence theorem about critical sets is assumed. Example 16.30.1 (A nonorthogonal linear parametrization has a Gram determinant) . F1CF07E63C19 Let $F(s,t)=(s,2t,s+t)$ on $(0,1)^2$. Then \[  (DF)^*DF=\begin{pmatrix} 2

& 1

\\ 1

& 5

\end{pmatrix}, \qquad J_2DF=3, \qquad \mathcal H^2(F((0,1)^2))=3.  \] Projection of the image to the first two coordinates has area two. Multiplying the lengths of the two tangent columns would incorrectly give $\sqrt{10}$ for the surface Jacobian. Proof The columns are $(1,0,1)$ and $(0,2,1)$, with squared lengths two and five and inner product one. Their Gram determinant is $10-1=9$. The map is injective, so Lemma 3.13.1 gives image area three. The first two coordinates form the rectangle $(0,1)\times (0,2)$, of area two. The product of column lengths is the area of the rectangle they would span if orthogonal; the actual parallelogram includes their nonzero angle through the Gram determinant. $\square$ Example 16.30.2 (A circle traversed several times counts every sheet) . 2834169DC9FF For an integer $q\geq 1$, let $\gamma _ q(t)=(\cos (qt),\sin (qt))$, $0\leq t<2\pi $. Then every point of the unit circle has exactly $q$ preimages, and \[  \int _0^{2\pi }|\gamma _ q'(t)|\, dt=2\pi q =q\, \mathcal H^1(S^1).  \] The image alone has length $2\pi $, independently of $q$. Proof The speed is the constant $q$. Writing a point of $S^1$ by its angle modulo $2\pi $, the equation $qt=\theta $ modulo $2\pi $ has precisely $q$ solutions in the half-open parameter interval. Apply Theorem 3.13.8 to the globally smooth map and that measurable interval. For $q=1$, the formula yields $\mathcal H^1(S^1)=2\pi $ directly; the general case gives the displayed multiplicity factor. Using a half-open interval prevents an extra endpoint preimage at $(1,0)$, although a single target point would not change the length integral. $\square$ Example 16.30.3 (A cusp has a harmless isolated critical parameter) . E40769F1A941 The curve $\gamma (t)=(t^2,t^3)$, $-1\leq t\leq 1$, is injective and has derivative zero only at $t=0$. Its length is \[  \mathcal H^1(\gamma ([-1,1])) =\int _{-1}^1|t|\sqrt{4+9t^2}\, dt =\frac{2}{27}\bigl (13^{3/2}-8\bigr ).  \] Thus failure of immersion at one parameter does not invalidate the area identity. Proof Equality of the second coordinates $t^3$ implies equality of the parameters, proving injectivity. The derivative is $(2t,3t^2)$, with the displayed norm. The locally Lipschitz area formula applies on the closed parameter interval by regarding it as a measurable subset of an open interval. Evenness gives twice the integral on $[0,1]$. Since the derivative of $(4+9t^2)^{3/2}$ is $27t\sqrt{4+9t^2}$, integration gives the stated value. The critical parameter and its image both have zero one-dimensional measure; the geometric cusp at the image is not being declared a smooth point. $\square$ Example 16.30.4 (A strictly increasing Lipschitz map can collapse a positive-measure set) . A0852DCD693D Let $E\subset [0,1]$ be the compact nowhere-dense set of measure $1/2$ in Proposition 16.11.2 . Define \[  f(x)=\int _0^ x\chi _{[0,1]\setminus E}(s)\, ds, \qquad 0\leq x\leq 1.  \] Then $f$ is one-Lipschitz and strictly increasing, maps $[0,1]$ onto $[0,1/2]$, and satisfies $f'=0$ almost everywhere on $E$ and $f'=1$ almost everywhere on its complement. Nevertheless $\mathcal L^1(f(E))=0$. Moreover \[  f_\# (\mathcal L^1\llcorner [0,1]) =\mathcal L^1\llcorner [0,1/2]+\nu , \qquad \nu =f_\# (\mathcal L^1\llcorner E),  \] where $\nu $ is singular continuous and has mass $1/2$. Proof The integral gives absolute continuity, the derivative values almost everywhere, and the one-Lipschitz bound. Every interval of positive length in $[0,1]$ meets the open complement of $E$ in a nonempty interval, because $E$ is nowhere dense. Its integral increment is therefore positive, proving strict increase. The endpoint value is $f(1)=1-|E|=1/2$. Extend $f$ constantly outside $[0,1]$ to a Lipschitz map. Corollary 3.13.9 applied to $E$ gives $|f(E)|=0$. Since $f$ is injective, every singleton has at most one preimage; hence $\nu $ has no atoms. Its support lies in the compact null set $f(E)$, and its total mass is $|E|=1/2$, proving singular continuity. On the complement of $E$, the derivative equals one almost everywhere. The weighted area formula, Proposition 3.3.1 , applied to indicators of target Borel sets and using injectivity, gives \[  f_\# (\mathcal L^1\llcorner ([0,1]\setminus E)) =\mathcal L^1\llcorner f([0,1]\setminus E) =\mathcal L^1\llcorner [0,1/2].  \] The last equality ignores only the null set $f(E)$. Adding the contribution from $E$ proves the decomposition. This example produces the singular measure by a Lipschitz map of a restricted positive-volume set; it does not require the usual Cantor function to be Lipschitz. $\square$ Example 16.30.5 (The graph retains the area that a scalar image loses) . 6D7A40B6E600 For $f$ and $E$ in Example 16.30.4 , the graph map $G(x)=(x,f(x))$ is injective and \[  \mathcal H^1(G([0,1]))=\frac{1+\sqrt2}{2}, \qquad \mathcal H^1(G(E))=\frac12, \qquad \mathcal L^1(f(E))=0.  \] A vanishing scalar derivative on $E$ does not make the graph derivative vanish there. Proof The first coordinate makes $G$ injective, and its speed is $\sqrt{1+|f'|^2}$ almost everywhere. This equals one on $E$ and $\sqrt2$ on its complement. The area formula on $[0,1]$ gives $|E|+\sqrt2(1-|E|)=(1+\sqrt2)/2$. Applying it only to $E$ gives length $1/2$. The scalar image assertion was established in the preceding example. In the graph, the derivative has the nonzero first component one even where the second component vanishes. $\square$ Example 16.30.6 (Graph regularization can have a linear Jacobian error) . 61971AD697D0 For an integer $m\geq 1$, let $f:\mathbb R^ m\to \mathbb R^ m$ be $f(x)=(x_1,\ldots ,x_{m-1},0)$, with the initial list empty if $m=1$. For $0<\varepsilon \leq 1$ and $F_\varepsilon (x)=(f(x),\varepsilon x)$, \[  J_ mDf=0, \qquad J_ mDF_\varepsilon =\varepsilon (1+\varepsilon ^2)^{(m-1)/2}.  \] In particular this Jacobian is of order $\varepsilon $, and cannot be bounded by $C\varepsilon ^2$ with $C$ independent of small $\varepsilon $. Proof The Gram matrix $Df^*Df$ is diagonal with $m-1$ entries equal to one and the last equal to zero. Lemma 3.13.6 adds $\varepsilon ^2$ to every entry. The square root of the product gives the displayed expression. Its ratio to $\varepsilon $ tends to one, while its ratio to $\varepsilon ^2$ tends to infinity. The linear upper bound used to discard critical images is sufficient, including in this worst-rank example. $\square$ Example 16.30.7 (A Lipschitz interval map has an infinite exceptional fiber) . E9BF0D2FEB22 On $[0,1]$ define $f(0)=0$ and $f(x)=x^2\sin (\pi /x)$ for $x>0$. This map is Lipschitz, and \[  f^{-1}(0)=\{ 0\} \cup \{ 1/j:j=1,2,\ldots \} .  \] Thus its multiplicity is infinite at zero, but is integrable with respect to target Lebesgue measure and is finite almost everywhere. Proof For $x>0$, \[  f'(x)=2x\sin (\pi /x)-\pi \cos (\pi /x), \qquad |f'(x)|\leq 2+\pi .  \] The mean-value theorem gives this Lipschitz constant between positive arguments; continuity at zero passes the bound to an endpoint argument. The zero set follows from the zeros of sine. Extend the map to a Lipschitz function on the line, and apply Proposition 3.13.10 to $[0,1]$. It gives integral at most $2+\pi $ and finite multiplicity almost everywhere. Infinite multiplicity at one null target level is compatible with that conclusion. No boundedness of the multiplicity at every point is claimed by the area formula. $\square$ Example 16.30.8 (Rank loss can give infinite fibers on a null image) . 61CF60B70046 For $f:(0,1)^2\to \mathbb R^2$, $f(x,y)=(x,0)$, the two-dimensional area Jacobian is zero everywhere. Every point of $(0,1)\times \{ 0\} $ has an uncountable fiber, yet \[  \int _{\mathbb R^2}\# f^{-1}(z)\, d\mathcal L^2(z)=0.  \] The integrand is infinity on a null line segment and zero elsewhere. Proof The derivative matrix has rank one, so its determinant and area Jacobian vanish. At an image point $(x,0)$ the fiber is $\{ x\} \times (0,1)$, whose counting measure is infinite. The image line segment has zero two-dimensional measure by diameter covers. A nonnegative extended-valued function supported on a null set has integral zero, regardless of infinite values there. This computes both sides of the area formula and separates target measure from the cardinality of an individual fiber. $\square$ Example 16.30.9 (A branched power map counts degree in its area) . 65DF2FEAFF73 For integer $q\geq 1$ and $R>0$, let $f(z)=z^ q$ on the complex disk $D_ R$. Its real two-dimensional Jacobian is \[  J_2Df(z)=q^2|z|^{2q-2}, \qquad \int _{D_ R}J_2Df\, dA=\pi qR^{2q}.  \] The image disk has area $\pi R^{2q}$; its nonzero points have $q$ preimages in $D_ R$. Proof At $z\ne 0$, the complex derivative is $qz^{q-1}$, which acts on the real plane as a rotation followed by dilation by its modulus. Its real area Jacobian is the square of that modulus. The same formula holds at zero, with value one if $q=1$ and zero if $q>1$. Polar integration gives \[  2\pi q^2\int _0^ Rr^{2q-1}\, dr=\pi qR^{2q}.  \] Every nonzero image value has exactly the $q$ distinct complex roots, all of modulus less than $R$; the value zero has only one preimage. The area formula therefore integrates multiplicity $q$ on the image disk except for a null target point. This is a branched parametrization of a plane; it should not be confused with an injectively parametrized singular complex curve in higher codimension. $\square$ Example 16.30.10 (A product map has a logarithmically unbounded density) . 716A1D1732A4 For $f(x,y)=xy$ on $Q=(-1,1)^2$, \[  f_\# (\mathcal L^2\llcorner Q) =-2\log |t|\, \chi _{\{ 0<|t|<1\} }\mathcal L^1.  \] The density is defined by the displayed expression for $0<|t|<1$ and by zero elsewhere; its value at zero may be changed freely. It is unbounded near zero but integrable, with total mass four. There is no atom at zero, although that fiber is the union of two crossing segments. Proof For a nonnegative Borel test function $\phi $, ordinary one-dimensional substitution at each fixed $x\ne 0$ gives \[  \int _{-1}^1\int _{-1}^1\phi (xy)\, dy\, dx =\int _{-1}^1\frac1{|x|}\int _{-|x|}^{|x|}\phi (t)\, dt\, dx.  \] Tonelli makes the density at $0<|t|<1$ equal to $2\int _{|t|}^1dx/x=-2\log |t|$. Its integral is four since $\int _0^1-\log t\, dt=1$. The zero fiber consists of the two coordinate segments and has zero area, so it carries no pushforward atom. Away from $x=0$, parametrize a fiber by $(x,t/x)$. Its speed divided by $|Df|$ equals \[  \frac{\sqrt{1+t^2/x^4}}{\sqrt{x^2+t^2/x^2}}=\frac1{|x|},  \] which gives the same inverse-Jacobian density by Proposition 3.12.2 . The crossing at zero affects one exceptional level only. $\square$ Example 16.30.11 (Radial powers give integrable power singularities) . 777E36C53AD3 Let $m\geq 2$, $R>0$, $\alpha \geq 1$, and $f(x)=|x|^\alpha $ on $B_ R(0)\subset \mathbb R^ m$. Then \[  f_\# (\mathcal L^ m\llcorner B_ R) =\frac{m\omega _ m}{\alpha }\, t^{m/\alpha -1} \chi _{(0,R^\alpha )}(t)\mathcal L^1.  \] When $\alpha >m$ this density diverges at zero, but its integral is $\omega _ mR^ m$ and it has no atom there. Proof The map is locally Lipschitz for $\alpha \geq 1$. At a positive level $t$, its fiber is the sphere of radius $r=t^{1/\alpha }$, with area $m\omega _ mr^{m-1}$, and its gradient has norm $\alpha r^{\alpha -1}$. Their ratio is $(m\omega _ m/\alpha )t^{m/\alpha -1}$, as in Proposition 3.12.2 . Equivalently the sublevel volume is $\omega _ m t^{m/\alpha }$, giving the same derivative. Its value tends to zero at the origin, which also shows there is no atom. The exponent $m/\alpha -1$ is always greater than $-1$, so the singularity remains integrable; integration up to $R^\alpha $ yields the original ball volume. $\square$ Example 16.30.12 (Distance slices of an offset affine plane) . 93DDA071D85B Let $m\geq 2$, $d>0$, $P=\mathbb R^ m\times \{ d\} \subset \mathbb R^{m+1}$, and $\rho (x)=|x|$. For $r>d$, \[  \mathcal H^ m(P\cap B_ r)=\omega _ m(r^2-d^2)^{m/2}, \qquad \frac{d}{dr}\mathcal H^ m(P\cap B_ r) =m\omega _ mr(r^2-d^2)^{(m-2)/2}.  \] The derivative equals the inverse-Jacobian fiber integral. The unique closest point is critical and contributes no atom. Proof In the coordinates $x=(u,d)$ of the plane, the condition $|x|<r$ becomes $|u|<\sqrt{r^2-d^2}$. This gives the volume and its derivative. On the fiber, the tangential gradient norm is $|u|/r=\sqrt{r^2-d^2}/r$, while its $(m-1)$-measure is $m\omega _ m(r^2-d^2)^{(m-1)/2}$. Dividing gives the displayed derivative. The only critical point is $u=0$, a set of zero $m$-measure. The volume tends to zero as $r\downarrow d$ and has no jump there. This contrasts with a whole sphere centered at the origin, where every point lies in one critical distance level. $\square$

text: Example 16.30.6 (Graph regularization can have a linear Jacobian error) . 61971AD697D0 For an integer $m\geq 1$, let $f:\mathbb R^ m\to \mathbb R^ m$ be $f(x)=(x_1,\ldots ,x_{m-1},0)$, with the initial list empty if $m=1$. For $0<\varepsilon \leq 1$ and $F_\varepsilon (x)=(f(x),\varepsilon x)$, \[  J_ mDf=0, \qquad J_ mDF_\varepsilon =\varepsilon (1+\varepsilon ^2)^{(m-1)/2}.  \] In particular this Jacobian is of order $\varepsilon $, and cannot be bounded by $C\varepsilon ^2$ with $C$ independent of small $\varepsilon $. Proof The Gram matrix $Df^*Df$ is diagonal with $m-1$ entries equal to one and the last equal to zero. Lemma 3.13.6 adds $\varepsilon ^2$ to every entry. The square root of the product gives the displayed expression. Its ratio to $\varepsilon $ tends to one, while its ratio to $\varepsilon ^2$ tends to infinity. The linear upper bound used to discard critical images is sufficient, including in this worst-rank example. $\square$

title: Example 16.30.7 (A Lipschitz interval map has an infinite exceptional fiber)
search_title: A Lipschitz interval map has an infinite exceptional fiber
section: 16.30 Examples of area, critical sets and pushforward densities
text: Example 16.30.7 (A Lipschitz interval map has an infinite exceptional fiber) . E9BF0D2FEB22 On $[0,1]$ define $f(0)=0$ and $f(x)=x^2\sin (\pi /x)$ for $x>0$. This map is Lipschitz, and \[  f^{-1}(0)=\{ 0\} \cup \{ 1/j:j=1,2,\ldots \} .  \] Thus its multiplicity is infinite at zero, but is integrable with respect to target Lebesgue measure and is finite almost everywhere. Proof For $x>0$, \[  f'(x)=2x\sin (\pi /x)-\pi \cos (\pi /x), \qquad |f'(x)|\leq 2+\pi .  \] The mean-value theorem gives this Lipschitz constant between positive arguments; continuity at zero passes the bound to an endpoint argument. The zero set follows from the zeros of sine. Extend the map to a Lipschitz function on the line, and apply Proposition 3.13.10 to $[0,1]$. It gives integral at most $2+\pi $ and finite multiplicity almost everywhere. Infinite multiplicity at one null target level is compatible with that conclusion. No boundedness of the multiplicity at every point is claimed by the area formula. $\square$

title: Example 16.30.8 (Rank loss can give infinite fibers on a null image)
search_title: Rank loss can give infinite fibers on a null image
section: 16.30 Examples of area, critical sets and pushforward densities
text: Example 16.30.8 (Rank loss can give infinite fibers on a null image) . 61CF60B70046 For $f:(0,1)^2\to \mathbb R^2$, $f(x,y)=(x,0)$, the two-dimensional area Jacobian is zero everywhere. Every point of $(0,1)\times \{ 0\} $ has an uncountable fiber, yet \[  \int _{\mathbb R^2}\# f^{-1}(z)\, d\mathcal L^2(z)=0.  \] The integrand is infinity on a null line segment and zero elsewhere. Proof The derivative matrix has rank one, so its determinant and area Jacobian vanish. At an image point $(x,0)$ the fiber is $\{ x\} \times (0,1)$, whose counting measure is infinite. The image line segment has zero two-dimensional measure by diameter covers. A nonnegative extended-valued function supported on a null set has integral zero, regardless of infinite values there. This computes both sides of the area formula and separates target measure from the cardinality of an individual fiber. $\square$

title: Example 16.30.9 (A branched power map counts degree in its area)
search_title: A branched power map counts degree in its area
section: 16.30 Examples of area, critical sets and pushforward densities
text: Example 16.30.9 (A branched power map counts degree in its area) . 65DF2FEAFF73 For integer $q\geq 1$ and $R>0$, let $f(z)=z^ q$ on the complex disk $D_ R$. Its real two-dimensional Jacobian is \[  J_2Df(z)=q^2|z|^{2q-2}, \qquad \int _{D_ R}J_2Df\, dA=\pi qR^{2q}.  \] The image disk has area $\pi R^{2q}$; its nonzero points have $q$ preimages in $D_ R$. Proof At $z\ne 0$, the complex derivative is $qz^{q-1}$, which acts on the real plane as a rotation followed by dilation by its modulus. Its real area Jacobian is the square of that modulus. The same formula holds at zero, with value one if $q=1$ and zero if $q>1$. Polar integration gives \[  2\pi q^2\int _0^ Rr^{2q-1}\, dr=\pi qR^{2q}.  \] Every nonzero image value has exactly the $q$ distinct complex roots, all of modulus less than $R$; the value zero has only one preimage. The area formula therefore integrates multiplicity $q$ on the image disk except for a null target point. This is a branched parametrization of a plane; it should not be confused with an injectively parametrized singular complex curve in higher codimension. $\square$

title: Example 16.30.10 (A product map has a logarithmically unbounded density)
search_title: A product map has a logarithmically unbounded density
section: 16.30 Examples of area, critical sets and pushforward densities
text: Example 16.30.10 (A product map has a logarithmically unbounded density) . 716A1D1732A4 For $f(x,y)=xy$ on $Q=(-1,1)^2$, \[  f_\# (\mathcal L^2\llcorner Q) =-2\log |t|\, \chi _{\{ 0<|t|<1\} }\mathcal L^1.  \] The density is defined by the displayed expression for $0<|t|<1$ and by zero elsewhere; its value at zero may be changed freely. It is unbounded near zero but integrable, with total mass four. There is no atom at zero, although that fiber is the union of two crossing segments. Proof For a nonnegative Borel test function $\phi $, ordinary one-dimensional substitution at each fixed $x\ne 0$ gives \[  \int _{-1}^1\int _{-1}^1\phi (xy)\, dy\, dx =\int _{-1}^1\frac1{|x|}\int _{-|x|}^{|x|}\phi (t)\, dt\, dx.  \] Tonelli makes the density at $0<|t|<1$ equal to $2\int _{|t|}^1dx/x=-2\log |t|$. Its integral is four since $\int _0^1-\log t\, dt=1$. The zero fiber consists of the two coordinate segments and has zero area, so it carries no pushforward atom. Away from $x=0$, parametrize a fiber by $(x,t/x)$. Its speed divided by $|Df|$ equals \[  \frac{\sqrt{1+t^2/x^4}}{\sqrt{x^2+t^2/x^2}}=\frac1{|x|},  \] which gives the same inverse-Jacobian density by Proposition 3.12.2 . The crossing at zero affects one exceptional level only. $\square$

title: Example 16.30.11 (Radial powers give integrable power singularities)
search_title: Radial powers give integrable power singularities
section: 16.30 Examples of area, critical sets and pushforward densities
text: Example 16.30.11 (Radial powers give integrable power singularities) . 777E36C53AD3 Let $m\geq 2$, $R>0$, $\alpha \geq 1$, and $f(x)=|x|^\alpha $ on $B_ R(0)\subset \mathbb R^ m$. Then \[  f_\# (\mathcal L^ m\llcorner B_ R) =\frac{m\omega _ m}{\alpha }\, t^{m/\alpha -1} \chi _{(0,R^\alpha )}(t)\mathcal L^1.  \] When $\alpha >m$ this density diverges at zero, but its integral is $\omega _ mR^ m$ and it has no atom there. Proof The map is locally Lipschitz for $\alpha \geq 1$. At a positive level $t$, its fiber is the sphere of radius $r=t^{1/\alpha }$, with area $m\omega _ mr^{m-1}$, and its gradient has norm $\alpha r^{\alpha -1}$. Their ratio is $(m\omega _ m/\alpha )t^{m/\alpha -1}$, as in Proposition 3.12.2 . Equivalently the sublevel volume is $\omega _ m t^{m/\alpha }$, giving the same derivative. Its value tends to zero at the origin, which also shows there is no atom. The exponent $m/\alpha -1$ is always greater than $-1$, so the singularity remains integrable; integration up to $R^\alpha $ yields the original ball volume. $\square$

title: Example 16.30.12 (Distance slices of an offset affine plane)
search_title: Distance slices of an offset affine plane
section: 16.30 Examples of area, critical sets and pushforward densities
text: Example 16.30.12 (Distance slices of an offset affine plane) . 93DDA071D85B Let $m\geq 2$, $d>0$, $P=\mathbb R^ m\times \{ d\} \subset \mathbb R^{m+1}$, and $\rho (x)=|x|$. For $r>d$, \[  \mathcal H^ m(P\cap B_ r)=\omega _ m(r^2-d^2)^{m/2}, \qquad \frac{d}{dr}\mathcal H^ m(P\cap B_ r) =m\omega _ mr(r^2-d^2)^{(m-2)/2}.  \] The derivative equals the inverse-Jacobian fiber integral. The unique closest point is critical and contributes no atom. Proof In the coordinates $x=(u,d)$ of the plane, the condition $|x|<r$ becomes $|u|<\sqrt{r^2-d^2}$. This gives the volume and its derivative. On the fiber, the tangential gradient norm is $|u|/r=\sqrt{r^2-d^2}/r$, while its $(m-1)$-measure is $m\omega _ m(r^2-d^2)^{(m-1)/2}$. Dividing gives the displayed derivative. The only critical point is $u=0$, a set of zero $m$-measure. The volume tends to zero as $r\downarrow d$ and has no jump there. This contrasts with a whole sphere centered at the origin, where every point lies in one critical distance level. $\square$
